items.title: Japan's Nuclear Revival Hits Setbacks After Scandals, Accidents
body: Japan’s nuclear revival is facing fresh setbacks after a summer of scandals and regulatory hurdles delayed reactor restarts, threatening the country’s plans to expand atomic power as electricity demand and energy costs rise.

BloombergNEF expects nine reactors totaling 9.6 gigawatts of power to restart through 2040, down from a previous outlook of 11 units. Japan will fall at least 11.7 gigawatts short of its 2040 target of generating 35 gigawatts of electricity from nuclear, BNEF said.
The weaker outlook comes after Chubu Electric Power Co. withdrew applications to restart two units at its Hamaoka nuclear plant after being accused of fabricating seismic data for the facility.

Hokkaido Electric Power Co.’s effort to restart its reactor is also facing delays after a fatal accident during construction of a seawall at its Tomari nuclear plant and the rejection of proposed safety measures by regulators. BNEF subsequently pushed its forecast for the restart of Tomari No. 3 back a year to 2028.

Japan has been pushing for the resumption of reactors shut in the aftermath of 2011 Fukushima disaster, in order to curb reliance on expensive imported fossil fuels. The delays threaten to keep power prices elevated, and expose the country to volatile liquefied natural gas and coal markets, just as the artificial intelligence boom is expected to lift electricity demand.

“We expect Japan data center power demand to double by 2030 from current levels,” said Robert Liew, director of integrated energy research at Wood Mackenzie Ltd. “If not using nuclear, alternative sources of baseload power will be required from either more coal or LNG imports.”
Nationwide spot electricity prices recently hit the highest level since 2022 due to the near-closure of the Strait of Hormuz, which has choked about a fifth of global LNG supply.
Japan’s strict regulatory regime and pockets of local opposition means only 15 of the nation’s 33 operable reactors are currently online.
Read More: Japan’s Chubu Electric Halts Plans for Nuclear Restart

The problems in Hokkaido jeopardize the northern island’s plan to become a major data-center hub, as electricity demand there is forecast to grow faster than any other part of Japan, according to the Organization for Cross-regional Coordination of Transmission Operators. The No. 3 unit at Tomari, Hokkaido’s only operable nuclear power plant, could meet as much as a third of the island’s power demand if restarted, according to BNEF.

Japan’s government set a goal in June to replace as many as 14 retiring reactors with new units by the 2050s. The country is aiming for about 20% of its power mix to come from nuclear energy by 2040, compared to 9% today, but still well below almost a third before the Fukushima disaster.

items.title: Japan's Inflation Slows Before Expected BOJ Interest Rate Hike
body: Japan’s inflation slowed for the first time in four months, largely reflecting the effect of government subsidies, in data released hours before the Bank of Japan is expected to announce an interest rate hike.

The consumer price index excluding fresh food rose 1.7% in August from a year earlier, easing from a 1.8% pace in July, the Ministry of Internal Affairs and Communications said Friday. Economists had expected the rate to remain unchanged.

While the data showed a slight slowing of inflation, the reading isn’t likely to change the calculus on Friday’s BOJ rate decision, especially given widespread expectations that the price trend will pick up in the coming months.
The index excluding both fresh food and energy, a measure closely watched by the BOJ for signs of underlying inflation, climbed 1.9%, as did the overall CPI gauge.

The figures were released hours before the BOJ’s policy decision, with economists unanimously predicting a quarter-point rate increase to 1.25%. If softer price momentum were to continue, it could complicate the BOJ’s communications strategy as authorities look to keep normalizing policy settings.
Read: BOJ Set to Hike Rate, Marking Fastest Pace Since 1990: Day Guide

As has been the case for some time, the overall reading was distorted somewhat by government measures aimed at easing the burden on households from the soaring cost of living. In the latest month those steps, led by measures to cap prices for gasoline, reduced the headline CPI figure by 0.62 percentage point.

“Government subsidies, including those for energy, have had a fairly significant impact in slowing inflation,” said Masato Koike, senior economist at Sompo Institute Plus. “But overall, inflation remains relatively solid. Looking ahead, given the situation in the Middle East, a number of companies have already announced plans to raise prices, so I think the underlying trend remains strong.”

The consumer price data come as other price indicators point to rising pressure on companies. Japan’s corporate goods prices rose 7.6% in August from a year earlier, beating expectations, as high energy prices combined with the weak yen and a tight labor market to push up input prices throughout the supply chain.

That’s forcing companies to pass on more of the burden to customers. The number of food and beverage products subject to price increases this month is 83% higher than a year ago, according to Teikoku Databank.

The gain in prices for processed foods slowed to 2.7% from 3% in the previous month, while growth in prices accelerated for household durable goods, durable goods for education and recreation and medical fees. Costs for lodging slipped 1.4% lower in August. Prices for rice, which surged a year ago, fell 15.7%.

Markets will be closely monitoring Governor Kazuo Ueda’s post-decision press conference to see how he characterizes recent price developments as well as the outlook for further rate increases. Pricing in the overnight swaps market shows traders are assigning a 90% probability to another rate hike by year-end.

In the latest economic outlook report, the BOJ said that inflation would accelerate to “clearly above 2%” in the second half of this fiscal year, citing higher chip prices driven by strong global artificial intelligence-related demand and the weaker yen.

As public frustration over the rising cost of living grows, Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi’s government has rolled out a range of measures to ease the burden on households. Steps include subsidies to curb gasoline prices and reduce electricity and gas bills. Education-related assistance has also been rolled out.

The cabinet approved Tuesday an outline for a temporary consumption tax cut on food starting next April, advancing Takaichi’s campaign pledge from the February election. The plan calls for lowering the tax rate on food and soft drinks to 1% from 8% for two years as a stopgap before transitioning to a broader tax-credit system.
Koike said Governor Ueda is likely to signal more rate hikes ahead when he speaks later Friday.

“I don’t think the slowdown in the latest reading will make it any harder for Ueda to explain the rate hike today or make him more hesitant to signal additional tightening ahead,” Koike said. “I think there’s a good chance we’ll hear some fairly hawkish comments.”

items.title: Sheinbaum Says Mexico Is Closer to Trade Deal After Trump Call
body: Lea la nota en español
Mexican President Claudia Sheinbaum discussed bilateral trade with her US counterpart Donald Trump in a phone call, according to several people familiar with the discussion.

The conversation took place on Wednesday as officials from both countries have held trade talks aimed at resolving disputes over US tariffs and rules of origin for Mexican exports, among other outstanding issues. The call follows the collapse of US-Canada trade negotiations late last month.
Trump hinted at a possible US-Mexico breakthrough on trade at a campaign event on Wednesday, saying a “great deal” was close at hand.
The White House didn’t respond to a request for comment.

The next round of trade talks between US and Mexican negotiators is expected to kick off in Washington on September 28, one of the people said. Politico first reported the phone call earlier on Thursday.

items.title: Wells Fargo, Citi Strategists See Weak Yen on BOJ Letdown
body: Strategists including those at Wells Fargo & Co. and Citigroup Inc. expect the yen to weaken as they anticipate the Bank of Japan will disappoint investors after its meeting on Friday by being less hawkish than the market expects.

The strategists are bearish on the Japanese currency, with Citigroup seeing the yen potentially reaching 159 per dollar over the next few weeks. The yen was little changed at 156.02 per dollar as of 8:31 a.m. in Tokyo on Friday.

Swaps traders are almost fully pricing in a quarter-point raise from the BOJ on Friday. The focus now is more on BOJ Governor Kazuo Ueda’s comments after the decision for hints on the central bank’s path ahead, with markets forecasting more rate increases by the end of the year.

“The hurdle for the BOJ to meet these expectations is high, and even higher to exceed them,” Wells Fargo strategist Chidu Narayanan wrote in a Thursday note. “The risk is skewed toward a more dovish-than-priced outcome.”

The yen had weakened after the Federal Reserve raised rates for the first time in three years on Wednesday and Chairman Kevin Warsh signaled the central bank would keep doing so as it fights inflation.

The reversal in the Japanese currency came after a sharp rally earlier this month when it reached its strongest level since mid-February, surpassing the peak it hit after the US and Japan’s rare yen-buying intervention in late July. The yen has faced pressure in recent years, largely because of a vast interest-rate gap with other major economies.

Despite the short-term downside risk for the yen if the BOJ fails to satisfy the market, Citigroup strategist Daniel Tobon said in a note Thursday that he sees recent policy moves as part of a broader “regime change” that could strengthen the yen in the longer term.
“A lot of the really big concerns that we’ve had on the yen, they’re slowly moving in the right direction,” Tobon said.
ING Bank NV’s head of G10 FX strategy Chris Turner expects the yen to weaken to the 157 or 158 level if the BOJ fails to signal more interest-rate increases.

Elsewhere, Georgette Boele, senior FX strategy at ABN AMRO, sees the yen strengthening in the second half of 2027, when she expects the Fed and the European Central Bank to cut interest rates. For now, however, she expects the currency to languish around the 154 level versus the dollar until the first quarter of 2027.
“We expect higher energy prices to halt the yen’s recovery for now,” she said.

items.title: Thames Water Seeks to Buy Time as MPs Push for Nationalization
body: Thames Water’s senior creditors should be blocked from taking full control over the utility, a group of British lawmakers said Friday.

Alistair Carmichael, chair of the Environment, Food and Rural Affairs Committee, accused creditors of the UK’s biggest water and sewerage company of “joyriding in the family car.” The committee said the government and regulator Ofwat should withdraw from negotiations with the creditor group London & Valley Water, or LV&W.

Doing so would likely trigger Special Administration, the committee said, a form of temporary nationalization, but would ultimately put the company on more sustainable footing and be cost neutral for taxpayers.

Thames, which supplies 16 million people in and around London, has effectively been in the hands of its creditors since shareholders walked away in 2024. It is drowning in more than £18 billion ($24.1 billion) of debt and is working on another loan to take it through next year as talks with Ofwat continue.

In the report published Friday, the EFRA committee said creditors currently fall through regulatory cracks as their position as “economic owners” means they do not have to go through due diligence in the same way that shareholders would.
A spokesperson for LV&W said the group is committed to ensuring Thames Water provides the service that customers and local communities deserve.
Read More: Why Thames Water Is Edging Closer to State Control: Explainer

Efforts to attract new shareholders in Thames last year failed when when KKR & Co. walked away. Since then, Thames’ senior creditors have been trying to secure government backing for a private-sector rescue of the utility, which would see them become “ultimate controllers” and give them the ability to materially influence Thames’ direction.

LV&W is preparing a significantly revised rescue proposal aimed at winning over the new government. The previous plan was criticized by former Environment Secretary Emma Reynolds. The new plan includes taking bigger losses on their debt and increasing the £3.35 billion of new equity previously pledged, Bloomberg News reported.
The group’s spokesperson said its proposal will address all feedback from Ofwat and ministers and is the fastest route to fix Thames Water’s problems.

The EFRA committee said the government should tighten the rules for putting a company into special administration as the current legislation is too vague and risks a legal battle. However, the MPs stopped short of Thames Water to be permanently nationalized, saying the company should enter SAR until a new owner can be found.

Prime Minister Andy Burnham’s team had signaled before taking office that it was prepared to put Thames into special administration. But like the government before it, Burnham’s administration has run up against a fundamental obstacle: officials first have to establish whether Thames meets the legal threshold for a performance-based SAR.
His government is still studying whether to put Thames into special administration, Bloomberg reported this week.
A spokesman for the Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs said Thames has been failing the public for a long time, and that it is looking at every option, including SAR.
A spokesman for Thames Water said that it didn’t want anything to delay from its current recapitalization and turnaround plan, which is needed to protect customers and the environment.

items.title: Tibet Wine Industry Grows at World's Highest Vineyard
body: At 3,600 meters (11,811 feet) above sea level in Tibet, grapes grow against the odds. Winters freeze the ground along the Yarlung Tsangpo River, ultraviolet radiation is intense, and the surrounding mountains rise from an arid plateau. Yet here, Pazhu Winery is producing thousands of bottles of chardonnay, ice wine and an indigenous red called Yajiang No. 1.

For generations, livelihoods in Shannan, an area often referred to as the cradle of Tibetan civilization, have centered on herding yak, sheep and goats, or growing barley on unforgiving patches of land. That routine is changing as China’s decade-long gambit to make Tibet a wine-producing region finally bears fruit. Pazhu now operates vineyards across the region, including one recognized by Guinness World Records as the highest in the world.

Pazhu has yet to turn a profit, but that may be beside the point. The winery is part of a broader effort by Beijing to promote what it calls common prosperity among China’s ethnic groups and more closely integrate restive frontier regions such as Tibet, where the government has faced allegations of repressing religious and ethnic traditions. Beyond building a local wine industry, the vineyard is creating jobs, attracting tourists and showcasing the government’s poverty-alleviation and modernization policies.

The winery has 80 full-time workers, earning as much as 8,000 yuan ($1,191) per month, deputy general manager Li Xiaoping told me during a government-organized trip to Tibet in July. An additional 3,000 people from 10 nearby villages take turns working in the vineyard, part of what Li calls a “near-to-home work” model.

Suolang Bianba knows what that means in practice. Before joining Pazhu full time, he traveled far from his village to find construction work. Now he can earn a living close to home. “I had to search for work,” says Suolang, who was handpicked to speak with the media as one of the most experienced employees. “Now, there is no need for that. I can work near my home all year round.”
“This has benefited lots of people,” he adds. “Our family income has significantly increased.”

President Xi Jinping has prioritized economic development and closer integration of regions like Tibet, where Beijing has exercised ultimate authority since 1959 when the Dalai Lama fled into exile as the People's Liberation Army crushed an armed uprising against Chinese rule. Subsequently, China has poured hundreds of billions of yuan into infrastructure including highways and railways, and last year it began construction of a $167 billion hydropower project set to dwarf the Three Gorges Dam.

Economic integration has come alongside a push for greater cultural and political conformity. An ethnic unity law that took effect on July 1 promotes a stronger shared national identity and greater assimilation with the majority Han Chinese culture. Critics say the law further erodes educational and religious freedoms for minorities in regions like Tibet and its northern neighbor Xinjiang.

Beijing’s message of ethnic unity was hard to miss during my weeklong trip to Tibet, organized by the government to showcase development projects and is the only way foreign journalists can travel to the region. At the Xizang Museum in Lhasa, the region’s capital, exhibits traced centuries of ties between Tibet and China, from Tang dynasty Princess Wencheng’s marriage into Tibetan royalty to China’s role in driving out Mongol forces. Western powers were portrayed as having driven a wedge between the two, eventually compelling Beijing to send forces into the region.

The two-hour drive from Lhasa to Pazhu, which at times left me dizzy due to the high altitude and thin air, was punctuated by security checkpoints and roadside slogans commemorating the anniversary of Tibet’s “liberation” — reminders that this was no afternoon in Napa or Sonoma.

While the political backdrop and high altitudes make Pazhu unusual, its commercial challenges are familiar: falling wine consumption and fierce competition. It’s trying to carve out a niche in a difficult domestic market dominated by established regions such as Ningxia and Shandong. Once a major driver of global wine demand, China has seen its consumption fall sharply since 2017. Younger consumers in particular have gravitated toward lower-alcohol drinks, pushing domestic wineries to emphasize quality and distinctive terroirs over volume.

Pazhu’s wines aren’t cheap, with bottles selling for as much as 777 yuan. Years of experimenting with imported grapes and cross-pollination at high altitude produced Yajiang No. 1, with notes of dark fruit, herbs and minerals the winery attributes to the local soil. It’s fruity, with tannins as smooth as any New World wine.
For now, Pazhu’s wines are sold mostly in mainland China, though shipments to Hong Kong and Macau started this year. “The dream is to be able to sell our wines around the world,” Li says.

Profitability, though, is only one measure of success. “Improving the living conditions of local residents through industrial development is the core social responsibility goal of the project,” Li says.

items.title: Todd Boehly's Chelsea Dream Succumbs to Reality of Football
body: When Todd Boehly attended his first Chelsea match after agreeing to buy the club in 2022, supporters greeted him with a playful chant: “Boehly, Boehly, give us a wave.” He didn’t respond, perhaps because he didn’t get what they were saying. The opportunity wouldn’t come again.

Within months, those same die hard Chelsea fans in the Matthew Harding Stand had turned on the American. Four years later, majority shareholder Clearlake Capital has now agreed to buy him out and a draw a line under a period of ownership turmoil after the two parties fell out.

Although Chelsea managed to pick up two trophies during his tenure and a focus on a roster of young players has made some money, Boehly never won back fans. In 2024, the US financier summed up the problem facing countless owners who have little experience of European football.
“The good news is people care so much,” he said. “And the bad news is people care so much.”
Boehly was hands on from the beginning in a sport he knew little about and one that’s burned many an owner, particularly in the lucrative, yet febrile English Premier League.

He installed himself as interim sporting director despite having no experience of football recruitment. He met agents, contacted club executives and pursued multiple targets at once. Years later, Boehly would admit that he had “no idea what made a good football player,” joking that his logic on signing one star player had been simple: “If Man City wanted him, I want him.”

Boehly was at the vanguard of a now established trend in European football: US billionaires who made their money in high finance looking to snap up what they saw as cheap, underdeveloped, yet famous football teams.

Among his consortium was Mark Walter, chief executive officer of Guggenheim Partners, and Swiss billionaire Hansjörg Wyss. California-based private equity firm Clearlake Capital, led by Behdad Eghbali and Jose E. Feliciano, provided most of the capital for the deal, owning about a 60% stake.

Although Boehly owned a relatively small stake in Chelsea, he became the public face. He arrived in May 2022 promising that Chelsea’s new owners were “all in — 100%.” The pledge covered the men’s and women’s teams, the academy and the club’s stadium complex at Stamford Bridge. He had already tried to buy the club in 2019 and, during the 2022 bidding process, sat anonymously among supporters.

To outsiders such as Boehly, Chelsea was a famous club. It was also based close to central London, and the opportunity to redevelop the stadium and boost revenue seemed like an easy win. It also had a strong brand. Under the previous owner, Roman Abramovich, fans had become used to success. The Russian’s 19-year reign delivered 21 trophies.

The reality was different. Despite its success, Chelsea has a small fan base compared with rivals such as Liverpool, Arsenal and Manchester United.  Planning rules in London and ownership disagreements hamstrung redevelopment plans. Perhaps most significantly, Chelsea’s previous success was tarnished.

Abramovich was forced to sell the club following Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine due to his links to President Vladimir Putin. During the takeover process, the new owners wrote to the Football Association, the sports governing body in England, flagging transactions that were the subject of an ongoing tax investigation.

The offences took place between 2009 and 2022 during Abramovich’s ownership and involved  illegal agent and third-party payments. Chelsea was fined £10 million and given a suspended two-window transfer ban following an FA investigation and an appeal.

All this was unknown to fans during the early days of the Boehly era. Within months, Chelsea’s performance nose-dived, and fans were singing the name of Abramovich during games. The new owners also failed to make a good impression with the Chelsea manager Thomas Tuchel, now manager of the English national team.

During an initial transfer strategy session, the ownership reportedly alienated Tuchel by inadvertently proposing a tactical lineup featuring 11 outfield players alongside a goalkeeper, according to       The Athletic    . Chelsea denied the mistake ever occurred.

Days after securing Pierre-Emerick Aubameyang for €12 million — a target brought in largely due to his prior relationship with the manager — Tuchel was dismissed. Boehly later  attributed the split to a missing “shared vision” rather than any single defeat. His replacement, Graham Potter, signed a five-year deal only to be fired seven months later.
Following a chaotic rotation of coaches, Chelsea closed out the first campaign under Boehly’s chairmanship in 12th place, marking their worst league finish in nearly three decades.

There were moments when Boehly appeared to embody   every dated anxiety about American money entering English football. He proposed a Premier League North-versus-South All-Star game and spoke about stadiums becoming lifestyle destinations where supporters would stay and spend longer.

Before a Champions League quarter-final against Real Madrid in 2023, he predicted Chelsea  would win 3-0. They lost the tie 4-0 on aggregate. Days later, angry supporters confronted him during a home defeat by Brighton.

Wall Street financing was also brought to the club. European football’s Financial Fair Play rules limit club spending on transfers and wages to a percentage of annual revenue, aimed to prevent wealthier clubs from using vast financial resources to dominate competitors by completely overhauling their squads.

Chelsea found a solution often used by financial firms looking to defray the costs of mergers or expenses over a longer period. Instead of booking the hit of buying a player this year, Chelsea spread the cost across a series of years. Chelsea also sold two Stamford Bridge hotels to itself for £76.5 million, a transaction approved by the Premier League.
“We are not spending the money,” Boehly       said     in 2024. “We are investing the money.”

By now, the relationship between Boehly and Clearlake had failed. Differing opinions on Chelsea’s recruitment policy, the team’s underperformance and the failure to make progress on building a new stadium,   all contributed to the rift.

Eghbali and Clearlake assumed greater control of football operations, while Boehly returned attention to his other businesses. In March 2025, he acknowledged that the stadium question could determine whether the partners stayed together or “went different ways.”

The owners prioritized signing young talent on long-term contracts, outlaying more than £1.5 billion on nearly 50 players through July 2025. The massive outlay on transfer fees created significant financial pressure for the club. Chelsea reported the largest ever pretax loss recorded by a Premier League club for the year ending June 30, 2025.

There was vindication on the pitch. Chelsea’s 2025 Conference League and Club World Cup triumphs brought the ownership its first major men’s silverware. After the 3-0 victory over Paris Saint-Germain in the Club World Cup final, Boehly thanked supporters for “sticking with us.” The young squad, so often presented as proof of recklessness, had begun to resemble a coherent team.
Yet the trophies didn’t repair the ownership split. A   federal probe of Walter’s businesses also prompted him to reshape his holdings, stirring up deal talks on multiple fronts.

Late in the night on Wednesday, Chelsea announced that Clearlake would buy the interests of Boehly and Mark Walter and take full control, with Eghbali and Feliciano also investing their own money into the club. Boehly is set to leave as chairman. He said it has been an honor.

items.title: China's 'Iron Lady' of Appliances Eyes Europe Winters for Growth
body: Gree Electric Appliances Inc., one of China’s largest home appliance makers, sees Europe’s cold winters as its next growth opportunity after record summer temperatures fueled an air-conditioning boom that nearly doubled its sales in parts of the region.

“People often assume that warmer weather creates an air-conditioning market, but Europe still has long winters during which people need heating,” Dong Mingzhu, Gree’s longtime chairwoman, said in an exclusive interview with Bloomberg TV in Singapore.

The opportunity in Europe would be small if Gree focused on cooling alone, Dong said. The company has developed technology that can both cool and heat homes while consuming less energy than conventional oil or gas heating, she added.

Chinese air-conditioner makers like Gree and Midea Group Co. are tapping into Europe as a new growth market as demand for their products spikes with extreme summer temperatures. Gree reported that sales in some European countries including Norway and Denmark jumped 92% in the first half.

Dong, 72, earned the nickname “Iron Lady” in China’s business world for her hard-driving style. She joined Gree as a saleswoman in 1990 and helped turn the company, which began as a small air-conditioner factory, into one of China’s leading appliance makers.
Read More: Europe’s Heat Wave Is Bright Spot for China’s Portable AC Makers

Whether Europe’s surge in demand will be sustainable remains unclear, and analysts said the gains are unlikely to fully offset weakness at home. China’s increasingly saturated home-appliance market and subdued consumption have weighed on manufacturers, with Gree’s first-half net profit falling around 7.8% from a year earlier to 13 billion yuan ($1.9 billion).
Although Gree is a household name in China, overseas revenue accounts for only about 15% of group sales, according to Citigroup Inc.
Gree is also grappling with soaring copper prices, which Dong said have wiped 2 billion yuan to 3 billion yuan ($298 million to $447 million) from profits this year.

China’s property slump has weighed on Gree, but Dong said the company isn’t reliant on new home sales to drive demand. About 600 million Gree air conditioners have been in use for more than a decade and many are due for replacement, she said.
“The solution is not to rely on property development,” Dong said. “I think at any time, we should insist that the solution to a changing market is to keep upgrading technology.”

items.title: China's $33 Billion REIT Experiment Sputters Due to Weak Demand
body: One of China’s less publicized avenues for pumping funding into the country’s struggling property market is running into the same problem that’s long plagued the industry: supply is overwhelming demand.

The market for publicly listed REITs, introduced in 2021, is showing signs of fatigue, with a glut of deals in the pipeline — more than $13 billion worth of offerings — set to add to the supply, including two that will begin raising funds next week. That deluge threatens to undermine a market that has grown to $33 billion as Beijing seeks to tap its massive capital markets to fund real estate projects and ease the burden on local governments.

Beijing has been looking for new ways to fund infrastructure projects, including rental housing, traditionally the domain of local government financing vehicles. As the property downturn since 2021 squeezed their cash flows, Beijing has increasingly relied on REITs to recycle some of the investment already in real estate assets.
Among a series of regulatory changes and other fixes, REITs were initially greeted with enthusiasm, particularly as a way to mobilize deep pools of liquidity for infrastructure projects.

Now they are emerging as the latest corner of China’s capital markets where supply is overwhelming demand, raising questions about the financing tool that has helped shift the cost of funding roads, industrial parks and utilities away from local governments and toward the market. The struggles expose a mismatch between infrastructure funding needs and low investor interest outside China’s tech ambitions.

“The REIT market slid into a deep correction as a flood of new supply collided with deteriorating fundamentals, unwinding the crowded trades that had supported the sector years ago,” said Zhao Yunjiao, an analyst at CSCI Pengyuan Credit Ratings. “The result has been a market characterized by low odds of gains and steep drawdowns, disrupting the trading dynamics that once supported the sector.”

Roughly 30 REIT products are awaiting regulatory approval to raise a combined 90.4 billion yuan ($13.5 billion), on top of another 3.9 billion yuan of issuance expected in the coming weeks, according to figures compiled by Bloomberg.

The pipeline is equivalent to about 40% of the value of the market’s 89 currently listed products, fueling concern that investor demand may no longer be deep enough to absorb the steady flow of new offerings, especially as returns have fallen short of expectations.

Just next week, the Yinhua Yuehai Water Resources fund will look to raise as much as $255 million and the Huatai Zijin Huazhu Anzhu fund will price its $196 million initial public offering. The queue is still building. New World Development Co. on Thursday said it had applied spin-off a Shanghai commercial building to list as a REIT on the city’s exchange pending regulatory approval.

While the trusts are pitched as bond-like investment vehicles that offer stable yields and predictable cash flows, their market performance has undercut that appeal. They have fallen 10.4% over the past six months by weighted average, while only half of this year’s debuts are trading above their listing price.

One example is an E Fund product tied to an industrial zone in Guangzhou, which has lost more than 50% since its 2024 listing, though its annualized dividend yield is still merely 4.5%. It suffered a net loss of 8 million yuan in the first half, and said that tenants remain under financial strain while competition is intensifying.
Oversubscription levels have halved from a year ago. A China Securities Index gauge of REIT products is down 28% from its 2022 peak, and trading has slumped to a quarter of the highs two years ago.

The surge in supply is no accident, even given that weak secondary market backdrop. Regulators have spent years expanding the market, broadening eligibility from industrial parks and office buildings to rental housing, shopping malls, hotels and other commercial assets. A once tightly controlled pilot has matured into a regular issuance program with streamlined approvals.

More recently, Beijing has cast REITs as a pillar of its new property-financing framework, encouraging issuance backed by rental housing and urban-renewal projects. Exacerbating the market’s caution, the wave of issuance also coincides with a deterioration in the investment case.

“The concept made sense: unlock capital tied up in assets owned by state firms and local-government financing vehicles and recycle it into new investment,” said Cai Yibin, chief investment officer at Xiamen Chuangzhao Private Fund Management. “But some assets were packaged too aggressively and listed at peak performance. Once fundamentals like rent and occupancy rate softened, investors started questioning the valuations.”

Among recent listings, the CICC Xiamen Affordable Rental Housing Closed-end Infrastructure Fund offered an annualized cash dividend yield of 2.4% in the first half according to a filing, while the Huatai Zijin Suzhou Hengtai Rental Housing Closed-end Infrastructure Fund yielded just 3.4%.

Backed by assets with operating lives exceeding 50 years, the products offered only a modest premium over the 30-year Chinese government bond yield of 2.15%, leaving little compensation for the additional risks investors assume.

Even the market’s more glamorous sectors have struggled to attract buyers. Data-center REITs have joined shopping malls, logistics parks and highways in trading below investor expectations, with a pair of such funds both trading below their offer price, at annualized cash dividend yields at 4.4% and 3.1%. While that is higher than the 1.7% on China’s 10-year government bond, it pales in comparison to the 30% gain in the CSI Telecommunication Services Index this year.

“When debuts were generating easy gains, even investors with little interest in REITs piled in. But if prices keep falling after listing, institutions eventually stop participating,” said Cai. “Then issuance becomes difficult and the market risks turning stagnant.”

items.title: NY Penn Station's Tracks Bar Reopens After Seven-Year Absence
body: New York City commuters can once again raise a Guinness at Tracks Raw Bar & Grill in its longtime Penn Station home, where the well-loved watering hole has returned after almost seven years.

Tracks, which opened in the basement of the much-maligned transit hub in 2003, was forced to close down in 2019 during the renovation of Long Island Rail Road’s concourse within the station. The bar moved to street level nearby when construction began, but officially reopened in its original location inside the terminal on Thursday.

After an almost $4 million renovation, commuters and neighborhood residents and workers have returned for the oysters, sushi and other seafood dishes. Thirsty travels can relax at the long, narrow bar where departure monitors keep LIRR riders abreast of track announcements.

At its grand re-opening celebration on Thursday, local politicians along with Janno Lieber, the head of the Metropolitan Transportation Authority, joined commuters and neighborhood residents inside for a pint.
“Tracks is always known as a place where blue collar and white collar, we all got together, a true melting pot,” owner Bruce Caulfield told reporters.

Reverend Brian Jordan, pastor at the nearby Church of St. Francis of Assisi, was on hand to bless the establishment — and its beer taps. The gang of suits then raised a glass of Guinness for a celebratory toast.
“God is great. God is good. God is our neighborhood,” Jordan said in a blessing behind the bar with a pint held high. “We’re right here in Penn Station. We’re open for Tracks! God Bless it!”
Tracks is one of Penn Station’s oldest retail tenants. It opened a second location in 2025 in Grand Central Madison, the new LIRR concourse at Grand Central Terminal.

If the original Tracks lacked swanky decor, it always offered location, convenience and a cold drink. The updated interior and lighting are a nice change, said Nicole Lyons, 42, who lives in the area.

“It’s so iconic and I feel like the old Tracks was dark,” Lyons said while sipping a glass of rose wine. “This one is so welcoming and inviting. It’s going to be great for all generations and even non-drinkers.”

items.title: Bathla, Centuria, Sydney Airport, Labor immigration policy: Australia Briefing
body: The fallout from the collapse of property developer Bathla continues to roll through the real estate and private credit markets this morning. A major Bathla backer - Centuria Bass Credit - is exploring options to sell some of its debt tied to the builder, Richard Henderson reported, in the latest sign that creditors might be looking to trim their exposure.
Meanwhile, my colleague Amy Bainbridge spoke to big investment platforms about how they are scrutinizing Bathla-exposed private credit funds they offer — or offered — their clients.

A key element of the current discussion about Bathla and its lenders is the opaqueness of private market investments in Australia compared to markets like the US and UK, something the regulator made a point of highlighting in recent months, even well before Bathla went into administration. Morgan Stanley’s banking analysts this week pointed to the need for more transparency for major banks who lend to the construction industry to allow for a better assessment of credit risk tied to developers, as Joe Flynn reported. - Adam Haigh, editor

Australia’s major airlines backed a proposal to close Sydney Airport’s control tower overnight to free up air traffic controllers, the latest step to address a persistent labor shortage that’s disrupting flights and raising safety concerns. At least six safety incidents, close calls and mistakes on the tarmac since late July has shone a light on the lack of controllers and the impact on air travel.

Labor is moving to reduce immigration, planning a clampdown on people who have overstayed their visas as well as restricting most student-visa holders from bringing family members into the country. Home Affairs Minister Tony Burke outlined the changes at the National Press Club on Thursday, saying the reforms “are to ensure that our migration system can be better targeted to the current needs of Australia.”

The Japanese yen has been trading near multi-decade lows — but one big Australian investor has bet on the currency’s recovery. This week, host Rebecca Jones talks to Bloomberg’s Chief Asia Rates Correspondent Ruth Carson about why Australian Retirement Trust is buying the yen, what’s driving Japan’s currency, and what a rebound could mean for Australian investors, businesses and anyone planning a Japanese ski holiday.
Listen and follow The Bloomberg Australia Podcast on Apple, Spotify, YouTube or wherever you get your podcasts.

Australia’s central bank should stand ready to hike interest rates given inflation risks remain tilted to the upside, the International Monetary Fund said, adding the government could also support disinflation by reining in spending. Meanwhile, HSBC said the housing downturn will help the RBA reduce inflation to its target band.

The government is considering a ban on smart glasses in federal buildings, citing privacy and security concerns over using the devices to record people without their knowledge. “We need clear and consistent guidance for public servants,” Minister for the Public Service Katy Gallagher said Thursday.

Stocks joined bonds higher as falling oil prices lent support to optimism that inflation can be kept under control a day after the Federal Reserve raised interest rates for the first time since 2023. Equities notched their biggest gain in six weeks, with the S&P 500 up 1.1%, while the tech-heavy Nasdaq 100 added 1.7%. Australian equity-index futures edged higher.

The US is expected to delay the announcement of new tariffs over allegations of trading partners’ excess manufacturing capacity at least until after next week’s planned summit between Presidents Xi Jinping and Donald Trump, Bloomberg reported on Thursday.

A senior Glencore executive who led the company’s relationship with Radiant World has been suspended as the company reviews its dealings with the embattled iron ore trader, according to a person familiar with the matter. Peter Hill, head of trading for steelmaking raw materials including iron ore and coking coal, has been stood down from his duties pending the outcome of a review.

The current round of panic over artificial intelligence is based on the conviction that the technology has slipped out of human control to do its own bidding in several recent incidents. But other experts in the field are pushing back, claiming that such talk allows companies to sidestep accountability for real-world impacts of their technology.

South Korean President Lee Jae Myung will seek to reverse hemorrhaging public support and get his policy agenda back on track at a high-stakes Friday press briefing, even as a barrage of criticism from Donald Trump narrows his room to maneuver.
All times Sydney:• 9.30 a.m. — RBA Governor Michele Bullock addresses committee in Canberra

US Secretary of State Marco Rubio is the first person to act as both the nation’s top diplomat and the president’s national security adviser since Kissinger during Richard Nixon’s presidency a half-century ago. Rubio is one of a small number of officials who can walk in to see President Trump without an appointment. He’s used that access to cultivate a friendly working relationship with someone he trashed as a “con man.” But as the Iran war drags on, inflation persists and Trump’s approval ratings dwindle, some people in Rubio’s camp have quietly explored whether he should exit the administration — and if so, when.

items.title: Pennsylvania's Josh Shapiro Calls for Tougher AI Safeguards
body: Pennsylvania Governor Josh Shapiro called for tougher safeguards around artificial intelligence Thursday, wading into a growing debate over the risks of the rapidly advancing technology while arguing the US can continue to reap its economic benefits.

“I don’t think it’s inevitable that AI is going to take over the world, or that someone will misuse it to kill us or to do harm. But I do have real concerns, as do many Pennsylvanians and many Americans,” said Shapiro, a possible 2028 Democratic presidential hopeful. “And I don’t think that the very real concerns of our neighbors that they overwhelmingly express about this technology is a hoax, as our president has called it.”
Shapiro delivered the keynote address at the AI Horizons summit in Pittsburgh, a two-day summit featuring executives, researchers and policymakers from the technology industry.

Shapiro’s comments come amid a renewed debate over the pace and risks of AI development. Anthropic researcher Jacob Coxon last week quit over safety concerns, saying that people building AI believe it could “kill us all by the end of the decade,” fueling calls for stronger safeguards. Microsoft co-founder Bill Gates last month in an essay warned that tech companies are minimizing the perils AI poses to humanity, even as he also emphasized its potential benefits.

Last month, Shapiro signed an executive order establishing new guardrails for data centers in a state that has become a hot spot for data center development. Shapiro’s order requires projects to obtain local approval before seeking state permits and tax credits, as well as cover their own power usage and abide by water conservation standards. It also bans non-disclosure agreements in the permitting and approval process. The governor said the standards were designed to protect local communities from “predatory” data center developers.

Pennsylvania’s move is part of a broader political backlash over the power, water and land consumed by data centers. Texas Governor Greg Abbott, a Republican, has increased scrutiny of data centers’ energy and water use, while New York Governor Kathy Hochul, a Democrat, has implemented a temporary ban on new large data centers.
Read More: Gates Criticizes Tech Companies for Downplaying AI’s Risks
Meanwhile, President Donald Trump this week dismissed as a “hoax” warnings from tech leaders that AI was advancing at a degree that could eventually destroy humanity.

Shapiro’s tougher approach marks a shift from last summer, when the governor celebrated the announcement of Amazon’s $20 billion investment in two new data center campuses, declaring the state was “all in” on AI. The investment, which includes campuses in Luzerne and Bucks counties, was billed as the largest private-sector investment in state history and was expected to create at least 1,250 permanent jobs as well as thousands of construction jobs.

In Pennsylvania, like elsewhere across the US, data centers have become a flashpoint in the midterms as the governor vies for reelection against Republican State Treasurer Stacy Garrity, who has called for a pause on new data center projects. Both Shapiro and Garrity have accused one another of flip-flopping on the issue. Garrity, in a press release Thursday afternoon, said voters aren’t “fooled by the blind political ambitions of Josh Shapiro.”
A poll conducted Aug. 17-21 by The Philadelphia Inquirer, The New York Times and Siena University found 6 in 10 likely Pennsylvania voters opposed construction of AI data centers in the US.
Read More: How Data Center Backlash Is Shaping the US Midterms: Explainer

The tension between embracing AI and limiting its physical footprint is particularly visible in Pittsburgh, a former steel center that has sought to remake itself as a hub for technology, robotics and advanced manufacturing.
Pittsburgh Mayor Corey O’Connor said he welcomes AI investment to make Pittsburgh a “smart city” that embraces tech to improve services and boost the economy.

“Whether it’s 3D printing or different types of manufacturing, all of those things coming to Pittsburgh creates opportunities and more jobs,” he said, adding “We don’t have to add data centers to the grid in the city of Pittsburgh.”

Shawn Steffee, a member of Boilermakers Local 154 in Pittsburgh, said AI-related investment could help create jobs in western Pennsylvania, a region whose economy was historically anchored by steel and coal.

“Let’s get moving. I’m ready to build it for Governor Shapiro, I’m ready to build it for Senator McCormick,” he said, referring to Republican Dave McCormick. “I don’t care if you’ve got a D an R or an I next to your name.”

items.title: S&P 500 Volume Spikes on $7 Trillion Options Day: Markets Wrap
body: Asian stocks and bonds rose tracking a rally on Wall Street as a pullback in oil prices eased inflation concerns. The yen was mostly steady ahead of the Bank of Japan’s interest-rate decision, with traders expecting a hike.

MSCI’s regional equities gauge advanced 0.3% with South Korea’s Kospi index leading gains. That came after the S&P 500 Index rose 1.1% on Thursday, its biggest advance since early August. The tech-heavy Nasdaq 100 Index climbed 1.7%, while a key gauge of chipmakers jumped 3.1% as US stocks rebounded from losses triggered by the Federal Reserve’s first rate hike since 2023.

Adding to the positive tone, Brent crude declined for a third day Friday to just below $104.00 a barrel as supply concerns eased and traders turned to the next round of diplomacy that could shape the US-Iran war.

Oil’s retreat helped Treasuries rally across the curve in the New York session, with the 10-year yield falling nine basis points to 4.93%, having touched 5.02% Wednesday following the Fed move. Government bonds of similar tenor in Australia and New Zealand opened higher.

Lower energy prices could reduce pressure on consumer prices and give central banks more room to assess the impact of tighter monetary policy, offering support to both stocks and bonds. But the durability of that reprieve may depend on whether oil continues to retreat, with the US-Iran war and prospects for further diplomacy keeping the outlook for energy supplies uncertain.
“Sentiment has been lifted in part because crude oil has fallen for a second day, easing pressure on bond yields,” said Fawad Razaqzada at Forex.com.

Oil fell with Saudi Arabia seeking to restore about half the capacity of its key East-West pipeline within days after it was shut last week following drone strikes, easing some concerns over further supply losses stemming from the Iran conflict.

Meanwhile, Reuters reported that China asked Iran to help rein in Yemen’s Tehran-backed Houthi militants, a move that could potentially ease disruptions around the Bab el-Mandeb, another strait vital to global shipping and energy markets.
Elsewhere, gold jumped on Thursday, snapping a three-day decline, while a Bloomberg gauge of the dollar pared some of its gains since the rate increase.

UK government bonds also rallied after the Bank of England scrapped plans to sell long-dated gilts as part of its quantitative-tightening program. The decision offered relief to a battered market, where 10- and 30-year yields had climbed to their highest levels since 2007 and 1998, respectively.
The BOE left its benchmark rate unchanged on Thursday.

Meanwhile, Japan’s inflation slowed for the first time in four months, largely reflecting the effect of government subsidies, in data released hours before the BOJ. All respondents in a Bloomberg survey expect the central bank to raise its policy rate to 1.25% from 1% on Friday, with governor Kazuo Ueda scheduled to hold a press conference after.
The yen was little changed, trading around 156.15 per dollar.

“We expect the BOJ to deliver a 25 basis point hike to 1.25% on Friday - this is now the bare minimum and it would be pretty unimaginable at this point that we don’t get one,” wrote Anthony Malouf, a market analyst at Ebury. “Governor Ueda will have no choice but to also strike a hawkish note on policy for risk of undoing a lot of the good work achieved via FX intervention.”

items.title: Oil Traders Stymied by Iran War Stalemate: Evening Briefing Americas
body: On one hand, oil fell on Thursday. On the other, it’s still about $105 a barrel.

And the reason for that three-digit crisis continues to metastasize across the Middle East. More than six months after the US and Israel launched the Iran war, oil analysts at JPMorgan are stating what many traders have been saying privately for some time: predicting an end to the conflict has become near impossible.

Several economic red lines the bank had assumed the Trump administration wouldn’t cross — like oil rising above $100 a barrel, gas near $5 a gallon and surging US Treasury yields — have already been crossed. With no clear understanding as to what it would take for Donald Trump or Iran to back down, analysts warn, the future is looking very cloudy indeed.
US regulators are seeking interviews with employees of Guggenheim Partners as part of a federal investigation into potential wrongdoing at Chief Executive Officer Mark Walter’s business empire.

The Securities and Exchange Commission is said to have sent requests in recent weeks to current and former employees from the firm’s $367 billion asset manager, Guggenheim Investments. The interviews come after public assurances from officials at Guggenheim and the billionaire’s holding company, TWG Global, that they are working to resolve government inquiries.

Jeep parent Stellantis told workers at a Toronto-area factory that it sees “no long-term business case” for making vehicles there and that it’s exploring a sale of the facility. In a letter to workers at the plant, which hasn’t produced vehicles since late 2023, the carmaker said it’s facing untenable economic conditions.

The automaker has considered “a range of options” since it reversed plans to build the Jeep Compass SUV at the factory last year. The company made that decision after Trump made it clear he would put tariffs on foreign-made cars and trucks as part of his trade war on Canada.

Eat less and exercise? If not, maybe just the shot, then. Users of GLP-1 pills for weight loss curbed their snacking less than those taking the treatment through injections, according to new research from Bloomberg Intelligence.

Among those taking the drugs orally, 74% said they were eating fewer salty snacks, compared to 80% for those taking a GLP-1 via a shot. Similarly, 76% of pill users said they were eating fewer baked goods, lower than the 82% for those using injections. That pattern was repeated in other categories, including confections and shelf-stable foods like soup.

CoreWeave, a provider of computing that powers artificial intelligence systems, kicked off a fresh round of fundraising that includes a $3 billion convertible bond issue and a vehicle for potential share sales.

The relentless drive to fund AI infrastructure has prompted companies involved in the rapid buildout to tap a wide range of potential sources of cash. But investors have begun to show signs of fatigue after companies borrowed about $419 billion in global debt markets this year alone, according to Bloomberg-compiled data, driving funding costs higher for some as demand dipped.

items.title: Latest Oil Market News and Analysis for Sept. 18
body: Oil dropped for a third day as supply concerns eased and traders looked to the next round of diplomacy that’ll shape the US-Iran war.

Brent fell below $104 a barrel after losing more than 3% over the two previous session, while West Texas Intermediate was near $101. In the Middle East, Saudi Arabia has moved to restore the damaged East-West pipeline to its Red Sea coast, aiming to return about half its capacity within days. At the same time, some tankers continue to traverse the contested Strait of Hormuz.

President Donald Trump told Axios he was approaching a “big decision” on whether to re-escalate attacks on Tehran, with a meeting with Persian Gulf nations planned for next week in New York on the sidelines of the United Nations General Assembly. In addition, the US leader is due to hold a summit with Chinese counterpart Xi Jinping that may touch upon the war.

Ahead of that, Beijing privately asked Iran to help rein in Houthi militants after an appeal to China by Riyadh, Reuters reported. The Tehran-backed militant group has made advances in Yemen toward the Bab el-Mandeb chokepoint in recent days, while also attacking facilities in Saudi Arabia.

Crude is finishing up a volatile week with supply concerns at the fore, initially gaining ground on the Saudi pipeline disruption before retreating. Global benchmark Brent remains more than 70% higher year-to-date given the conflicts in the Middle East and Russia-Ukraine. That’s fanning inflationary concerns, with Goldman Sachs Group Inc. predicting more gains for gasoline.

JPMorgan Chase & Co. analysts including Natasha Kaneva said the length of the Iran war and impact on flows have become increasingly hard to predict. “For the first time since the start of the Iran conflict, we don’t have a baseline view,” they said. “We simply don’t know how to model the endgame.”

There’s no consensus on energy volumes transiting Hormuz, the waterway that links the Persian Gulf to global markets. While US Energy Secretary Chris Wright put a recent seven-day average at 11 million barrels a day, Clarksons Research estimates the daily figure at about 8 million barrels.

Risks to shipping in the waterway persist amid Iranian threats to vessels using routes it regards as unapproved. A Togo-flagged tanker was struck while transiting the conduit, state-run IRIB News reported, citing the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corp Navy. The report hasn’t been independently verified.

Meanwhile, Saudi Aramco has been looking to secure thousands of tons of diesel in the Mediterranean after strikes on its energy facilities. The pickup predates attacks last week on the East-West pipeline, but coincides with reported incidents involving fuel-making plants in recent months.

items.title: Can China Turn Its AI Reach Into Geopolitical Power?
body: When Chinese President Xi Jinping meets with President Donald Trump in Washington next week, any discussion about keeping artificial intelligence safe will be colored by a broader strategic question: which country stands to benefit most from guardrails. Calls by leading US labs to slow frontier development have heightened fears that China could catch up, with Trump dismissing AI concerns as a “hoax” that could play into Beijing’s hands.
The US has good reason to worry that China is closing the gap. Just look at how Chinese electric vehicles rose to dominance.

In 2011,  Elon Musk laughed when asked whether BYD Co. might one day compete with Tesla Inc. “Have you seen their car?” he responded. China’s EVs went on to improve so much that they spooked incumbents, triggered major US trade barriers and account for almost 75% of global production today.
Musk appears less inclined to again dismiss China, calling it “by far the strongest competitor in AI.”

China’s AI industry has come to look much as its EV sector did a decade ago: Local companies are competing fiercely and making the technology cheaper and better, even if that means years of price wars and consolidation before clear winners emerge. Constrained by US controls on advanced chips, Chinese firms have learned to squeeze more intelligence out of less computing power, challenging the so-called American frontier at a fraction of the cost and winning users around the world. That reach offers Xi the prospect of influence on a scale that closed American platforms struggle to match, particularly across the developing world.

But unlike cars, China is giving much of its AI away as open-weight models that anyone can download and run for free on their own computers. They lack the stickiness of operating systems like Google’s Android or Microsoft Corp.’s Windows, or the lock-in that comes with Huawei Technologies Co.’s 5G infrastructure. Developers can swap one open-weight model for another, whether it be US or Chinese, with relatively little friction as prices and performance change. That leaves a yawning gap between global popularity and monetization, and it raises questions about whether China can derive lasting geopolitical influence from its models.

Xi laid out his vision in July at a flagship conference in Shanghai, declaring that AI development “should not be a solo performance by a single country.” He announced the World AI Cooperation Organization, or WAICO, with 29 founding members including Russia, Pakistan and Indonesia, but none from the Group of Seven.

He didn’t name the US, but his message was clear: China will champion open models and share its technology, while the US keeps its best models proprietary and seeks to build an American-led supply chain less dependent on China. Xi reinforced that message at a gathering of BRICS countries earlier this month, proposing an “AI open-source community” among emerging markets and promising support and training for their AI development.

Whatever the strategic intent, that generosity has resonated. Alibaba Group Holding Ltd. said in August its open-weight models had accumulated more than 3 billion global downloads in six months, exceeding the downloads of those developed by Meta Platforms Inc., Alphabet Inc. and other US peers.

If those models were EVs, that kind of volume would translate directly into market share and revenue. But once a model’s weights — its core numerical parameters — are published, anyone can download them, run them on their own servers, modify them and even resell access. Users often have no obligation to pay anything to companies like DeepSeek or Z.ai Co. unless they are accessing the models through their servers.

The distinction between using a Chinese AI model and using Chinese servers that host that model was on full display when US lawmakers concerned about data security pressed Airbnb Inc. over its use of Qwen for customer service. Chief Executive Officer Brian Chesky said that the firm sent no data to any Chinese companies and that the lawmakers were “misunderstanding” the technology.

Even if open-weight models generate little direct revenue, the case for spreading them widely is clear: Get as many people and businesses using your technology as possible. US Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick made a similar argument in defending sales of second-tier chips to China, saying it was better to keep Chinese developers “addicted to the American technology stack” than push them toward self-sufficiency.
Read More: US Lead in the AI Race With China Is Rapidly Narrowing

But chips are much stickier than models. Nvidia Corp.’s hardware locks customers into CUDA, the software platform used to run complex computations on its graphics processing units (GPUs), making it painful to switch to rivals. By contrast, model makers have converged on standard interfaces created by OpenAI or Anthropic PBC, allowing developers to switch the brain of their applications from Claude to DeepSeek as easily as changing a URL.

Android is also open-source, but Google profits from its widespread adoption through app-store and advertising revenue. Most Chinese model makers have no equivalent source of income, nor Huawei’s ability to parlay 5G technology into long-term infrastructure contracts and licensing fees.

That interchangeability creates a hypercompetitive market with little lock-in. When DeepSeek’s updated V4-flash model proved almost 100 times cheaper than US flagships, its use surged almost instantly and helped propel the company’s market share on OpenRouter past Google to the top by number of requests. But users can move just as quickly in the other direction: OpenAI edged DeepSeek out of the No. 1 spot earlier this month as the American company’s cheaper GPT-5.6 Luna model gathered steam.

I’ve had a front-row seat to that fickleness. A year ago, I bought a Mac Studio with 96 gigabytes of unified memory — a stupid amount of RAM for someone who mostly works with words — because I wanted to see what running large models locally actually felt like. I also had some abandoned personal projects I wanted to vibe code back into existence. I took open-weight models from Qwen, Z.ai, Google and OpenAI — which last released a significant open model in August 2025 — for a ride with the ease of downloading different apps to your phone.

In r/LocalLLaMA, a Reddit community named after Meta’s earlier open-weight Llama models, users count down to new Qwen releases the way some people count down to Christmas. But there’s little loyalty: People gravitate toward the best model for their needs, often migrating overnight.

What that community has created paying demand for isn’t any particular model — US or Chinese — but more RAM and more GPUs. Apple announced upgraded Mac Studio desktop computers last month with up to 512GB of memory and an expanded memory bandwidth of up to 1.2 terabytes per second. By comparison, a base-model MacBook Air has 16GB of memory and one-eighth the bandwidth.

The Studio machines are marketed explicitly for running large language models locally, something made possible by the proliferation of capable open-weight models. That means China’s free AI is generating revenue for Apple and other companies that make the hardware needed to run it. Demand is so strong — and memory prices so high — that my computer is now worth more on the second-hand market than I originally paid for it.

Software companies have also found ways to capture value from interchangeable models. An industry has sprung up around the tools and software that make those models more useful than just chatting — a stickier layer of the technology stack that model makers themselves are now trying to move into. Anthropic has Claude Code, while DeepSeek released its own open-source coding tool in August. So far, nobody has established a durable lead.

Chinese companies may struggle to make much money from their models, but they have still eaten into the market share of America’s frontier labs by making intelligence dramatically cheaper. Anthropic and OpenAI both face pressure to cut prices. More broadly, AI-related investment accounted for about half of US economic growth this year — something Trump will care about if Chinese competition starts to dent the pace of investment.

Monetization, however, is only one measure of success. A thriving AI industry at home lets China lift productivity to support the economy without depending on foreign suppliers, in keeping with Xi’s drive for technological self-sufficiency. Abroad, particularly in developing countries priced out of the leading closed models, China can gain influence with its cheaper alternatives and by allowing anyone, including governments, to customize them.

Their spread also makes technological decoupling harder. US companies selling chips, cloud services and software can profit from Chinese models, giving them reason to oppose restrictions while creating an opening for Chinese hardware as it improves.

Washington responded to China’s EV dominance largely by shutting Chinese cars out of the US market. AI is different: The US sees it as a strategic race it has to win, not simply a foreign technology to keep at bay. So far, Washington has focused less on restricting Chinese models than on scrutinizing their producers over alleged theft of intellectual property. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has threatened sanctions over what he called “industrial-scale distillation” — extracting a rival’s capabilities by training on its outputs. “Open source is not open season on American IP,” Bessent wrote.

Most American tech companies don’t want a ban. When reports surfaced in July that the White House was considering broader restrictions on Chinese models, nearly 200 startups petitioned against the idea. Some 25 companies including Nvidia, Microsoft, Meta and Palantir Technologies Inc., later signed a letter defending open weights as a strategic asset, though OpenAI, Anthropic and Google were conspicuously absent from the initial list.

Washington may not need to go that far. China’s own caution could act as a handbrake on its AI ambitions. Beijing is wary of the technology destabilizing the labor market or creating safety risks, and Xi has repeatedly stressed the need for AI to remain under human control. China’s spy chief recently warned that adversaries could use AI for “cognitive warfare,” including fabricating rumors and inflaming social divisions.

A more likely source of confrontation is the US further restricting China’s access to advanced chips. That could tempt Beijing to reach for its leverage over rare earths, pulling the two largest economies back into a chips-versus-magnets standoff.

Neither side has yet won the race for self-sufficiency — in advanced chips for China or rare earths for the US. But there are signs Chinese companies are making up for the gap in compute. Last month, a free mystery model called Ox Alpha topped OpenRouter’s usage charts for several days before Z.ai revealed itself as the developer. More significantly, the company said it ran the model on about 100,000 Chinese-made chips.

Washington also sees geostrategic value in competing with China on open models, even as US companies remain divided over how much technology to give away. Meta, Google and Nvidia all actively support open weights, while Anthropic and OpenAI depend more on selling access to proprietary models. Musk, meanwhile, has promised to make his Grok 3 open-source, a vow he has yet to fulfill.
The technology industry has a name for China’s strategy: “commoditize your complement.” Make one part of a system abundant and cheap, and you can increase demand — and value — elsewhere in the stack.

But it is not yet clear what China’s models will complement. The obvious candidate is domestic hardware, but its chipmakers remain constrained by US controls on advanced tools. So far, cheap Chinese intelligence has also increased the value of foreign chips, computers and software. China has built great engines. Now it has to convince the world to pay for them — and the rest of the car.

items.title: DoubleLine's Gundlach Warns of Fiscal Crisis in Next Recession
body: DoubleLine Capital chief executive Jeffrey Gundlach warned that the next US downturn could trigger a debt crisis that sends long-term Treasury yields sharply higher — defying decades of conventional wisdom that bonds will always serve as safe haven during times of economic strife.

Such a scenario could push the Federal Reserve and the Treasury into unconventional policies, such as the central bank buying long-dated bonds in a repeat of Operation Twist, or even a debt restructuring. Gundlach said he’s focusing on low-duration assets to shield Doubleline’s funds against further increases in interest rates.

“If there’s a recession, there’s going to be incredible attention paid to the fiscal situation,” he said at an event in New York. “You would have the budget deficit go easily to 12% of GDP. That would create $3 trillion of interest expense probably per year, and you just can’t do it.”

Gundlach’s views, while extreme, reflect growing investor concerns over the diversification benefits of fixed income, which are traditionally seen as buffering losses from stock portfolios during economic downturns.

In recent years, the inflationary nature of recent shocks has pummeled bonds, sometimes leading them to sell off at the same time as equities. Should the next recession prove similarly inflationary, that would limit the scope for central bankers to stimulate the economy by lowering interest rates.
Read More: AMP Says Bonds No Longer a Hedge, Cuts From Some Pension Funds

Gundlach cited the breakdown of closely-watched market correlations, including the ratio of gold and copper to Treasury yields, since 2020 as evidence of a regime change where the secular direction for interest rates is higher. The dollar, meanwhile, doesn’t hold the same inverse relationship to US stocks, he said.
“We’re in backward land and in the next recession long-term rates are going to go up and they’ll go up because of the debt crisis that it’s going to usher in,” he said.
Gundlach founded DoubleLine in 2009 after a contentious exit from TCW, where he’d become a star bond manager. DoubleLine managed $95 billion in assets and had more than 250 employees as of March.

Gundlach said he is now “a little less negative on the long end” than he was a year ago but remains positioned for yields to ultimately move higher. He sees the potential for greater US policy interventions to cap the bond selloff should it continue.

One possibility would be a repeat of Operation Twist, in which the Federal Reserve would suppress long-end rates while keeping short-end rates elevated. “I think they would do that somewhere around 6.5%,” he said of the yield level likely to trigger action.
Another option would be a restructuring of Treasury debt — a risk he has warned about before. That would involve cutting coupon payments across outstanding bonds.
Read More: Gundlach Takes Longshot Bet in Case of US Debt Restructuring

“You could just say every Treasury bond that has a coupon above one, your coupon is now one. That would reduce your interest expense overnight by 75%,” Gundlach said. “Of course, every investor would erupt in anger and they’d never look to you again. You’d never be able to borrow money again.”

items.title: Stocks, Treasuries Bounce Back After Fed-Day Drop as Oil Slips
body: Good morning. Equities and bonds bounce back after their Fed-day drop as oil slips. Indian retail traders face a new reality after regulators stepped in to manage the country’s options boom. And a Monet masterpiece may fetch as much as €30 million at auction. Listen to the day’s top stories.

Stocks and Treasuries rebounded as oil slipped amid signs that supply disruptions in the Middle East are set to ease, feeding optimism that inflation can be reined in. Citadel Securities’ Scott Rubner said September will still be bumpy for equities but “the setup is beginning to change.” The Bank of Japan may deliver its second rate hike in three months, though strategists warn the yen may suffer unless officials convince markets that more tightening is in store. But a hike may also reduce the appeal of the yen carry trade by making the currency more expensive to borrow.

Donald Trump told Axios he’s nearing a decision over whether to restart attacks and “annihilate” the Iranian regime, ahead of a planned meeting with Gulf leaders next week at the United Nations General Assembly. JPMorgan oil analysts are saying the path to the end of the war is increasingly impossible to predict. The White House plans to sell Saudi Arabia up to 48 F-35 warplanes in a deal that may be worth as much as $24.3 billion.

Tata Sons said it would pursue a stock listing and give Chairman Natarajan Chandrasekaran another five-year term despite strong — and public — opposition from the founding-family patriarch, setting up a showdown at one of India’s oldest conglomerates. Tata Trusts called the reappointment “illegal.”

In trade news, the US is expected to delay announcing new excess-capacity tariffs until after the Trump-Xi Jinping summit, people familiar said. It’s uncertain whether the final rate will change from the level previously expected, which would restore Trump’s second-term duties on China to around 20%.

Jensen Huang said artificial intelligence systems must be safety-tested “rigorously” as he and other industry leaders met with King Charles III to discuss the risks of the new technology. The Nvidia chief executive officer told reporters he expects to sell twice as many chips in the coming year, sending shares higher.

A perfect storm of budget smartphones, dirt-cheap data and lower barriers to entry helped turn India into the world’s largest equity options market by contracts traded — with some first-time investors gambling away their life savings before regulators stepped in.

Japan is getting choosier about who gets to stay for good, writes Gearoid Reidy. The latest permanent-residency proposals aren’t perfect, but critics should look at the ructions elsewhere when mainstream politicians fail to manage a growing population of foreign labor.

items.title: Pizza Hut Eyes Bonds Backed by Franchise Fees to Aid Buyout
body: Pizza Hut Inc. is looking to finance its $1.5 billion buyout by selling a series of bonds backed by the fees it receives from franchising its restaurants, according to people with knowledge of the transaction.

UBS Group AG provided the funding and is due to lead a transaction that will be structured as a whole-business securitization, said the people, who requested anonymity because the discussions are not yet public. Pizza Hut’s debt is expected to get rankings from credit-rating companies before a deal will launch, the people added.

Earlier this month, LongRange Capital closed on its acquisition of Pizza Hut from Yum! Brands Inc. after a two-part sale was reached in June. Yum China Holdings Inc. had agreed to buy the China-based business for $1.2 billion, while LongRange acquired the rest for $1.5 billion.
A representative for Pizza Hut did not immediately respond to a request for comment. Representatives for LongRange and UBS declined to comment.
Read More: Yum Is in Exclusive Talks to Sell Pizza Hut to LongRange (1)
Whole-business securitizations are typically done on a so-called best-efforts basis. A special purpose vehicle is set up to protect holders of the debt from any bankruptcy proceedings.
Dunkin’ Brands Group Inc. used the method to raise $900 million in October, while Taco Bell Corp. and Domino’s Pizza Inc. have also recently raised capital through this type of debt.

While whole-business securitizations are considered a lower cost of capital for casual-dining businesses, some restaurant chains from Hooters to Red Lobster have loaded up on such debt, and gone bankrupt later.

FAT Brands Inc., which owns chains from Fatburger to Johnny Rockets, filed for bankruptcy in January. The company did not make interest payments due last October on some of its $1.2 billion in whole-business securitizations.
