items.title: Carry Trade Explained: Why the Japanese Yen Is Losing Its Appeal (JPY/USD)
body: For decades, the Japanese yen has been one of the world’s favored currencies for investors looking to borrow cheaply and put that money into assets offering higher returns.

The strategy, known as a carry trade, tends to be popular when market volatility is low and interest-rate gaps between countries are wide, often because central banks are pursuing divergent monetary policies. One may be raising borrowing costs to combat inflation while another keeps them low to boost economic growth.

The strategy can generate steady returns as long as exchange rates remain relatively stable. But sudden currency moves can quickly lead to large losses. When such trades unravel en masse, they can also amplify volatility in financial markets, prompting investors to exit riskier, higher-yielding assets and potentially triggering broader selloffs in bond and equity markets.

Now the dynamics that made the yen such an attractive funding currency are starting to shift. As the Bank of Japan raises interest rates, borrowing in yen is becoming more expensive and the potential returns from the trade are shrinking. That’s prompting some investors to look elsewhere, including to China’s offshore yuan.

In finance-speak, the “carry” of an asset is the return an investor earns while holding it minus the cost of financing it. A carry trade involves borrowing cheaply to buy a higher-yielding asset and profiting by “carrying” the position over time.

Suppose an investor borrows ¥1 million at an interest rate of 1%, converts the funds into dollars and invests them in a dollar fund yielding 4% interest. If the exchange rate remains stable, the investor earns the 3-percentage-point difference between the two interest rates. Investors often hold such positions for months or years to maximize returns, although they can unwind them quickly if market conditions change.
Investors who don’t want or aren’t able to buy assets in the higher-yielding currency can also access the carry trade through derivatives such as currency swaps and forward contracts.

For decades the yen was one of the world’s most preferred funding currencies because Japan kept interest rates exceptionally low after its asset-price bubble burst in the early 1990s. As the BOJ cut rates to zero — and later below zero — in an effort to revive economic growth, borrowing in yen became far cheaper than in many other major currencies. That made it attractive to both institutional and retail investors seeking to profit from interest-rate differences.

But the yen has started to lose its appeal as a funding currency since the BOJ abandoned its negative-rate policy in March 2024 and began raising borrowing costs. Repeated interventions since 2022 by Japanese authorities to boost a weak yen, including a historic joint operation with the US on July 31 this year, have added further risk for carry traders.

When choosing a funding currency, traders weigh not only how cheaply they can borrow but also the risk of exchange-rate volatility. Taken together, these factors — captured by what’s known as the carry-to-risk ratio — make two currencies stand out: the Swiss franc and China’s offshore yuan. The Swiss National Bank keeps its policy rate at zero and stands ready to intervene against excessive appreciation of the Swiss franc. Meanwhile, the offshore yuan has become increasingly attractive because of its low volatility, helped by the People’s Bank of China setting a daily reference rate around which the currency is allowed to trade.
Economists have likened the carry trade to picking up pennies in front of a steamroller — the money’s there for the taking, so long as you don’t dally and get crushed.

To make a profit, investors need the interest-rate differential to outweigh any losses caused by exchange-rate movements. That’s where the biggest risk lies. Currencies can move far more sharply than the interest-rate gap, quickly wiping out the returns from a carry trade.

In the carry-trade example above, assume after one year that the investment is worth $10,400. But in the meantime, the yen strengthened to ¥80 per dollar and the proceeds are now only worth ¥822,000 after paying the 1% interest on the yen loan. That’s less than the ¥1 million originally borrowed.
It’s hard to pin down exactly how much money is involved because carry trades take many forms and available market data rarely reveal strategies behind individual investor positions.

Bank for International Settlements researchers tried to gauge the scale of yen-funded carry trades in a September 2024 report. They estimated that about ¥200 trillion ($1.3 trillion) of net yen supply was absorbed by non-bank market participants. That included overseas investors hedging yen-denominated assets as well as speculators potentially borrowing the currency to fund carry trades, meaning only a portion of the total was necessarily related to the strategy.

More recent, but much narrower, data from the Commodity Futures Trading Commission show that hedge funds have cut their net short positions in yen futures and options by nearly two-thirds since the end of June, when bearish wagers reached a 19-year high. Such positions can serve as a proxy for speculative carry trades because the strategy involves betting against the funding currency. But they capture only a fraction of suspected carry trade activity in the $9.6 trillion-a-day global currency market.

When carry trades become popular, they can channel large amounts of money across borders into higher-yielding currencies and assets. When many investors do the same thing, those flows can materially weaken the lower-yielding currency while boosting the higher-yielding currency and the assets investors have bought. A weaker currency makes imports more expensive and can add to inflationary pressure, which may necessitate central bank interest-rate hikes. A stronger currency can hurt a country’s export competitiveness and may lead to monetary policy easing.

The biggest impact of a carry trade usually comes when the cycle suddenly goes into reverse. If a higher-yielding currency drops or borrowing costs in the funding currency jump, investors may rush to unwind their trades. For leveraged investors, mounting losses can also trigger margin calls, forcing them to sell assets to raise cash. That can cause a feedback loop in which falling asset prices generate further losses and forced selling. Because investors may sell other liquid assets to cover their losses, the turmoil can spread to a broader market selloff.
Because of these features, the carry trade is often seen as a source of global financial fragility and crisis contagion.

A sharp carry-trade unwind contributed to market turmoil in July and August 2024, after the BOJ raised interest rates and Governor Kazuo Ueda suggested further hikes. The prospect of higher Japanese borrowing costs prompted carry traders to unwind positions funded in the currency. That pushed the yen even higher against popular carry-trade targets such as the Mexican peso. Japanese equities also suffered as the unwinding of yen-funded positions added to broader market volatility. Between July 31 and Aug. 5, the yen strengthened by about 8% against the dollar, while the Mexican peso fell by about 13% against the yen. The Nikkei 225 Stock Average slumped 19% during this period.

items.title: Amazon Says AI Models Should Be Released When 'Ready and Safe'
body: Amazon.com Inc. said artificial intelligence models should be released only after rigorous testing, weighing in on the debate about the pace of AI development after top labs called for a slowdown following safety lapses.

“We don’t see it as a choice between progress and safety,” Amazon spokesperson Tom Parnell said in an email. “Models should be released when they’re ready and safe to use, which comes from rigorous testing and strong safeguards. There are risks if that doesn’t happen collectively, and we believe that as an industry, in partnership with government, we’ll work through the right protections.”

Amazon is partner of and investor in leading AI companies, including OpenAI and Anthropic PBC, whose executives have called for moderating the pace of cutting-edge AI work to assess the safety of the technology.
Read More: Amodei, Altman, Musk Call for Slowing AI Model Development

Amazon develops its own large language models, though they are not seen as rivals to the most powerful tools from OpenAI, Anthropic and top Chinese companies. The company’s Amazon Web Services unit also sells computing power and infrastructure management tools to the AI industry.
“AI is already delivering real value to customers, so getting this right matters,” Parnell said. Reuters reported the company’s comments earlier.
Read More: Are We Losing Control of AI? What’s Driving Fears

items.title: Alberta Separation Report Deals Blow to Premier Smith's Agenda
body: Welcome back to Canada Daily, the newsletter on business, economics and politics from Vancouver to Montreal and beyond. If this was forwarded to you, sign up.

Alberta Premier Danielle Smith has spent the summer touting a rosy outlook for her province, announcing major infrastructure projects (including two oil pipeline proposals and a Meta data center) and winning concessions from the federal government to back her goal of doubling oil production.

This week, however, cracks began to show for her government. First, the New Democratic Party scored a byelection win on Monday in a deeply conservative seat in south Calgary, a shock result even in the rollercoaster of Alberta politics.
And then on Wednesday, a delayed government-commissioned report from academics at the University of Calgary painted a grim picture of what Alberta separating from the country could look like.

With a referendum on the issue just weeks away, the byelection result may predict how even conservative voters feel about Smith calling a vote on a constitutional change that, if it happens, would break up Canada as we know it.

Any secession process would dent the province’s gross domestic product by at least 2.2% in the first five years in a good scenario, or more than 10% in a poor one, the academics found. Alberta would take on at least C$324 billion ($232 billion) of additional debt, between its share of Canada owes and the costs associated with separation.
Canada would also suffer greatly: a 15% loss of GDP, a wider federal deficit, a weaker dollar and a bigger trade deficit with the rest of the world.
While the report strongly suggests that secession would be messy, it also showed a potential upside, which may be seized on by separatists as mainstream evidence their cause has real legs.

In the long run, the report said the province may see a bump in GDP of 3.4% in 20 years compared with staying in Canada — on the assumption that independence went smoothly and the price of oil stays in line with expectations. Big assumptions, but ones that provide credibility to some separatists’ arguments coming from an established institution.

Voters are deeply divided, and there’s anger on both sides of the debate. Smith had managed to stay relatively insulated from the fallout from her decision to call a vote, but with referendum day swiftly approaching, the risks for her — and for the province and the country — are becoming clearer.

Also in this newsletter: Stellantis tells workers it has no future in Brampton. Canada tries to stop tech startups from moving to the US. Prime Minister Mark Carney seeks a deeper alliance with the European Union to defend shared values.
The following was produced with the assistance of Bloomberg Automation.

Some of the world’s biggest infrastructure investors are clubbing up to take over GFL Environmental in what could be one of the largest leveraged buyouts of the year. KKR, Energy Capital Partners and Blackstone are bidding together while Brookfield Asset Management and IFM Investors have teamed on a rival bid for the waste manager, according to people familiar with the matter. GFL closed up 5.2% in Toronto.

Canada auctioned long-term bonds at the highest yield in 19 years, as upside inflation risks create higher borrowing costs around the world. The government sold C$3 billion of notes due on June 1, 2059, at an average yield of 4.201% Thursday. That was the highest yield for an auction of Canada 30-year notes since July 2007, when a credit crunch began to ripple through global markets, eventually leading to a major financial crisis the following year.

Many Canadian startups have moved to the US to expand over recent years. Now, the problem is getting fresh attention from Canada’s government and business leaders, and they’re searching for ways to keep startups at home. Carney’s Canada Investment Summit this week resulted in a slew of patriotic announcements to rejuvenate Canadian business — including a new late-stage growth fund that Carney said will “help Canadian AI companies scale up and stay Canadian.”

Jeep parent Stellantis told workers at a Brampton factory that it sees “no long-term business case” for making vehicles there and that it’s exploring a sale of the facility, increasing the likelihood of a work stoppage. “Strike action remains a real possibility,” Unifor National President Lana Payne said at a news conference in Toronto. The parties have been an impasse since last week, when Roshel, a Canadian armored vehicle manufacturer, said it had signed a memorandum with Stellantis outlining steps toward a sale of the plant.

Carney called for a closer alliance between Canada and the EU in a bid to establish a bulwark strong enough to ward off intimidation from world powers like the US and China that could threaten their sovereignty. Carney welcomed a speech made by European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen, when she proposed that Canada become the first “associate member” of the EU. President Donald Trump threatened a new round of tariffs against the bloc if he deems the new relationship to be harmful to the US.

Oil dipped on signs that war-driven market tightness may still persist even as some supply disruptions in the Middle East ease. Global benchmark Brent fell 1% to settle under $105 a barrel, while West Texas Intermediate dipped 0.5% to settle near $102. Saudi Arabia is seeking to return about half the capacity of its key East-West pipeline within days after shutting it last week following drone strikes, easing some concerns about lost crude oil cargoes stemming from the Iran conflict.

Canadian government-owned Trans Mountain has been meeting with new Asian oil buyers in an effort to diversify its customer base for crude exports, the company’s chief administrative officer said. Jennifer Pierce returned last weekend from a trip to visit with customers in China, Korea and Japan as well as “future customers” in India, Singapore, Brunei, Thailand and Vietnam, she said at the Oil Sands Expo in Fort McMurray, Alberta on Wednesday.

Alberta plans to change the fees it charges oil companies to encourage investment in the industry and grow production to fill a proposed million-barrel-a-day pipeline. The revised royalty regime, to be announced in November, will be structured to encourage Canada’s oil sands companies to invest in new production, Smith said on Wednesday.
The S&P/TSX Composite Index rose 1.1%, with the 10 best-performing stocks all in the mining sector.

Trillion-dollar startups, once-unthinkable compensation packages and bidding wars for workers who can build and deploy artificial intelligence have created the impression of a Bay Area labor market on fire. But even as debate swirls about AI’s potential dangers and the need for regulation, the technology has already had a profound disruption on jobs. Many of the workers who helped power San Francisco’s last boom are struggling to find their place in this one. Tech-industry employers filed layoff notices for more than 14,500 Bay Area workers in the 12 months that ended in June, almost double the count for the previous fiscal year, a Bloomberg analysis of data from California’s Employment Development Department shows.

items.title: Rubio's Diplomatic Finesse Has Been Most Effective With Trump
body: I’m Nancy Cook, Bloomberg’s senior national political correspondent, and each weekday I’ll be coming to you with inside-the-room reporting and insights that reveal what’s really happening in Washington — and how it affects you. Email me with feedback and comments here.
What is Marco Rubio’s end game, given his many high-profile jobs within the Trump administration and his own political ambitions?
That’s the subject of the new Businessweek cover story out tonight which I co-wrote with our all-star State Department reporter, Eric Martin.

The curious factoid about Rubio is that he has mostly abandoned the typical secretary of State agenda of constantly flying all over the world to meet with foreign dignitaries. Trump never wanted him to do that, our sources told us.

Instead, Trump has farmed out much of the negotiations and diplomacy on the world stage to advisers like Steve Witkoff, Jared Kushner or Vice President JD Vance while Rubio spends most afternoons working out of his office in the West Wing.

He ended up with that prime real estate once he took on the additional job of national security adviser — and it affords him close proximity to the Oval Office, Vance and chief of staff, Susie Wiles, who he has known for many years given their shared history in Florida politics. (One of the screens in Rubio’s office is tuned to Trump’s hyperactive Truth Social feed, a real-time gauge of the president’s state of mind).
And his fidelity has paid off.

Whereas Trump once nicknamed him “Little Marco” during the 2016 campaign when they ran against one another, Trump now just calls him “Marco,” and the two of them frequently joke around and chat about football games, or boxing matches they’ve watched on TV.

Rubio’s portfolio has allowed him to make big moves in the Western Hemisphere. “After the military strike on Venezuela this January, Trump put Rubio in charge of overseeing the caretaker government of Delcy Rodríguez, the Maduro deputy Trump effectively installed as leader of the country. Rubio keeps in close touch with Rodríguez, and she clears major decisions with him,” as Martin reports.

Rubio is also leading the way on tightening sanctions against Cuba, the country his parents fled and where he’s long wanted to see regime change. Where his fingerprints are less obvious is on the war in Iran.

“When Henry Kissinger was secretary of State and national security adviser, he was everywhere, on every major topic of the day,” says Steve Bannon, the MAGA elder and former Trump adviser. “We’re in a war that’s been going on for six months, looks like it could go on for six years, and Rubio is in the witness protection program. The American people want to know exactly how we got into this mess and how we’re going to get out.”
Looming over all of this is the political equation of whether Rubio will run for president in 2028.
Donors widely favor him as Trump’s heir apparent, but he has repeatedly suggested Vance would be the best nominee and has deflected questions about his own future.

“Political speculation is a sport that people like to participate in and write stories about,” Rubio told my colleague Martin in an interview. “I’m not offended by it. I’m just not going to spend any more time talking about it.” — With Joshua Green

The Trump administration will allow the core members of an Iranian delegation to travel to the United Nations in New York for the General Assembly next week, the State Department said, even as the US and Iran remain at war in the Middle East.

Trump said “major progress” was being made to establish a new US Army base in Poland, even as the Pentagon plans to reduce American forces in Europe. The US already has about 10,000 troops stationed in Poland.

Maria Elvira Salazar, a Republican congresswoman representing Miami, told Trump in a 30-second ad that some of his immigration efforts have gone “too far” as she battles to retain her seat in a district heavily affected by the administration’s policies.

Cyber threats against nearly 20 commercial vessels are being tracked by US government agencies, according to US officials familiar with the matter. In late August, several ships were targeted in potential attacks, one US official said.
The State Department notified Congress that it plans to sell Saudi Arabia as many as 48 F-35 warplanes in a first-time sale that could be worth as much as $24.3 billion.
New residential construction in the US declined unexpectedly in August to one of the weakest paces since the coronavirus pandemic, reflecting a plunge in starts of multifamily projects.

A Washington federal judge ordered the Kennedy Center to provide more information about the recent closure of the decades-old performing arts venue and to notify court challengers about any future “demolition” or broader renovations of the building.

State leaders are cracking down on data center developers’ use of secrecy as a bargaining chip when bringing their projects to town by preventing them from entering into nondisclosure agreements with municipal officials.

The Senate’s version of the farm bill isn’t expected be put to a vote in the chamber before the elections and instead senators and House lawmakers will informally work out differences in conference, Senate Agriculture Committee Chairman John Boozman said yesterday.

Today on Bloomberg Television’s Balance of Power early edition at 1 p.m., hosts Joe Mathieu and Kailey Leinz interviewed Jessica Taylor, Senate and Governors Editor at the Cook Political Report, on key races.
On the program at 5 p.m., they talk with Senator Alan Armstrong, an Oklahoma Repubican, about US energy production and the soaring cost of diesel fuel.

On the Trumponomics podcast, host Stephanie Flanders is joined by Bloomberg Opinion columnist John Authers and Jamie Rush of Bloomberg Economics to discuss how demographics, rising government debt and the artificial intelligence investment boom are reshaping the price of money — and why 5% could prove to be a floor rather than a ceiling. items.title: Ukraine War Enters Its Fifth Winter
body: This is Bloomberg Opinion Today, a technological jolt of Bloomberg Opinion’s opinions. Sign up here.

It has been 1,666 days since Russian forces launched a full-scale invasion in Ukraine. A lot has changed in the world during that time, and yet the war seems stuck in a kind of limbo. Just read this description from the Editorial Board. It was published today, but could have been written last September, or two Septembers ago, or three:

To move the needle, those Western backers need to buck Putin’s expectations and ensure his efforts fail. On Thursday, EU Commission President Ursula von der Leyen announced a new disbursement of €3.3 billion ($3.8 billion) for missiles and drones. That’s welcome news, yet the editors say the US needs to supply its own Patriot interceptors, despite low inventories. “Even a modest US contribution would cast doubt on Russia’s plans for a winter air offensive,” they write.

Yet even that, Marc Champion says, might be wishful thinking. President Donald Trump spent the week blaming Ukraine for his own problems, namely $6-per-gallon diesel prices. He also revived a false claim about the Biden administration giving Ukraine $300 billion, demanding that Kyiv or Europe give him the money back — more than half of which the US never gave away in the first place.

“It’s important to recognize why the president has chosen this moment to cook up these false narratives,” Marc writes. “The short answer is, of course, the midterms. Trump’s war in Iran is unpopular at home and he’s looking for ways to distance himself from its ill effects.” We don’t need to wait for another 1,666 days to pass to know that’s not a winning strategy.
Phew!! Federal Reserve Chair Kevin Warsh does in fact know what a rate hike is.

On Wednesday, he presided over the first the first increase in the benchmark federal funds rate since 2023. Naturally, a lot of investors are already asking, “same time next month?” As Jonathan Levin writes, “rate hikes are generally a package deal,” unless your name is Alan Greenspan. Will Warsh follow in the Maestro’s footsteps and skip the next hike, as Greenspan did in 1997? Perhaps. There are plenty of similarities between this moment and that one: “Warsh finds himself adjusting to a potential technological jolt from artificial intelligence that could drive up productivity and growth, and change assumptions about how interest rates work,” Jonathan writes. “Greenspan was contending with the start of the internet revolution.”

Yet traders anticipate about three more increases by late 2027, so there’s really no telling what Warsh will do next. As John Authers says, the new Fed chair “framed the hike as part of a ‘discipline’ and ‘the removal of some accommodation’ — implying more to come.” Fascinating times for those fluent in Fedspeak:

What’s interesting about this new hike is that support for it was unanimous. Trump, talking to reporters, appeared to think that his chairman was held hostage by other central bankers: “You might as well vote with the board because it’s not going to matter. The board is very hostile, very political.” But most people didn’t see it that way. John says the unanimity was “widely interpreted as showing that Warsh was beginning to exert control.”
Bonus Wall Street Reading: What bond investors can learn from Tina Turner’s career. — Allison Schrager
On first glance, you might think the below chart illustrating the dominance of the superpeso is excellent news for Mexico. Who wouldn’t want to top the charts and lead the world?

Yet Juan Pablo Spinetto points to growing evidence that the superpeso is doing more harm than good to Mexico’s economy. “A Big Mac in Mexico already costs almost $6.50. So does a gallon of premium gasoline. The shiny new iPhone 18 Pro? That will set you back 29,999 pesos, or about $1,765 at 17 to the dollar, nearly 50% more than the US pre-tax list price. And I won’t get into what private-school tuition costs in Mexico City even before converting it into dollars,” he writes.

More broadly, inbound air travel and tourist spending is down. Remittances are losing value. And domestic goods appear to be losing ground to imports. “It’s time to stop pretending that a stronger FX is always good news, as Mexico’s leftist government has oddly done since the days of President Andrés Manuel López Obrador, who turned the macho peso into a leitmotif of economic soundness,” he writes.

What’s the remedy? It’s tough to say, but JP says a rushed FX intervention is not the answer: “Policymakers should weigh the risks carefully and deploy any creative solutions at a gradual pace that doesn’t threaten the country’s hard-won financial reputation.”

Here’s an idea for next year’s Iowa State Fair: A game called, “Is it cake or is it coal?” But here’s the catch: There’s no cake. It’s allllll coal. The Hawkeye State, which Mark Gongloff points out has long been a renewable-energy paragon, is consuming more and more of the black stuff in order to keep up with the AI boom. “Just that little bit of extra burning coal had an immediate impact on air quality, according to a report by the Iowa Environmental Council, a nonprofit watchdog group. Emissions of fine particles known as PM2.5 increased by more than 50% at each of the state’s two biggest electric utilities. These sink deep into the lungs, can enter the bloodstream and generally wreak havoc on human bodies.”

Do any Chelsea Football fans read this thing? If so, I’d love to hear what you think about the club’s new price tag, which was revealed after owner Clearlake Capital agreed to buy out the chairman and director. “Can the £5 billion figure be rationalized?” Chris Hughes asks. “Soccer club valuations, typically based on revenue multiples, were boosted by the World Cup, he notes, but Chris says Clearlake has a tough task ahead. “The strategy thus far has been to fill the squad with younger players who have more of their career ahead of them. With acquisition costs smoothed out over long contracts, there’s some financial logic to this approach. But results on the pitch have been mixed at best, even with the addition of genuine superstars such as Cole Palmer,” he writes.
The Kennedy Center ... demolition?
How India built (and broke) the options casino.

items.title: India Recruits Its Diaspora Into the Campaign for the Rupee
body: Prime Minister Narendra Modi had a message for hundreds of overseas Indians gathered at Paris’ Salle Pleyel concert hall in June: India was counting on its diaspora to send back dollars.

As the war in Iran raged, the world’s third-largest oil importer was staring at a surging energy bill. This raised concerns about India’s need for greenbacks to pay for imports and sent the rupee to a record low. “I would urge all of you to deepen your engagement with India,” Modi told the packed crowd at a community event in the French capital. “This will give new strength to India’s development journey, while also giving you an opportunity to serve the land of your ancestors.”

Back home, Indian authorities had already begun laying the groundwork to support the rupee, which had weakened to an exchange rate near 97 per dollar, from about 86 a year ago. Reserve Bank of India Governor Sanjay Malhotra and other senior officials at the central bank had been meeting with commercial financial institutions. One idea was to raise dollars through state banks, according to people familiar with the discussions who asked not to be named because the talks were private. That move was ruled out as bankers warned that borrowing when the rupee is weak could be seen as a sign of stress, spooking investors and ultimately making the borrowing more expensive.

And so policymakers turned to a familiar move: encouraging commercial banks to attract foreign-currency deposits from Indians living overseas. The RBI would cover banks’ cost of protecting against swings in the rupee, in effect allowing them to offer higher rates. A similar measure proved highly effective in 2013, when expectations of tighter US monetary policy triggered an exodus of foreign capital from emerging markets and sent the rupee plunging.

The response was emphatic again. The Foreign Currency Non-Resident (Bank) deposit plan, or FCNR (B), attracted $127 billion, a record for such Indian programs, allowing authorities to close the hedging-cost incentive a month before schedule. The success highlights how India’s 35 million-strong diaspora has grown into an economic powerhouse and a key financial backstop.
The RBI didn’t respond to a request for comment.

The diaspora has transformed over the past three decades. Once dominated by blue-collar workers mainly in the Persian Gulf, it’s now thick with well-heeled professionals from the likes of Alphabet Inc.’s Sundar Pichai and International Business Machines Corp.’s Arvind Krishna as well as doctors and bankers.

Beyond bank deposits, remittances to India — typically cash sent home by workers to family — were more than $150 billion in 2025, according to World Bank data. That’s more than twice the amount sent to Mexico, the world’s second-largest recipient. Remittances do more than bolster India’s supply of foreign currency. They support household consumption, savings, education and health care, providing a steady source of income even during economic shocks.

Read more: Immigration Crackdowns Put an $800 Billion Lifeline at RiskAbu Dhabi-based engineer Avijit Chatterjee is one of the overseas savers drawn to the FCNR (B) program. He put in $40,000 in June. Chatterjee, 46, says his foreign-currency deposits now total $100,000, driven purely by the prospect of higher returns as he builds a nest egg for retirement in India. When the RBI was offering its incentives, commercial banks offered rates as high as 7.75% for depositors willing to tie up their money for a few years. “I need dollars without any exchange-rate risk, also to help sustain my son’s education abroad,” Chatterjee says over a Zoom call.

Piyush Jhunjhunwala, the 44-year-old founder of Stockify Fintech in Dubai, says patriotism played a part in his decision to put $1 million in an FCNR (B) plan, with the help of leverage from also borrowing dollars at a lower rate than the deposit pays. Such leverage can squeeze returns if short-term borrowing costs move the wrong way, but it can also amplify gains as the deposit pays more than the loan. “When I heard of the FCNR scheme, it was exciting because this is like a once-in-a-decade kind of an opportunity,” says Jhunjhunwala, who’s lived in Dubai for two decades. “This is our opportunity to give back and help our homeland.”

As the diaspora has grown wealthier, Indian banks, asset managers and property developers are competing for its accumulated savings in Dubai and Singapore, as well as Europe. They’re also tapping investment funds by using international financial hubs, such as India’s Gujarat International Finance Tec-City, or GIFT City. The special economic zone has its own regulatory and tax framework to attract global capital.

In July, bankers at HSBC Holdings Plc held roadshows for high- and ultrahigh-net-worth Indians in Hong Kong, Manila, Singapore and the Middle East, in an effort to attract deposits, according to a person familiar with the events who was not authorized to speak to the news media. Dozens of prospective clients attended one gathering in Manila, another person said. They asked bankers about using leverage, its risks and how their dollars would be deployed. HSBC did not respond to a Bloomberg email seeking comment.At Singapore-based investment firm Lighthouse Canton, nonresident Indians, or NRIs, now account for about half of its $7 billion global assets, from a minuscule amount about eight years ago, says Shilpi Chowdhary, the firm’s group chief executive officer. They’re increasingly dipping their toes into equities, startups and venture capital funds, moving beyond long-popular property investments. “India will always be a preferred choice because we understand India,” Chowdhary says. “It’s a known devil.”
In 2024, Indian regulators relaxed restrictions on NRIs investing in foreign funds set up in GIFT City. Since then, diaspora investments there have topped $7 billion.

There are also signs that diaspora wealth could provide a particularly durable source of capital. Zerodha, one of India’s largest stockbrokers, says its more than 50,000 NRI clients tend to invest more and hold for longer than domestic counterparts. Earlier this year their accounts were worth almost 10 times as much on average as those of resident investors.

Property remains a major draw. Inflows into India’s property market reached a record of more than $14 billion in 2025, according to CBRE Research, with foreign investors — including high-net-worth individuals and NRIs — making up about a quarter of the total. At DLF Ltd., India’s largest real estate developer, NRIs accounted for 27% of sales in the year through March 2025, up from 23% a year earlier.

The Indian rupee climbed the week the fundraising came to an end, but the flood of money from the diaspora wasn’t enough to trigger a strong rally. That’s partly due to India’s waning appeal among foreign investors: The country replaced Indonesia as Asia’s least-preferred stock market in an August survey of fund managers by Bank of America Corp.

Many experts argue that India should put greater emphasis on attracting more long-term and less expensive sources of dollars, especially foreign direct investments — that is, active ownership stakes in businesses. Unlike bank deposits, dollars from FDI don’t have to be paid back. India attracted almost $100 billion of gross foreign direct investment in the year ended March 2026, according to official figures.

That’s less than the $150 billion-plus in remittances in 2025, which help too. Former RBI Governor Duvvuri Subbarao referred to remittances as “good money” given they have grown from a modest source of foreign exchange into an important buffer for India’s external finances. “We need to make it easier for the diaspora to send money here,” Subbarao says, suggesting easing the tax burden and lowering transaction costs among potential measures. “It makes sense to bank on the diaspora.”

Devesh Kapur, a professor of South Asian studies at Johns Hopkins University’s School of Advanced International Studies, refers to the diaspora as “insurance.” But he says direct investment would make it even more powerful. He draws parallels with Chinese living outside the mainland, which historically sent less money home through remittances. Instead, entrepreneurs in Hong Kong, Taiwan and elsewhere in East Asia helped finance factories in the mainland, Kapur says, bringing manufacturing expertise, supply chains and international networks that led to China’s emergence as an export powerhouse.
“One of the biggest weaknesses of India’s link with its diaspora and the diaspora’s links with India is the extreme reluctance to invest in FDI as opposed to safe, easy returns,” Kapur says.

There are also questions about whether the diaspora can be a reliable backstop indefinitely. A global immigration crackdown is slowing the flow of Indians overseas. Second- and third-generation Indians may have weaker ties to their ancestral homeland and weigh investment opportunities elsewhere, fund managers warn.

The challenge for India will be to maintain their ties. “Provided we can tap them and ensure that they maintain an emotional connect with India,” Subbarao says, “that will be good for India.” —With Advait Palepu

items.title: Crypto Finds an Innovative Way Around the Will of Congress
body: Scott Patterson writes about how the digital-asset sector appears to be coming out a winner even after US legislation they championed was rejected by lawmakers.

On Tuesday, the crypto industry watched its hopes for sweeping market-structure legislation disappear on the Senate floor. The Clarity Act fell well short of the 60 votes needed to advance, putting on ice a bill its supporters hoped would usher in a golden age of blockchains and tokenization.

But there was an obvious Plan B: the regulators. Within minutes, crypto supporters were calling on the Securities and Exchange Commission and the Commodity Futures Trading Commission to pick up where Congress had left off. “@SECPaulSAtkins and @ChairmanSelig, you’re up!” White House crypto adviser Patrick Witt wrote in a post on X.

Crypto industry leaders echoed the call. “I do have faith that the SEC and CFTC will drive on with rules for the road,” Mike Novogratz, CEO of crypto giant Galaxy Digital, wrote in separate post on the industry’s favorite social-media platform.

By Thursday morning, that Plan B was already taking shape. The SEC unveiled its long-waited innovation exemption, which gives the industry the greenlight to start issuing digital versions of stocks. The exemption, in the works for more than a year, is poised to ignite a scramble among crypto firms racing to tokenize US stocks, with different models competing for market share. Some firms, such as Securitize Corp., are working directly with public companies to bring tokenized shares to US crypto markets. Securitize’s own shares jumped the most on record. Others will provide third-party tokens that don’t involve close cooperation with issuers.

Critics of the program blasted it as a dangerous experiment on a market that functions efficiently. The exemption for tokenized stocks “will exacerbate market fragmentation and worsen price discovery,” said Amanda Fischer, policy director for Better Markets.

Most crypto market participants celebrated the move as a hopeful sign that the regulators are taking up the baton after Congress fumbled it. The show of confidence by an industry that just saw its landmark legislation blow up on the Senate floor is to be expected — what else can it do?

The CFTC is also plunging ahead with its pro-crypto agenda. On Thursday, it moved to expand crypto and prediction market trading via online platforms. The agency’s guidance provides exemptions for software providers from registration requirements.

In August, CFTC Chairman Mike Selig told Bloomberg Television that the crypto industry would get market structure rules even if Congress failed to pass the Clarity Act. “It’s really important that we have market structure,” Selig said then ahead of the agency’s inaugural Innovation Advisory Committee meeting. “We can do that through rules, we can do that through laws.”

The fly in the ointment, as most know very well, is that federal-agency regulations are a lot less sticky than legislation approved by Congress. The next administration, if Democrat, could claw back rules it sees as too generous to the industry or too dangerous to investors and the broader economy.

It won’t be as simple as the stroke of a pen. Businesses that take off over the next few years under the new regulatory regime will certainly defend themselves in the halls of the agencies and in court if necessary. Regulators taking actions that can significantly impact those businesses will need to justify their actions with well thought out economic analysis.

Still, there’s little question that an innovation exemption and other rules the regulators pass in the next two years will widely be seen as weak tea compared with the 600-plus pages of rules laid out in the Clarity Act.
Strategy Inc.’s flagship preferred security is a whisker away from its original offering price after a bruising selloff, helped by one committed buyer: the company itself.

Circle Internet Group Inc. CEO Jeremy Allaire says he still believes the Clarity Act could become law even though it failed to pass the US Senate. The bill would mainly let the Commodity Futures Trading Commission regulate the digital assets industry. He speaks on “Bloomberg Open Interest.”

items.title: Korea's Lee Vows Not to Get Drawn Into Iran War as Support Sinks
body: South Korean President Lee Jae Myung will seek to reverse hemorrhaging public support and get his policy agenda back on track at a high-stakes Friday press briefing, even as a barrage of criticism from Donald Trump narrows his room to maneuver.

Lee has seen his approval ratings plunge in the past two months, hitting a record low of 38% last week. That comes as the Trump administration slams Seoul over its purported unwillingness to help reopen the Strait of Hormuz and slow movement on its $350 billion US trade deal.

At home, many South Koreans have soured on Lee over the economy. Even as the global AI build-out reaps record profits for chip giants SK Hynix Inc. and Samsung Electronics Co., voters are seeing little impact on their lives, with surveys highlighting growing discontent on issues such as Seoul’s high property prices.

If Lee can’t turnaround his ratings and retain support from his base, he risks being relegated to “early lame-duck status,” said Jeong Han-wool, director of the Korean People Research Institute. In this situation, even if his party’s control of parliament means he can enact some policies, he’d face “criticism whatever he does.”

To stop the bleeding, Lee ordered a sweeping reshuffle of his cabinet weeks ago, changing out his finance, defense and justice ministers among others, with his top policy advisor Kim Yong-beom stepping down, writing that it was time for the government to refocus not only on “the percentage of growth but also about how many lives have been transformed by that growth.”

But that reset and shift in messaging have failed to boost Lee’s approval ratings. When the president speaks to the media Friday, he will “clearly lay out and explain his position and direction on major issues,” Lee’s office said.
Read more: Korea’s Gender Minister Nominee Pulls Out in Fresh Blow to Lee

Lee has also been struggling to balance Seoul’s all-important relationship with security ally Washington, which stations around 28,500 soldiers in the South in part to help protect it from the nuclear-armed North. Trump canceled long-planned joint military drills with Seoul, citing his friendship with Kim Jong Un and Seoul’s purported refusal to help with Iran.

Washington has also been complaining about what it sees as lack of follow-through on Seoul’s investment commitments. While the two countries are nearing an announcement on the first project, South Korea recently asked for more time to fine-tune the deal.

In a bid to smooth ties, Lee’s administration has said it is exploring options to help support the effort to reopen the Strait of Hormuz — through which, before hostilities broke out in February, South Korea used to receive more than 70% of its oil needs. The president faces strong domestic opposition to sending troops to help secure the strategic waterway under US pressure.
Read more:  Korea’s Lee Faces Pushback as Trump Ups Pressure Over Hormuz

“Any mission would require Seoul to balance the US demands with the risk of Iranian retaliation, military readiness on the Korean Peninsula, and domestic political opposition,” Bloomberg Economics’ Hyosung Kwon and Adam Farrar said in a note. “Trump’s transactional approach to alliances means friction in one area is almost certain to bleed into other issues.”

items.title: FCC Approves Foreign Funding for Paramount-Warner Bros. Deal
body: The Federal Communications Commission approved Paramount Skydance Corp.’s request to allow foreign financing in excess of 25% in its proposed acquisition of Warner Bros. Discovery Inc., saying that doing so would “serve the public interest.”

Paramount told the regulator that the foreign investment will help it improve its broadcast stations’ news gathering both nationally and locally. It said the international ownership will “not result in a transfer of control of Paramount” and that the “Ellison family will retain a majority of the voting interests and control.”

Paramount Chief Executive Officer David Ellison has secured sign-off on the deal from top antitrust officials, although it is now tied up in lawsuits led by state attorneys general and the Writers Guild trade union. Ellison is the son of Oracle Corp. co-founder Larry Ellison, who will help fund the proposed acquisition. The elder Ellison is a big supporter of President Donald Trump.

FCC Chairman Brendan Carr, whose agency reviewed the deal because it involves the ownership of broadcast TV stations, previously said he was waiting for clearance from a joint federal committee called “Team Telecom,” which includes the Departments of Justice, Defense and Homeland Security. In a statement, a Paramount spokesperson said Team Telecom had also approved the financing on Thursday.

The parent of CBS and other media businesses has proposed buying Warner Bros., which owns the CNN news channel among other assets, for $110 billion, including debt. The transaction includes $24 billion in equity from three Middle East sovereign wealth funds.

According to the FCC filing, 49.5% of Paramount’s Class B shares will be controlled by foreign owners. The Ellison family and RedBird Capital Partners will collectively hold the largest equity stake in the combined company and 100% of the voting shares, “with no other equity participant having any governance rights,” the Paramount spokesperson said.

Anna Gomez, the lone Democrat among the FCC commissioners, said in a social media post that the regulator “just let some of the most repressive governments in the world indirectly control nearly all of a combined Paramount-Warner Bros.”
Gomez said she had sought to bring the decision up to a full commission vote. The ruling instead came from the FCC’s Media Bureau.
“An investment this large in one of America’s biggest media companies doesn’t just buy equity, it secures influence over what gets said and made,” she said.

items.title: Ahead of Midterms, The Battle For America's Working Class
body: Never miss an episode. Follow The Big Take daily podcast today.

The “working class” in America used to conjure a vivid image: factory workers, blue-collar jobs and a political coalition born out of the Industrial Revolution. But as Republicans and Democrats try to court voters ahead of midterms, a question keeps coming up: What is the working class today?

On today’s Big Take podcast, host Sarah Holder talks to Bloomberg Opinion columnist Allison Schrager, labor activist Bertha “Mama Cookie” Bradley and Distinguished Professor of Law Joan C. Williams about the moving target of defining and catering policy to working Americans.

items.title: Suspended Glencore Exec Told Radiant 'Say Nothing on Email'
body: A senior Glencore Plc executive last year urged counterparts at Radiant World not to communicate by email, according to WhatsApp messages from the company’s head of iron ore seen by Bloomberg News.

“Say nothing on email,” Peter Hill wrote in one WhatsApp message in early April 2025. In other messages dating from 2023 to 2025 he highlighted Glencore’s role as an important backer of the Radiant World group of companies, and suggested that he was the ultimate decision maker for various aspects of Radiant World’s trading.

The messages raise questions about the depth of Glencore’s involvement with the Radiant World network of companies. Glencore was a key backer of Radiant World, Bloomberg has previously reported, but the relationship has ended in acrimony in recent weeks with Glencore publicly accusing the Radiant World group of fraud while Radiant World has filed a $2 billion lawsuit against Glencore.
Hill was suspended from his duties pending the outcome of a review into Glencore’s dealings with Radiant World, Bloomberg reported on Thursday.
Read: Glencore Suspends Executive Who Led Radiant World Business

Screenshots of some of the messages were shown to Bloomberg News; in other cases, their contents were relayed by people familiar with them, who asked not to be identified due to the sensitivity of the matter. Bloomberg News was not shown the full context of the conversations in which the messages were sent.

A spokesperson for Glencore declined to comment on the messages. Hill didn’t respond to calls or messages and the Glencore spokesperson said he declined to comment. A spokesperson for Radiant World didn’t respond to a request for comment.

The relationship between Glencore and Radiant World has come into focus after Radiant World, Sapphire Minmetals and several related companies filed the lawsuit against Glencore in Singapore this week. Glencore has said that the “claims are meritless and we will contest them vigorously” and that Radiant World is suing it “for telling the truth about their fraud.”

Radiant World has been accused of fraud in court documents by at least two of its lenders after Bloomberg reported concerns that it had been providing falsified documents to banks to raise money. Glencore, long its key backer, has cut ties and taken a $480 million provision on its outstanding exposure to the group, which includes Sapphire Minmetals, a closely connected but legally separate trading company. Radiant World has denied wrongdoing.
Read: How Radiant World’s ‘Prince’ Has Banks Chasing Fake Invoices
Some of the WhatsApp messages from Hill were sent from his personal mobile phone, while others were sent from his Glencore phone, according to the people familiar with the matter.

In one series of messages in December 2023, Hill appeared to be discussing a forthcoming conversation with Societe Generale SA about its lending to Sapphire Minmetals. (Company filings show that Societe Generale lent money to Sapphire to finance prepayments to Glencore for iron ore supplies, in deals that were guaranteed by Glencore itself.)
“Soc gen asking to speak to me about sapphire prepayment,” Hill wrote. “What argument did you use for them,” he said.

In another message, in May 2023, he implied that there had been certain issues with the way that Glencore and Radiant World had conducted their relationship in the past. “i don’t for a second doubt your integrity but there’s a big challenge and we just need to work on it together and sometimes that requires some hard chats and some adjustments to how things have been done,” he wrote.

In other messages, Hill suggested that Radiant World could only do certain trades with his authorization. The Radiant World companies had been hit by a spike in iron ore prices in 2021 when they built up a debt of approximately $1.1 billion to Glencore, according to the Singapore lawsuit.
“you need to hear and listen to what i’m saying - if I say stop, i need you to stop, if i say jump i need you to jump,” Hill wrote in a message in September 2023.

Later, in October 2025, Hill offered a window into the pressure he was facing internally within Glencore. In a message on Oct. 20, 2025, a few days after Bloomberg published a profile of Radiant World and for the first time reported historic allegations of fraud against it, he wrote that Chief Executive Officer Gary Nagle and Glencore’s board had “just ripped me a new asshole.”

In recent years, Hill’s star had appeared to be rising in Glencore. He was approached by Vitol Group in 2024 but decided to stay at Glencore, Bloomberg has reported. In August 2025, he was promoted from head of iron ore to run the trading of all steelmaking commodities, including coking coal, where Glencore had just become one of the leading players thanks to its acquisition of Teck Resources Ltd.’s coal business.

In one of the messages before the breakdown of the relationship, he offered hope for a rosier future. “$350m to go mate.. then we in golden territory,” he wrote in February 2023. “Maybe we go buy a mine together!”

Hill’s role as head of steelmaking commodities made him the Glencore executive with direct responsibility for the Radiant World relationship. Still, he is not the only person in Glencore who was involved in the relationship.

Jyothish George ran Glencore’s iron ore unit from 2014 to 2021 and is now head of trading for all metals and bulk commodities. And Radiant World’s lawyers, in a letter to Glencore last month, named five other Glencore employees as having been involved in the relationship, while the Radiant World lawsuit also claims that Glencore’s top management, including CEO Nagle, Chief Financial Officer Steve Kalmin and former CEO Ivan Glasenberg, were aware of and approved Glencore’s continued exposure. Glencore hasn’t yet directly addressed those claims in its response to the Radiant World case.

items.title: Braskem Creditors Shun Debt Plan, Push Owners to Inject Cash
body: Leia em português

Braskem SA’s bondholders are balking at a restructuring proposal presented by the petrochemical giant, increasing pressure on Petrobras to commit fresh capital into the business, according to people familiar with the matter.

Tensions in talks to rework a $11 billion debt pile escalated after Braskem controllers Petrobras and IG4 Capital Group softened the language around a capital injection, the people said, asking not to be named discussing non-public information.

Under Braskem’s latest proposal, presented in late August, creditors would provide about $2 billion of new money, according to some of the people. Roughly $1.25 billion would be used to repurchase existing debt at as much as 50% of face value, while the remaining $750 million would go toward working capital, they said.

The terms mark a departure from initial discussions, which did not contemplate a debt haircut. Creditors are also demanding shareholders make an enforceable commitment, with some making it clear there is no deal without a capital injection, the people added.

Petroleo Brasileiro SA, as Petrobras is formally known, has become increasingly involved in the negotiations — and while it wants to avoid having Braskem file for bankruptcy, it has so far been unwilling to provide the type of enforceable capital commitment sought by creditors, the people said.

The two sides remain so far apart that some creditors consider not submitting a counter proposal at all, some of the people said. The gap between the sides remains wide enough that the possibility of a bankruptcy filing — a so-called judicial reorganization — has returned prominently to the discussions, they added.
Braskem and IG4 declined declined to comment. Petrobras didn’t immediately reply to a request for comment.
Read more: Braskem’s $11 Billion Debt Rework Puts Spotlight on Petrobras
Valor Econômico newspaper had initially reported on Wednesday that Braskem had presented a proposal for its creditors, without further details.

Braskem, the largest petrochemicals producer in Latin America, has seen years of turbulence, with cash dwindling after an environmental disaster at one of its salt mines and a long stretch of depressed prices in the petrochemicals sector. Several failed attempts by troubled conglomerate Novonor SA to sell its controlling stake further added to the woes.

The petrochemicals producer had filed for an emergency protection from creditors in June, buying time for it to get enough creditors to agree to the out-of-court rework. Then in August it became the latest Brazilian company to be forced to restructure its debts after falling behind on its obligations. About $7 billion of the amount covered in the rework is owed to bondholders, people familiar said at the time.

The initial plan presented by Braskem included fresh equity after a so-called “Relief Period,” during which it would seek to turn around its operations and address its capital and liquidity needs, documents show. That could happen through a public offering of nonvoting shares, some of the people said at the time.
Now, some creditors do not see a follow-on offering as enough, the people said.
Read more: Braskem Reaches Deal on $11 Billion Out-of-Court Debt Rework

The parties have until Oct. 9 to agree on a term sheet — a particularly significant deadline because it falls in the middle of Brazil’s election period and could determine whether negotiations continue or the company moves closer to a bankruptcy process, a delicate matter with state-owned Petrobras as a shareholder. The company has until late November to come up with a final plan with support of more than half of its creditors and avert a bankruptcy filing.
Yields on Braskem’s dollar notes due in 2030 have surged to about 26%, levels typically associated with distressed debt.

items.title: Private Credit Funds Exposed to Bathla Face Platform Scrutiny
body: Investment portals in Australia are removing or closely monitoring access to private credit funds that own stakes in collapsed Sydney property developer Bathla Group, amid heightened regulatory scrutiny on unlisted markets.

Customers on Macquarie Group Ltd.’s wealth management platform can no longer invest new money in two Bathla-exposed private credit funds after the funds gated redemptions and stopped taking new applications. Elsewhere, the CVS Lane First Mortgage Fund and the CVS Lane Property Finance Fund, which both have some exposure to Bathla, are closed to new members even as they remain on Netwealth Group Ltd.’s platform for existing customers.

Wealth portals offer individual investors a broad investment menu via a financial adviser and are a fast-growing segment of Australia’s booming A$4.8 trillion ($3.4 trillion) pension industry. The securities regulator’s focus on private credit funds has been in the spotlight after the insolvency last month of Bathla, owing private lenders more than A$3 billion.

“New work has been flowing in around people wanting to get advice around what to do,” said Alex Jamieson, who manages around A$450 million for clients across Australia at Jamieson Private Wealth. “It’s probably the start of a growing concern rather than the finishing point.”

Platform providers have faced heightened regulatory scrutiny in the wake of two high-profile fund collapses in recent years, the Shield Master Fund and First Guardian, where thousands of investors lost money. Fast-growing platforms are drawing flows from some large pension funds as older members seek financial advice and look for personalized investment options, a Conexus Financial report this year showed.

The Macquarie Wrap system removed the Bass Property Credit Fund and the Centuria Bass Credit Fund from its offering to investors after both funds gated redemptions and stopped taking new investor applications last month.

Spokespeople for Macquarie and Netwealth declined to comment. Centuria Bass has temporarily paused redemptions and applications to both funds, a spokesperson for Centuria Bass said. When applications and redemptions restart, Centuria Bass will work with the relevant platform to restore availability of the funds, they said.
Not all platforms are taking immediate action, though they are watching the situation.
For AMP Ltd., where a small Bathla exposure across its North platform is limited to two funds, investors are free to buy and sell as they please.

AMP said direct Bathla exposure across its North platform is limited to the Trilogy Monthly Income Trust, which has a less than 3% exposure to Bathla, and the La Trobe Australian Credit Fund, which has less than 0.05% exposure.
“AMP’s investment governance bodies continue to monitor developments and assess any implications for investors,” an AMP spokesperson said.

Trilogy has said no single loan in its portfolio respresents more than 5% of funds under management and redemption procedures remain unchanged for the monthly income trust. A representative for La Trobe didn’t reply to requests for comment.
Listen and follow The Bloomberg Australia Podcast on Apple, Spotify, YouTube or wherever you get your podcasts.

“Both funds are on the platform” at Netwealth, said a CVS Lane spokesperson, who declined to comment on how much money was invested in the options. The trustee has temporarily suspended applications and redemptions for both funds and this will be reviewed at the end of October, they said.
Another platform provider, HUB24, didn’t respond to requests for information about the investment options offered on its platform with exposure to Bathla.

The financial regulator has been increasing its supervision of the private credit industry by requesting more detailed data from funds. In June, the Australian Securities and Investments Commission said the private credit sector is “on notice” and surveillance across wholesale and retail funds was “well progressed and multiple enforcement investigations are underway.”

ASIC has also warned platform trustees must do due diligence before offering members options via investment menus or approving options for use by advisers. In a review expected to be published by the end of the year, ASIC is also looking at the ways private credit funds are distributed to retail investors.

items.title: Australian Airlines Back Plan to Shut Sydney Tower Overnight
body: Australia’s major airlines backed a proposal to close Sydney Airport’s control tower overnight to free up air traffic controllers, the latest step to address a persistent labor shortage that’s disrupting flights and raising safety concerns.

“It sounds like an opportunity we should absolutely explore,” said Stephen Beckett, chief executive officer of Airlines for Australia & New Zealand, the group that represents Qantas Airways Ltd., its low-cost carrier Jetstar, and Virgin Australia Holdings Ltd. “There seems to be some merit to this proposal,” he said in an interview.

At least six safety incidents, close calls and mistakes on the tarmac at Sydney since late July have put a spotlight on the lack of controllers and the impact on air travel. Qantas CEO Vanessa Hudson last month called for the issue to be fixed after 60,000 passengers were affected by flight delays in July alone. The proposal to close the tower was raised at the meeting of a taskforce specially formed last month to address the disruption in Sydney.

Sydney Airport’s existing 11pm-6am curfew means commercial air traffic would be largely unaffected by any tower closures. But a plan to have no operational tower at Australia’s biggest aviation hub, even temporarily, reflects the urgency of the labor shortfall. Flights exempt from the curfew, such as those dealing with emergencies or carrying medical patients, would have to fend for themselves when landing or taking off.
Read More: Two More Close Calls at Sydney Airport Add to Safety Concerns

Airservices Australia manages the country’s airspace and employs air traffic controllers at airports. Beckett said the roster of controllers at Sydney has been too fragile for too long. “That’s had a significant impact on passengers,” he said.

The unexpected absence of just one controller at the airport on Sept. 11 was enough to cause significant flight delays the same morning. Closing the tower at night would free up two controllers who could, in theory, be deployed during the day.

In an email, Australia’s Civil Aviation Safety Authority said, “Airservices Australia is exploring an option to temporarily vary the operating hours of Sydney Air Traffic Control Tower services overnight.” But CASA said it hasn’t received an application seeking approval for such a proposal.

Airservices Australia is “considering all options to ensure the efficient use of our qualified workforce,” it said in an email. “Any changes to air traffic services at Sydney Airport would be subject to “thorough safety assessment processes,” including approval by the regulator.

items.title: Argentine Economy Posts First Quarterly Contraction Since 2024
body: Lea en español
Argentina’s economy contracted in the second quarter for the first time in two years, marking a setback for President Javier Milei’s administration.

Gross domestic product fell 0.6% in the April-June period from the previous three months, better than the -0.9% median estimate of analysts surveyed by Bloomberg. On an annual basis, the economy expanded 2%, according to government figures published Thursday.
Exports were the only category that drove growth in the quarter along with a pullback in imports. Government expenditure, consumer spending and capital formation all declined on a quarterly basis.
The unemployment rate ticked up during the same period to 7.9%. Joblessness ranks as Argentines’ top economic concern, according to an August poll by AtlasIntel.

Sluggish growth has become collateral for some of Milei’s policies to tame inflation and eliminate chronic deficits. The libertarian leader has kept a tight grip on the peso, letting it appreciate when adjusted for inflation, while opening up the historically protectionist economy to more global trade.

A stronger exchange rate and more global competition has hit manufacturing, retail and construction industries — the top three by employment — hard, resulting in job losses. The more competitive sectors driving Argentina’s growth — energy, mining and agriculture — are breaking export records, but employ far fewer workers.

On Tuesday, the government cut its 2026 GDP forecast to 3% growth from 5% previously, according to its annual budget proposal sent to Congress. Economists aren’t as optimistic: annual growth is projected to finish the year at 2.1%, down from a forecast of 3.5% last December, according to the central bank’s monthly surveys.

So far in the third quarter, the growth outlook hasn’t improved. Construction and manufacturing sectors both declined sharply in July, while tax collection in August was flat when adjusted for inflation, a discouraging signal for a turnaround.

items.title: Palantir CEO Says AI Firms Responsible for Their Own Actions
body: Palantir Technologies Inc. Chief Executive Officer Alex Karp said developers of artificial-intelligence systems need to be held liable for their own work as opposed to depending on government regulation.

“The first line of defense is you’re liable for your own actions,” Karp said in a CNBC interview when asked about the growing concerns that AI threatens humanity, prompting calls by Anthropic PBC CEO Dario Amodei and others for an industrywide slowdown in AI development. “The first step is to say, okay you’ve disclosed this, what are you doing about it?”

Amodei has proposed that independent, third-party evaluators be embedded within the operations of AI firms to ensure that they’re adhering to safety guidelines and guardrails. Karp described such regulation as complicated. “You need people who understand them,” he said. “Another problem we have is seemingly everyone who understands this is on some payroll. So it’s like, ‘Who are you going to trust?’”

Nvidia Corp. CEO Jensen Huang similarly said earlier this week that AI companies are responsible for ensuring they’re releasing products that are safe. Huang’s advice to AI firms: If the “product’s not going to be safe, take a pause and make sure you get it right.”

items.title: US Says Iranian Officials May Travel to New York for UN Meetings
body: The Trump administration will allow the core members of an Iranian delegation to travel to the United Nations in New York for the General Assembly next week, the State Department said, even as the US and Iran remain at war in the Middle East.

The officials from Tehran will be permitted to enter the US for the annual high-level week consistent with host country obligations, a State Department spokesman said in an emailed statement on Thursday.

The delegation will face travel restrictions within the US and won’t be permitted to buy luxury and other goods, in accordance with US policy, the spokesman said, adding that the delegation is smaller than last year.
The US and Iran remain in a standoff over a war that began with an American and Israeli attack on Tehran on Feb. 28 that killed Supreme Leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei.
Many of the top Iranian officials who weren’t killed in the initial weeks of the war have been hit with sanctions that would normally prevent them and their family members from traveling to the US.

On Wednesday, the State Department separately announced that the US was denying visas for top Palestinian Authority officials to attend the UN meetings, saying they have failed to comply with previous pledges under peace deals with Israel.
Read more: Iran, US Brace for Long War With Neither Side Ceding Ground

items.title: McDonald's Value Menu to Get Revamp as US Growth Slows
body: McDonald’s Corp. is switching up its value playbook following its slowest US growth in more than a year.

The company will work with franchisees in the coming weeks on a “longer-term” approach that appeals to value-conscious diners, according to a message to operators seen by Bloomberg News. In the meantime, McDonald’s is “building a near-term bridge plan” of temporary items and digital offers focused on what’s currently selling well. On its app, you can get a $2 breakfast sandwich or free fries with a $1 minimum purchase.

The move is accompanied by changes in the company’s training and support to franchisees. It’s the first sign of a shift under the company’s new US head, Skye Anderson, and comes ahead of its investor day next week. While McDonald’s has mostly outperformed fast-food competitors in recent years, it’s looking to avoid a prolonged slump in the US — especially as Burger King’s growth accelerates.

McDonald’s didn’t respond to a request for comment. The shares rose nearly 1% in New York trading on Thursday, touching a session high. The stock has declined 19% year to date through Wednesday’s close, adding pressure on management.
Sales at established McDonald’s US restaurants grew 0.8% last quarter — the weakest result since the start of 2025. Last month, Anderson was named to bring “focus and urgency” to the business.

McDonald’s got a boost in 2024 from its $5 meal deals as the burger chain looked to counter perceptions that its food had gotten too expensive. The latest memo shows the company is looking to sharpen its strategy on affordability.

“Compelling value remains critical to bringing customers through our doors and strengthening the baseline of our business,” the company said in the message, which was signed by leaders from corporate as well as from a franchisee group that’s involved in developing the plans.

Earlier this year, McDonald’s expanded its value offerings, introducing a lineup of at least 10 items under $3. But many franchisees, who have latitude to set their own prices, didn’t adhere to recommendations from third-party advisers, which hurt results, Chief Executive Officer Chris Kempczinski said on the company’s earnings call on Aug. 4. McDonald’s also pulled back on app-only offers and ended a buy one, get one for $1 promotion.

McDonald’s has already announced a multiyear plan to become a go-to dining destination that expands its appeal beyond those looking for a fast, cheap meal. This includes higher-quality food, such as hand-breaded chicken, and changes to the restaurants designed to make them feel more open. The Chicago-based company is also looking to offer friendlier service, and it wants all customers to be greeted when they enter its locations.

As part off those efforts, McDonald’s is pausing spot restaurant visits through March 31 for some franchisees in favor of targeted training aimed at improving diners’ experience, according to the memo. Staff will participate in sessions on hospitality and ensuring menu items are always prepared right.

“There’s more work to do in these areas,” McDonald’s said in the message. “A customer’s last visit is often what determines whether they will return, which is why every interaction should reflect the best of McDonald’s.”

The Big Mac seller is facing fierce competition from Burger King, which last quarter grew at a faster pace thanks to a revamp of its signature Whopper and ongoing restaurant remodels. That chain, which is owned by Restaurant Brands International Inc., has also appointed a manager in charge of addressing any issues diners have during their visits.

McDonald’s US sales declined in July and August, according to debit- and credit-card data tracked by Bloomberg Second Measure. The upcoming investor day, scheduled for Sept. 23, “could prove a crucial clearing event” for management to prove that it has a credible plan, Jefferies analyst Andy Barish said in a recent investor note.
“For the stock to rebound, management will have to convince investors the recent same-store sales slowdown is fixable (soon),” Barish wrote.
