items.title: Japan Raises the Bar on Residency. Cue the Outrage
body: From the US green card to the UK’s “indefinite leave to remain,” permanent residency in a country that’s not your own can be a prickly issue. Japan is now getting choosier about who gets to stay for good.

Under Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi, the country has tightened various rules around immigration, including higher renewal fees for visas and stricter enforcement of overstayers. The latest proposal is to raise the bar on permanent residency, adding requirements for minimum salary and Japanese language ability.

Critics, and some residents, are up in arms at the suggested changes. The Asahi daily deemed them “a revision that will doom the dreams and enthusiasm of foreigners.” Some liken the moves to anti-immigration crackdowns taken by the Trump administration and other right-wing governments. “Japan should not shut the door on permanent residents,” said the Mainichi.

But the changes are boringly conventional by the standards of peers. They draw a clearer line between permission to come to Japan for work and the right to remain permanently, part of a long-delayed overhaul that, by shoring up a patchwork of outdated rules, explicitly acknowledges Japan’s substantial future need for foreign labor.

The proposals are still subject to change before introduction next year, but envisage taking into account language proficiency, requiring a household income above the national average, and examining applicants’ ability to remain solvent after retirement. These are not unreasonable.

Japan was long an outlier in requiring neither language ability nor an explicit minimum salary, instead largely gatekeeping PR behind the number of years spent in the country — seemingly assuming that only the very dedicated would stay so long anyway.

Indeed until quite recently, it made remarkably little distinction between a Goldman Sachs banker and an English teacher when it came to awarding permanent residency. Assuming candidates had put in the years and met vague guidelines on good behavior, the country didn’t really seem to care. The total number of foreigners was so low for so long, it wasn’t that important anyway.

This began to change in 2017, when a fast-track PR system for “highly skilled professionals” was added by then-Prime Minister Shinzo Abe, who promised access to permanent residency that would be among the fastest in the world. By further separating permission to work from an entitlement to remain permanently, the latest changes merely advance this policy.

Any time there is a change to Japan’s immigration system, there are predictable complaints that foreign workers will look elsewhere. As far back as two decades ago, supposedly draconian fingerprinting at the border was set to scare foreigners away; during the pandemic, longer border closures than similar countries was expected to scare potential employees away forever. Instead, the number of foreign workers has continued to hit records. These latest changes will have just as much long-term impact on the country’s ability to attract talent, which is to say, precisely none.

The proposal has similarities to policies in places such as Singapore or South Korea, nations that increasingly rely on foreign labor but have selective standards for permanent residency and (explicitly or implicitly) examine language, salary and level of integration. And conditions would nonetheless be far less onerous than in many states that, despite dangerous or outright abusive working conditions, continue to attract foreign labor.

Concern about scaring away the most attractive talent is also overstated: Abe’s fast-track “green card” remains in place, with exceptions for highly skilled workers to quickly acquire permanent residency in a points-based scheme. The ultra-fast track “J-Skip” program for very high earners also remains.

By maintaining these carve-outs, the government thinks it can become more choosy, keeping only the most skilled and determined, while maintaining a more fluid base of non-permanent labor. And it’s probably right. Critics often fail to appreciate that the Japan of today is no longer a country that needs to bend over backwards to advertise itself as a destination.

It also no longer needs, to quote the title of a book on a government scheme to bring foreign teachers to rural areas, to “import diversity.” These days, the foreign population is flourishing, for the simple reason that business needs them. For those seeking opportunity beyond their home country, economic incentives will almost always trump other concerns.

The proposals are not perfect. Income is only a rough proxy for economic value; Japan will in future likely have to make exceptions for sectors where workers are needed but poorly paid, most notably nursing and care work. Authorities should allow a crossover period to grandfather in residents who were expecting to qualify under the current rules. And most importantly, these changes should be communicated far more clearly. Much of the confusion among the foreign community is due to continuous piecemeal leaks of policy to domestic media, who can report the changes out of context.

But critics who damn every change should look at ructions elsewhere to see what happens when mainstream politicians fail to create a structure that acknowledges and manages a growing population of foreign labor. Japan isn’t pretending anymore that it doesn’t have an immigration strategy. That means it must grow more selective about who gets to stay.

items.title: The Whole Indian Options Trade Was Too Good
body: Programming note: Money Stuff will be off on Monday, back Tuesday.
A fact about human nature that I once did not appreciate, and that I really really really appreciate now, is that it is very fun to gamble on stock options. Like:
Offset against all of this is the fact that options trading is essentially zero-sum, and negative-sum after transaction costs paid to brokers and market makers.

And so, if you want to build an efficient machine to extract money from people at scale, selling them stock options is pretty good. There are some obvious design tweaks to maximize the money you can extract:

You see elements of this playbook everywhere. US stock options used to mostly expire monthly, but there has been a huge push to zero-day options (ones that expire in a day), because: more chances to win. And agentic trading, where customers can automatically make hundreds of trades per day, is the next frontier in frequency. US brokerages used to charge commissions for trading stocks or options, but now they don’t, because: lower barriers to entry.

You also see people expand this playbook to other, uh, I guess the polite term is “asset classes,” though my hypothesis here is that the correct term is “bets.” Most notably, a theme of this column over the last year or two has been the huge cultural push, in the US, to make sports betting feel more like stock options. Right now, you can go on your brokerage app and make sports bets, and Robinhood will explain that sports bets are an “emerging asset class,” and US financial regulators will talk about “competitive, fair, and efficient markets that protect the price discovery process of trading in the centralized derivatives markets” for sports bets. And when you bet on sports, the person on the other side of your bets will not be a Las Vegas casino but rather a billionaire’s sophisticated quantitative trading firm that is best known for trading stock options. Your sports bet feels, in many respects, like an options trade, and you can feel smart and prestigious if you win, and imagine feeling smart and prestigious if you lose. (And it’s sports so it’s fun.)
Bloomberg Markets Magazine has a feature on “How India Built (and Broke) the World’s Biggest Options Casino,” which lays out this playbook with great clarity:
This was an extremely successful money-extraction endeavor:
And then the money extraction got to be too much, so regulators just shut it down:

The end. There was a large fun casino that extracted a lot of money from retail gamblers, regulators found that bad, they shut down the casino, and it stopped extracting a lot of money from retail gamblers. You could imagine objections:

All of those objections strike me as basically self-refuting but there they are. (“Casinos are fun, these people are adults, and if they want to blow their money on dopamine let them” is a better objection.) Also here’s this:
Right, no, that was the trick!
I wrote once about egg market manipulation:

That’s the core idea of market manipulation: You find some small illiquid market that determines the price of some much larger and more liquid market. You buy $100 million worth of stuff in the large liquid market, without moving the price much. Then you buy $1 million worth of stuff in the small illiquid market, causing the price — in the illiquid market, and also in the liquid one — to double. You sell your stuff in the large liquid market for $200 million (it’s doubled), again without moving the price much. Then you sell your stuff in the illiquid market, maybe driving the price down to zero, but so what: You lose $1 million on your small-market manipulative trades, and make $100 million on your large-market manipulated trades.

In general, this is hard to pull off, because what markets have structures like that? Why would some giant liquid market depend on some small illiquid market for its pricing? There are a few salient examples — eggs, Indian index options, interest-rate swaps in the 2000s — but they’re kind of weird.
But maybe that’s the wrong way to think about it. The other day, I quoted a judge’s opinion in an insider-trading lawsuit, saying:

You could tell a story like this: The marginal prices of stocks are set by, you know, four hedge funds; they are set by “algorithms, AI agents and career traders” reading “tea leaves to make split-second decisions.” The stock market is big and liquid. But the tea leaf market is weird and small. The marginal price setters in stock markets are looking to some data sources to set prices, and those data sources might be small and niche and manipulable, and if you can manipulate them you might have a big impact on stock prices.

Arguably the biggest market in the world right now is, like, “AI.” Trillions of dollars of stock market capitalization, of data-center financing, of expected capital expenditures and revenues, all depend on the path of artificial intelligence adoption. The modern debt market is basically built on the value of computer chips as debt collateral. If there is news suggesting that AI progress will be faster or slower than expected, that causes huge shifts in value.

Meanwhile we’ve talked occasionally about compute futures. Several exchanges are working on developing financial futures products to price and hedge the expected future cost of computing power. This has an obvious use case in the AI buildout; I wrote once:
But this is all pretty early and small right now; the compute futures are more of a proof of concept than a robust liquid market for AI computing.

Here is a fascinating story from Semafor reporting that “the US Commerce Department last month ordered Kalshi to take down one of its products tracking the price of AI compute,” and has “also pushed the Commodity Futures Trading Commission … to effectively freeze approval of new compute contracts for 60 days.” (“’This story is false,’ a Commerce spokesman said,” though.) Why? “It’s unclear why Commerce is worried about the nascent market,” but:

That is: Maybe you can spend a small amount of money to manipulate the market for the value of computer chips as long-term debt collateral. The whole AI economy is, arguably, built on that value. If it goes down, maybe hedge funds will notice. Maybe that will crash the prices of AI stocks and bonds. Maybe you can make a lot of money in the biggest market by spending a little money in the compute futures market.

When a company wants to borrow money, its lenders will want to know if it can pay them back. The main way to figure this out is by comparing the company’s earnings to its debt. The lenders will take some measure of the earnings (often Ebitda, earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortization) and compare it to some measure of the debt (often the total amount of debt, or the interest expense). If the company made $50 this year and wants to borrow $100 for five years, that’s probably fine: It will earn back enough to pay off the debt in two years, and its $50 of earnings is more than enough to cover, like, $8 or $10 or $14 of annual interest on $100 of debt. If the company made $8 this year and wants to borrow $100, that’s harder.

Of course, this isn’t really what the lenders want to know. They don’t want to know how much money the company made this year. They want to know how much money the company will make over the next five years. For many companies, much of the time, this year’s earnings are the best data point for estimating the next five years’ earnings, but that’s not always true. What if they go down? Lenders will often protect themselves by including maintenance covenants in their loans: If the company makes $50 a year and wants to borrow $100 for five years, the loan might have a covenant saying “if the company’s earnings fall below $20 in a year, it has to pay the money back immediately.”The phrasing will generally be that the covenant requires some maximum leverage ratio (debt to Ebitda) or some minimum fixed charge coverage ratio (Ebitda to fixed charges), and failing to meet that ratio can trigger an event of default and, eventually, acceleration. That way, if the company becomes a lot riskier after taking out the loan, the lenders can demand their money back early, or at least use that demand as leverage to negotiate other protections.
But, again, the thing that the lenders really want to know is how much money the company will make over the next five years, so there is room for negotiation and interpretation. Like:

One way that this all plays out is that companies and lenders use projected earnings, not just historical earnings, in negotiating loans. But “projected” often sounds kind of fake, so another (also kind of fake-sounding!) way that this plays out is with “Ebitda add-backs.” Basically:

Of course this still leaves tons of room for negotiation and interpretation. The company will tend to think that many of this year’s expenses are not indicative of its future earnings power and should be ignored. The lenders will be more conservative. But, you negotiate, and maybe you reach an agreement. If a loan has maintenance covenants, they will probably require the company to maintain a certain level of “Adjusted Ebitda,” which will be defined as earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation, amortization, and any other add-backs that the lenders have agreed to.

During the Covid-19 pandemic, we talked about the “corona clause,” an Ebitda add-back that was added to some loan documents to basically back out the costs of Covid from covenant calculations. I wrote:

That was written in March of 2020, and my main point was that a series of debt defaults triggered by covenant breaches wouldn’t really help anyone. With hindsight, though, possibly a better point would have been “the effects of Covid-19 on borrowers’ income really will be temporary, so ignoring those effects might more accurately reflect the borrowers’ actual recurring earnings power.”

Anyway. Take some arbitrary corporate borrower. It has $100 of earnings this year. You want to know how much money it will make over the next five years. A decent starting point, knowing no specific facts about the company, would be $100 per year, grown at some reasonable rate. We are not currently in a big pandemic that shuts down all economic activity, but we are in the early-ish stages of a possibly world-changing boom in artificial intelligence. So … uh … what about that? You could spitball:

These are all dumb, and in the real world lenders negotiate with actual companies and try to underwrite the course of their actual businesses. Still it is plausible to think that, for many businesses, AI could cause changes to their costs and/or revenues that are (1) quite large, (2) somewhat knowable and (3) not reflected in current earnings.
Here’s a fun Bloomberg News story about AI Ebitda add-backs:

I kind of take Sabahi’s point that future cost savings from AI do not actually increase last year’s earnings, but I also take Emeria’s point that it is pretty conventional, in credit markets, to pretend that they do.

I mentioned last week one of my favorite tropes of financial journalism, a profile of a rich hedge fund manager who is not like other rich hedge fund manager, he’s down to earth and not flashy, and his biggest indulgence outside of work is some hilariously on-the-nose rich-guy thing. “When he goes to his house on Nantucket, he only sometimes flies private,” or “his only real indulgence is several yachts.”

Here is a Wall Street Journal profile of Jacob Coxon, the former Anthropic researcher who became famous for quitting because he thinks Anthropic is going to kill everyone. He’s not like other AI doomers, though:
Except for …

Like, before reading this article, I would have guessed that the No. 1 and No. 2 indicators of “most likely to quit Anthropic over safety concerns” are (1) “rationalist” and (2) living in a group house after college. But actually those are No. 2 and No. 3, and being on the UK IMO team pretty much dooms you to quit Anthropic. And he had all three!

Anyway I don’t think “guy who quit Anthropic over safety concerns who is not like other guys who quit Anthropic over safety concerns” will ever be as big a genre as “hedge fund guy who is not like other hedge fund guys,” but it is a really good one. And “discuss grim scenarios at happy hours” is perfect.

items.title: Four Big Deals That Reveal the State of Podcasting
body: Welcome back to Soundbite. This week has unofficially been dubbed “podcast week” in New York because of a couple conferences happening, the Interactive Advertising Bureau’s annual podcast upfronts and more. As part of the hoopla, lots of deals have been announced, and I’ve had conversations with people in and around the space. Today, I break down what we can discern about the state of the industry from four pieces of percolating news. Also: how big was Giggly Squad’s new deal?
If you appreciate this kind of work, please support it and subscribe. Reach me through email.
Up first, here’s what I’m reading and writing this week.

Hannah Berner and Paige DeSorbo, the hosts of Giggly Squad, announced this week that they’re taking their show to SiriusXM Holdings Inc. after years with Acast AB. The Hollywood Reporter notes the deal covers four years and will involve the women creating new programs to complement their original podcast starting next year. What went under-covered is the fact that this is quietly one of the biggest podcast deals of the year. According to people familiar with the negotiation, offers to the women came in between $35 million and $40 million a year.Representatives for DeSorbo, Berner and SiriusXM didn’t respond to requests for comment.

That makes their payout nearly as high as the second most popular podcast in the US, based on the Edison Research rankings. Ashley Flowers’ Crime Junkie is making $150 million through its deal with Fox, according to the Wall Street Journal. For comparison: Giggly Squad didn’t make the Edison rankings during the past quarter.

So what’s going on here? For one: Berner and DeSorbo have toured the US and sold out two shows at Radio City Music Hall, meaning sponsorships could be on the table for these in-person hangs. At the same time, the women speak to a valuable audience of Gen Z and Millennial women, which few top podcasters reach. Alex Cooper of Call Her Daddy has built her entire brand (and an ad agency) around reaching these same women. Cooper also works with SiriusXM. Generally, podcasting continues to be male-dominated, so speaking to different demographics could be a way to stand out — and rake in loads of cash as a result.

The women also maintain large social media followings that could give brands additional real estate beyond the podcast itself, and their lo-fi video production provides even more visual space to plaster a brand. During recent recordings, the hosts have been seen with Dunkin’ cups on their coffee table.

Still, it’s a massive number that feels reminiscent of the podcast-gold-rush days, when creators could secure eye-popping upfront payments with the promise that they’d increase their output and convert audiences into consumers of certain products. It certainly feels like we’ve re-entered a seller’s market in podcasting, which brings us to our next big deal this week….

I reported last week that Kevin Roose and Casey Newton, the former hosts of Hard Fork, were out shopping for a deal for their next tech podcast. Offers were reaching as high as $5 million a year, I reported. The day after I published my story, the two men signed their deal with their new distributor: NPR. Admittedly, I didn’t see that one coming.

On paper, the pairing makes sense. Roose and Newton are seasoned journalists who, while both now independent, cut their teeth at legacy institutions. For NPR, Roose and Newton represent a fresh opportunity to bring in “creators,” but with trust that the duo value fact-based reporting and won’t devolve into conspiracy theories or other algorithm-chasing bait.

The move comes only a few months after the public media outlet named Nadine Zylstra — a veteran of YouTube, Pinterest and Sesame Workshop — its chief content officer. Clearly, Zylstra, who helped build YouTube’s push into originals, believes the organization can and should look outside the newsroom for talent to populate its airwaves and feeds. Roose and Newton will also be recording video episodes, another change for NPR.

Of course, this sea change arrives against a backdrop of a difficult time in public media after the Trump administration spearheaded a campaign to revoke funding for radio stations and TV channels. NPR raised money on the back of that moment and said in April it had received $113 million in philanthropic gifts. Now it seems the institution is using some of that windfall to flip its model, as it tries to figure out how to survive on its own.

One fun thing about the podcast business currently is that there’s no consensus on its limitations. One moment, industry executives can be sitting in an upfront presentation focused on the power of audio, and the next, find themselves in a windowless room near Penn Station waiting to hear about a mysterious deal involving Steven Bartlett, the host of Diary of a CEO. Indeed, I found myself in this subterranean space on Tuesday.

Bartlett and Jamie Salter, founder of Authentic Brands Group, announced a strategic venture in which they’re aiming to deploy $400 million into creator businesses. The basic idea is that Bartlett can help these stars scale their content operations while Authentic can build ancillary businesses around them, like product lines and more. (See what Authentic has done with Shaquille O’Neal over the past couple of years: launching a dunk league, a Netflix docuseries and re-releasing a rap single.)

Authentic often looks to acquire name, image and likeness rights of stars, so this will be a test of whether digital creators can really transfer their online celebrity into successful brands and more. Oftentimes, NIL deals come about in the twilight years of a celebrity’s career, and Authentic also owns the rights to deceased stars like Marilyn Monroe and Elvis Presley. All of which raises the question of what happens when creators see this as a retirement strategy that could help them exit the content-creation business. Does their name continue to remain relevant?

Wondery tried to pioneer the podcasters-as-IP-machines model with the launch of products and merch stores via Amazon.com Inc. To date, the results of that experiment remain somewhat fuzzy. Wondery’s chief brand officer, Nicole Blake, left last year, and the studio was divvied up among various stakeholders within Amazon.
We’ll see how this effort goes.

The New York Times Co. confirmed this week that Serial Productions, its long-form, limited-series outfit, is launching a bi-weekly program dedicated to storytelling about New York City. Not only is it an always-on show, but the team is planning to create standalone video and multimedia programming to accompany the podcast.
This feels like a significant moment.

Sarah Koenig and Julie Snyder, the founders of Serial, announced the show on stage at the Sounds Profitable Podcast Business Summit and retold their arc of rising in the industry. Namely, when they created the first season of Serial, the idea of telling one story over multiple episodes was “pretty novel and also something you couldn’t really do on radio.”
Podcasting, Snyder said, offered a format for this type of consumption. But now, the changing realities of media seem to be forcing Snyder and Koenig to switch formats yet again.

The forthcoming series is “absolutely a departure for us, but remember, Julie and I worked at This American Life,” said Koenig. “We worked for Ira for decades, so this is in our blood. We know how to make episodes sort of in a weekly way.”

Not long ago, telling a single audio story across many episodes felt revolutionary. Nowadays, it’s almost impossible to go silent for a period of time without fearing (and likely experiencing) a loss in audience. Even The Daily, which also pioneered the idea of a daily format in podcasting, went to seven days a week recently — aiming to prevent a drop-off in listeners over weekends and creating a space for less news-driven conversations. Koenig and Snyder didn’t say anything specifically about the future of limited series at the Times. But given their stature, their shift in format seems like an acknowledgement, at some level, that limited series are becoming even more difficult to get through to publication.

items.title: Intense Heat Strains Power Grids for 100 Million North Americans
body: Power grids serving more than 100 million North Americans are bracing for a demand surge as unseasonable heat strains electrical equipment scheduled for repairs.

Temperatures are running more than 20F (11C) above normal in some areas served by the Midcontinent Independent System Operator, with triple-digit heat forecast around the South through at least Sunday, according to the US National Weather Service.
St. Louis is forecast to reach 99F (37C) and is under a heat advisory through late Saturday, according to the National Weather Service. That’s about 18F higher than normal for this time of year.

Meanwhile, a neighboring grid managed by PJM Interconnection LLC that encompasses Chicago, Washington DC and Virginia’s Data Center Alley issued an alert that reserve power supplies are under strain in some areas and ordered some major, non-residential customers to cut back.

The searing weather arrived just as power-plant operators were scheduled to take key systems offline for autumn maintenance. MISO reported roughly 51 gigawatts of generation outages Thursday even as demand is forecast to reach 105.2 gigawatts.
PJM expects electricity usage to surpass 132 gigawatts, with nearly 37 offline.

PJM officials requested Wednesday that the US Department of Energy waive some emissions rules so plants can operate at full tilt. The agency also authorized the deployment of backup generation resources Thursday to mitigate any potential shortages.
Spot power prices in the largest US grid jumped above $4,300 per megawatt-hour on the benchmark Western hub just after 6 p.m. local time Wednesday.

Aging generating stations are coming off a summer of brutal heat that prompted repeated federal orders to run at full blast. That’s put additional stress on a system facing growing industrial and data center demand.
PJM’s generation fleet “is starting to show signs of its age when trying to stay working,” said Gary Cunningham, a director at Tradition Energy.
Wholesale power prices probably will remain elevated across Virginia, Ohio, Kentucky and western Pennsylvania through Thursday, Cunningham added.

Autumn in the Northern Hemisphere is typically an ideal time to conduct maintenance on power gear as milder weather eases air-conditioner use. But erratic weather linked to both human-caused climate change and natural phenomena like El Niño is squeezing the repair calendar.

Increasingly, plant operators are finding there is no off-season. The artificial intelligence boom is also boosting overall electricity demand, which means critical equipment doesn’t get much of a break.
Read More: Power Grids Hit Tipping Point as US Heat, AI Boom Elevate Risks

Unseasonable weather “plays well into the narrative of PJM needing more generation capacity, and needing it NOW, even before new demands to meet data center requirements come,” Cunningham wrote in an email.

items.title: Existential Angst Dominates Debate Over Tech From Anthropic, OpenAI
body: The current round of panic over artificial intelligence is based on the conviction that the technology has slipped out of human control to do its own bidding in several recent incidents. To some disillusioned AI researchers — and some senior employees at leading AI companies — this is an early sign of a true threat to human civilization. But other experts in the field are pushing back, claiming that such talk allows companies to sidestep accountability for real-world impacts of their technology. Critics see AI’s environmental impacts, the threat of job displacement, or the potential for mass surveillance as more urgent targets for policymakers.

Concerns that AI software posed an existential threat began ramping up this summer.  In July, OpenAI said that its advanced AI models hacked Hugging Face Inc., another AI startup, during an evaluation meant to test their cyber capabilities. Unlike the AI models the company releases to the public, the software was being tested without guardrails that would normally stop it from carrying out such actions, which is a common AI industry practice. OpenAI acknowledged in a subsequent report that it could have reacted sooner, and that its employees didn’t act on signs that the models left their digital sandbox and broke into Hugging Face without being instructed to do so.

More unsettling details emerged about the behavior of technology from OpenAI and several key competitors, including Anthropic and Meta, during other evaluations. When Jacob Coxon, a former Anthropic and OpenAI employee, accused the industry of “gambling with our lives,” Evan Hubinger, a safety researcher at Anthropic, responded by saying the company actually did believe AI might kill every human on earth. He added that he saw the chances this could happen within the decade at over 10%.

The normie world was getting a glimpse into a long-running conversation within the field. Before there were chatbot subscriptions to sell or IPOs to price, researchers understood their work as a high-risk, high-reward proposition for civilization. For years, some leaders within the AI industry have taken these ideas to extremes, saying AI might eventually cure all human disease, replace all human labor, kill all humans — or all of the above.

Building such a technology inspired a sense of mission, both self-flattering and frightening, that has shaped AI culture since before the technology became a blockbuster business. In 2023, months after ChatGPT was released, Yoshua Bengio and Stuart Russell, two of the field’s founding figures, were the top signatories on a statement calling for a pause on the development of the most powerful AI, citing “profound risks to society and humanity.”

Critics have consistently dismissed such arguments as self-serving fearmongering. For an individual researcher, to see your work as capable of ending humanity is also to consider it the most important work there is. For companies, talk about existential risk was an effective recruitment strategy in AI’s early days, since many highly sought-after researchers wanted to work at places that took such risk seriously.

More recently, it has even seeped into product marketing. During the World Cup this July, Anthropic aired an ad that opened with an image of a burning house, moved through a pit mine and panned across rows of headstones, as a worried-sounding narrator discussed potentially catastrophic impacts the technology could have. Eventually the soundtrack turned uplifting and it revealed its tagline for its Claude chatbot: “There’s hope in hard questions.”

Doomerism can also function as a defense strategy, and there’s controversy within the field about whether companies employ it in cynical ways. Talking about AI as an autonomous entity reframes safety failures as evidence that containment is not possible. This reduces the focus on how tech companies may have conducted their experiments unsafely, according to Subbarao Kambhampati, a computer science professor at Arizona State University. “It's a failure of the sandbox that you are essentially trying to pass off as, ‘The AI is going to become so effective and it’s going to kill us all,’” he said.

The fear has already begun shaping the way members of Congress frame the issue. Vermont Senator Bernie Sanders has proposed banning so-called superintelligent AI, saying that AI leaders have acknowledged the technology “is escaping their control.” Representative Ted Lieu said an OpenAI model “went rogue” and, along with Representative Nathaniel Moran, introduced the AI Kill Switch Act in July.

These bills almost certainly won’t become law this year, but the announcements show how much of the vocabulary of catastrophe has migrated from the industry into the rhetoric of federal lawmakers. Advocates of AI regulation also worry that bills that start from a premise that AI may kill us all will crowd out other ideas about regulating AI. “Before getting to ‘the world is going to end,’ we need to be breaking down, what are the mechanisms through which we envision that happening?” said Sarah Myers West, co-executive director of the AI Now Institute, a policy research organization. “What can we do to mitigate them?”  In a statement, OpenAI spokesperson Drew Pusateri said the Hugging Face incident “showed where our safeguards needed to be stronger, and we’ve acted on that by strengthening protections across our research systems.” On Wednesday, the company unveiled a new set of guidelines for how it will track, investigate, and let the public know about incidents of so-called misalignment. It also shared several previously undisclosed instances of such misalignment, in which its technology had done things like conceal or fabricate information to return results. None of those incidents involved compromising external networks, the company said.
Anthropic declined to comment for this article.

Melanie Mitchell, a Santa Fe Institute professor who studies how AI systems reason, took issue in a Sept. 10 essay that AI companies had ever lost control of their technology, and said talk of swarms of rogue agents breaking out of their cages distorted the public conversation. Such descriptions imply humanlike agency that AI models don’t possess, she wrote. Mitchell compared the OpenAI-Hugging Face hacking incident to a 2000 New Mexico wildfire, where officials conducting a controlled burn overlooked wind forecasts and watched the fire spiral out of control. The fault, she wrote, lies with the humans who trained models with methods that reward persistence and autonomous decision-making, then who failed to engineer safe testing conditions. She sees the biggest future dangers lying with humans who use AI models to cause harm.

Some people, including President Donald Trump, have rejected existential threats as a way to dismiss any suggestion that AI requires new regulations. But not every anti-doomer wants to let AI rip. Sara Hooker, co-founder of the AI startup Adaption Labs and a former research scientist at Google DeepMind, agrees with Anthropic Chief Executive Officer Dario Amodei when he expresses concerns about so-called recursive self-improvement, a term that refers to the theory that AI will eventually acquire the ability to alter its own code or otherwise improve its capability without human intervention.

Amodei has said he's worried that, once this process begins, it could set off a feedback loop that will outpace the ability of humans to control the ever-improving systems. “Left unchecked, it could outrun our ability to understand and control these systems, and so must be pursued very carefully, if at all,” he wrote on Saturday, in a lengthy blog post calling for slowing the pace of development of the most cutting-edge AI models. Anthropic’s rhetoric on existential threats has been consistently more aggressive than OpenAI’s. But OpenAI CEO Sam Altman quickly signaled support for Amodei’s position, as did SpaceXAI leader Elon Musk.

Hooker agrees that self-improving AI would be a real break from earlier systems. On the other hand, “do you jump from that to extinction? No,” she said. The estimates circulating this month from AI researchers trying to pinpoint the probability of the end of humanity, she added, come with “no accountability for where that number comes from.” Such talk has been common within the field, leading to its own kind of recursive feedback loop that has left AI researchers increasingly out of touch with the rest of the world.

Incidents like the Hugging Face hack raise plenty of concerns even for those who don’t see them as a threat to civilization. In addition to not using the safeguards it puts on publicly available products, OpenAI had trained the models it was testing to cooperate, rewarding them for reaching objectives collectively. Although the agents in this evaluation were meant to be isolated from one another, each had access to the same internal software which gave them a shared state to exchange information — something OpenAI called a message board. Agents found that the software could reach the internet even though they couldn’t, and got the software to fetch material from outside. The agents then hacked Hugging Face for datasets that would reveal how their work was graded.

As AI companies continue to work on developing safer testing methods, Kambhampati said that claims of out-of-control AI should not be used as a way to sidestep accountability. He pointed to Robert Morris, the Cornell graduate student who blamed a programming error after his 1988 worm disabled about a tenth of the computers then connected to the internet. A court rejected this argument, and Morris became the first person convicted under the Computer Fraud and Abuse Act. “You start a process that goes haywire and causes damage to my property, you are responsible, period,” Kambhampati said. “It’s true even when your dog does it.”

items.title: AI Pioneer Andrew Ng Calls Extinction Fears 'Science Fiction'
body: Artificial intelligence pioneer Andrew Ng said warnings about existential AI risks from researchers at top model makers are “science fiction” that may be detrimental to ensuring the technology’s maximum benefits to society.

Ng, who helped start Google Brain and Coursera Inc., said the tech industry previously stoked fears about the potential catastrophic harms of artificial intelligence earlier in the AI boom in an apparent bid to bolster publicity and shape regulation.
“I was quite dismayed over the past two weeks,” he said in an interview with Bloomberg TV on Thursday. “This wave of PR has kicked up again, for probably similar purposes.”

The high-profile resignation this month of former Anthropic and OpenAI researcher Jacob Coxon helped bring a long-simmering discussion about AI safety into the mainstream. Coxon accused both his former employers of “gambling with our lives” by “racing toward super-intelligent AI,” and said the people building AI believe it could “kill us all by the end of the decade.”
Earlier this week, an AI researcher who recently resigned from Google DeepMind also warned humanity is running out of time to prevent artificial intelligence from causing widespread harm.

Against that backdrop, AI leaders including Anthropic’s Dario Amodei and OpenAI’s Sam Altman are calling for the industry to pace development of cutting-edge models and take additional steps to safeguard future development.

Ng, who previously worked with both Amodei and Altman earlier in their careers, said there are certainly risks from AI, including with cybersecurity capabilities. But he described the concerns around human extinction as “much more science fiction than science.”

He also said there are “practical engineering problems” the industry can focus on to continue to improve and safeguard the technology, while working to ensure that AI can be used for “many of the wonderful things it can do.”

items.title: US Said to Hold Off on Tariffs Until After Xi-Trump Summit
body: The US is expected to delay the announcement of new tariffs over allegations of trading partners’ excess manufacturing capacity at least until after next week’s planned summit between Presidents Xi Jinping and Donald Trump, according to people familiar with the matter.

Bloomberg earlier reported that the administration intended to release a trade report on excess capacity before the US-China leaders’ meeting, which would recommend a 7.5% tariff on Chinese goods. The reason for the delay is unclear.

It’s also uncertain whether the final tariff rate will change from the previously expected level, which would restore Trump’s second-term duties on China to around 20%, a rate Beijing has previously said is consistent with its trade truce with Washington.

In March, the Trump administration launched an investigation into more than a dozen major trading partners under Section 301 of the Trade Act of 1974 over excess capacity concerns. Those expected levies, along with already-implemented duties related to forced labor, are expected to eventually bring tariff rates closer to Trump’s country-specific duties that were overturned by the Supreme Court earlier this year.
The Office of the US Trade Representative and the White House did not respond to requests for comment.
Inside US Trade first reported the delay.
US and Chinese officials are expected to discuss a number of issues during the summit, including the war in Iran, trade and artificial intelligence.

Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi discussed Middle East issues with US Secretary of State Marco Rubio in a phone call Thursday, according to China’s Foreign Ministry. Wang said the next stage of high-level exchanges between the two countries should be conducted in the spirit of equality, respect and mutual benefit.

items.title: Hyrox Needs to Remember Who Its Customers Are
body: Hyrox takes its sporting credentials seriously — it was, after all, co-founded by an Olympian. But the commercial success of the high-endurance fitness race isn’t built on the backs of elite athletes. It comes from attracting overachieving gym junkies.

Which is why the competition must now make amends to its core group of devotees after mishandling a hygiene controversy in Beijing over the weekend, especially as it sets its sights on becoming an even bigger force in global fitness. The women's world record holder, Australia’s Joanna Wietrzyk, was allowed to complete (and win) despite experiencing bowel incontinence partway through the race.

The viral episode caused an uproar among participants upset about the prospect of having to share dirty equipment, a reaction that quickly reverberated through the international community. There was also the issue of fairness. Existing rules penalize behaviors that can affect the cleanliness and safety of communal spaces, such as spitting. Allowing a competitor to continue after soiling herself struck many as a glaring inconsistency.

Organizers treated the event as a serious championship, where the overriding concern is preserving the integrity of the tournament by ensuring an athlete’s right to finish. Elite endurance sports have plenty of precedents of athletes pushing on through deeply uncomfortable — and potentially embarrassing — circumstances. Chinese runner Li Meizhen continued the Hengshui Lake Marathon in 2024 after unexpectedly getting her period, with blood visibly running down her legs. And in 2005, Paula Radcliffe had to relieve herself in public during the London marathon, which she won. Both were lauded for their determination.

But Hyrox is different. Racers complete eight rounds of a one-kilometer (0.6 mile) run, each followed by a functional workout station. Unlike a marathon or triathlon, the format requires competitors to cycle through stations with everyone using the same equipment. What might be treated as an individual athlete’s decision in a road race can become a hygiene issue in an indoor contest.

That distinction matters as the fitness brand founded in Germany nine years ago is gearing up to become an even bigger global player. Hyrox needs stricter rules for handling incidents involving bodily fluids. Hyrox co-founder Moritz Fürste, who won a gold medal for Germany in field hockey at the 2008 Summer Olympics, apologized for “not reacting immediately” during the race. With 1.4 million people taking part in more than 100 events in the last season, its policies and standards must reflect its growing ambition.

Investors are already buying into the hype. A group led by private equity firm L Catterton, backed by LVMH Moët Hennessy Louis Vuitton SE, bought a majority stake in the company last week from Infront Sports & Media AG, backed by Dalian Wanda Group Co. The deal reportedly valued Hyrox at about €600 million ($700 million) with a price-to-sales ratio of about 2.6 times this year’s expected revenue. At that multiple, the deal was roughly on par with the 2020 sale of the Ironman triathlon franchise by Wanda Sports to Advance Publications Inc.

There’s already evidence that Hyrox’s growing popularity is starting to pay off. Puma SE, its longtime sneaker and apparel partner, launched a dedicated fitness racing shoe last year and has characterized the relationship as a strategic tie-up involving sportswear and community building (Wietrzyk is a sponsored athlete).

Puma Chief Executive Officer Arthur Hoeld said during the firm’s latest earnings call that Hyrox-related products helped contribute “strong growth” to the footwear segment. Rivals Nike Inc. and Adidas AG have also entered the racing category with shoes like the Hybrid RN and Adizero Dropset Elite, respectively.

Other companies are piling in. Amazon.com Inc. became a global partner in August, launching dedicated Hyrox storefronts selling everything from sports nutrition to training equipment, while AirAsia Group became an  airline partner earlier this year. Continuing this commercial momentum depends on keeping racers coming back.

After the Beijing controversy gained traction online, Hyrox offered refunds and the rulebook has been updated, giving race officials the power to withdraw athletes if bodily fluids present a safety risk. These were the correct responses, but the episode offers a broader lesson.

A fast-growing global franchise needs rules designed not just to protect the integrity of competition, but also the overall experience of entrants. Consistency, hygiene and consideration for fellow participants aren't peripheral concerns.

Hyrox has successfully persuaded mainstream gym goers to train like serious athletes. But the competitive instincts of people at the front of the race shouldn’t ruin the experience of those behind them. For Hyrox to go the distance, it needs to do better in catering to the masses.

items.title: Venezuela comienza a levantar bloqueos a sitios de noticias tras años de censura
body: Read the story in English
Venezuela comenzó a levantar los bloqueos impuestos durante años a sitios web de noticias, aunque algunos siguen sin estar disponibles.
La flexibilización de la censura a la prensa es la señal tentativa más reciente de liberalización política tras la captura en enero del líder venezolano Nicolás Maduro por parte de Estados Unidos.
Suscríbase       aquí     al boletín Morning Briefing Español y conozca nuestro canal de       WhatsApp

Los proveedores de internet recibieron instrucciones de la presidenta encargada Delcy Rodríguez, respaldada por Estados Unidos, para restablecer el acceso a sitios web de noticias nacionales e internacionales, informó el regulador de telecomunicaciones del país el jueves por la mañana en un comunicado.

La medida se produce antes de una segunda ronda de conversaciones políticas respaldadas por Estados Unidos en Caracas más tarde el jueves, en las que se espera que se discutan garantías civiles y políticas, incluida la libertad de expresión.

Al menos una docena de medios previamente bloqueados —incluidos los sitios venezolanos El Pitazo, Runrunes y Efecto Cocuyo, además de Semana, de Colombia, y la agencia española de noticias EFE— ya eran accesibles a través de los principales proveedores de internet a primera hora del jueves, según el grupo de derechos digitales VE Sin Filtro. La mayoría de los sitios de noticias extranjeros seguían bloqueados, dijo por mensaje de texto a media mañana Andrés Azpurua, director de la ONG.

La medida desmantela de forma selectiva un sistema de censura en línea que se expandió durante el gobierno de Maduro y restringió el acceso a medios considerados críticos de su régimen. Más de 200 dominios de internet seguían bloqueados previamente este mes, la mayoría relacionados con noticias, según VE Sin Filtro.

La libertad de prensa se deterioró drásticamente durante los 13 años de Maduro en el poder, cuando las autoridades censuraron sitios web de noticias, cerraron estaciones de radio y utilizaron leyes y presión regulatoria contra periodistas y medios independientes. La ofensiva contra la prensa se intensificó en períodos de agitación política y elecciones, lo que llevó a muchos venezolanos a recurrir a redes sociales, aplicaciones de mensajería y redes privadas virtuales para acceder a información independiente.

La decisión se produjo horas después de que el Programa para la Paz y la Convivencia Democrática, respaldado por el gobierno, recomendara a Rodríguez eliminar las restricciones a los sitios web de noticias tras consultas con medios públicos, privados e independientes.

Tras la salida de Maduro del poder, funcionarios del gobierno, incluida Rodríguez, regresaron a X, plataforma que Maduro había ordenado bloquear durante el volátil período posterior a las disputadas elecciones de 2024. A fines de junio, los venezolanos comenzaron a informar que el acceso a la red social había sido restablecido.
Nota Original: Venezuela Unblocks Some Media Ahead of Talks, Others Still Dark

items.title: Knicks Halt Ticket Sales After Error Sends Prices Over $1,200
body: The New York Knicks suspended individual ticket sales after an internal error resulted in sky-high prices to see the NBA champions play their season opener in October.
The cheapest available tickets Wednesday on Ticketmaster and resale websites like StubHub were over $1,000.

Madison Square Garden Sports Corp., which owns the Knicks, said in a statement that ticket prices will be set at 12% on average over last year’s prices when it restarts individual ticket sales. Those who purchased tickets already will be refunded the difference.
“Our intention was never to overcharge our loyal fans, and we thank everyone for their support of the Knicks and their patience as we get this right,” the statement said.
The Knicks will open the season at the Garden on Oct. 20 against LeBron James and the Philadelphia 76ers, which will also include the championship ring ceremony and banner-raising.

In June, the Knicks ended a 53-year championship drought for the franchise. The five-game series against the San Antonio Spurs saw tickets sell for thousands of dollars and scored massive television ratings, ranking as the most-watched NBA Finals since 1998.
The lowest-priced tickets for the season opener cost $1,251 on resale sites, according to aggregator TicketData. The New York Post first reported the pricing error.

items.title: Regulatory Capture Isn't What You Think It Is
body: Hello and welcome to the newsletter, a grab bag of daily content from the Odd Lots universe. Sometimes it’s us, Joe Weisenthal and Tracy Alloway, bringing you our thoughts on the most recent developments in markets, finance and the economy. And sometimes it’s contributions from our network of expert guests and sources. Whatever it is, we promise it will always be interesting.

If you like chatting with us, check out the Odd Lots Discord, where you can hang out and talk with us and with other listeners 24/7.Today’s newsletter is written by Odd Lots producer Cale Brooks, and it is about what undergirds the current debate over AI regulation.

In light of AI founders like Sam Altman and Dario Amodei calling for a “pacing” of frontier technological development and the public reaction to the recent AI whistleblowers, there’s an emerging debate over the efficacy and desirability of regulation. The various proposals and calls for regulating AI have been met by insistences that regulation might lead to “regulatory capture.”

Most of these arguments have been made along the classic line that sticking regulatory bodies on the industry not only shields the current front runners from market discipline but also builds a moat that new entrants can’t traverse. But whichever particular concern is raised, these calls share a common outlook: Regulating an industry leads to regulatory capture, we’re told, because regulation is responsible for a reduction in competition, more bureaucracy, and a hit to economic growth, all of which hurts the public interest.

The historic evidence for this claim is pretty thin. And that’s because to make the claim that the regulators have been captured by the industry under regulation requires more than just observing the industry benefiting — often this is the point of regulation. It requires a demonstration that the regulators have been led astray from carrying out their public responsibilities. As the political scientist Daniel Carpenter has concluded in his assessment of the regulatory capture literature, “The process by which policy and institutions are directed away from the public interest and toward a special interest is crucial and often missing from analysis.”

It’s clear why regulation could be desirable from the perspectives of the big AI labs, who want to ward off smaller competitors. It’s also clear why they would prefer to self-regulate their “pace,” despite the imperatives of competition. But business intent cannot be the sole foundation for regulatory capture, regardless of how strong or restrictive the regulation is in implementation. To prove capture, it has to be contrasted with a defined sense of the public interest, another concept which has been pulled in many directions. Is the public interest a specific government mandate? Is it whatever improves business prosperity? Or is it the majority of Americans or even the majority of human beings?

However defined, it’s evident that regulation for the public interest has not impeded capitalism, and realistically has always been an inherent part of economic development. While it’s true that regulation could result in the current industry leaders feeling some institutional protection, as other tech giants before them have experienced, this has never stopped the tectonic shifts of creative destruction. This occurs both within an industry, as fixed capital becomes a double-edge sword along the lines of the classic The Innovator’s Dilemma, and across industries, as firms who utilize AI economize on their inputs or make other cost-saving substitutions. Regulation does not mean the end to competition, but it does mean a shift in who has a say over the social impacts of private investment decisions.

There is also historical precedent for an industry’s insiders calling for regulation. In the early 20th century, the business magnate Samuel Insull also urged the government to regulate the burgeoning electric utilities industry when his ComEd empire was expanding rapidly across the Midwest but also struggling to turn a profit as the energy market was maturing. The electrical grid was successfully regulated mostly as a public utility for about three decades until the 1970s wave of electricity deregulation.

It could instead be argued that the real regulatory capture occurring right now is the deferral by the federal government to impose some checks and balances on the industry, given that the public is becoming quite clearly hostile to AI.

This current capture occurs in two ways. There are huge sums of money flowing into congressional races to oppose politicians calling for AI regulation — which is textbook regulatory capture. And then there is the pressure of keeping economic growth up, weighing on both the governing political party along with a fair number of members from the opposition. More specifically, it’s the capture of this particular growth model built around AI technology, which is of course ephemeral and certainly changeable, but also currently fueling much of our retirement accounts, even if the employment and income effects are fairly restricted. Both of these means of capture have led to an unresponsiveness of the current administration to the majority’s feelings on technological development.

It’s not at all obvious that the AI industry as it’s currently constituted, with the number of players or the flow of funding rushing in or the purported importance of the technology as a general purpose input to all other industries, will remain this way in the near future. But given the emerging mass concern over the quality, utility, and safety of the industry’s product, it seems likely that regulation will play an increasing role in the pace of AI development, much like it was for electricity.

Francis Fukuyama’s 1989 essay “The End of History?” was published a few months before the fall of the Berlin Wall, and its argument seemed to foretell the end of the Cold War and what it would mean for liberal democracy to no longer have an ideological foe. He revisits the essay in his new memoir In the Realm of the Last Man, and he wonders whether its argument still holds up in our world of AI and global populism. For today’s episode we talk to him about the memoir, the internet and social media, and what will come after liberalism. Watch: Bloomberg / YouTubeListen: Apple / Spotify

items.title: Guggenheim Staff Face SEC Interviews in Probe of Walter's Empire
body: US regulators are seeking interviews with employees of Guggenheim Partners LLC as they hunt for evidence of potential wrongdoing at Chief Executive Officer Mark Walter’s business empire.

The Securities and Exchange Commission sent requests in recent weeks to current and former employees from the firm’s $367 billion asset manager, Guggenheim Investments, according to people with knowledge of the matter. People who have managed portfolios of assets for insurance companies are among those the agency is seeking to interview.
Some facing SEC requests are in the process of lining up attorneys to advise them on how to respond, the people said, asking not to be identified discussing the confidential inquiries.
“We are cooperating with the investigation,” Guggenheim Investments said in a statement. An SEC spokesperson declined to comment.

The interviews show watchdogs continue to dig deeper after public assurances from officials at Guggenheim and the billionaire’s holding company, TWG Global, that they are working to resolve government inquiries. Though it’s unclear what questions the SEC is asking, US prosecutors are known to have sought information on at least a couple of fronts.
Read More: Mark Walter’s Insurers, Guggenheim Probed by Prosecutors

Accounting practices at Guggenheim were the focus of a whistleblower report last year, the company has acknowledged. That focused on concerns about how revenue fees were disclosed at Guggenheim Private Investments, a unit that manages private funds for institutional investors, Bloomberg has reported.

Prosecutors later expanded their inquiry to examine separate dealings at Walter’s insurance companies, people with knowledge of the matter have said. This year, two of the insurers disclosed more than $20 billion of loans that should have been labeled as affiliated transactions but weren’t. In June, the insurers — Delaware Life Insurance Co. and Clear Spring Life and Annuity Co. — disclosed that they’d received subpoenas from the Manhattan US Attorney’s Office.
Still, some of the employees the SEC is now seeking to interview haven’t been directly involved with GPI or the insurers, some of the people with knowledge of the matter said.
Executives at Guggenheim Investments have sought to reassure lenders about its accounting practices.

The firm has been “very open with regulators and very cooperative,” Anne Walsh, chief investment officer of the asset-management business, told Bloomberg Television last month. “We’ve engaged with our auditors and we feel that the accounting treatment was appropriate.”

Separately, TWG has said that its insurance arm has submitted plans to state regulators to resolve any concerns. It added: “There is no victim here. No one has been harmed, and no one has claimed they were harmed.”

Walter — known best beyond Wall Street for his stakes in storied sport franchises — has meanwhile been exploring deals that would free up cash. Last month, he agreed to sell his stake in the Los Angeles Lakers to Bob Iger and Josh Kushner in a deal that valued the team at $12.5 billion.

On Wednesday, Chelsea Football Club owner Clearlake Capital agreed to buy out Walter and his longtime associate Todd Boehly. That deal was expected to pay Walter a premium to his original investment, a representative told Bloomberg last week.
TWG has said it isn’t looking to sell sports assets at “fire sale” prices, and Walter has said that he didn’t initiate the Chelsea transaction and intends to make other sports acquisitions.

items.title: Fed Hike Means Bumpy Roads for Credit Card, Auto Loan, Mortgage Borrowers
body: Federal Reserve Chairman Kevin Warsh on Wednesday defied pressure from President Donald Trump as the US central bank raised interest rates. Warsh framed the decision as reacting to an economy that continues to speed up while inflation remains too high. Sarah Foster, who writes about personal finance in New York, explains how the new rates may affect your wallet. Plus:  Fender is making enemies with a messy fight over an iconic guitar (free link).

Following the Federal Reserve’s policymaking over the past few years feels a bit like getting stuck in rush hour traffic while leaving John F. Kennedy International Airport: You’re stopping, you’re going, you’re getting jerked around. You may even have a tinge of motion sickness.

The Fed’s rate-cutting cycle officially came to an end on Wednesday, almost two years to the day after it began. The US central bank lifted its benchmark by a quarter of a percentage point, its first hike since 2023. And there could be more. Sixteen officials on the Federal Open Market Committee also projected at least one additional increase this year.

As a former Fed reporter who now covers money, I’ve been a passenger on this ride for a while: The meetings can bring a few twists and turns, but consumers often feel the bumps before policymakers even act.

We’re already seeing higher interest rates. Mortgage rates have been barreling toward the dreaded 7% threshold for four weeks now, hitting 6.95% in Freddie Mac’s latest weekly rate survey. It’s sapping the steam out of an already weak housing market. MBA’s refinance index fell 8.8% to its lowest level since May 2025. Sales of previously owned homes in the US slowed last month to their weakest pace in more than a year. The run-up in mortgage rates follows surging longer-dated bond yields, which this week hit the highest level in almost two decades.

To be sure, more borrowing costs are poised to follow after Wednesday’s rate increase. Credit cards, auto loans and home equity lines of credit (HELOCs) all get more expensive when the Fed’s benchmark goes up. Fixed-rate borrowers won’t feel a difference, but if you carry variable-rate debt, your interest payments could rise within one to two billing cycles. Borrowing costs for new loans could start to increase immediately. From an investing perspective, markets may also be choppy. The stock market doesn’t always take to rate-hiking cycles well.

Your destination, however, might not need to change. If the past decade has shown anything, it’s that there will be cycles of higher rates and lower rates, and the best investing strategies are built for the long haul, namely through diversification. If you’re carrying credit card debt, a rate hike also doesn’t change the urgency of paying that off. The average credit card APR was already double-digits.

Like a stop-and-go taxi ride, though, shifting between monetary policy cycles can leave someone feeling disoriented. Renters might be stuck on the sidelines for longer; borrowers who are locked in a mortgage rate that’s stretching their budgets once again have fewer opportunities to refinance. A few months ago you might have been planning your finances for a lower-rate era. Now you’re left bracing for higher — for even longer.

Step into Carl Verheyen’s home in Topanga, California, and you’ll see his lifelong commitment to the guitar everywhere you look. “There’s about 30 or 40 guitars under there,” he says, opening a closet door under a staircase. The unused fifth bathroom? “Twenty-two in the shower.” Nearby, shelves hold his 18 solo albums, CDs from a career that’s included sessions with Dolly Parton, Miley Cyrus and the Bee Gees, and magazines with published articles about him. “My ego shelf,” he says with a smile.

Verheyen has a test for every electric guitar he considers buying: Hold it by the headstock at the end of the neck, pluck an open B string, then feel and listen to how the wood vibrates. The guitar speaks or it doesn’t. His collection includes three vintage Fender Stratocasters — one from 1958 and two from the early 1960s. Those vintage Strats have become one of the most recognizable guitar shapes in music: a slim, contoured body with a narrow waist and two sweeping horns reaching up around the neck.

Then there’s his signature model: a Strat-style guitar built by LsL Instruments, a husband-and-wife shop in Santa Clarita, California. It’s the result of a failed courtship with Fender. In 2009, Fender flew Verheyen to its headquarters, then in Scottsdale, Arizona, hoping to build a model based on his 1961 seafoam-green Stratocaster, one of the guitars Verheyen played in arenas with Supertramp. Over a martini lunch, the team proposed a $6,000 limited-edition replica — what Verheyen dismissed as a “lawyer guitar.” He wanted something players could afford. He wanted to work side by side with a builder. Fender put him in touch with its factory in Corona, California. The Corona people referred him back to Scottsdale, saying he needed to deal with corporate first. “It was so lame, I just gave up,” he says.

Then Lance Lerman of LsL called. He listened to what Verheyen wanted and built it — scratches, nicks and Verheyen-specified adjustments included — a near replica of the 1961 Strat that Fender also wanted to re-create. Now, watching Fender and its lawyers threatening LsL and scores of other builders, Verheyen says he’s unlikely to play his Fenders much in public. In the studio, sure, but onstage? “I’m just not sure I want to be seen playing Fender publicly,” he says.
For Fender, the Stratocaster’s greatest triumph has become its greatest vulnerability, Paul Sloan writes. Go inside the battle to stop competitors from riffing on its designs. (🎁)

items.title: US to Sell F-35s to Saudi Arabia in $24.3 Billion Deal
body: The State Department notified Congress that it plans to sell Saudi Arabia up to 48 F-35 warplanes in a first-time sale that could be worth as much as $24.3 billion.

“This proposed sale will support the foreign policy and national security objectives of the United States by improving the security of a major non-NATO ally that is a force for political stability and economic progress in the Gulf region,” the State Department said in a statement.
The sale of the Lockheed Martin Corp. fighter jet to Saudi Arabia has been in the works for a number of years.
Israel, which operates the jets and has flown them in combat missions, has expressed concerns about the possible sale — the first to a Middle East nation other than Israel.

President Donald Trump signaled in November the US would sell F-35s to the Kingdom, offering Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman a prize he’s long cherished, ahead of a visit to the White House that month.
Read More: Trump Approves F-35 Jets for Saudi Arabia Ahead of MBS Visit
F-35 aircraft are the world’s most advanced jets, and the Saudis have long wanted them, according to officials familiar with the negotiations.

The F-35’s advanced technology is also one reason why the deal may be challenged. Saudi Arabia has deepened ties with China in recent years, and there are concerns that selling them to Riyadh could allow Beijing to end up gaining access to some of the most sophisticated American military systems.
Read more: Why Selling US F-35 Jets to Saudi Arabia Is Fraught: QuickTake

“Saudi Arabia and China have a history of security cooperation, including combined military exercises,” said Justin Leopold-Cohen, a research analyst with the Foundation for Defense of Democracies. “That should be a deal breaker for Washington, as it could lead to exposing the planes to unnecessary risks.”

Under American law, Israel is also guaranteed weapons needed to maintain its “qualitative military edge” over Arab nations. US officials have said they can provide that assurance regardless of F-35 sales, without specifying publicly what they would offer Israel.

“We should always be a few rungs above. And if they give them the F-35, we’ll get the B-2, for argument’s sake,” Eli Cohen, a member of Israel’s security cabinet, told Channel 14 in November, referring to the stealth bomber used by the US to attack Iranian nuclear sites in June.
The “Israeli edge must be preserved and insisted on,” he said.

items.title: Russia Ties Nestle, Auchan Asset Grabs to Europe Aid for Ukraine
body: Russia seized control of the local assets of Swiss food giant Nestle SA and French supermarket chain Auchan, placing their stakes in Russian businesses under temporary administration.

President Vladimir Putin ordered stakes in the assets to be handed to a company called AO L.E.V. Menedzhment, according to a decree published Thursday on the country’s official legal portal. The little known entity was registered in 2024 in Moscow, according to Russian registry data.
Russia has used the temporary-management mechanism since 2023 to take control of assets belonging to companies from countries it considers “unfriendly.”

More than 1,000 companies have left Russia or scaled back their operations since the Kremlin’s war on Ukraine began in 2022, according to the Yale School of Management. Still, many multinational companies, including PepsiCo Inc. and Mondelez International Inc., continue to operate in the country.

The Russian authorities previously imposed temporary administration on assets belonging to foreign companies including Danone SA and Carlsberg A/S, with some of those businesses later sold to Kremlin-linked owners.

Nestle, which has operated in Russia since the 1990s, scaled back its business after 2022, suspending some brands and halting non-essential imports and exports, advertising and capital investment. Earlier this year, a little-known company, KS Logistics, asked Putin to place Nestlé’s local entities under temporary management, the Kommersant newspaper reported, a move that could potentially pave the way for a change in ownership.
Nestle told the outlet then it hadn’t received any inquiries from Russian authorities and that its offices and factories continued to operate.
Nestle wasn’t able to comment immediately on today’s developments, while an Auchan representative didn’t immediately have a comment on them.

Auchan was among the early wave of major Western retailers to expand into Russia, opening its first store there in 2002. The retailer went on to build a sprawling presence and now operates 230 supermarkets and hypermarkets across the country, according to its website.

items.title: What the Bassman-Simplify Asset Management Clash Tells Us About the ETF Industry
body: Welcome to ETF IQ, a weekly newsletter dedicated to the $22.5 trillion global ETF industry. I’m Bloomberg News reporter Isabelle Lee, in for Katie Greifeld.

Everybody loves a little drama. But the escalation of a clash between bond veteran Harley Bassman and his former employer Simplify Asset Management raises questions for the broader ETF industry, particularly around how asset growth is measured and the complexity of fee structures when funds invest in other funds.

Bassman, in a letter to Simplify’s shareholders, said he’s “deeply concerned” about management and oversight of the firm. A recap for those who haven’t been following: He’s separately suing Simplify over the compensation he says he’s owed (which the company disputes). He also remains the ETF issuer’s fourth-biggest common shareholder.Bassman laid out several questions for the firm’s board. The letter indicates that he thinks Simplify is overstating its growth, charging investors fees it shouldn’t, and overriding strategies to make what he describes as idiosyncratic bets, my colleague Justina Lee reported.

Simplify has more than $13 billion in assets under management, with over 40 funds spanning strategies as varied as private credit and Chinese commodities. But around 38% of that top-line figure traces back to other Simplify ETFs, according to data compiled by Bloomberg. Bassman called this “Russian-doll stacking.”
“Many of these questions point to a disturbing lack of management and fiduciary oversight which, if left uncorrected, will continue to damage Simplify and our investment,” Bassman wrote.

Regardless of whether Bassman is right, it’s worth assessing whether the ETF industry’s rapid expansion has created structures that make asset growth, fees and investment decisions harder for investors to evaluate at a glance.

Paul Kim, co-founder and chief executive officer of Simplify, described the letter as “mostly a one-sided narrative from an ex-employee.” He also said the firm has “grown by helping our clients with their portfolio objectives.”
He also said the Simplify products invested in the firm’s own funds are primarily used for cash management or fund-of-funds strategies.
We tend to think of the ETF flywheel pretty simply: Great performance attracts attention, attention attracts assets, assets attract even more attention, and so on.
Only, sometimes, it doesn’t seem to work that way.

Take the Breakwave Tanker Shipping ETF. BWET has surged about 4,900% over the past year, and, on a year-to-date basis, is the world’s best-performing ETF, according to Bloomberg Intelligence’s Eric Balchunas and Rebecca Sin. That’s thanks to exposure to futures tracking the cost of shipping oil from the Middle East.
Even so, cash hasn’t exactly poured in. BWET ranks outside the top 1,000 ETFs by inflows. It has raked in only $134 million year to date.

“This unusual gap suggests an ETF can perhaps be too shiny for investors,” Balchunas and Sin wrote. “Obscure exposure, limited investor familiarity, and a rally that may already look extended can outweigh even eye-popping performance.”
Both describe BWET’s performance as “unprecedented” for an ETF, especially one that’s not a leveraged fund.
So what’s going on? Well, a couple of things.

BWET holds futures tied to the cost of transporting crude oil from the Middle East and West Africa to China and other destinations. It’s the only freight-futures ETF focused exclusively on crude-oil tankers, according to Bloomberg Intelligence, making it sensitive to disruptions to global oil shipping because of the war in Iran.
Another potential reason: fees. BWET charges a 3.5% total expense ratio, roughly six times the average ETF fee, according to Bloomberg Intelligence.
And then there is timing.

“Although the ETF’s positions established before the war have driven extraordinary short-term returns, once those contracts expire, the fund will face the same uncertainty as other investors over the duration and outcome of the conflict,” Balchunas and Sin wrote. “After such an extreme rally, investors may be reluctant to chase further gains.”
Nate Miller, vice president of product development at Amplify ETFs (BWET’s issuer) said flows have been modest because investors see freight markets as a tactical allocation.

“In some ways, this is similar to where Bitcoin was in its early years,” he said. “The investment case was compelling to some, but broad adoption took time because the asset class was unfamiliar, difficult to access, and outside most investors’ traditional frameworks. Specialized exposures often need time, education, and growing investor awareness before flows begin to catch up with performance.”

This case just highlights that in a hyper-competitive ETF market, where almost anything can be packaged into an investment product, getting traders to actually care — and stick around — is becoming a much harder problem to solve.

Bloomberg Head of Games Joel Weber put Scarlet Fu, Eric Balchunas and me to the test. I’m happy to announce I did not get zero! Take it for yourself and find out what you score. Answers are at the end of this newsletter.
Which of these BlackRock ETFs has seen the biggest outflows so far this year?
Which ETF will be the first new ETF to launch on the Texas Stock Exchange?
Mutual funds that convert into ETFs are having a moment. What percentage saw their flows improve in the year after converting?

David van Adelsberg, founding partner & CEO at Irrational Capital, stopped by the ETF IQ show to discuss the Harbor Human Capital Factor US Large Cap ETF (HAPI), which tracks companies based on the happiness of their employees. How fun!
Top holdings include Apple, Amazon, Microsoft, Nvidia, Alphabet and Meta Platforms, according to the firm’s website.
Catch ETF IQ next week, live on Monday at noon Eastern. Catch it on Bloomberg Television’s ETF IQ, on the Bloomberg Terminal at TV GO.
IQ Test Answers: IVV, PWRX, 78%
