items.title: Trump Pulls Mullin's Pick to Lead ICE After Republican Pushback
body: The Trump administration has withdrawn the president’s nominee to lead US Immigration and Customs Enforcement, a setback for Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin that leaves the agency leading a mass deportation push without a permanent director.

Lance Schroyer, an Oklahoma state trooper and ally of Mullin, was nominated to lead ICE in June. The nomination stalled after Senator Rand Paul, a Kentucky Republican who leads the Senate Homeland Security Committee, pressed the Department of Homeland Security for more information about the deadly shootings of two US citizens in January.
The White House, which didn’t immediately respond to a request for comment, withdrew Schroyer’s nomination on Thursday.
ICE has been without a confirmed director since the end of the Obama administration.

Schroyer had previously acted as a senior advisor to Mullin, a former Republican senator from Oklahoma. During his time with the highway patrol Schroyer also oversaw the state’s agreements with ICE under the 287(g) program, which offers local authorities immigration enforcement authority.
The program has rapidly expanded under the Trump administration and helped ICE increase its arrests in recent months, hitting monthly records of about 50,000 in July and August.
Read more: US to Offer $1,000 Bonuses to Police for Help Arresting Migrants

ICE has been in the spotlight since the start of the Trump administration after the president campaigned on a harsh crackdown that would lead to millions of deportations. Since Trump took office, ICE has recorded more than 630,000 arrests. Between January 2025 and July 11 the agency has deported roughly 590,000 people, according to ICE data.

Agents have also repeatedly clashed with protestors and drawn criticism for heavy handed tactics and arresting people without criminal records. Federal agents have shot and killed several people, including US citizens Renee Good and Alex Pretti in Minneapolis during a months-long surge there.

items.title: CFTC to Expand Crypto, Predictions Trading Via Online Platforms
body: The Commodity Futures Trading Commission moved to expand crypto and prediction market trading via online platforms by exempting some software providers from registration requirements.

In staff guidance issued Thursday, the CFTC said that “passive software” providers that are partnering with regulated entities wouldn’t face enforcement penalties for failing to register as brokers, so long as they never take custody of a user’s assets.

Historically, companies that solicited or accepted trade orders, sent them to futures commission merchants and were compensated through fees or commissions would have to register as brokers. In March, the CFTC granted a no-action letter to Phantom Technologies Inc. waiving that requirement. Phantom has partnered with Kalshi to bring predictions trading through its more than 20 million crypto wallet holders.
Phantom laid the groundwork for platforms that never take custody of users assets or make decisions for their trades, Chief Executive Officer Brandon Millman said in a statement.
“This is how it should work: software built to protect consumers, paired with regulated partners, giving more people safe access to the financial services they want,” Millman added.
It’s a business model that has been embraced by others in the prediction markets industry as well, including Crypto.com and ProphetX, both of which operate CFTC-registered platforms.

“You could use this to put a prediction market basically anywhere,” said Aaron Brogan, founder of Brogan Law, which specializes in emerging companies and regulated businesses. “Anything that can trade on a DCM could, in principle, be covered by this,” he said, referring to designated contract markets.
The CFTC’s new guidance is in place until the effective date of an agency rulemaking or other guidance, the agency said.

The announcement comes after a group of senators from both parties blocked crypto market legislation sought by the industry on Tuesday. CFTC Chairman Michael Selig and Securities and Exchange Commission Chairman Paul Atkins have vowed to move forward with rules for the digital asset industry in the absence of legislation.

items.title: Spanish Copper Manufacturer Cunext Is Said to Consider an IPO
body: Spanish copper manufacturer Cunext Copper Industries SL is considering holding an initial public offering, according to people familiar with the matter.

Cunext, which makes power and data cables from copper and aluminum in facilities in Spain and Italy, is hiring advisers to work on the potential offering, the people said, asking not to be named as the information is private.
Founded in 1917, Cunext makes a range of specialist cabling. The firm had revenue of more than €2 billion ($2.3 billion) last year, a company official told Bloomberg.
Deliberations are ongoing and no final decisions have been made, the people said. A representative for Cunext declined to comment on the IPO plans.
Read more: Europe IPOs Must Raise $5 Billion This Fall to Beat 2025’s Haul

A potential offering would add to a pipeline of possible IPOs in Spain that includes Blackstone Inc.’s Hotel Investment Partners, which could raise around €800 million, Bloomberg reported previously. Vortex Energy-backed Ignis, which is also planning an IPO to raise as much as €600 million.
New listings have been rare in Spain in recent years. The bourse only held two IPOs this year after two major deals last year, according to data compiled by Bloomberg.

items.title: Bill to Limit College Player Transfers Nears Final Senate Vote
body: The Senate advanced a bill to limit college athletes to one school transfer during their careers and help regulate the fast-changing landscape of collegiate sports.

The bipartisan Protect College Sports Act, which also addresses a range of other issues including media rights and fee caps for agents, moved forward on a 77-22 vote Thursday. The Senate still has to vote on final passage of the measure.

The Senate is rushing to move the legislation before its members leave Washington for the midterm elections, though bill still must pass the House, which just left for a seven-week break. Senate Republican Ted Cruz of Texas and Democrat Maria Cantwell of Washington sponsored the measure amid changes that allow payers to be paid and students to perpetually transfer teams.

New Jersey Democrat Cory Booker, who played football at Stanford, excoriated the bill at length on the Senate floor as a gift to the college sports “cartel” and their wealthy donors, with athletes treated far worse than coaches, who often make millions of dollars a year.

“We’re coming in and taking away their leverage, their bargaining power,” Booker said of the athletes. “Why are you treating the college kids different than you’re treating the coaches if it’s all about the money?”

A group of athletes represented by a group called Athletes.org said in a letter this week they agree college sports needs “clear, enforceable national rules,” but lasting stability cannot come from rules imposed on athletes without being negotiated with them.

“The PCSA responds by placing a federally-imposed hard ceiling on athlete compensation while leaving every other major expense uncapped,” the group wrote. “This includes coaching salaries, coach buyouts, administrative compensation, athletic department staffing, facilities and facilities upgrades.”

Backers of the legislation say athletes still would be compensated but would be encouraged to stay at a single school for most of their university years. President Donald Trump held a college sports summit that encouraged legislation on the matter.

New York Yankees President Randy Levine, a vice chair of Trump’s college sports roundtable, said a recent incident where the Louisiana State University football program under Coach Lane Kiffin sought to add former NFL players to its roster reinforces that the system needs federal intervention.
Watch:  Yankees, Vanderbilt on the Evolution of College Sports (Video)
“Are we going to have student athletes or professional athletes?” Levine said at Bloomberg Power Players New York. “What happened with LSU has crystallized the problem.”
At the same time, colleges are racing to generate more revenue to stay competitive when recruiting and paying players.
Read More: College Sports Go Pro on Player Pay, Arenas, $50 Million Coaches
They’ve been renovating or building new stadiums and arenas with luxury amenities, showing how the new financial model in college sports looks a lot more like professional teams.

The biggest college sports conferences agreed last year to a revenue-sharing plan with players, which amounts to about $21.6 million per school for athletes across all sports for the 2026-27 academic year. The figure is expected to increase 4% each year — but could effectively more than double if the bill passes through Congress.

items.title: Venezuela Unblocks Media, Some Sites Still Dark
body: Lea en español
Venezuela began lifting years-long blocks on news websites, but some remain dark.
The easing of press censorship is the latest tentative sign of political liberalization following the US capture of Venezuelan leader Nicolás Maduro in January.

Internet providers have been instructed by the US-supported acting president, Delcy Rodríguez, to restore access to national and international news websites, the country’s telecommunications regulator said Thursday morning in a statement.
The move precedes a second round of US-backed political talks in Caracas later Thursday, where civil and political guarantees, including freedom of expression, are expected to be discussed.

At least a dozen previously blocked outlets — including Venezuelan sites El Pitazo, Runrunes and Efecto Cocuyo, as well as Colombia’s Semana and Spanish news agency EFE — had become accessible across major internet providers by early Thursday, according to digital rights group VE Sin Filtro. Most foreign news sites remain blocked, Andrés Azpurua, the NGO’s director, said via text message by mid-morning.

The move selectively dismantles a system of online censorship that expanded under Maduro and restricted access to outlets believed to be critical of his regime. More than 200 internet domains remained blocked as of earlier this month, most of them related to news, according to VE Sin Filtro.

Press freedoms deteriorated sharply during Maduro’s 13-year rule as authorities censored news websites, shuttered radio stations and used laws and regulatory pressure to target journalists and independent outlets. The press crackdown intensified around periods of political unrest and elections, pushing many Venezuelans toward social media, messaging apps and virtual private networks to access independent reporting.

The decision came hours after the government-backed Program for Peace and Democratic Coexistence recommended that Rodríguez remove restrictions on news websites following consultations with public, private and independent media.

Following Maduro’s ouster, government officials, including Rodríguez, returned to X, which Maduro had ordered blocked in the volatile aftermath of a disputed 2024 election. By late June, Venezuelans began reporting that access to the social media platform had been restored.
Read More: Venezuela’s Leader Returns to X in Reversal of Maduro’s Ban

items.title: Former Trafigura CEO Contender Hallouche Starts New Energy Firm
body: Hadi Hallouche, who helped run Trafigura Group’s oil business and was a CEO contender before departing last year, has set up a new trading firm called Oxitera SA.
The company will trade oil, liquefied natural gas and power with offices in Geneva and Houston, Hallouche, the firm’s chief executive officer, said in a statement on the company’s website.

As the war in the Middle East disrupts energy flows, commodity trading houses are once again enjoying bumper profits close to records set in the aftermath of Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine. Profits at Mercuria Energy Group and Gunvor Group have more than doubled, while Trafigura’s first-half profits saw a 173% rise.
“The commodities landscape is undergoing a tectonic shift. The strategic nature of commodities has never been clearer; and technology has never been more transformational,” Hallouche said.

One of several protégés of Trafigura founder Claude Dauphin, Hallouche was long seen as a rising star who had built the company into a significant player in liquefied natural gas trading and went on to jointly run its oil division and manage its fuel distribution business Puma Energy.

But expectations that he might become just the third CEO in the company’s history were dashed when he was dropped from Trafigura’s reconstituted executive committee in 2023. He left the firm in the middle of last year.

Hallouche is being joined in the startup by several former Trafigura senior executives. Nicolas Marsac, who was head of Trafigura’s structured finance, is the new company’s chief financial officer, and Margaux Moore is the chief of staff. Career oil trader Conor McFadden is Oxitera’s head of North America, while Laura Tolub is joining as head of European gas and power.

items.title: Germany Plans Sharp Expansion of Gas Tender to Boost Storage
body: Germany is planning to sharply expand an existing tender that pays suppliers to keep gas available for winter, in a move designed to encourage traders to fill the country’s unusually low storage sites.

The government and the nation’s gas-market manager Trading Hub Europe GmbH intend to increase upcoming tenders by 5 billion cubic meters or roughly 50 terawatt-hours, according to a person familiar with the matter. That’s enough extra gas to fill about 20% of storage.

Germany’s sites are just 56% full, the lowest seasonal level since records began in 2009. The tenders give traders an incentive to put more gas into reserves without the government buying it directly. Suppliers that sell THE an option to call on gas this winter need to ensure they can deliver it — encouraging them to inject gas into caverns now and keep it there.

Stockpiling has been particularly difficult this year because the Middle East conflict has driven up near-term gas prices compared to winter, making summer injections uneconomic. European gas futures have more than doubled since the start of the war and earlier this month reached their highest since late 2022.

The Economy Ministry plans to expand THE’s regular tenders for so-called long-term options, or LTOs, Bloomberg reported Wednesday. If completely filled, the additional 5 billion cubic meters would represent a substantial increase on the volumes contracted so far this year, the person said, asking not to be identified discussing private deliberations.
During the last heating season, THE held two LTO tenders, paying traders about €110 million ($126 million) to hold 21 terawatt-hours of gas in storage — equivalent to about 8% of Germany’s capacity.
THE hasn’t called on any of those contracts this year, a company spokesperson said. The last time it tapped LTO volumes was during the energy crisis in late 2022.

The mechanism is distinct from the emergency intervention used during the crisis, when THE spent billions buying gas to fill storage. LTOs are ordinarily used to ensure gas is available to address regional grid bottlenecks.

The size of the tenders is calculated by Germany’s gas-grid operators and agreed jointly with THE, according to another person familiar with the matter. A decision on the additional volumes could come as early as Monday.

The Association of Transmission System Operators Gas didn’t comment on ongoing discussions with authorities. A spokesperson for THE said that it will publish the bidding documents “shortly”. The Economy Ministry referred questions to THE.

“Given the current low gas storage levels, it makes sense for the market manager to issue calls for bids, thereby incentivizing traders to inject gas”, said Andreas Schroeder, Head of Energy Analytics at research firm ICIS. The alternatives could be considerably more expensive, he said.
Industry group BDEW also backed the approach, saying LTOs can help secure sufficient supplies without displacing the market’s normal role in filling storage.

items.title: Trump DOJ Blasts States' Legal Challenges to Major US Mergers
body: The US Justice Department official overseeing antitrust enforcement criticized state attorneys general who have sued to block major corporate mergers the agency had already cleared, saying the federal government should take the lead on deals involving national businesses.

“A state represents only the citizens within its borders, and when the federal government makes the determination that a merger is in the public interest of the entire nation, including the citizens of all 50 states, a state cannot go to court and claim the public interest” supports it, “especially when other states and the federal government disagree,” said Associate Attorney General Stanley Woodward, the No. 3 Justice Department official.

“When a merger harms local markets, we want the states in the room,” Woodward said at an antitrust conference in New York in his first public remarks on the job. “When it is national, we expect to lead.”

The Trump administration has been at odds with dozens of state attorneys general on several antitrust cases this year. That includes two deals in which the states sued to block deals the Justice Department cleared — Paramount Skydance Corp.’s proposed acquisition of Warner Bros. Discovery Inc. and Nexstar Media Group Inc.’s purchase of Tegna Inc. Both trials are scheduled for next year.

While the Nexstar deal is being challenged by a bipartisan group of attorneys general, only Democrats have signed on to the case against Paramount. The Republican attorneys general from Iowa and Montana have separately filed a long-shot US Supreme Court action seeking to block that pending merger case.

On Tuesday, the Justice Department weighed in on the states’ challenge of the Paramount deal, saying they should have to post a bond in order to move forward with their case. The company has asked that the states post a nearly $1.9 billion bond pending the outcome of the trial, scheduled for March.

Litigation by the states has gone beyond just mergers. After the DOJ reached a surprise settlement with Live Nation Entertainment Inc. and its Ticketmaster unit earlier this year, the states pushed ahead with the legal fight and won a jury verdict saying the company illegally monopolized the live events industry and overcharged for tickets. The states are pushing for a breakup of the company.

Woodward – who is overseeing the antitrust division after President Donald Trump removed his first antitrust chief in February – characterized the state actions as “political resistance to the Trump administration,” saying they have sought to “weaponize” the US merger laws that require companies to hold off on closing deals until after a federal antitrust review.

The states have been “sticking their feet in the door at the last minute rather than pursuing their interests earlier or seeking post-closing review of a transaction,” he said. “This type of gamesmanship should not be permitted by federal courts.”

Colorado Attorney General Phil Weiser, a Democrat who is running for state governor, this week claimed the Trump administration was an “inconsistent and unreliable enforcer of antitrust law.” He said the current merger review system “was set up on the premise the federal government would be acting on the merits.” That doesn’t reflect “the realities we’re in,” he said.

Weiser called on Congress to amend the antitrust laws to allow state attorneys general access to the same information the Justice Department receives about mergers and potentially provide funding to the states for enforcement. Woodward, for his part, called Weiser’s criticisms “misplaced laments” and suggested that Congress could instead change the law to give the federal government sole authority over national transactions while leaving local ones to the states.

items.title: Airtel Money Is Said to Trim IPO Size Ahead of Deal Kick Off
body: Airtel Money’s owners are considering raising less money than previously sought in the company’s initial public offering, a listing process that could start as soon as next week, according to people familiar with the matter.

The money transfer and payments company’s IPO is now expected to raise at least $800 million in London, the people said, asking not to be identified as the information is private. That is substantially lower than the previously targeted deal size of $1.5 billion to $2 billion that Bloomberg News reported in April.

Airtel Money is now considering a valuation of $8 billion to $9 billion to align with technology stock valuations, the people said, lower than the $10 billion sought previously. The firm’s valuation in the offering was reduced following feedback from investors, some of the people said.
Airtel Money is part of Airtel Africa Plc, with other investors like Mastercard Inc. and the Qatar Investment Authority holding minority stakes, according to its website.

Even at a reduced size, the deal would be one of the larger offerings held on the LSE in recent years, delivering a boost to the exchange. London’s bourse has been experiencing a prolonged drought of first time offerings since 2022, a trend that has led to reforms of its listing rules.
The filing could come early next week, and the unit is looking to start trading on the LSE in October, the people said.
The details of the offering, including the deal size and timing, could still change, the people said. A representative for Airtel Africa declined to comment.

Airtel Africa is mostly owned by Indian billionaire Sunil Mittal’s Bharti Enterprises Ltd and is Africa’s third-largest wireless carrier. It has long been planning an IPO of Airtel Money after years of rapid growth.

Airtel Africa’s mobile money segment reported revenue of $1.4 billion for the year ending on March 31, a 28% increase on the year before, according to an investor presentation. The company’s shares have traded flat this year, currently up just 0.4% through Thursday’s close.

items.title: Dallas Has Capital-Markets Moments With Funding, IPOs and a Tug of War
body: Welcome to Bloomberg’s Texas Edition — covering all the industries and people driving America’s second-largest economy, from finance and oil to tech and sports. Join us each week for an inside look at Texas through a Bloomberg lens.   Sign up here   if you’re not already on the list.
Dallas is making a statement in capital markets.
It’s a little subtler than the big-ticket announcements like Morgan Stanley joining Goldman Sachs with an office campus near downtown. But one deal at a time, the headlines are there.

Bloomberg’s Bailey Lipschultz broke the news that Addison-based Firehawk Aerospace, which builds rocket motors, is in talks to raise funds at a $1.25 billion valuation. Firehawk’s investors include 1789 Capital, the venture firm where Donald Trump Jr. is a partner, and the firm is expected to participate in the funding round, people familiar with the matter said. 1789 Capital led a Series C round for Firehawk last year.

The past few days also have been pivotal for the Texas Stock Exchange. Bloomberg scooped Texas Capital Bancshares’ switch from Nasdaq to join the Dallas-based exchange. It was the fifth company to make the move.

“We’ve been considering it since the day we knew it was going to come to fruition,” Texas Capital CEO Rob Holmes told Bloomberg’s Joe Lovinger — just ahead of Ruston, Louisiana-based Origin Bancorp becoming the first out-of-state listing.

The list goes on and on. Dallas-based Copart just agreed to its biggest-ever acquisition, at $1.9 billion. Dallas PE firm Trive Capital saw Lyntris, created by the combination of two of its portfolio companies, go public last month. Coppell-based Csquare, which owns and operates more than 60 data center sites in the US, Canada and UK, raised $1.05 billion in a July IPO.

And that doesn’t even include the three-country tussle over troubled nickel and cobalt producer Sherritt International, which includes two Dallas-based investors on opposite sides of the trade. Oil tycoon Albert Huddleston is the latest suitor for the company, which was already in talks with the family office of Dallas real estate executive Ray Washburne. Toronto-based Sherritt is among the top foreign investors in Cuba. If that tug of war wasn’t intriguing enough, the contest also involves Citigroup and Office Depot. Thanks to M&A going back almost 100 years, those companies hold long-dormant claims on Cuban property seized in the 1959 revolution.
Texas Capital CEO Rob Holmes joined Romaine Bostick and Isabelle Lee on BTV’s The Close after the bank’s announcement of its listing shift to the Texas Stock Exchange.

Houston’s oil-capital status got a boost this week as the host city for the Group of 20 energy summit. Venezuela sent a team as the White House seeks closer ties with Caracas, though the officials weren’t part of formal talks. Chevron said its $7 billion expansion there will be funded by local production, not outside cash. While that meeting held the focus, ExxonMobil Holdings quietly held talks with Venezuelan officials in Caracas about re-entering the country, according to a scoop by Kevin Crowley, Jennifer A. Dlouhy, Ari Natter and Eric Martin. Meanwhile, energy investment banker Dan Pickering cautioned against getting too enthusiastic about foreign drillers’ new access to Venezuelan fields. Costs and a history of nationalizations loom large over future deals, Pickering said at another Houston conference.

Texas’ Railroad Commission race was thrust into the national spotlight after Republican nominee Bo French’s racist X post denigrating non-white UT fans celebrating the Longhorns’ stunning comeback against Ohio State. French, who posted a photo showing mostly brown-skinned students in UT spirit wear, stood by his online remarks afterward, but Texas GOP figures including Senator John Cornyn condemned him. Governor Greg Abbott distanced himself from the comments, saying, “That is not my message,” but didn’t denounce French. Democratic nominee Jon Rosenthal, a Houston state representative, said he had his best fundraising day of the campaign after the uproar.

Sysco’s $29.1 billion acquisition of Jetro Restaurant Depot is still making news in capital markets. The Houston-based company plans a $1 billion share sale to partially fund the takeover, with the stock on offer at prices of $80.20 to $81.90. That’s as much as a 4% discount to Monday’s closing price. The managers on the offering read like a Wall Street A-list: Goldman Sachs Group and Toronto-Dominion Bank are leading the charge, joined by Bank of America, JPMorgan Chase and Wells Fargo.

One up-arrow for JD Vance, one down-arrow for his boss, according to David Drucker.  Donald Trump’s performance at last week’s Republican convention earned a harsh review from Drucker, who called the president “a generational political talent” out of office but “an incompetent campaign doppelganger as president.” Trump’s twin prime-time speeches in Dallas included mockery of Americans’ concerns, hardly a winning strategy, Drucker wrote. Vance fared better in the estimation of Nia-Malika Henderson, who wrote that even Trump — famously disinclined to share the spotlight — is appreciative of the vice president’s chops. Dallas showed him to good advantage, and she added: “Come 2028, Vance will be a tough out.”

It’s that time of year again. Ahead of the State Fair of Texas opening Sept. 25 in Dallas, the all-important question is: What are the new foods this year? I got you covered.You will obviously need a drink. You can start with the “All Shook Up”, a milkshake featuring banana pudding ice cream, a peanut butter cookie and bacon. Because of course a milkshake has bacon. Deep-fried appetizers include ranch dressing and bourbon banana bread. There are entrees like the focaccia alla porchetta e salsa verde, fried-green-tomato lobster bruschetta and Texas brisket pierogies. Top it off with triple-chocolate flautas for dessert. This is just a small part of the list. Have a great weekend.

Calling all senior executives across capital markets, institutional investment, private equity and emerging growth companies. Bloomberg Invest is coming to Dallas on Oct. 27. Join us for exclusive conversations with TXSE CEO Jim Lee and the NYSE and Nasdaq, Carlyle’s David Rubenstein alongside Ross Perot Jr. discussing real estate and Texas’ most prominent financial leaders, including JPMorgan’s Elaine Agather, Arctos’ Ian Charles, and Goldman Sachs’ Aasem Khalil. Space is limited—register your interest to attend today.

items.title: Merz Says US Friendship Since War 'Probably Over' for Now
body: German Chancellor Friedrich Merz said the era of “unconditional” ties between the US and Europe built since World War II are over, at least for now, the latest pronouncement of a breakdown in relations under Donald Trump’s presidency.

“This era of unconditional transatlantic friendship is probably over for the foreseeable future,” Merz told party members in Berlin on Thursday. “On the other side of the Atlantic, we are seeing a change in political attitudes, a change in the assessment of the transatlantic alliance, which we might not have thought possible.”

Merz, giving a stump speech at his conservative party headquarters ahead of the Berlin state election on Sunday, contrasted the current US relationship to past visits by American presidents to the German capital, citing famous speeches by John F. Kennedy and Ronald Reagan.

His comments came the same day that he spoke on the phone with Trump, where the two “emphasized the special bond between Germans and Americans,” according to a German government spokesman. The pair also discussed US efforts to end Russia’s war against Ukraine, as well as the ongoing trade friction in the Strait of Hormuz and Red Sea.

Merz’ speech came as Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney welcomed an overture to become an “associate member” of the European Union this week. Trump responded by threatening a new round of tariffs against the 27-member bloc if he deems the new relationship to be harmful to the US.

Trump lauded a shock victory by Germany’s far-right Alternative for Germany in a state election earlier this month, an event that’s shaken the country’s political establishment and raised calls for Merz to step aside.

Merz has a track record of provoking the Trump administration with his rhetoric. In April, he told a group of school students that US negotiators seeking a way out of the war with Iran were being “humiliated.” The US president responded with an announcement of the withdrawal of some 5,000 troops from the country.

The comments echo those made by then-Chancellor Angela Merkel, who in May 2017, during Trump’s first term, told a rally that reliable relationships forged since World War II “are to some extent over.” The comments triggered global attention.

items.title: Poland Says Russia Plans to Strike Ukraine's NATO Allies
body: Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk warned that Russia plans to launch “hybrid-style” drone and missile strikes against nations supporting Ukraine, including NATO-member Poland, as the war enters its most crucial phase.

The Kremlin’s main goal now, as supported by evidence gathered by intelligence services, is to destroy Ukraine’s economy and logistics and weaken NATO’s resolve by attacks on its member states, Tusk said in parliament on Thursday. It’s the “most likely scenario,” the premier told lawmakers.

Poland, as a key conduit for aid to Ukraine, has suffered a spate of suspicious incidents, with multiple cyberattacks on public utilities like water, energy infrastructure and hospitals, and damage to the rail line between Warsaw and the Ukrainian border attributed to Russian intelligence. A Russian missile crashed in eastern Poland in late July.

“There is a real risk that drones or other types of missiles may fly into the territory of one or more NATO countries on the eastern flank, even cause destruction,” Tusk said. Russia’s “official narrative will be that this is an accident and that there is no reason for anyone to think about any response from NATO.”

His comments were made hours before he sets out on a visit to Ukraine. They come as Moscow has recently intensified attacks against Ukraine, including at targets close to the Polish border, while NATO jets shot down a drone of Russian origin over Lithuania on Tuesday.

“Sustained, very frequent and intense attacks are expected on six major Ukrainian cities, including the destruction of warehouses, all types of products essential for the country’s defense, and, as we have witnessed very strongly in recent weeks, the railway infrastructure,” Tusk said.

items.title: Bank of England Holds Rates, Overhauls Gilt Sales Plan
body: The Bank of England held interest rates at 3.75% today but warned that a hike may be necessary if inflationary pressures intensify as a result of the conflict in the Middle East. Six of nine policymakers chose to leave the level unchanged, including Governor Andrew Bailey, as the committee split along the same lines as in their last meeting in July.

Bailey said the global energy shock so far has had a limited effect on prices and wages in the UK. “But the longer this volatility persists, the bigger the impact it will have on inflation, and the more likely it is we will need to raise Bank rate,” the governor added.

Alongside the decision came an announcement that the BOE is scrapping plans to sell long-dated gilts as part of a major overhaul of its quantitative tightening program that will see the £488 billion ($650 billion) portfolio unwound by 2034. Borrowing costs dipped after the announcement. The yield on 30-year bonds fell more than 10 basis points, the biggest drop in four months, after touching the highest level since 1998 recently. Two-year yields, more sensitive to monetary policy, also dipped.

Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney called for a closer alliance with the European Union in a bid to establish a more united front to ward off intimidation from world powers like the US and China. Carney welcomed a speech made by European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen, when she proposed that Canada become the first “associate member” of the EU.

“We do not seek power to dominate others,” Carney told European lawmakers in Strasbourg, France, today. “On the contrary, we are pursuing resilience so no one can control our open markets, impair our sovereignty, threaten our territorial integrity, or undermine our freedoms, our democracies, our rule of law.”

Turkish officials are trying to stop a meltdown at some of the country’s most prominent asset managers from infecting the wider financial industry. Regulators announced a wave of measures today to stem the turmoil. These include plans to liquidate about $20 billion in funds run by Tera Portfoy and others, as well as criminal complaints against dozens of people and trading bans over alleged share-price manipulation.

Several top finance executives were detained while others were given a travel ban. The developments have put a spotlight on the risks created by Turkey’s fast-growing fund industry, where some managers built large positions in relatively illiquid shares. At the center of that has been Tera Portfoy, an asset manager founded by Emre Tezmen with about 730 billion liras ($15 billion). The initial reaction in the broader stock market was positive, with the main index steadying after a three-day selloff that wiped almost 10% off the benchmark.

Some of the biggest figures in artificial intelligence gathered in Scotland today for a meeting convened by Britain’s King Charles III. The summit was focused on the mounting risks of AI. While executives didn’t make public commitments, some address the safety concerns directy.

“Those of us building AI must test systems rigorously,” Nvidia Chief Executive Officer Jensen Huang said in brief remarks. “When a product is not safe enough, we should hold it back.” OpenAI’s Chief Financial Officer Sarah Friar and Google DeepMind co-founder Demis Hassabis were also in attendance at at Dumfries House, along with leaders from other technology companies, nonprofits and educational institutions.

Sweden’s center-left opposition bloc won the tight general election held Sunday by a narrow margin. The result prompted Prime Minister Ulf Kristersson to resign and close off the prospect of the far right entering government for now.

A final tally of late votes and overseas ballots was completed today, giving the Social Democrat-led bloc 176 seats against 173 for the current premier and his allies. Just over 50,000 votes separated the sides. Social Democrat leader Magdalena Andersson is now expected to begin what could be tricky talks with allies who disagree with each other over key areas from tax policy to the future of nuclear power.

The world’s banks allocated 15% more capital to the energy sector last year than in 2024, arranging and underwriting deals worth $2.3 trillion, according to a study by BloombergNEF. Against a backdrop of rising demand spurred by AI data centers, cooling technologies and the proliferation of electric vehicles, banks stepped up low-carbon financing by 16%, with such deals reaching a five-year high, BNEF wrote today. Deals backing oil, gas and coal, meanwhile, rose 13% last year, it said.

The study maps out the role played by the global financial system in enabling the low-carbon transition. The headline figures disguise significant regional differences, though. For example, Wall Street banks trail their counterparts in Europe by a wide margin.

items.title: Florida Republican Knocks Trump for Betraying Hispanic Voters
body: Maria Elvira Salazar, a US House Republican representing Miami, told President Donald Trump that some of his immigration efforts have gone “too far” as she battles to retain her seat in a district heavily impacted by the administration’s policies.

Salazar, who has been in Congress since 2021 and was endorsed by Trump, said the president was alienating many of his own supporters in a 30-second ad filmed in front of the White House. She warned Trump to “be careful” of what his advisers are telling him about immigration policy.

“In July, 50% of the 50,000 people that were detained had no criminal record,” the 64-year-old former Spanish-language television anchor said. “The same Hispanics who helped you get to the White House in 2024 feel betrayed today.”

Trump won Miami-Dade County in the 2024 general election with support from large sections of the Cuban and Venezuelan communities that have settled in the area. His tough-on-socialism approach resonates with many who have immigrated to South Florida over generations, but those same neighborhoods are grappling with harsh immigration raids and deportations that are spooking residents and hitting businesses.
Read More: Republicans at Risk of Losing Latino Support Ahead of Midterms
Neither White House officials nor the Department of Homeland Security immediately responded to a request for comment.

ICE agents made about 12,600 arrests across Florida in June and July. About half of those people had no criminal history, according to arrest data compiled by the Deportation Data Project at the University of California at Berkeley and UCLA. Roughly 16% of those arrested had criminal convictions, according to the arrest data.

Florida has become a key state partner in the Trump administration’s mass deportation campaign. State law mandates that all 67 county jails participate in the federal 287(g) program that grants immigration authority to local officials. Statewide there are more than 300 such agreements in place, including with the Florida Department of Law Enforcement and the Florida Highway Patrol.

Last year Republican Governor Ron DeSantis opened a tent jail at a decommissioned airfield in the Everglades, naming the facility Alligator Alcatraz. The jail faced multiple lawsuits alleging inhumane conditions and was shuttered earlier this year. A Homeland Security inspector general report released earlier this month found that the facility violated multiple detention standards, including holding migrants in cramped and at times unsanitary conditions. Someone detainees were at times held metal cages the size of a phone booth. The cages were described to inspectors as “calming areas,” the inspectors found.
The IG report noted that while the facility was owned and operated by Florida it operated with oversight from US Immigration and Customs Enforcement.
Salazar is being challenged by fellow Latino Eliott Rodriguez, a political newcomer who also built his career as a local news anchor.
In a statement, Rodriguez scoffed at Salazar’s complaints, saying she sought Trump’s endorsement and supported Alligator Alcatraz.

“She voted for all this. She gave Trump the money and the tools to do this,” Rodriguez said in his statement. “Now, just 47 days before the mid-term election she is trying to convince voters that she disagrees with Donald Trump’s inhumane practices on undocumented people who have no criminal record?”

While the Cook Political Report rates Florida’s 27th District as “likely Republican,” Rodriguez’s campaign team released a survey on Monday that showed the two candidates polling at about 45% each. Democrats need to flip just a handful of seats to win control of the House.
South Florida has one of the biggest immigrant populations in the US. Recent decisions to end Temporary Protection Status for Venezuelans and Haitians have drawn criticism from local officials.
Trump won Salazar’s district — where roughly three in four residents identify as Latino — by 15 percentage points in 2024, while the congresswoman beat her Democratic opponent by 21 points.

Salazar has been sounding the alarm on Trump’s immigration policies for months, citing the December election of Miami’s first Democratic mayor in almost three decades as evidence of her concerns. That loss for the party was an early warning sign of what could be coming, Salazar said in an interview with Bloomberg News earlier this year.
DeSantis has made helping Trump’s immigration round-up a cornerstone in his administration.
“I’m not talking about giving them amnesty,” Salazar said. “I’m talking about giving them a dignified life in this promised land.”

items.summary_zh: 佛州共和党众议员萨拉查警告特朗普移民政策过火，称迈阿密西语裔选民感到被背叛，6至7月佛州约1.26万人被捕，半数无犯罪记录。

items.title: US to Reopen Largest Port for Mexican Cattle Shipments
body: The US is reopening its biggest port for Mexican live cattle shipments, marking a significant step in the Trump administration’s efforts to ease the pressures of a domestic cattle shortage.

The port in Santa Teresa, New Mexico, is the second to reopen, after the US in late 2024 stalled livestock shipments from Mexico in order to prevent the spread of the deadly New World screwworm. It’s far larger than the Arizona plant that resumed operations last month: nearly 500,000 cattle were shipped through the Santa Teresa port in 2024, amounting to about 40% of the US’s total imports from Mexico, according to the US Agriculture Department.
The port is scheduled to reopen on Sept. 24, and agency staff are already preparing on site, Agriculture Secretary Brooke Rollins said in a Thursday press conference.

Mexico used to ship over a million head of cattle each year to be raised in the US and then processed. The lack of that trade has hurt meatpackers, which have closed beef processing facilities over the past year as they struggle to procure enough animals to keep plants running at capacity. The halt also has contributed to record consumer beef prices, which has been a major concern of the Trump administration.

The US aims to resume shipments through more ports. Rollins said the USDA is “looking every day at reopening the Columbus, New Mexico, port,” and has previously said the agency is assessing its Nogales, Arizona, location.
More than 6,000 cattle have entered the Douglas, Arizona, port since the trade resumed at the end of August, according to USDA data.

Plant closures, along with increased live cattle from Mexico and higher ground beef imports — have helped beef processing margins turn positive for the first time since April, according to data from HedgersEdge. President Donald Trump last month said he would allow up to 300,000 tons of ground beef to enter the country under lower tariffs, though the USDA’s forecasts suggest only a portion of that will be filled.
The outlook for the meat industry’s recovery remains precarious, and the country’s largest meatpacker, Tyson Foods Inc., recently cut its annual outlook twice within a month.
Read More: Tyson Cuts Profit Outlook Again on Worsening Beef Fallout

Meanwhile, concerns over the screwworm in the US have faded, with only two active cases remaining in Texas. Infestations of the parasite, which can be deadly if left untreated, have totaled less than 50 since its detection in the US in June. Still, there are nearly 2,000 active cases in Mexico. The US has been dispersing sterile male flies, which contain the disease by mating with wild female flies to curb reproduction. The US is looking to build a new dispersal facility in Arizona, and a larger plant to produce those flies in Texas is slated to open in spring 2027.

“We’re not yet at eradication, I want to make sure everyone understands that,” Rollins added. “That may go up a case or two, and may go up a little bit more. But we are so proud of the fact that we only have two active cases in the US.”

“All the boxes have been checked. We feel really good about all the protocols that are in place,” Rollins said. “If there is one question and we’re not 100% sure in the safety and the protocols, then we will push it back.”

items.title: France Seeks to Pare Deficit After Missing Its 2026 Target
body: French Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu will propose a vast effort to control spending and narrow the deficit after failing to do so in 2026, setting the stage for a parliamentary battle that risks toppling the government just ahead of presidential elections.

The budget bill will aim to reduce the gap to 5% of economic output in 2027 from 5.4% in 2026, the finance ministry said. The government previously targeted a 5% deficit this year, but a slump of growth and rising interest costs has put that out of reach.
The narrower shortfall next year will come mainly from a €54 billion ($62 billion) “effort” to contain spending, Lecornu said in an interview with Le Figaro.

“By putting the brakes on health insurance spending from this summer, we have started to structurally mitigate the shock, but we must press on,” Lecornu said. “The constraints of reality apply as much to the government as the parliament and candidates in the presidential election.”
But the premier said he also plans to partially extend a tax on big business first introduced as one-off in 2025. The new version would target €5 billion revenue instead of €8 billion.

France is struggling to get a grip on runaway public finances as economic growth slows sharply and a fragmented parliament pushes back against austerity measures. The risks for next year are particularly acute as opposition parties are reluctant to compromise with President Emmanuel Macron’s outgoing administration just seven months ahead of elections.
Jordan Bardella, the head of the far-right National Rally, said he would wait for more details on the project.

“A budget that would penalize those in France who are working or have worked without addressing the waste of public funds would be unfair,” he said on BFMTV late Thursday. He added that his party would present a “counter-budget” in the next few days.

The political and fiscal uncertainty has added to selling pressure on French assets amid a global rout on bond markets. Last week, the yield-premium on French 10-year bonds over German equivalents broke through highs not seen since the euro zone’s debt crisis and now stands around 96 basis points.

The government has already slashed its growth forecast to 0.5% for this year, while the 2026 budget law was based on a 0.9% expansion. Last week, Finance Minister Roland Lescure already warned that the initial goal of a 5% deficit this year was “no longer an option.”
If there are no changes in next year’s finance bill to curb the trend increase in spending, the deficit would widen to as much as 6.5% of economic output after 5.1% in 2025, Lecornu told Le Figaro.

Lecornu said the efforts to curb spending would include €2.5 billion at the labor ministry, €2 billion from freezing a wage index for public sector workers, and another €2 billion from changes to sick leave compensation.

Savings from changing tax breaks for pensioners or the indexing of their pensions would be less than €6 billion and decided during debate in parliament, he added. The full details of different proposed measures will be unveiled later this month.

items.title: Spanish Renewables Firm Ignis to Unveil IPO Plans This Month
body: Spanish renewable energy company Ignis Energia SL expects to unveil its stock listing plans this month as it seeks to capitalize on growing demand for data center projects in the country.

Ignis is currently aiming to announce its plan on Sept. 28, people with direct knowledge of the plans said, asking not to be named discussing non-public information. The Vortex Energy-backed company will seek to raise as much as €600 million with the IPO, people familiar with the matter said previously.
A representative for Ignis declined to comment.

Ignis — which focuses on developing, supplying and managing renewable energy for data centers, industrial customers and power generation plants — is counting on a growing number of projects to power artificial intelligence in Spain.

The Spanish government is preparing a new set of rules for data centers that could include the requirement that each new megawatt of power demand be paired with newly installed renewable energy capacity.

Renewable energy stocks have been under pressure as the appeal of the sector’s steady cash flow diminishes with rising interest rates and the recent concerns over the pace of AI developments. In Spain, the problem is compounded by an abundance of solar energy that at times has pushed power prices to zero as the country lacks enough energy storage infrastructure.
Storage is one of Ignis’s focus. The company earlier this year signed an agreement with French energy giant Engie SA to secure revenues generated by a portfolio of energy storage projects in Spain.
Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez said Thursday in an opinion piece published by Bloomberg that “access to the electricity grid is a scarce strategic asset.”

“Spain wants to fully capture the opportunities created by data centers and AI. Yet the challenge is making sure the infrastructure expands in line with the capacity of the power system, that valuable energy resources are directed toward useful projects and that this all makes Europe less dependent technologically,” Sanchez wrote.

Spain this week announced it will ramp up investment in its electricity network, with the government planing to invest more than €17 billion ($19.6 billion) in the grid through 2030, Bloomberg News reported.

items.title: Orban Son-in-Law Sells Bank Stake During Hungary Graft Crackdown
body: Viktor Orban’s son-in-law is selling most of his stake in a listed bank at a time when key businessmen with ties to the previous regime are being swept up in corruption probes.

Istvan Tiborcz’s BDPST Group agreed to sell a 20.48% share in Granit Bank Nyrt., according to a stock exchange filing Thursday. The sale follows a deal announced last week to dispose another 9.9% stake in the bank. If both transactions go through, Tiborcz will retain control of about 10% in Granit, a small digital bank which also owns local brokerage Equilor.
Read More: Hungary’s Magyar Unveils Plan to Cleanse Orban’s ‘Mafia State’

Prime Minister Peter Magyar’s administration is stepping up a corruption crackdown as well as efforts to claw back misappropriated state assets. Magyar won a landslide election in April on those pledges. The European Union had withheld billions of euros in funding on graft concerns under Orban’s 16-year rule.

Tiborcz, who’s denied that his political connections to his father-in-law enriched him, became one of Hungary’s wealthiest businessmen during Orban’s rule. He owns Hungary’s biggest luxury hotel portfolio as well as a controlling stake in listed hauler Waberer’s International, among other assets.
This week, Daniel Jellinek and Norbert Szivek, two prominent businessmen who had been past business partners of Tiborcz, were detained in a corruption case. They’ve denied wrongdoing.
Read More: Unwinding Orbán’s Graft in Hungary, From Advertising to Zebras

On Thursday, the government backed a decision to allow the tax authority to conduct comprehensive probes of the assets of politicians, going back as far as 20 years. Magyar said the probes would extend to the families of politicians, including those of former prime ministers, and will seek to shed light on the “fairy tale” wealth accumulation of the former political elite.
“Our goal isn’t vengeance,” Magyar said after a cabinet meeting. “Our goal is for the law to apply everyone.”
items.title_zh: 欧尔班女婿在匈牙利反腐行动中出售银行股份
items.summary_zh: 欧尔班女婿蒂博尔茨拟出售Granit银行20.48%股份，此前已售9.9%，匈牙利新政府正加大反腐力度。

items.title: Bank of England's QT Tweak Gives Andy Burnham's Labour Breathing Space
body: Is the Bank of England in hock to Andy Burnham?

Some people, particularly in today’s political climate, might be inclined to think so after the Bank revealed that it would overhaul its controversial quantitative tightening programme. Whether or not the details of it mean anything to you, let’s first consider this afternoon’s immediate consequence: the government’s borrowing costs enjoyed the steepest daily drop in four months. A nice little boon, as debt-servicing is Britain’s biggest bill after pensions/benefits and the National Health Service.

There’s also a knock-on effect beyond the Treasury. The softening of financial conditions we’ve seen this afternoon will feed into the retail market and should halt — or partly reverse — the recent upward pressure on mortgage rates. The average five-year fix rose this week to its highest level since 2023, back when UK credibility was still recovering from the Liz Truss debacle, so any relief will be appreciated by leveraged homeowners whose deals are soon to expire.

Lower (or perhaps I should say, less high) rates of course make other types of borrowing easier (or less punishing) too, which would be positive for output across the economy — another boon ahead of Labour’s first budget under the Burnham government, due on Oct. 28.
Thus it’s unsurprising that Bank of England Governor Andrew Bailey addressed the question of timing head on during a TV interview this afternoon.

“We’ve been planning and working on this for a long time, I can assure you, this work did not start when we had a change of government back in the early summer,” the governor said. “So there’s no question of in any sense favouring a particular government.”
He continued: “We were planning this work well before the conflict broke out in the Middle East, so it’s not a reaction to market conditions at all.”

Beyond conspiratorial paranoia, there’s no reason not to take Bailey at his word. The effect of QT in shuffling up gilt yields has been a gripe for some time and the longer the asset-selling went on, the greater the need to think about the detail of how it worked.

There is one lingering question, though: if the Bank’s been discussing this with the Treasury and Debt Management Office for some time, as Bailey says, why does the Treasury now need a six-month pause in Bank asset-sales to thrash out the details?

Perhaps there’s a technical reason that’s beyond me, but it seems like a rather convenient hiatus for Burnham’s government. The PM has spoken repeatedly of his desire to give voters more “breathing space” in their personal finances, an aim complicated by the persistent conflicts in Ukraine and the Middle East.

Today, the Bank of England helped a little — with both the QT changes and its less-hawkish-than-expected interest rates statement. Threadneedle Street can’t do anything to fend off a global energy price shock, but it has, inadvertently, given Burnham’s Labour government a bit of breathing space of its own.
Want this in your inbox each weekday? You can sign up here.

Hi, I’m Morwenna from the MT blog. There’s a palpable sense of relief in gilt markets this afternoon. A lot of that’s down to changes to the BOE’s QT programme, as Julian mentions above, which is helping lower longer-dated yields. But the fact that the central bank didn’t hike rates — and the vote wasn’t closer — will have also come as some relief and shored up the shorter-end of the curve.

Markets are no longer fully pricing in four hikes by the end of next year and certainty of a quarter-point tightening has been pushed out to December, albeit still with an 88% chance seen of it coming at the next meeting.

All the evidence suggests that the case for a hike is building. Those who voted to hold indicated a prolonged conflict in the Middle East could push them closer to the hawkish camp. The BOE’s inflation forecasts have moved higher due to energy prices, with CPI now seen potentially topping 4% by early next year. And worries about the labour market and economic growth seem to have diminished.

Right now, there are plenty of reasons inflation could rise further, eventually delivering so-called second-round effects. Governor Bailey, in a broadcast interview this afternoon, acknowledged the pass-through of higher energy costs to inflation has been “subdued” so far, but that it is “early days.” And there is a risk, as identified by the hawks, of waiting too long.

items.title: Glencore Suspends Executive Who Led Radiant World Business
body: A senior Glencore Plc executive who led the company’s relationship with Radiant World has been suspended as the company reviews its dealings with the embattled iron ore trader, according to a person familiar with the matter.

Peter Hill, head of trading for steelmaking raw materials including iron ore and coking coal, has been stood down from his duties pending the outcome of a review that the London-listed company announced earlier this week, the person said, asking not to be identified as the matter isn’t public.

Hill’s role makes him the Glencore executive with direct responsibility for the Radiant World relationship. Glencore has taken a $480 million provision on its exposure to Radiant World and associated companies, Bloomberg reported previously, while the Radiant World group this week filed a $2 billion lawsuit against Glencore.
A Glencore representative declined to comment. Hill didn’t answer a call to his mobile phone.

Several top commodity traders stopped doing business with Radiant World amid concerns it had provided falsified documents to banks to raise financing, Bloomberg previously reported. Radiant World has denied wrongdoing and said it conducts its business to the highest commercial and legal standards.
Glencore said earlier this week that it was conducting a review of its historic business activities with Radiant World, Sapphire Minmetals and associated companies.

Glencore for years was Radiant World’s most important backer, Bloomberg has reported previously. A letter from Radiant World’s lawyers, previously reported by Bloomberg, cited a November 2024 WhatsApp message from Peter Hill, Glencore’s head of steelmaking raw materials, in which he said that Glencore had “basically bank rolled your entire existence for the last few years.”

However, the relationship soured this year, with Glencore beginning to withdraw after banks started to approach it with Radiant World invoices with its name on it, which it could not verify as genuine, Bloomberg reported earlier.

After Radiant World filed its suit this week, Glencore in response directly accused it of fraud, saying that it had “confirmed evidence” that Radiant World and associated companies had sent falsified invoices, contracts and emails.
“We take these issues seriously and are conducting a review of our historic business activities with Radiant World” and associated companies, Glencore said.

Radiant World said earlier this week it rejects the allegations of wrongdoing that have been made against it. “This is, and has always been, a commercial dispute arising out of a genuine and longstanding trading relationship,” it said.
Hill has run the iron ore division since 2021, and was previously seen as a rising star within the business as he rapidly increased the unit’s trading volumes.

He was promoted last year, when he was elevated from head of iron ore to run trading for all steelmaking commodities, including coking coal, where Glencore had just become one of the leading players thanks to its acquisition of Teck Resources Ltd.’s coal business.

items.title: Botswana Says It Won't Be 'Reckless' Over De Beers Investment
body: Botswana won’t risk its financial wellbeing when it increases its investment in De Beers, the world’s biggest diamond company, Vice President Ndaba Gaolathe said.

The country, which has developed one of Africa’s richest economies on a per capita basis by partnering De Beers in diamond mining, wants to deepen its involvement in the industry as Anglo American Plc seeks to dispose of its 85% stake in the gem company.

Duma Boko, the country’s president, had previously said Botswana would seek to get control of the company. But the government has since indicated that it could settle for merely increasing its stake from the current 15%.

“I can assure you that Botswana as a government, the Ministry of Finance, is not reckless and careless,” Gaolathe said at Chatham House event in London Thursday, dismissing concerns that the country would over-extend itself financially. “We’re very particular about how we invest.”

Anglo is trying to sell De Beers as the diamond industry endures one of its deepest and longest downturns due to the rise in popularity of synthetic stones and a decline in Chinese luxury spending. Since diamonds were discovered in Botswana in 1967, the industry has bankrolled its development but the demand slump has tipped the economy into recession.

A group led by former De Beers Chief Executive Officer Gareth Penny has been selected as the preferred bidder. Anglo is discussing selling its stake for about $1 billion, a fraction of what it was once worth, people familiar with the situation told Bloomberg in July.
Botswana, while keen to “go to the next level” in the diamond industry, is looking for other sources of revenue, Gaolathe said.
Botswana is the world’s largest producer of rough diamonds by value, with the stones making up the bulk of foreign currency receipts as well as about a third of budget revenue.
“We have no choice to diversify or we perish,” he said.

items.title: US Weighs Antitrust Guidance on AI Safety, Top DOJ Official Says
body: The Trump administration is considering whether to update interagency antitrust guidance on cybersecurity to address a new wave of threats posed by artificial intelligence, according to Associate US Attorney General Stanley Woodward.

At an event in New York on Thursday, Woodward said that existing guidelines spell out the extent to which companies can coordinate on hacking risks without running afoul of rules prohibiting anticompetitive behavior. While Silicon Valley leaders have called in recent days for an exemption from antitrust scrutiny to allow them to work together on safety, Woodward said that so far no one has contacted his office on the matter.

“To the extent that anybody at any of the frontier labs wants to come see us about a concern, they would get a meeting,” said Woodward, the department’s No. 3 official and the head of its antitrust section. “That meeting hasn’t been requested.”
Read More: OpenAI Says It’s Working With Anthropic, Google on AI Safety

During the Obama administration, the federal government issued guidance clarifying that companies could coordinate on sharing cybersecurity threat information to better protect networks and deter attacks. A similar approach has been floated by the tech industry for artificial intelligence.

Anxiety over AI’s existential risks has risen since the publication Saturday of an essay by Anthropic PBC Chief Executive Officer Dario Amodei that warned of new threats posed by the technology. Amodei pledged to slow development of cutting-edge models and said the industry would benefit from a narrow antitrust waiver to allow AI companies to work together more on safety issues.

While Woodward signaled some openness to discussing the industry’s concerns, the head of the Federal Trade Commission, which shares jurisdiction over competition enforcement, expressed skepticism about companies’ desire for an exemption.

FTC Chair Andrew Ferguson said Tuesday he would be “deeply suspicious” of requests for relief and said that the AI companies are “asking for barriers to entry” that will insulate their companies from challengers.
Read More: FTC’s Ferguson ‘Deeply Suspicious’ of AI Antitrust Exemption

Some of the leading US AI developers have already begun safety discussions. OpenAI global policy chief Chris Lehane said Tuesday the company has been working for several weeks on AI risks with Anthropic and Google DeepMind, a unit of Alphabet Inc. He added that their work on security has ample precedent, citing the airline industry as an example. “There are many instances over time where companies are trying to help each other on safety,” he said.
During his appearance on Thursday, Woodward said the administration was watching the issue “very closely” but was waiting still to hear from the industry.
As of now, he said, officials “have not had any outreach from companies.”

items.title: NY Attorney General Urges AI Whistleblowers to Come Forward
body: New York Attorney General Letitia James encouraged workers at artificial intelligence companies to confidentially report activity they think is dangerous or illegal to her office.

In a Thursday press release, James pointed to an online portal she said whistleblowers could use to contact state law enforcement. “Those developing AI have a responsibility to ensure their products are safe,” she said.

James’ appeal comes as leading AI labs issue increasingly stark warnings about the technology’s risks. Anthropic PBC Chief Executive Officer Dario Amodei and OpenAI Inc. CEO Sam Altman have both suggested that development of AI models should be slowed and called for greater regulatory oversight.

OpenAI has disclosed cases involving AI agents behaving in unexpected ways, while Anthropic has reported concerns involving its own advanced models. Anthropic researcher Jacob Coxon resigned last week over safety concerns, saying that people building AI believe it could “kill us all by the end of the decade,” fueling calls for stronger safeguards.

The Trump administration has so far rejected calls for federal AI regulation, but New York and California have both passed state laws targeting the sector. New York’s law, which takes effect Jan. 1, requires frontier-model developers to report critical safety incidents to a new office within the Department of Financial Services within 72 hours.

items.title: ECB's Zigman Warns Growth Is at Risk If Inflation Isn't Tackled
body: The European Central Bank must get inflation under control as failing to do so would endanger economic expansion, Governing Council member Ante Zigman warned.

With stronger-than-expected growth in the second quarter, officials must focus on bringing inflation that’s currently above 3% back to the 2% goal, the Croatian central-bank chief told Bloomberg Television’s Oliver Crook on Thursday.

There’s “a lot of optimism for growth,” he said in his first interview with international media since taking office in June. “We really need to care about inflation, which also at the end can jeopardize the growth.”

Having just hiked interest rates for a second time, the ECB is gauging how much more it must do to get inflation back to target. With oil and natural gas prices jumping again, analysts see price gains climbing toward 4% in the coming months, though at the same time, the euro-area economy is so far weathering the Iran war fallout.

Markets are pricing at least three more hikes in the deposit rate from its current level of 2.5%. That would push far beyond the so-called neutral range, where borrowing costs neither stimulate nor curb economic activity.
Officials including Bundesbank President Joachim Nagel have said mildly restrictive policy may be needed. Others like Executive Board member Piero Cipollone warn against tightening excessively.
Zigman said the ECB mustn’t focus too much on where the neutral rate is exactly. “For us it’s important, and especially for myself, that all inflation indicators are under control,” he said.

While price growth is elevated, he stressed that this hasn’t yet fed through to other parts of the economy, with wages still contained. He rejected the idea that the ECB is already in the adverse scenario in its latest outlook.

“For now, it’s still mostly related to the energy, mostly related to the geopolitics, which we know very well can be changed in a very short period of time,” he said. “Those other segments of inflation are still contained and we don’t see any major second-round effects.”
Asked about a potential back-to-back hike next month, Zigman said he expects “very intensive discussion and it’ll depend on the data which we are going to have at that moment.”
However, he emphasized that investors’ bets on aggressive tightening will not determine the ECB’s next steps.
“The markets are always speculating and they have their expectations and their rationale,” Zigman said. “We are not going to make our decision based on the market expectations.”

items.title: Belgium Ramps Up Budget Talks to Tackle €10 Billion Shortfall
body: The Belgian government is intensifying budget talks in a bid to find around €10 billion ($11.5 billion) in savings by 2029, the latest effort by the country to reassure investors ahead of a deadline next month.

The cabinet is due to meet Friday for the latest round of negotiations on its budget plans for the coming years. The government, led by Prime Minister Bart de Wever, earlier this year agreed to find €10 billion in annual savings or additional revenue by the end of its term in 2029.

Belgium’s central bank governor Pierre Wunsch gave a presentation to senior cabinet members in Brussels on Saturday, where he set out his analysis of the country’s challenging fiscal picture, according to people familiar with the discussions. Ministers also held initial talks on the menu of budget options available during the meeting, the people said.

Technical discussions between representatives of the country’s five-party coalition government have been taking place this week ahead of Friday’s meeting, which could still be pushed back due to scheduling changes.

De Wever warned about the parlous state of Belgium’s public finances at a committee hearing in Parliament on Wednesday. Holding up slides from the National Bank of Belgium and the IMF, he argued that cutting expenses was key to the budgetary effort.

“The confidence of financial markets needs to be strengthened again, against the background of our historical track record,” he said. “That confidence has become very shaky, to the point where we are running very significant risks.”
Belgium, a country of 11 million people which hosts the headquarters of the European Union and NATO, has faced a persistent drumbeat of negative views about the outlook for its budgetary situation.

Morgan Stanley rates strategists said last week they believe there is “scope for investors to price a greater risk premium” over the possible challenge in finding a budget deal, recommending investors sell 10-year Belgian debt and buy equivalent EU peers. The country has already faced two ratings downgrades this year and two in the prior year.

During his presentation, central bank chief Pierre Wunsch presented senior cabinet members with the evolution of revenue and expenses over the past 20 years, emphasizing the challenge raised by a large rise in government expenditure, according to three people familiar with the presentation.
A spokesperson for the Belgian central bank confirmed the presentation but declined to comment on the substance.
Belgium had the highest budget deficit in the euro area last year, at 5.2% of gross domestic product. The country’s central bank expects that to widen to 5.7% in 2028.

But the country’s five-party coalition has divergent views on how to reach the €10 billion budget goal they set themselves in July. The country is famous for its fractious governments and complicated institutional structure. Last week’s cabinet meeting led to another spillover of tensions, with some parties trading insults in statements and on X in its aftermath.

The coalition government aims to find a budget accord ahead of a mid-October state of the union speech by de Wever as well as an Oct. 15 European Union deadline for the submission of national budgets. The coalition government last year missed its own and European deadlines for the budget, striking an accord only at the end of November.

items.title: SpaceX Discusses Buying Data for AI Models From Failed Startups
body: Elon Musk’s SpaceX has held internal discussions about buying customer and operational information from troubled or defunct startups, according to people familiar with the matter, targeting a more affordable data source to improve its artificial intelligence models.

The approach would mirror Google’s offer to purchase business data from Spirit Airlines for AI training purposes after the discount carrier wound down operations. The Alphabet Inc. company’s $10 million bid sparked some data privacy concerns, including from former flight attendants.

The talks within teams inside SpaceXAI, the company’s AI unit, are informal and may not result in a deal, said the people, who spoke on condition of anonymity as the information is not public. SpaceX did not respond to a request for comment.

Musk’s space, satellite communications and artificial intelligence conglomerate is locked in a heated battle to build more advanced AI offerings that rival the likes of Anthropic PBC and OpenAI as it works to sign up more business customers. Like other AI companies, SpaceXAI, formerly known as xAI, is focused on securing high-quality data sources that can be used to boost the performance of its models on various tasks. The firm is targeting operational data and customer information to train Grok, among other sets, some of the people said.

The strategy of using external datasets marks a departure of sorts for SpaceXAI, which has previously relied on data from Musk’s social network, X, as well as a fleet of in-house specialists known as AI tutors to train and refine its artificial intelligence software.

SpaceXAI is still using its internal tutors to help engineers make AI systems better at specialized skills such as finance, science and even humor, but the team has gone through a series of exits and strategy changes. SpaceXAI paused hiring for AI tutors, Bloomberg News reported in June, and later swapped leadership.

Jack Garabedian, a staffer that had spent years working at SpaceX’s Starlink satellite-internet service, recently took over the team, replacing college-aged engineer Diego Pasini, Bloomberg previously reported. Since then, Garabedian has worked to quell discontent on the team, establishing processes and meetings as well as clear goals for AI training data, said the people.

In an internal newsletter seen by Bloomberg News, the data team highlighted some of its achievements for July, including progress made on a new AI model and coding agent. “None of these land as polished products without the quiet, exacting work of annotation, preference alignment and validation that happens every day on this team,” the newsletter said.
While SpaceX’s AI team considers using more outside data sources, it also continues to rely on information from within Musk’s empire, including employees.
“We are going to be training Grok on the sum total of all SpaceX information,” Musk told SpaceX personnel during a recent meeting. “It’ll be trained on you.”
