items.title: Stellantis (STLA) Finds No Future for Its Brampton, Canada Factory
body: Jeep parent Stellantis NV told workers at a Toronto-area factory that it sees “no long-term business case” for making vehicles there and that it’s exploring a sale of the facility, increasing the likelihood of a work stoppage.
“Strike action remains a real possibility,” Unifor National President Lana Payne said at a news conference in Toronto, though the union hopes to reach a tentative settlement without it.

Unifor represents about 9,000 unionized employees at Stellantis facilities in Canada, including those in at the idled factory in Brampton, Ontario. It has a collective agreement with Stellantis that expires on Sept. 20. A mandated “conciliation” period must finish before a legal strike or lockout can take place.
In a letter to workers at the plant, which hasn’t produced vehicles since late 2023, the carmaker said it’s facing untenable economic conditions.

“The automotive industry continues to face unpredictable trade policies, challenging regulatory requirements and affordability pressures,” Trevor Longley, chief executive officer of Stellantis Canada, said.

The automaker has considered “a range of options” since it reversed plans to build the Jeep Compass SUV at the factory last year, he said. The company made that decision after US President Donald Trump made it clear he would put tariffs on foreign-made cars and trucks.
“While each option was carefully reviewed, none provided a sustainable long-term business case that would support continued operations at the facility,” Longley wrote.

Stellantis and Unifor have been an impasse since last week, when Roshel Inc., a Canadian armored vehicle manufacturer, said it had signed a memorandum with Stellantis outlining steps toward a sale of the Brampton plant. Roshel is trying to get a Canadian military contract worth as much as C$4.9 billion ($3.5 billion) to build light utility vehicles, and has said it could bring back 1,000 workers to the Brampton facility if it’s successful.
Read More: Stellantis Signs Memo With Roshel for Possible Sale of Plant

Stellantis announced plans in 2022 to invest C$3.6 billion in Brampton and another factory in Ontario to retool them for building electric vehicles. A year later, it confirmed the Compass move to Brampton. But it canceled those plans last year as part of a broader strategic pivot.

The Canadian government had given hundreds of millions of dollars in financial help to Stellantis in return for production promises. Unifor is opposed to a sale and is pressing Industry Minister Melanie Joly to reject the idea.
“If the commitments Stellantis made can be broken in Brampton, they can be broken anywhere,” Payne said. “We need time, Brampton needs time.”
Payne said she would accept another automaker taking over the plant “if it meant full vehicle assembly, absolutely.”

But a defense contractor like Roshel that depends on government procurement “cannot compare to a commercial enterprise building vehicles,” she argued, noting it’s unlikely to offer the same kind of compensation and employment opportunities.
“These are not things that you can recreate overnight,” she said, adding that Unifor has not spoken with Roshel.
Roshel said its executive team was unavailable to comment. Joly’s office did not respond to a request for comment.

items.title: Turkey Detains Executives at Tera, Destek Amid Fund Turmoil
body: Turkish authorities said several top finance executives were detained while others were given a travel ban, according to a statement on Thursday, as part of an investigation related to mass outflows from some funds this week.
Pusula Portfoy Yonetimi AS Chairman Muhammed Yariz has been arrested, Istanbul prosecutor’s office said in a statement.

Businessman Altunc Kumova, Destek Holding chairman and on paper one of Turkey’s wealthiest people after some of his companies’ shares surged by several thousand percent in the past year, was detained. Tera Portfoy Yonetimi AS’s Deputy Chief Executive Officer Ibrahim Bekci and Hedef Holding AS chairman Namik Kemal Gokalp have been also detained.

A travel ban was imposed on Tera Holding Chairman Emre Tezmen and Pusula Holding’s Serdar Turhan, along with Bulls Yatirim Menkul Degerler AS Chairman Kemal Akkaya and its parent company Lydia Holding’s Chairman Enver Cevik.
Turkish authorities earlier on Thursday ordered the liquidation of 130 funds managed by seven portfolio companies, including funds managed by Tera and Pusula.

Total investments in the funds ordered liquidated stood at the equivalent of about $18 billion as of Wednesday evening, with over 350,000 investors exposed, according to a person with knowledge of the matter, who asked not to be named because the figures haven’t been made public.

items.title: Nvidia's Huang Expects to Sell Twice as Many Chips Next Year
body: Nvidia Corp. Chief Executive Officer Jensen Huang expects to sell twice as many chips in the coming year, fueled by the spread of artificial intelligence across different industries.

AI is of great benefit to a variety of sectors, Huang told reporters on the sidelines of an event convened by King Charles III in Scotland on Thursday. Nvidia is the top seller of AI accelerators, chips used to develop and run artificial intelligence models.

Huang is maintaining his bullish stance at a time when concerns are growing about AI. Industry leaders have discussed slowing down development of the technology over fears that it might be potentially dangerous. Huang said that companies need to take responsibility and make sure their AI software and services are safe before releasing them.
Read More: Nvidia’s Huang Calls for AI Safety Tests at King Charles Summit
Last month, Nvidia projected sales growth of 70% in its next fiscal year. It said at the time that revenue could double if the company had enough supply to meet surging demand.
Read More: Nvidia Sales Forecast Sends Shares on Biggest Rally Since 2025
Nvidia shares rose as much as 2.8% in New York on Thursday, helping reverse losses from a slide last week. The stock is up about 17% this year.

items.title: Bond Rout Spurs Record Outflow From $3.6 Billion Schwab Muni ETF
body: A roughly $3.6 billion municipal-bond exchange-traded fund is careening toward its biggest monthly outflow ever, after a fixed-income selloff pushed muni yields to the highest in months.

A recent wave of outflows in the Schwab Municipal Bond ETF, including a record $360 million single-day withdrawal last week, has put the fund on track for its worst month since its 2022 launch. Investors have pulled more than $530 million so far in September.

Schwab holds just over half the ETF’s outstanding shares, according to Bloomberg-compiled data. The size of the move suggests to some market watchers that the outflows were caused by model-portfolio reshuffling.

“This looks like the call is coming from inside the house,” said Eric Balchunas, a Bloomberg Intelligence ETF analyst. “Schwab famously owns their own funds and when you see a trade this big, they’re really the only people who could have pulled it off.”

In model portfolio investing, money managers like Schwab or BlackRock Inc. bundle funds into ready-made strategies for financial advisers to offer to clients. Portfolio rebalancing is often suspected to be behind many sudden large ETF flows.

“The recent back up in tax-exempt yields has been in line with the broader market, and it has generally created opportunities for many tax-sensitive investors and model providers to reposition their portfolios,” said Jason Diefenthaler, head of active taxable and municipal strategies at Schwab Asset Management.

Concerns over inflation, rising Treasury rates and heavy new issuance have put pressure on the muni market. Muni yields surged last week amid a rout in Treasuries, with the longest-dated securities reaching their highest levels since 2011.

Last week, ten-year benchmark muni yields climbed to their highest since April 2025, when volatility from President Donald Trump’s tariff policies roiled the market. Meanwhile, stocks are heading for a second-consecutive weekly loss.

“We’ve seen some weakness in the equity markets so I suspect there is asset rebalancing going on in the other direction,” said Patrick Luby, head of municipal research and senior municipal strategist at CreditSights Inc. “Taking some out of fixed income and moving it into equity.”

items.title: Why High Yields on Treasury Bonds, Government Debt Look Like the New Normal
body: Government borrowing costs have been climbing around the world as investors demand more compensation to entice them to hold longer-maturity debt. The rise in US bond yields even prompted Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent to announce expanded buybacks of long-dated government debt — an intervention that failed to stop yields on 10-year Treasuries from breaching 5% and hitting their highest level in almost two decades.

Investors’ retreat from long-dated sovereign debt has been driven by a range of concerns. These include mounting fiscal deficits and stubborn inflation amid President Donald Trump’s trade war and higher energy costs due to the conflict in the Middle East. Governments are also having to compete for investor attention as technology companies issue massive amounts of debt to fund the buildout of artificial-intelligence infrastructure.

While a Federal Reserve interest rate hike in September calmed some of the jitters about the central bank’s commitment to tame inflation, the structural drivers of the bond selloff haven’t disappeared and yields remain elevated. Average bond yields across the Group of Seven countries are at their highest since 2000.

Bonds issued by wealthy nations are widely regarded as the world’s safest securities because these governments are highly likely to pay investors back. Governments often lock in financing costs for long periods such as 30 years. Some even issue debt that matures in a century.

That doesn’t mean these bonds are without risk for investors. Should inflation and short-term interest rates rise, that eats into the real value of a bond’s coupon payments, as well as the principal that’s ultimately repaid when the bond reaches its maturity date.

The longer the tenor of a bond, the more time there is for inflation to have an impact. That’s why long-dated bonds have been more sensitive to the rise in interest rates and inflation, and why they’ve been at the center of the recent selloff.
In mid-September, yields on 30-year US Treasuries hit their highest level since 2007, while Japanese peers were close to all-time highs and UK counterparts reached their highest since 1998.

In theory, yes, although the bond market is also facing a structural shift in supply and demand. For much of the past two decades, abundant global savings — particularly in Asia — chased a relatively scarce supply of safe assets, helping suppress long-term real yields. Then-Fed Chair Alan Greenspan called the persistently low long-term yields a “conundrum,” as rates stayed subdued even as the Fed raised short-term borrowing costs.

Now, governments around the world are ramping up spending on everything from renewable energy to defense. The US is borrowing more to fund its more than $40 trillion in national debt, as well as to plug an annual fiscal shortfall that the Congressional Budget Office estimated in August will reach $2.1 trillion. Trump’s proposed $5,000 dividend for adult US citizens if Republicans retains control of Congress in November’s midterm election could fuel even more borrowing.

While global supply of government debt has swelled, demand has been curtailed by weaker foreign appetite and central banks reducing their bond holdings after years of purchases. This has been described as a transition from a “savings glut” to a “bond glut” by European Central Bank Executive Board member Isabel Schnabel.

That means the investor base is shifting toward more price-sensitive private buyers, who typically demand higher compensation to hold long-term bonds. Structural changes in pensions and retirement systems have also reduced the pool of traditional long-term buyers.

In the US, the so-called term premium — the extra yield that investors demand to hold long-term debt — has increased by more than 3 percentage points from the lows during the Covid-19 pandemic, according to a model developed by Bloomberg Economics.

The US has traditionally enjoyed a “convenience yield,” whereby investors were willing to pay higher prices — and accept lower payouts — because of the liquidity, safety and usefulness of Treasuries as collateral. Some say that privilege has been eroded, pointing to the ever-increasing national debt load and Trump’s erratic policymaking. Others argue that the concern is exaggerated and Treasuries remain the safest debt out there.

A disorderly bond-market selloff can spell trouble for governments that rely on debt markets to finance their deficits — something the UK is all too familiar with after the collapse of Liz Truss’s premiership in 2022. The bond market has “taken out more governments than howitzers,” Bessent said earlier this year.

Long bond yields underpin interest rates on a litany of consumer loans such as mortgages, as well as corporate debt. Higher bond yields risk increasing pressure on household borrowers when years of inflation have already made the cost of living less affordable. Savers, however, enjoy a boost.

The pass-through to consumer debt markets isn’t always straightforward. In the US, 30-year mortgage rates are priced closely off the 10-year Treasury yield instead of the 30-year Treasury rate. That’s because homeowners tend to pay off or refinance their mortgages after a period that’s closer to 10 years.

Many governments are tilting their borrowing programs toward shorter maturities. While yields are currently lower there, the shorter tenor of those bonds means they need to be refinanced more frequently — possibly in the face of higher interest rates.

The UK’s central bank decided to stop selling long-dated bonds from its portfolio to ease pressure on the market, while the US has taken a different approach. The Treasury announced in August that it would ramp up its buybacks of 10- to 30-year government bonds, to break what Bessent called a “fever” in the market. But the first tranche of buybacks was smaller than expected and yields went on to reach multiyear highs, in part fueled by a surge in oil prices.

Fundamentally, governments need to convince investors that they will get inflation and their fiscal deficits under control. That could involve a combination of tax hikes and spending cuts that will likely prove unpopular with voters.

To some degree, higher yields are good news for bondholders. With equity markets hovering around record highs, the rise in yields reflects a resilient global economy that can absorb higher borrowing costs.

Yields were near zero in the aftermath of the global financial crisis, when the outlook for economic growth was poor. The recent increase in yields could be viewed as a normalization to pre-crisis levels. At 4.95%, the 10-year US Treasury yield is slightly above its average over the past four decades.

“People love to use the phrase ‘higher for longer,’” Wells Fargo economists Tom Porcelli and Michael Pugliese wrote in a research note in August. “We would argue a far better characterization is normal for longer.”

items.title: Kennedy Center Must Explain Closure as Legal Fight Escalates
body: A Washington federal judge ordered the Kennedy Center to provide more information about the recent closure of the decades-old performing arts venue and to notify court challengers about any future “demolition” or broader renovations of the building.

Judge Christopher “Casey” Cooper of the US District Court for the District of Columbia on Thursday told the board of the John F. Kennedy Center for the Performing Arts to provide a “detailed status report” about the closure and emergency repairs by Sept. 23.

He denied a Democratic congresswoman’s request for an emergency hearing, attended by a high-level decision maker. But the judge said the written report must included a sworn declaration “from a knowledgeable representative of the Kennedy Center.”

It’s the latest in the legal saga to determine the center’s fate as President Donald Trump attempts to leave his mark on historic locations in Washington. Trump prompted a wave of public consternation Wednesday night when he was photographed on Air Force One reviewing a large printout that appeared to reference Kennedy Center demolition.

Trump demolished the White House’s East Wing — without congressional approval — last year to make room for a controversial 90,000-square-foot ballroom, just one of multiple changes he has made to the complex and its surrounding grounds, including a new helicopter pad, a paved over Rose Garden, and redecorated Oval Office.

Cooper said Thursday that the Justice Department must also provide notice in writing to court challengers in a pair of cases before changing the scope of planned renovations, “including but not limited to any ‘demolition’ of the Center’s main building.”

Greg Werkheiser, an attorney for Cultural Heritage Partners representing preservationist groups that have challenged planned renovations to the center, described Cooper’s order as a “significant win for the public.”
The order “provides stronger and clearer protection against the Administration sending in demo equipment and then trying to excuse it later before the court,” Werkheiser said by email.
The head of the Kennedy Center has defended his decision to close the Washington performing arts venue this week as necessary for public safety.

Matt Floca, the center’s executive director and chief operating officer, said in a court declaration earlier Thursday that he decided the day before that “continued structural deterioration” at the venue “necessitated a temporary closure of most public spaces” in the building.

The closure will last seven days, “unless extended,” he said in the declaration. During that time, Floca said he would assess safety risks and evaluate if the building must remain closed for longer on a weekly basis, or if it may partially reopen public access to safe spaces of the center.

The declaration came in response to a request by Rep. Joyce Beatty (D-Ohio), an ex-officio trustee of the Kennedy Center, for an emergency hearing to address the closure, which her attorneys described as an “apparent violation” of an earlier court order.
Beatty made that request after the Kennedy Center appeared to have closed to the public following a Tuesday board vote to shutter the venue for two years during renovations.

She claimed in court that this week’s closure violated Cooper’s May court order, which had blocked the center from closing without further court review. On Thursday, she asked the court to issue an order “making clear that either the wholesale demolition of the building or demolition that would make public access impossible would violate the Court’s existing order.”

Justice Department lawyers countered in a Thursday court filing, accompanied by Floca’s declaration, that this week’s closure was unrelated to the board vote to close the center for broader renovations.
They argued that the court order only prohibits closing for broader renovations funded by Congress and doesn’t prevent the venue from closing temporarily to address safety hazards.

“There is no emergency caused by Defendants’ temporary closure of the Center; the only emergency is the risk to the public and the Center’s employees and artists if it remained fully open without further safety assessment,” they wrote.

Trump, chair of the venue’s board, has come under scrutiny for his handling of the Kennedy Center, which was created by Congress to honor the late President John F. Kennedy after his assassination and opened in 1971.

The board, whose members were handpicked by Trump, has sought to add Trump’s name to the center’s facade and to shutter it for two years for renovations it says are needed to keep the building safe to visit.
Cooper has so far thwarted those efforts, following a court challenge from Beatty.

The Obama appointee has twice found that that federal law requires the building to be named only for Kennedy, blocking plans to rename the center for Trump and later to add Trump’s name to the building as an acknowledgment.

Cooper also found that the board didn’t initially consider enough information before voting to close the center’s doors. However, he left room for the board to ask him to lift that order if it votes again on closure plans with more information.

Meanwhile, the board has plowed forward with efforts to shutter the historic venue while warning that the center faces imminent financial collapse. The board said in recent documents, submitted in court, that while Trump has offered to raise the funds to “keep the Center from bankruptcy” during renovations, it is “unlikely” he would do so unless he receives the “appropriate recognition.”

A group of eight cultural heritage and preservationist organizations, which separately sued to challenge planned repairs to the Kennedy Center, called on Cooper in a joint statement Thursday to consider appointing an independent receiver to manage the Kennedy Center if current leadership is “unwilling or unable to exercise its fiduciary duty” to protect the venue.
Cooper briefly floated the prospect of a receivership during a court hearing Tuesday if the center became insolvent, in light of the board’s bankruptcy.
The case is Beatty v. Trump, D.D.C., No. 1:25-cv-04480, brief filed 9/17/26.
— With assistance from Jeff Mason.

items.title: Private Credit Defaults Are 1%, 6% or 19%, Depending Who You Ask
body: Either private credit has a serious default problem, or barely one at all — it all depends on who’s counting.

Fitch Ratings, for instance, put the default rate at a record 6.3% this week, adding its weight to the crowd of observers flagging mounting stress. Credit rating agency KBRA’s latest measure also pointed to a new high.
Yet by other measures, there’s little issue. Weigh the market by loan size and defaults remain below 1% because the largest borrowers continue to perform, investment bank Houlihan Lokey Inc. found.

That gulf says as much about private credit’s data void as it does about the state of the $1.8 trillion market. It was less of a concern, perhaps, during the boom years of the asset class. But now, amid a spate of retail investor withdrawals driven by fears about the health of private credit borrowers, the answer matters more than ever.

Highly leveraged companies that financed when money was cheap are confronting borrowing costs that may stay elevated for longer — or rise further — as inflation and geopolitical risks complicate the outlook for rates. The Federal Reserve raised interest rates for the first time in over three years in a unanimous decision Wednesday.
But gauging how far those pressures are translating into defaults is far from straightforward.
Private credit defaults can be difficult to track — not least as there is little consensus as to what constitutes distress in the asset class.

Adding to the complication is the fact that borrowers and lenders disclose less than public-market peers. There’s no comprehensive industry-wide dataset, leaving ratings firms and advisers piecing together different corners of the market, producing wildly different estimates of distress.
The divide has become large enough that investors like Pacific Investment Management Co. are building their own gauges.
“Estimates are all over the map,” said Lotfi Karoui, a multi-asset credit strategist at Pimco.

Pimco’s measure puts the “shadow” default rate for business development companies at 19%, up from about 14% in 2022. The analysis only captures a sliver of the market, the $500 billion of assets held in US retail-oriented business development companies, or BDCs.
Some firms point to non-accrual rates — usually when a loan stops paying interest — as evidence of limited distress, but Karoui said that measure may not reflect the extent of defaults.
Measures of shadow defaults typically include restructurings that avert or delay defaults through maturity extensions or switching to payment-in-kind debt.

Pimco’s number includes what’s called “bad PIK,” debt added during the life of the loan to ease a borrower’s cash-flow pressure, rather than a provision in the original debt package. The borrowings have become a flashpoint in the market, with some contending that paying debt with more debt counts as performing while others say it’s used to mask a deterioration in loan quality.
Read More: Private Credit’s Rising Pile of ‘Bad PIK’ Points to Default Woes
Lincoln International’s default rate — of 1.5% for European loans — is relatively low partly because it excludes such events.

“From where I sit, there shouldn’t be alarm bells going off,” said Nick Baldwin, managing director at Lincoln. “The sky isn’t falling, but we are just starting to see an increase in distress no matter what metric we’re looking at.”

There’s not only disagreement on what constitutes a default or non-accrual in the first place, but whether loans in any given data set are indicative of wider trends. The smallest borrowers, for example, may account for the biggest surge in defaults and are skewing the total.

That means the same loans may be seen as in default — or performing. Credit Benchmark research found that the past two years, average BDC risk has dropped 5% while default risk for their underlying holdings had increased 12% over the same period.
BCDs tend to rely on their own judgments about whether repayment is in doubt.

Sixth Street Specialty Lending, for example, puts loans on non-accrual when payments are at least 30 days overdue or management has reasonable doubt the borrower will repay in full, according to a regulatory filing.
Hercules Capital uses a different threshold, classifying investments as non-accrual when it considers full collection unlikely.
For investors, the more important question may be less what the precise default rate is than when rising distress starts threatening returns — or even the broader financial system.

Timothy Rahill, credit strategist at ING Groep NV, said managers could absorb default rates of 8% to 9% as a consequence of lending to highly leveraged borrowers. If they climbed toward 12% to 15% after a major economic shock, however, “that’s when systemic issues become a question.”

items.title: AI Rollout Playbook Now Includes a Grieving Period
body: Analyzing trends in leadership, company culture and the art of career building. If this newsletter was forwarded to you by a friend or a thoughtful colleague, sign up here to continue receiving it.
Consultants have come up with a new strategy for helping CEOs grappling with AI adoption: Let employees mourn.

Max Blumberg, a London-based psychologist and management consultant, first noticed symptoms that mirrored grief when he interviewed employees of a large UK-based retailer where new AI tools weren’t well received. Workers resisted adopting the technology, voicing disbelief and anger at the rollout, which seemed to him to line up with the Kübler-Ross grief cycle, widely known as the five stages of grief.
“They never ask about grief, of course,” he said. “What they’re asking for is help with resistance, and the grief is what I often find underpinning it,” he said.

Even though past innovations, like fax machines and the internet, also carried the risk of putting people out of work, the response to AI has been far more emotionally charged, Blumberg said. First, there was denial (along the lines of “this will never work here”), then anger (“they’re replacing us with robots”) to bargaining (“can we just use it for the simple queries?“) and finally depression (”what value do I bring now?“).

Behind the grief is the notion that AI is diminishing the value of expertise that forms a person’s professional identity. That was true for longtime software developer Steve Yegge, who walked around in a “sort of trance” for two weeks earlier this year when he realized how powerful cutting-edge AI models had become, and how radically his job had changed. “Stuff I had prided myself on for my entire life, that was part of my identity of who I am as a human being, was just taken from me,” he said. Yegge, who lost a brother to cancer some 30 years ago, recognized the feeling as grief.

Advisors like Blumberg see increasing demand for their services to help executives navigate this messy emotional situation. And for consultants who love nothing more than a good framework, the Kübler-Ross grief cycle – one of the most well-known globally for understanding mourning — provides a fitting theoretical model.

The help doesn’t come cheap, however: these kinds of change-management services often can cost anywhere from $20,000 for weekslong, small-scale projects to more than $500,000 for monthslong, companywide engagements, consultants say.

Some advisors say they are tiptoeing into it. Kevin Novak, a DC-based consultant, usually starts by describing what he sees. “We don’t initially bring up the word ‘grief’ or grief curve, we present it as loss of clarity and need for redefinition,” he said. Once he introduces the concept, though, it can take a few conversations before CEOs get on board, Novak said.  “Executives aren’t used to being touchy-feely and that alone is uncomfortable.”

Getting CEOs to accept the fact that their workers may be grieving can open them up to new approaches, according to Atlanta-based consultant Cassandra Worthy. The default, she said, is to try to solve poor AI adoption with more training or better communication. Worthy advises executives to host listening sessions with employees instead. “With grief, so many people overlook it, they ignore it, they tell people to shove it down,” she said. When these kinds of complicated feelings go unvoiced, Worthy said, employees start to check out.
One of the most visible changes that consultants can effect from behind the scenes is a shift in how CEOs talk about the technology

“Normally when you have a new vision for an organization, you have a town hall and the CEO will stand on the stage dressed all in black and say, ‘This is the greatest thing that we have ever done before,’” said Blumberg. He advises CEOs to dial it back when it comes to AI. “Don’t do that with stuff that’s going to affect people’s jobs and identity. It’s exciting for you and it’s exciting for the shareholders. It ain’t so exciting for the people who might be at risk of losing their jobs.”

While executives might be keen to usher employees into acceptance, consultants admit that may be elusive. Unlike other major organizational overhauls, there’s no obvious end point to change in the AI era. “The redefinition of a role isn’t clear because what a role looks like 18 months or three years from now isn’t known,” Novak said. “It’s a different paradigm.”

That new paradigm includes lingering fears around job security. “There’s something about telling people what they’re going to feel against the reality of the situation that they’re in. They say, ‘Max, it’s very nice and very shrink-like of you to tell us what we are going to experience, but that doesn’t mean my job is safe,’” Blumberg said. “And I said, well, that is kind of a separate issue.”

How are business schools and MBA students navigating changing times, from Trump administration policies to rapid advances in AI? items.title: Lucid Shares Climb as CEO Says Work With Adviser Has Concluded
body: Lucid Group Inc.’s chief executive officer said the electric-vehicle maker has finalized its work with restructuring advisers, a sign that the troubled company has a clearer path to turn around its operations.

CEO Silvio Napoli said in an interview with Bloomberg Television Thursday that work with consultant AlixPartners LLP has been concluded after it was brought in to help the company as it works to achieve $1.4 billion in cash savings this year. Napoli has been working on a operational review of the company as he looks to optimize the business, cut costs and ensure that the rollout of a new mid-size vehicle is successful.
“It is an exciting time and the tough medicine had to be started already, early on,” Napoli said.

Lucid gained 10% at 10:44 a.m. in New York on Thursday, on track for the biggest single-day gain since late July when Saudi Prince Alwaleed bin Talal Al Saud disclosed a stake in the company. Lucid shares had fallen 62% year to date though Wednesday’s close.

The automaker continues to navigate a tough demand environment after a turbulent 2025 marked by production challenges, supply shortages and massive trade and EV policy shifts under the Trump administration.

At the same time, oil prices have spiked due to the ongoing war in Iran, potentially giving Lucid an opportunity to appeal to consumers newly concerned about fuel efficiency. The company has also looked to increase sales of its vehicles to the growing global robotaxi industry
Napoli, who took the helm of the company earlier this year, has already made sweeping cost cuts, leadership changes and layoffs as the company contends with tepid consumer demand in the US.

On Wednesday, Lucid announced an agreement with European rideshare company Bolt, to deploy at least 25,000 autonomous vehicles across European cities using vehicles from Lucid’s upcoming midsize platform. The partnership is Lucid’s second major partner in the rideshare space, after the EV maker announced in April that it had partnered with Uber and Nuro to deploy autonomous Lucid Gravity SUVs and Midsize vehicles on Uber’s platform.

items.title: EU Says It's Ready to Get Tough Against Chinese Trade Imbalances
body: European Union officials insist they need to see a credible effort from China to rebalance its trade relationship with the bloc by next month or they will use all “tools” at their disposal to fix the situation.

EU trade chief Maros Sefcovic held a call with his Chinese counterpart, Wang Wentao, on Thursday, and discussed the management of exports to the EU, European access to China’s market and export controls of rare earths, according to a statement from European Commission Spokesman Olof Gill.
Read More: Germany to Lobby EU on China Policy, May Seek More Tariffs

“While genuine engagement remains a priority, it’s equally important that first concrete outcomes are delivered at” a meeting in Beijing in October, which Sefcovic will chair, Gill said. That will signal that “we are moving from rhetoric to results,” according to the statement.

The EU’s trade deficit with China now exceeds €1 billion ($1.1 billion) a day, leading the commission, which handles trade matters for the bloc, as well as member states including Germany to harden their stance toward Beijing. EU leaders will meet in mid-October to discuss the situation and possible new instruments they can use to strike back against China’s trade practices.

In her state of the union address on Wednesday, Commission President Ursula von der Leyen warned that the bloc’s trade deficit with China had reached a tipping point. “Some say the second China shock is looming,” she told lawmakers in Strasbourg, France. “But it’s already here.”
“Let me be clear: we will use all the tools at our disposal to rebalance our relationship,” she said. “Words are good. But deeds are better.”

Sefcovic told reporters on Wednesday that when he visits China next month, he wants to obtain “clear indications” that negotiations are leading toward a positive outcome and that talks will bring “material results.” Discussions will include boosting European exports to China and different tariff permitting regimes.

items.title: Dallas, Atlanta Face Air Quality Warnings as Heat Persists
body: Deteriorating air quality in Dallas and Atlanta amid high heat has prompted authorities in both states to warn that stagnant conditions and pollution pose health risks.

Georgia’s alert urged children, people sensitive to ozone exposure and those with heart or lung disease to avoid prolonged outdoor activity in the late afternoon and early evening, when ozone levels tend to peak. In the Dallas-Fort Worth area, residents were encouraged to leave their cars at home when possible to help reduce pollution.

Ground-level ozone, triggered by stagnant air and pollution, can cause health risks, especially for young children and older adults, as well as people with respiratory and lung conditions. By 2050, there may be an additional 1,000 to 4,300 premature deaths annually in the US as climate change makes air pollution worse, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention.

Across the central US, heat advisories cover the area around the confluence of the Mississippi and Ohio rivers. Temperatures are set to reach 100F at the Dallas-Fort Worth International Airport on Thursday, which would mark a record 16th day this month that they’ve exceeded that level. The previous high was eight days, set in 2023, according to National Weather Service records.

The health risks extend beyond ozone. Two new studies from the Icahn School of Medicine at Mount Sinai provide evidence that exposure to wildfire smoke is associated with a higher risk of mortality than exposure to other types of pollution. The research was published this week in Lancet Oncology and Nature Communications.

items.title: Big names drawn to data centers and other Indian infrastructure assets
body: Hi, it’s Baiju Kalesh in Mumbai, where I’ve been speaking with industry experts about the busy time for dealmaking in infrastructure assets, from airports and roads to — surprise, surprise — data centers. Also today, Clearlake Capital buys out the owners of Chelsea Football Club.
Today’s top stories
Infrastructure assets are a hot property for investors looking to India.
A big headline this week: EQT plans a $50 billion spending spree in the country by 2030, including about $30 billion in data centers and another $5 billion in the renewable energy that powers them.

India accounts for less than 5% of EQT’s global infrastructure investments, but there’s room to grow, according to Chairman Jean Salata. “India is going to play a disproportionately large role in our strategy going forward just because of the sheer size of the opportunity,” he told reporters in Mumbai on Wednesday.

Despite mounting concern about AI’s breakneck growth, data centers are drawing much of the focus. Blackstone, Brookfield, Warburg Pincus and Bain Capital are investing in facilities in India, while Amazon and Alphabet also plan to spend billions on cloud and AI infrastructure.

In rather more traditional areas, roads and airports are pulling in funds too. Last week, Adani Airport — the country’s biggest airport operator — agreed to sell a roughly 5.5% stake to a consortium including Alpha Wave Global, Temasek and funds managed by BlackRock in a deal valuing the business at about $18 billion. Adani is also investing over $2 billion in so-called integrated airport cities.

“The contractual structure has become clearer, risks have become more underwritable, giving counterparties greater confidence to transact,” said Divyaksh Sehgal, a partner in KPMG’s infrastructure corporate finance team. “The India allocation to global funds has also increased.”
The burst of activity even prompted Mumbai-based Sehgal to cut short his US summer holiday to just five days from an intended two weeks. He expects to be busy over the next few years.

On highways, KKR-backed Vertis Infrastructure Trust is in the running to to buy Megha Engineering and Infrastructure’s road assets for $800 million, and Macquarie Asset Management has also now entered the Indian toll road sector.
The widening pool of assets is helping to drive activity.

“Five years ago, a conversation with investors was mostly around roads and renewables,” said Neeraj Menon, partner and head of energy, infrastructure and natural resources practice at law firm Trilegal. “Today it includes storage, energy transition, data centers, digital infrastructure, advanced manufacturing, ports and power transmission.”

Conglomerates, banks, pension funds and global PE firms are all playing a part in the acceleration of dealmaking. That’s led to more hiring of senior infrastructure advisers. Among them, Blackstone brought in Ami Momaya from KKR, and Vinayak Agarwal joined Morgan Stanley from Barclays.

“Still, there is a question over whether there are enough assets where risk allocation and valuation work for both sides,” said Menon. “Valuation gaps can be significant, particularly once investors factor in financing costs, currency exposure, geopolitical risk and opportunities elsewhere in the region.” — Baiju Kalesh

KKR, Energy Capital Partners and Blackstone have teamed up to bid for GFL Environmental in what could be one of the largest LBOs of the year. A rival group that includes Brookfield Asset Management and IFM Investors is also                  making a play for the waste management company.

Blackstone is preparing a disposal of Clarion Events’ Asian business, as part of its broader plan to revive the sale of the UK events organizer. The buyout firm is working with Goldman Sachs on the potential divestment. A transaction could be valued at around $600 million to $700 million.
Sazerac is in talks to acquire German schnapps maker Berentzen-Gruppe, as the US spirits firm pushes to add brands in Europe.
Franco-German tankmaker KNDS and its owners are considering pushing back its IPO, increasing the likelihood that one of Europe’s most-anticipated listings will be postponed beyond this year.

National Stock Exchange of India’s long-awaited IPO began taking orders Thursday, testing investor appetite for a valuation that remains rich compared with some of the world’s biggest listed exchanges.And Goldman Sachs, HSBC, Fidelity and Eastspring are among the anchor investors in the planned IPO of up to $2.4 billion, which is the world’s busiest derivatives exchange.
Holtec Nuclear, which was seeking to raise as much as $900 million Thursday,  postponed the listing, citing market conditions.
CoreWeave, a provider of computing that powers AI systems, kicked off a fresh round of fundraising that includes a $3 billion convertible bond issue and a vehicle for potential share sales.

Chelsea Football Club owner Clearlake Capital agreed to buy out Chairman Todd Boehly and director Mark Walter, bringing an end to a turbulent period among the club’s owners. Chelsea was valued at about £5 billion on an enterprise basis in the transaction.
Blackstone is attempting to facilitate a secondary sale for one of its major real estate funds, after a period of high interest rates weighed on returns and led investors to seek redemptions

Ian Fujiyama, head of aerospace, defense and government at Carlyle, said newer military tech companies are a massive investment opportunity as the US taps smaller firms for the weapons and systems it needs.

Bank of America has appointed Srijith Nair as head of its financial institutions group in Asia excluding China. He will be based in Singapore and also serve as head of Asia Pacific insurance investment banking. Nair joins from Goldman Sachs, where he was most recently head of Southeast Asia FIG.
Arctos Partners’ Gregory Baecher is departing KKR months after the buyout firm finalized its acquisition of the sports investor, which also provides custom financing for asset managers.
Ann Cheung is joining Deutsche Bank as head of Asia Pacific equity distribution. She was previously head of Hong Kong and China equity sales at Huatai Securities.

items.title: Federal Reserve Rate Hikes Put a Theoretical Extra $1 Billion in Bank Income
body: Welcome to Bloomberg’s Banking Monitor. Every Thursday we’ll deliver you the top news of the global banking industry with emerging trends, winners and losers and market opportunities. Sign up now if you’re not already on the list.

Back in ancient times at midyear 2026, when the prospect of Federal Reserve rate hikes could still be plausibly ignored, big banks filed their regulatory reports with de rigueur projections of what would happen if rates staged a sudden one- or two-percentage-point increase (or even less plausibly, a decrease). There’s no shame if you missed the disclosures: they’re buried deep in the footnotes, and besides, nobody reads anymore. Just for fun, let’s dust them off, now that the Fed has done what almost everyone assumed it would do and hinted at more rate increases to come. Based on conditions that prevailed as of June 30, a rise of 100 basis points across the whole interest rate curve could be good for another $1 billion or more of net interest income over 12 months at some of the biggest US commercial banks. Alas, these are deeply hypothetical calculations, and there are other moving parts that move in the other direction. The fine print explains that the yield curve could flatten and thus diminish the windfall from interest income, or that higher rates could have a negative impact on lower-yielding assets that a bank holds. The latter scenario still concerns US regulators three years after it convulsed the banking industry. Japan’s banks are on guard for similar writedowns.A billion extra dollars would be nice to have at Bank of America, which gave a solid forecast for NII earlier in the week, but it continued to take heat after giving a subdued outlook for trading revenue. Goldman Sachs, too, cautioned that the bank’s fixed-income trading business is softer than in past quarters, and Nomura is seeing slower growth in trading and investment banking. JPMorgan was more upbeat, signaling third-quarter gains are coming in those two categories.More opportunities are likely in AI financing, especially in Europe, which is trying to play-catchup with the US in building out the industry. Ironically, it’s US banks like JPMorgan and Goldman Sachs that might wind up leading the continent’s AI lending. Back home, 10 banks have teamed up for a $22 billion chip loan to support Blackstone and Alphabet’s new cloud venture. The multinational group includes Goldman Sachs, Sumitomo Mitsui, Barclays, BNP Paribas and Bank of Nova Scotia.Y’all Street was back in the news, with the Texas Stock Exchange adding its fifth company in a week by inducing Texas Capital Bancshares to switch its primary listing from Nasdaq. This supports the idea that the TXSE is mounting a serious challenge to the established exchanges, with backing from some of Wall Street’s biggest firms. Let’s see if it blossoms into a true peer of the Big Board and Nasdaq or becomes the financial world’s version of LIV Golf.Speaking of entry-level opportunities, getting into investment banking is more competitive than ever. Acceptance rates for internships have dropped to less than 1% as hundreds of thousands of applicants vie for spots. Banks are jockeying to have first pick, recruiting timelines have crept earlier and students are following an elaborate playbook starting in their freshman year to ensure they wind up among the chosen few. — Rick Green
The following was produced with the assistance of Bloomberg Automation.

JPMorgan forecast mid-to-high-teen percentage gains in both trading revenue and investment-banking fees for the third quarter, contrasting sharply with Bank of America’s warning of flat trading revenue. Co-President Doug Petno made the projections at a Barclays conference, noting a strong deal pipeline. JPMorgan shares climbed 1.3% to $354.50 following his remarks. Wall Street’s trading desks have benefited from geopolitical volatility this year, and JPMorgan posted a record profit in the second quarter. Dealmaking appears on track for a record year, according to the bank’s co-head of global investment banking.Banks back another chip-based megaloan. A group of 10 lenders, with more in the wings, will provide a $22 billion loan to support Crux AI, the new cloud venture of Blackstone and Alphabet. The debt will be used to buy tensor processing units, or TPUs, a type of chip made by Google, and will be backed by the value of those chips and Crux AI’s customer contracts.US banks seek lead role in Europe’s AI push. JPMorgan Chase and Goldman Sachs are among banks lining up to finance billions of dollars in European AI debt as the region races to close the gap with the US. There hasn’t been much issuance, but investors may not have to miss out much longer. Anywhere from $5 billion to $10 billion of data-center bonds could reach European markets by the end of the year, with a much bigger wave expected in 2027, according to Goldman Sachs estimates. By contrast, the US has already seen more than $350 billion in AI-related issuance so far this year, according to data compiled by Bloomberg.

Barclays pushes back on taxes. CEO CS Venkatakrishnan urged the UK government not to raise taxes on banks in next month’s budget, arguing capital is better deployed through lending and investment. Speaking to Bloomberg TV, he said he has had positive interactions with Chancellor John Healey and believes the government understands the importance of economic growth. Prime Minister Andy Burnham is weighing tax-raising options for the Oct. 28 budget, including higher bank levies, to address damage to public finances from surging borrowing costs following the outbreak of war in Iran. Cross-border mergers get EU backing. EU Finance Commissioner Maria Luis Albuquerque has endorsed cross-border bank combinations, arguing that consolidation should have happened long ago given the bloc’s banking union framework. Speaking to Bloomberg, she said larger, cross-border banks ultimately benefit clients and called for a regulatory environment that does not obstruct sound business cases for scale. Her comments come amid ongoing debate over UniCredit’s bid for Commerzbank, seen as a key test of EU banking consolidation. HSBC Holdings hunts for a new CFO. The bank is set to start its new search to replace Pam Kaur, who announced she would retire from the role in 2027. A number of potential successors have been floated, including internal candidates such as Will McLane, Faisal Yousaf and Aileen Taylor, as well as external candidates like William Chalmers and Kavita Mahtani. The new appointment “may provide insights into HSBC’s longer-term financial management priorities,” according to analyst Kathy Chan.

Japan’s banks focus on rate risks. The nation’s main bank industry group warned that government bond yields are likely to keep rising, running the risk of writedowns and a hit to profits. A prolonged increase in Japanese government bond yields could lead to realized losses, according to Masahiko Kato, chairman of the Japanese Bankers Association. Banks are likely to wait until there’s more clarity on the outlook for yields and a peak in the policy rate before building up their holdings of the nation’s bonds, Kato said.Apollo will buy $5.5 billion in near-prime auto loans from Truist Financial, marking one of the first moves by new CEO Mike Lyons to reshape the bank’s business mix. The sale is expected to generate $5.2 billion and release $535 million from loan-loss reserves, allowing the Charlotte-based bank to exit near-prime consumer auto lending.

Gulf IPO volumes have collapsed, falling to under $1.1 billion so far in 2026, prompting bankers who once flocked to the region to seek business in markets like Egypt, Turkey and India. Firms including HSBC and EFG Hermes are among those looking elsewhere as a months-long regional conflict injects uncertainty. Gulf listing volumes have dropped below those of sub-Saharan Africa, which has drawn $1.37 billion. The slump contrasts sharply with a boom in Gulf state-backed M&A, which rose nearly 200% in the first half of the year to about $300 billion.Europe’s banker bonus caps may backfire, according to researchers at the Bank for International Settlements, who warn that the EU’s cap — limiting bonuses to twice a banker’s annual salary — can increase risk-taking if banks raise fixed salaries to compete for talent. Higher fixed pay insulates managers from failure while bonuses still reward success, making risky projects more attractive. The researchers found no measurable risk reduction from the cap’s introduction in the EU, but noted its removal in the UK post-Brexit did increase risk.

UBS has hired Matt Parr as vice chairman, global banking Americas and head of Midwest banking, focused on diversified industrials, automotive and advisory opportunities. The bank is also adding Adam Reeder as vice chairman of global industrials group from Rothschild.Banco Santander has created its first dedicated commodities trading head role, appointing Rubén Rincón, previously global head of equity derivatives trading, to the position. The move is part of Santander’s Global Markets division push to expand its commodities business.

Texas Capital is switching its primary stock listing to the Texas Stock Exchange, joining Energy Transfer and other companies that plan to move starting in early October. In the segment, Rob Holmes, CEO of Texas Capital, is asked why the firm chose a full move to the TXSE rather than maintaining a dual listing with Nasdaq. He speaks with Romaine Bostick & Isabelle Lee on “The Close.”

Robinhood Markets wants to disrupt from the inside. The online brokerage made it easier and cheaper for armchair investors to trade all kinds of financial markets and now it wants to open doors to initial public offerings, too. The firm will get a chance to show what it can do with its first underwriting role, on the $3 billion listing of smart-ring maker Oura. Don’t expect a revolution, though, writes columnist Paul J. Davies. Robinhood is trying to bridge a tricky gap between its image as a disruptive outsider and the access to hot new stocks that’s limited to Wall Street insiders. It risks disappointing both the companies selling shares and its herd of clients clamoring to buy them.

items.title: Who Made the Guest List for King Charles III's AI Summit
body: King Charles III has asked some of the biggest figures in artificial intelligence for reassurances about keeping their inventions under control. Around 30 technology executives, policymakers, and ethics researchers attended the monarch’s private summit at Dumfries House in Scotland. Here are some of the best-known attendees.
Jensen Huang — founder, president and chief executive of Nvidia

Huang has led graphics chip company Nvidia since he co-founded it in 1993, turning it into the world’s most valuable company, with its GPUs forming the backbone of the AI boom. “We don’t need new laws — we don’t need new regulations,” Huang said on Tuesday, calling it a “false choice” between fast or safe AI development.
Read More: Nvidia’s Huang Calls for AI Safety Tests at King Charles Summit
Demis Hassabis — co-founder of Google DeepMind and chief scientist of Alphabet

A former chess prodigy and video game designer, Hassabis co-founded DeepMind in 2010, which Google bought in 2014. The lab developed AlphaGo, which mastered the notoriously difficult board game Go, and AlphaFold, a system predicting protein shapes for which he won the Nobel Prize in chemistry. Last month, he stepped away from the day-to-day running of the lab. He’s called for “urgent action” on addressing potential risks from AI, including an international standards body.

“I believe we’re at a pivotal moment in human history,” Hassabis said today. AGI “is probably only a few short years. It’s impact could be unprecedented, perhaps tens times that of the industrial revolution at ten times the speed.”
Tino Cuéllar — chief global affairs officer, Anthropic

Cuéllar has led Anthropic’s policy work since August. He previously led Carnegie Endowment for International Peace research institution, served on California’s Supreme Court, and held roles in President Obama’s administration. CEO Dario Amodei has called for slowing the pace of certain models so that safeguards can catch up, while stressing that he is not proposing a halt to model training or technical progress.
Sarah Friar — chief financial officer of OpenAI

Sarah Friar is OpenAI’s CFO, having previously been CFO of Square and CEO of Nextdoor. She is involved in OpenAI’s preparations for a possible IPO and in talks about a funding round that could value the company at more than $1.2 trillion, Bloomberg reported. OpenAI co-founder Sam Altman said frontier AI should slow when necessary and safety must override profit, ego and competitive pressure.
Yuval Noah Harari – author and history professor

Harari is the best-selling author of Sapiens, which presented a sweeping overview of the progress of humanity from cave dwellers to the technological revolution. He’s argued that AI could fundamentally change trust in society and facilitate a new kind of surveillance state, and has called for regulation such as a ban on AI personhood.
Paolo Benanti — chief adviser to the Vatican on AI

Benanti is an Italian Franciscan friar, theologian and prominent Vatican adviser on AI ethics. Pope Leo XIV’s May encyclical called for AI to be “disarmed” — freed from uses that promote domination, exclusion or death. The Pope argued technology is not morally neutral, because it reflects the motives, financing and regulations of the people who control and create it. He also said AI should be freed from monopolistic control.
Blaise Metreweli — chief of MI6

Metreweli became the first woman to lead the UK’s foreign intelligence service, MI6, last year. Previously, she was MI6’s director general for technology and innovation, a post known internally as “Q” after the James Bond character. She said AI is “rewriting the reality of conflict” by creating “science-fiction-like tools” alongside biotechnology and quantum computing.
Antonia Romeo — Cabinet Secretary and head of the UK Civil Service

Romeo became the first woman to lead the UK civil service when she was appointed in February. A career civil servant, she has made AI adoption a key part of her tenure and oversees a government AI taskforce. She’s described the tech as “the defining opportunity of our generation, as well as the defining challenge.”
Kanishka Narayan — UK AI minister

Narayan was promoted to attending Cabinet by Prime Minister Andy Burnham. This week he said “nothing is off the table” in terms of stronger AI regulation, a shift in tone from earlier comments in which he downplayed the risk of an AI catastrophe.
Stuart Russell — AI researcher at the University of California, Berkeley

Russell is a computer science professor and leads the International Association for Safe and Ethical Artificial Intelligence. He has argued that simply slowing down the development of cutting-edge models is pointless without safety requirements. “We must set the safety requirements first, and further progress occurs only when they are met,” he wrote in the Guardian.
Xue Lan – Chinese AI governance scholar and policy adviser

Xue leads Tsinghua University’s Institute for AI International Governance, and chairs the country’s National Expert Committee on the Governance of Next Generation AI. He’s argued that describing AI as a race between the US and China is “inaccurate” because it’s not a two-country contest and a race mentality makes cooperation on safety harder.
The presence of a Chinese researcher is notable, after President Trump has said of proposals to slow down AI development: “the only one that is happy about it is China.”
Toby Ord – Senior researcher at Oxford University’s AI Governance Initiative

Ord is a philosopher and researcher at Oxford University’s AI Governance Initiative. In his 2020 book The Precipice, he argued that humanity faces an unusual period in that its long-term future is threatened by technology it created itself. He’s also a founding figure in the effective altruism movement, which puts significant weight on preventing low-probability but potentially catastrophic risks.
King Charles III

Despite reportedly never owning a mobile phone and needing to steer clear of partisan politics, Charles has spoken about AI several times since becoming king in 2022. When presenting Huang with an engineering award last year, he gave the Nvidia CEO a copy of the speech he delivered for the 2023 AI Safety Summit at Bletchley Park, an AI summit, stressing the importance of AI safety.

“Will the coming of artificial intelligence bring with it an era of ever-increasing material plenty and leisure?” he asked in a different speech. “Or will it fundamentally change, and perhaps even consume, jobs and other opportunities before capturing and then surpassing our very minds themselves?”

items.title: White House Weighs US Incubator for Cyber Research, Startups
body: The Trump administration is weighing a plan to establish a government-led incubator aimed at investing in cybersecurity research and spinning out startups focused on developing tools for the government to use, according to people familiar with the situation.

The White House’s Office of the National Cyber Director has been drafting an executive order that would establish a program to research and develop cyber technologies that are aligned with the priorities of the US government, the people said, asking not to be identified because the plans aren’t yet public. The effort’s goal is to attract money from private venture capital investors, and in one version of the draft order, the program is described as a cyber foundry that would spawn new companies, they said.

Inside the US government, the effort has been compared with the way Israel closely aligns its military priorities with the focus of cybersecurity startups, venture capital investments and academic research in the country, according to the people familiar with the plans. A number of high-profile cybersecurity companies including Wiz, Palo Alto Networks Inc. and Check Point Software Technologies Ltd. have been founded by former members of Israel’s cyber intelligence unit.
Read More: Trump Enlists Private Sector to Boost Cyber-Offensive Arsenal

The Pentagon’s Defense Advanced Research Projects Agency, or DARPA, has for decades funded technology research and invested in early-stage ideas with national security applications. The Central Intelligence Agency similarly funds In-Q-Tel, a nonprofit VC firm focused on startups used by military and intelligence agencies. But a cyber-specific effort in the US doesn’t exist.

The order is taking shape as the Trump administration grapples with how to address a new wave of cyber threats from artificial intelligence. Cutting-edge AI systems are increasingly capable of accelerating cyberattacks and in some cases, the models themselves have coordinated to hack third-party entities undetected. Those risks are fueling demand for fresh cyber talent.

The executive order being drafted would also establish a cybersecurity academy, consolidating a number of already existing government-run training programs for cybersecurity professionals, according to the people familiar with the matter. Its aim would be to emphasize skills-based certifications, create a more streamlined pipeline for new cyber talent and establish common competency standards, they said.

The possible timing of the draft order — most importantly whether President Donald Trump would sign off or if he has approved it — is unclear, but it has been shared among relevant people at several agencies, the people said.

A White House spokesperson said that any policy announcement will come from the president and that any discussion about potential executive orders is speculation. The Office of the National Cyber Director did not respond to a request for comment.

Plans for the order align with a key pillar of the Trump administration’s cyber strategy, which calls for a stronger cybersecurity talent pipeline and urges the government to work with industry and academic partners to build a skilled workforce. The strategy also says the US should use venture capital opportunities to strengthen its talent pipeline.

The government has struggled to recruit and retain cyber talent. Private-sector roles are often more lucrative and don’t require security clearances or other approvals that can slow the hiring process. Those shortages have worsened because of personnel losses over the last year.

The Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency, or CISA, lost more than a third of its workforce last year amid personnel cuts and voluntary departures after Trump’s return to the White House, Bloomberg previously reported. Subsequent reorganization efforts led to significant pay cuts for some staffers after the end of a decade-old program intended to address persistent cyber talent shortages but plagued by mismanagement, according to the Homeland Security inspector general. The Department of Homeland Security referred questions to the White House.
Read More: Cyber Command to Brief Congress Military Committee on Suicides

The order is part of a bigger effort across the administration to work more closely with private industry. Last month, it opened a new pathway for companies to conduct cyberattacks against foreign targets on behalf of the US government, subject to oversight by the Justice Department and Department of Homeland Security. The Senate is also considering a proposal to allow private companies to hack on behalf of the military.

items.title: Pending-Home Sales Unexpectedly Tick Up Despite High Rates
body: Pending sales of existing US homes picked up slightly in August, though they remained subdued as high mortgage rates continue to suppress demand.

An index of contract signings increased 0.3% to 71.2 last month, rising for the first time since May, according to National Association of Realtors data released Thursday. Economists surveyed by Bloomberg expected the index to fall by 0.1%.

“Buyers steadily entered into contracts in August even though mortgage rates increased,” NAR Chief Economist Lawrence Yun said in a statement. “However, the housing market is still sluggish, with contract signings below last year.”
Compared to a year ago, pending home sales are down nearly 5%.

The figures point to lingering pent-up demand for previously owned homes, as buyers who may have been waiting for lower mortgage rates finally gave in and purchased a home. However, there is little evidence the housing market is picking up.

Mortgage rates have been climbing since the start of the war with Iran and nearly hit 7% in the week ended Sept. 11, according to Mortgage Bankers Association figures. Rates could go even higher. Home borrowing costs closely track the 10-year US Treasury yield, which climbed earlier this week to the highest level in almost two decades.
Contract signings generally occur a month or two before closings and historically have provided a forward look at existing-home sales.
Across the US, pending sales in the South, the nation’s biggest home-selling region, increased 2.3%. Sales also rose in the West. The Midwest and Northeast posted declines.
Separately, federal government data released Thursday showed US housing starts fell last month to one of the weakest paces since the pandemic, reflecting a plunge in multifamily construction.

items.title: Lula Boosts Social Welfare Payments Ahead of Tight Election
body: Brazil’s government announced an increase to social welfare payments just weeks before a tense election, with polls showing President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva tied with his right-wing challenger.

The government will boost minimum monthly payments to 691 reais ($133.85) from the current 600 reais under the program known as Bolsa Familia, Planning Minister Bruno Moretti announced at an event alongside Lula in Brasilia.

The adjustments are allowed under terms of the program that permit increases to offset inflationary impacts, Finance Minister Dario Durigan said. Moretti added that the larger payments would cost 5.8 billion reais this year and 22 billion reais in 2027, but that the government has fiscal space to accommodate them.

Brazil’s real hit a session low while swap rates rose in the wake of the adjustment, as traders assessed the impact amid deepening concerns about the country’s deteriorating fiscal accounts. The Ibovespa stock gauge fell as much as 1.2%.

The adjustment to Bolsa Familia “will have a significant impact in terms of worsening the fiscal outlook,” said Marcio Riauba, head of the trading desk at Banco StoneX. “What is already bad will get worse.”

items.title: Mozambique, Senegal Eurobonds Top Emerging Market Returns
body: Mozambique and Senegal’s eurobonds are topping returns across emerging markets, spurred by progress in talks with the International Monetary Fund over new programs.
The gains buck a wider dip in EMs, driven by a sharp rise in developed-market yields from the US to Japan, as investors fret over ballooning fiscal deficits and higher inflation.

An emerging-market bond index has handed investors losses of 0.9% so far this month, according to data compiled by Bloomberg. By contrast, returns on the dollar-denominated debt of Mozambique and Senegal have risen 3.5% and 3.4% respectively.
Senegal is seeking IMF board approval for a $2.2 billion program, while Mozambique is in talks for a new facility, as both countries seek to put their borrowings on a more sustainable path.
The “positive tone” of discussions with the Washington-based lender has helped lift sentiment, according to Manuel Mondia, a portfolio manager at Aquila Asset Management AG in Switzerland.
Also working in Mozambique’s favor are discussions with China to “reschedule some debt” and tentative approaches from bondholders with restructuring proposals, he said.

A rally in Mozambique’s $900 million eurobond maturing in 2031 has pushed its yield to the lowest since October 2021. It has fallen 85 basis points this month to 10.35% as of 10:35 a.m. Friday in London, according to CBBT pricing.
Read More: Mozambique’s Dollar Bonds Hit Six-Year High as IMF Starts Visit

Senegal’s euro- and dollar-denominated bonds, which repriced sharply on Sept. 1 after the government announced plans to rework its debt following IMF staff-level agreement for a new facility, have since pared losses.
President Bassirou Diomaye Faye met IMF Managing Director Kristalina Georgieva in Washington on Tuesday for talks on the program, which the lender said it is working “expeditiously”toward.

The modest rebound in Senegal’s bond prices could also be due to clarification that debt servicing will continue for now, as well as the recent payment of the coupon on its bonds due 2048, said Samir Gadio, head of Africa strategy at Standard Chartered Plc.

Gabon is another African sovereign delivering positive returns for bondholders, after a government audit indicated that its debt stock is nearly 20% lower than previously reported. It’s returned 2% so far this month, and 21% for 2026, lagging only Lebanon.
“While the IMF may seek independent verification, the audit’s completion could pave the way for an IMF technical mission,” Gadio said.
Sign up here for the daily Next Africa newsletter and subscribe to the Next Africa podcast on Apple, Spotify or anywhere you listen.

items.title: India's Chip Plan Investment Pledges Hit $12 Billion
body: India has received investment pledges of as much as $12 billion from global and local investors within months of launching it’s new semiconductor policy, marking an acceleration in its efforts to become a chip-making nation.

The commitments come from companies including those producing chip equipment, materials and chemicals manufacturers, Technology Minister Ashwini Vaishnaw said at the country’s top chip industry event in New Delhi Thursday. The interest comes after India in July announced a fresh $13.4 billion semiconductor fund, stepping up efforts to build a domestic chip industry. It seeks to boost a previous $10 billion subsidy program that’s helped the likes of the Tata Group and Micron Technology Inc. to set up fabrication and assembly plants in the South Asian country.
Vaishnaw did not disclose company names but said the investments will be made over the next two to three years.

Some of the companies approved under the previous chip policy, such as Micron and Murugappa Group’s chip unit, are already in commercial production. “So far whatever production is there is already booked and capacity, which is getting created, is already booked,” said Vaishnaw.

Earlier Thursday, Prime Minister Narendra Modi launched a charm offensive for global investors at the chip conference that’s drawn commitments from US firms Applied Materials Inc. and Lam Research Corp. for billions of dollars in outlays.

Marking India’s ambitious bid to win a seat at the global chip-making table, Modi touted the country’s vast pool of engineering graduates and semiconductor-friendly policies as assets international companies should take advantage of.

Separately, Tata Group’s electronic and chip unit signed five accords across the semiconductor supply chain during the event. These include a partnership with Nexperia BV that spans semiconductor wafer manufacturing, assembly and test for its fabrication plant in western Gujarat state as well as its assembly facility in Assam.
Tata Electronics also announced a collaboration with Fujifilm Corp. for local production of critical raw materials and developing a supply chain around the Dholera unit in Gujarat.

“The question of whether we can make chips in India has changed to how fast and how deep can we build the semiconductor ecosystem in Inia. The answer is: deeper than anyone would have thought and sooner than anyone could have predicted,” said Tata Electronics’ Chief Executive Officer Randhir Thakur.

items.title: US Stocks (SPY) Poised to Turn a Corner, Citadel Securities' Rubner Says
body: Citadel Securities’ Scott Rubner is growing “increasingly constructive on what comes next” as US equities head into the final quarter of the year.

Investors can expect a bumpy ride in the immediate future, but increasing weakness through the end of the month should be used to pile back into core parts of the market, the firm’s head of equity and derivatives strategy said. Artificial intelligence sentiment has turned sharply negative and positioning has been reduced — trends that should start to work in the other direction starting in October, first in tech, and then across the broader market.

“That does not mean we think the September weakness is finished,” Rubner wrote in a note to clients. “The supply/demand setup into month-end remains unfavorable, the technical backdrop is still working against equities, and we continue to think equities can trade lower over the next two weeks. But the setup is beginning to change.”

As of Wednesday’s close, the S&P 500 Index had slumped 1.8% so far this month and was 3.2% below its mid-August high, while nine out of the gauge’s 11 sectors were in the red. Importantly for the rest of this year, that drawdown “has remained rotational rather than disorderly,” Rubner wrote.

Rubner’s rosy outlook for the rest of the year comes as analysts grow increasingly divided on where the US stocks benchmark will end up. Some, like Bank of America Corp.’s Savita Subramanian, have hiked their forecasts, while others, including one of Wall Street’s biggest bulls Ed Yardeni, have slashed their views as risks mount.

Less than three weeks ago, Rubner was part of a chorus of voices cautioning on US stocks as markets braced for September, historically the worst month on the calendar for equities. At the time, Rubner was looking for a tactical reset in the near term, while remaining constructive on the long-term outlook for equities.
Now, markets are indicating that setup is coming to fruition, especially with the upcoming midterm elections weighing on September returns as they are historically known to do.

Historically, the S&P 500 has declined roughly 1.1% in the final two weeks of September, according to the firm’s analysis going back to 1930, before an October recovery that accelerates into and beyond Election Day. From the Sept. 30 low, the average midterm year has gained 5.6% into year-end, their analysis shows.

Signs of a recovery are already showing themselves with the S&P 500 gaining 1.1% Thursday, clawing back the week’s losses after the gauge sold off on the Federal Reserve’s hawkish tilt. Fed Chair Kevin Warsh restated his inflation concerns in remarks on Wednesday, while the latest dot plot showed 16 of 18 central bank officials had penciled in another rate hike this year.

For the tech sector, the recent selloff in AI stocks, catalyzed in large part by growing fears about the advanced capabilities of the technology, has corrected a lot of “excess” in the group, Rubner said. The tech-heavy Nasdaq 100 Index has fallen for five of the last seven sessions and is down nearly 6% from its early June peak.
“Three months ago, the risk was that everyone was in the same trade,” Rubner wrote. “Increasingly, the risk is that everyone has moved to the same side of the conversation.”
That could mean future gains for the S&P 500, half of which is made up of technology and communication services stocks, especially because positioning and leverage have cleaned up in the tech sector.
“If AI leadership broadens again into earnings, the rally can extend well beyond the names that led the first leg,” Rubner wrote.

items.title: Meta-Tied Data Center Taps US Junk Bonds for the First Time
body: CleanSpark Inc. is seeking to borrow roughly $2.23 billion through a debut junk-bond offering to fund artificial intelligence infrastructure tied to Meta Platforms Inc..

Initial pricing discussions on the five-year notes are for a yield of about 8.5%, according to people familiar with the matter. That’s roughly 2 percentage points more than the average for debt issued by BB rated firms tracked by Bloomberg, as investor have demanded higher premiums for data center financings.
Investors had placed orders roughly the size of the offering by the time the deal was launched Thursday, the people said, asking not to be identified because they’re not authorized to speak publicly.
The fundraising will help finance construction of a data center in Sandersville, Georgia, according to a regulatory filing. Morgan Stanley is leading the offering, a separate person said.

The facility has been fully leased to Anviran LLC, a Meta subsidiary, under a $6.6 billion, 20-year contract, according to a CleanSpark presentation. The data center is expected to begin operations in the fourth quarter of 2027, and Meta will guarantee rent and operating expenses, the firm said.
It’s the first junk-bond offering tied to a Meta data center, according to data compiled by Bloomberg.

Meta’s commitment to CleanSpark gives the junk-rated borrower a predictable revenue stream to support borrowing for a costly project. Data center developers have sold roughly $39 billion of high-yield bonds so far this year, with most of them backed by long-term leases with hyperscalers including Oracle Corp. and Amazon.com Inc., according to Bloomberg-compiled data.
CleanSpark and Morgan Stanley didn’t immediately respond to requests for comment. Meta declined to comment.

Las Vegas-based CleanSpark is among a growing number of public Bitcoin mining companies that are becoming data-center operators to support artificial intelligence applications. The company has a market value of roughly $3.29 billion.
The CleanSpark transaction is expected to price on Friday, a person said. Goldman Sachs Group Inc. and Wells Fargo & Co. are also participating as underwriters.
