items.title: Israel's Need for $8 Billion of Extra War Funds Leads to Election Showdown
body: Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s government is struggling to strike a deal to fund the Israeli military’s request for $8 billion before next month’s election.

Netanyahu this week failed to secure opposition leader Yair Lapid’s support to allocate 25 billion shekels ($8.2 billion) in extra funding to the military, whose finances have come under strain from almost three years of fighting in Gaza, Yemen, Lebanon and Iran, according to people familiar with the matter. They asked not to be identified because of the sensitivity of the issue.

After the meeting, Defense Minister Israel Katz appealed to Lapid to “support the IDF’s urgent request.” The extra funds are needed, he said, to pay reserve soldiers, protect Israeli border communities, and procure munitions.

“We face dramatic security challenges that require decisions and actions right now,” Katz said. “It would be wrong to tie the issue of security to the standard political debate with the government over various budgetary items.”
Netanyahu’s office and a spokesman for Lapid declined to comment. The Israel Defense Forces didn’t immediately respond to a request for comment.

The showdown is part of political maneuvering between the government and opposition ahead of the election scheduled for Oct. 27. The proposal would bring this year’s defense spending to about 183 billion shekels, or around 9% of Israel’s gross domestic product, one of the highest globally.

Military outlays have surged as Netanyahu’s government adopted a more preemptive military doctrine in the aftermath of the 2023 attack by the Iran-backed militant group Hamas — designated a terrorist organization by the US and much of the West — that triggered the war in Gaza and spilled over onto the wider region.
The opposition supports increasing military spending, though wants some expenditure cuts to balance the impact on the budget, one person close to the opposition leader said.

Lapid asked the government to scrap so-called coalition funds — which are estimated to cost about 5 billion shekels in 2026 — the person said, adding that Netanyahu rejected clamping down on those handouts. Those funds support his political allies, including the country’s ultra-Orthodox Jewish community.

Some of the fallout is already visible. Israel has missed its designated slot to order a squadron of Apache helicopters from Boeing Co., one of the people said, asking not to be identified while discussing private information. Boeing didn’t immediately respond to a request for comment.
The failure to reach a compromise is also putting pressure on military operations conducted by the IDF. It controls about 60% of the Gaza Strip and is occupying parts of Lebanon and Syria.

Netanyahu already approved a 15-billion-shekel budget supplement for the IDF in June. The other 25 billion shekels would be allocated following reviews over the next two months, two of the people said.
With Israel’s parliament in pre-electoral recess, any new funding would likely need to be legally signed off by the opposition.

Some of the fallout is already visible. Air-defense stockpiles need replenishing, one of the people said, noting that rebuilding those stocks requires multiyear contracts. The US, which started this year’s war against Iran alongside Israel, has also seen its stocks of high-end munitions drop significantly, according to several analysts.
Read more: US Munitions Shortfall Is a Crisis In the Making: Editorial

Israeli defense firm Elbit Systems Ltd. expects to shut down some production lines for tank rounds and other ammunition because of the government’s inability to sign new contracts, the same person said.

The Finance Ministry was forced to delay payments to some local defense companies, including Elbit, Israel Aerospace Industries and Rafael Advanced Defense Systems Ltd., according to one of the people, who didn’t elaborate on the amount currently owed to those firms.
Elbit, IAI and Rafael either declined to or didn’t immediately respond to requests for comment on the late payments.

Earlier this year, Netanyahu sought to advance a 12-year military buildup plan at a cost of as much as 400 billion shekels. The program is aimed at making Israel more self-sufficient for its defense needs. It’s expected to start next year, but that may depend on the election results.

items.title: Hungarian Startup Plans US Foothold With Non-Military Drones
body: ABZ Innovation, a Hungarian startup, is planning to begin non-military drone production in the US over the course of next year after expanding output at home, according to its chief executive officer.

ABZ opened a new production facility in Szentendre, north of Budapest, on Thursday, where it plans to ramp up production of heavy-duty agricultural and industrial drones, Karoly Ludvigh said in an interview. The facility will eventually produce 3,500 drones annually in two shifts to address an order backlog.

While the Russia-Ukraine and US-Iran wars have boosted demand for military drones, ABZ plans to focus on civilian use, which it sees as a niche market for clients looking to diversify away from China.
Read more: Trump’s 100% Tariff on Drones Deepens US-China Tech Decoupling

“It’s a constant topic for us,” Ludvigh said about whether ABZ may expand to dual use to include military drones. “But we don’t have to deal with it because all of our capacity is completely booked for our civilian drones.”
ABZ plans to set up a factory in the US next year, a move the CEO said would shield the company from potential tariffs.

The startup’s products can be used in various ways from spraying crops to cleaning buildings, cutting costs for farmers and for maintenance. Its biggest market is the US, accounting for more than a third of the planned 600 drones the company will sell this year, Ludvigh said.
ABZ received €7 million ($8 million) from venture capital firms earlier this year. Ludvigh declined to give the valuation from the funding round.
Another financing round is planned for next year to help cover the cost of expansion, the CEO said, with an initial public offering among the options under consideration for later.
Read more: Canada Targets Millions of Drones, With a Third for Ukraine

items.title: GM Defense Delivers First Patriot Missile Parts to Lockheed
body: General Motors Co. made its first delivery of Patriot missile parts to Lockheed Martin Corp. less than a month after forming a partnership, a sign that the automaker is pushing to help the defense industry rapidly rebuild the nation’s ammunition stock.

GM delivered castings that make up the outer shell of the PAC-3 missiles 22 days after signing a partnership agreement with Lockheed, according to a statement Thursday. President Donald Trump invoked the War Powers Act to press defense contractors and other US industrial companies to replenish a dwindling supply of missiles and munitions due in part to the war with Iran and the conflict between Russia and Ukraine.
GM shares rose 3.1% at 9:33 a.m. shortly after markets opened in New York on Thursday. They’d gained 3.7% this year through Wednesday’s close. Lockheed shares were largely unchanged Thursday.

Collaboration between the two companies shows the beginnings of the kind of factory conversion to weaponry that made Detroit’s automakers the Arsenal of Democracy during World War II. Auto plants were converted to make tanks, military trucks, bomber planes and other war materials.

Though at a much smaller scale now, the deal helps Lockheed and potentially other defense contractors work faster to build missiles and support the military during conflicts around the globe. It also helps GM grow its budding defense unit, which mostly sells pickup trucks used in troop transport for the US Army.

Lockheed signed a deal with the Pentagon in January to triple Patriot missile production. Under the terms of its deal with GM, the Detroit-based company is making castings and other parts and lending mass-manufacturing expertise.
GM has discussed similar deals with RTX Corp. and L3Harris Technologies Inc. about similar collaboration, people familiar with the matter said in June.

items.title: Next Africa: South Africa's Next Crisis After Electricity Is Gas
body: Welcome to Next Africa, a daily newsletter on where the continent stands now — and where it’s headed. Sign up here. In today’s edition, we look at:
South Africa is accustomed to being mired in crisis.

It’s just coming out of more than a decade of crippling power outages and is now contending with collapsing water infrastructure. But it still hasn’t learned to anticipate where the next challenge will come from.
Businesses that account for 8% of the economy are imploring the government to help avert a so-called gas cliff in as little as two years.

That’s when petrochemicals giant Sasol says it will no longer have enough spare supply from its central Mozambican fields to meet the needs of natural gas-reliant industries such as glass and food manufacturers.
That’s led some companies to shelve investment plans and others to consider reverting to costly and dirty fuels, such as fuel oil and even coal.
There are two main reasons for the impending shortage.

The government hasn’t moved fast enough to have its own utility or private investors commit to building gas-fired power plants to guarantee the demand that will justify the cost of constructing import terminals for the product.
Secondly, a decade or more of legal challenges by environmentalists has stymied exploitation of ample offshore gas reserves.
Sasol has offered a temporary fix until 2030: gas made from coal. But companies say that could be prohibitively expensive and set back their environmental targets.
With time running out, they may have no choice.
As the commercial officer of the country’s biggest glassmaker says: “South Africa doesn’t do anything until it’s an absolute crisis.”

A Kenyan high court ruled that laws governing the nation’s public-private partnerships are unconstitutional as they exclude scrutiny and oversight from lawmakers. Thursday’s judgment is the latest blow to President William Ruto’s plans to fund $39 billion of mega-infrastructure projects.

Israel and Morocco agreed to deepen ties by reinstating direct flights and opening embassies, pressing forward with a normalization deal signed during US President Donald Trump’s first term. The countries are also discussing further economic and trade cooperation, and trying to finalize deals to protect investments.

Uganda’s central bank raised the cash-reserve requirement for commercial lenders to help defend the shilling. The currency has weakened almost 6% against the dollar in the past month, making it the world’s worst performer of those tracked by Bloomberg.

South African consumer confidence rebounded in the third quarter, but is expected to remain subdued as household finances come under strain from soaring oil prices and higher interest rates. Separately, key legislation including a bill that would impact a municipal election set for Nov. 4, is in limbo because of parliamentary delays.

South African police found the body of a ninth woman on the outskirts of Johannesburg, widening an investigation into a series of similar killings over the past two months. The deaths have heightened concerns about violence against women in a country with one of the world’s highest female-homicide rates.

Ethiopia’s stock exchange has given in-principle approval for 11 listings, potentially almost tripling the number of publicly traded firms. The bourse debuted in January 2025 to help attract capital into an economy that was largely closed to foreign investment for decades. It has a total of 22 market intermediaries, including seven investment banks.

As the US ramps up its oil and gas use, the rapid shift by emerging markets into alternative sources of energy — a trend that has been turbocharged by the war in Iran — is forcing a reset that will have consequences for global power dynamics, according to Al Gore. The former US vice president and climate activist says a “real sea change” is under way in parts of Africa, Pakistan and Thailand.
We’ll be back in your inbox with another edition tomorrow. Send any feedback to nextafrica@bloomberg.net.

items.title: Bose Unveils $199 Bose Sport Open Earbuds, Second-Gen Ultra Open Earbuds
body: Bose Corp. is expanding its line of wraparound, cuff-shaped earbuds with two new models: the $199 Sport Open and $299 Ultra Open.

Both are marked by their C-shaped “cuff” style, which hugs the earlobe almost like an earring. The Sport Open Earbuds have a lightweight, dust-resistant build, seven-hour battery life and textured physical buttons that should be easier to use during workouts. The new Ultra Open model, priced at $299, promises less lag, comes with a redesigned case that can wirelessly charge, and offers longer, nine-hour battery life. Both products, introduced Thursday, will be available to preorder on Sept. 19, with shipments beginning Oct. 1.

The new Ultra Open otherwise includes many of the same features offered by the original model introduced in 2024, including splash and sweat resistance, voice isolation for calls and automatic volume adjustments.

This wraparound form factor represents an increasingly popular and more fashionable style that promises robust audio quality without sealing off the ear canal, making it easier for users to stay aware of their surroundings. The trade-off, however, is that many open earbuds lack noise cancellation. To address that, Bose said its hardware design helps minimize sound leakage and that its digital signal processing can help balance clarity and deep bass sounds.

Similar to rivals such as Sony Group Corp., Lenovo Group Ltd.’s Motorola and Huawei Technologies Co., Bose is marketing its open earbuds as stylish accessories, in part by offering trendy, limited-edition colors alongside more standard black and white options. That includes eucalyptus green for the sports model, and cherry chocolate, olive green and sky pink for the upgraded Ultra.

The charging case for the upgraded Ultra Open earbuds offers an additional 19.5 hours of playback. The case for the athletic model adds as much as 22 hours. A 10-minute charging session can provide two hours of playback on the Ultra and one hour for the Sport version.

Both new models offer the option to set up customizable shortcuts for Spotify’s streaming service or quick access to a phone’s native voice assistant. Bose said it’s planning a firmware update for the new devices after their Oct. 1 release that will add more connectivity options, including for Google Find Hub, Alexa+ and shortcut support for Apple Music.

items.title: Carney Plays Down Trump Threat as He Touts EU Alliance
body: Welcome to the Brussels Edition. I’m Suzanne Lynch, Bloomberg’s Brussels bureau chief, bringing you the latest from the EU each weekday. Make sure you’re signed up.

If European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen surprised Brussels watchers yesterday with her bold offer of associate EU membership for Canada, today it was Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney’s opportunity to set out his stall.
Addressing the European Parliament in Strasbourg, Carney welcomed the “ambition” of von der Leyen’s proposal, noting that an overwhelming majority of Canadians support closer ties with Europe.
“A Canada-EU alliance would create a beacon for other democracies,” he said. “An alliance not defined by what we oppose, but about what we are for: freedom, solidarity, prosperity, sustainability.”

He shed some light on what Canada wants from the relationship –  greater cooperation in critical materials, defense industrial capacity, AI and space. He also floated an integrated market for financial services and Canadian participation in the EU’s popular Erasmus study-abroad program.

But he stressed that “we’re at the start of a road,” noting that there would be debates and a vote in the Canadian parliament on the final structure of any alliance, while next month’s EU-Canada summit in Montreal would provide more detail. US President Donald Trump may not have been present at today’s speech, but his dismissal of the new alliance as “laughable” and warning that he could impose fresh tariffs on the EU, loomed over the proceedings.

Carney played down the Trump threat, telling reporters after his speech that the proposed EU-Canada alliance will result in a “stronger, more resilient, and more sovereign Canada,” that would be a more effective partner with the US.
Nonetheless, his speech did include some some apparent digs at Canada’s closest neighbor.

“I am not proposing a third bloc in order to become a great-power rival, only with better manners,” he said to smiles as he wrapped up his speech. “We do not seek power to dominate others. On the contrary, we are pursuing resilience so that no one can control our open markets, impair our sovereignty, threaten our territorial integrity, or undermine our freedoms, our democracies, our rule of law.”

ECB Governing Council member Gabriel Makhlouf declined to rule out an interest-rate hike in October if circumstances require it. In an interview with Oliver Crook in Dublin, the Irish central bank chief said that while there’s currently no worrying sign of inflation spreading into wages, officials will take each decision on borrowing costs as it comes. “At a time of uncertainty, every meeting is a live meeting for the European Central Bank,” Makhlouf said when asked if that was the case for the next one on Oct. 29. “You can’t rule out anything that might happen in future meetings, nor can you rule them in.”

Europe is set for one of its smallest ever potato harvests after a succession of heat waves and lingering drought battered the water-hungry staple. The summer heat is likely to curb the crop in Europe and the UK by about 3.5 million tons, according to analysis from the Energy and Climate Intelligence Unit. That could cost farmers more than €800 million ($923 million), given the current range of prices, it said.

As threats to NATO territory intensify, Germany’s hospitals are preparing for the very worst. Across the country, government bodies are surveying Germany’s healthcare systems and infrastructure to see how — or if — they would stand up in a defense scenario. Focus has now turned to facilities like Ulm, a hospital in southwest Germany, which has an underground medical facility completed in 1979 at the height of the Cold War. It’s a rare example of a military medical bunker in good enough shape to be brought back into use.

items.title: SEC Issues Guidance to Tokenize Stocks After Clarity Act Failure
body: The Securities and Exchange Commission gave the green light for digital versions of securities to start trading in the US, moving forward with a plan that could reshape traditional market structure after crypto legislation failed a key Senate vote on Tuesday.

The guidance for the five-year plan shows that market regulators are ready to follow through on their promise and move forward digital asset regulation after senators from both parties blocked the Clarity Act on Tuesday. While the exemption would provide a boost to crypto firms eager to tap into US markets, many in the industry have said they are concerned a future administration could claw it back without legislation.

“Congress was unsuccessful in advancing the Clarity Act despite the tireless efforts of many,” SEC Chairman Paul Atkins said in a statement. “So today, the Securities and Exchange Commission is taking a significant step forward, within its statutory authority, to bring America’s capital markets into the digital age by facilitating onchain trading of certain tokenized stocks.”

The exemption, in the works for more than a year, is poised to ignite a scramble among crypto firms racing to tokenize US stocks, with different models competing for market share. Some firms, such as Securitize Corp., are working directly with public companies to bring tokenized shares to US crypto markets. Others will provide third-party tokens that don’t involve close cooperation with issuers.

The SEC had planned to unveil the innovation exemption in May, when it issued a proposal to regulate crypto issuance, but the agency postponed that release while negotiations over the Clarity Act were still in flux.

The order, which is effective immediately, will exempt so-called Tokenized Securities Venues, or TSVs, from certain regulations that apply to stock exchanges. Exempted tokens include a stock that’s tokenized by a public company as well as stock tokenized by a third party that isn’t directly affiliated with the company.

The plan won’t apply to tokens issued by third parties that are essentially synthetic, such as a security-based swap, the SEC said. Such tokens, often called “wrappers” that track share prices but don’t provide ownership benefits, have proliferated on crypto exchanges outside the US.

The number of tokens that can trade on each venue will be subject to certain limits, and those tokens will be required to provide standard shareholder benefits such as dividends and voting rights. Third-party venues will be required to notify issuers about their plans to tokenize their stock, giving the issuer an opportunity to object to the move.
That option could sharply limit the number of third party tokens available to investors if it is taken up by large number of public companies concerned about the risks of crypto trading.

The exemption is part of a series of steps the SEC has taken to open up crypto trading in the US, a key priority of President Donald Trump. The SEC in June proposed to eliminate the so-called trade through rule, which prohibits exchanges and other market participants from executing trades that “trade through” or execute at prices worse than the national best bid or offer.

The rule, which made speed a paramount trait of today’s computer-driven stock market, posed a problem for crypto platforms that wouldn’t be able to compete with the high-speed exchanges and other trading venues. By eliminating the rule, the SEC can give crypto platforms a better shot at competing with traditional exchanges.
The agency in August unveiled another proposal, called Regulation Crypto Assets, to exempt certain digital asset offerings from securities registration statements.

Advocates of tokenization say the shift to 24/7 trading of tokenized equities will reduce counterparty risk by providing nearly instantaneous trade settlement. That could be beneficial during times when traditional markets are shuttered but when real-time trading platforms, such as Robinhood Markets Inc., are active.  It could also allow retail traders to own fractions of more expensive stocks, or to include tokenized equities in automated trading through smart contracts.

Some groups have cautioned against providing exemptions from securities rules related to fair access, price transparency and investor protections. The Securities Industry and Financial Markets Association, a brokers trade group, has warned that the proliferation of tokenized stocks could result in market fragmentation.

items.title: Exxon Sounds Alarm Coal Use Is Accelerating Global Warming
body: ExxonMobil Holdings Corp. says the world is on course for rapid global temperature increases as coal use persists, pushing emissions beyond mid-century climate goals.

Carbon dioxide emissions will be 30 billion metic tons in 2050, almost three times the levels needed to limit global warming to 2C (3.6F) above pre-industrial norms, the company said in its annual Energy Outlook on Thursday.
The estimate is about 10% higher than a year ago as adoption of emissions-mitigation efforts such as carbon capture slows and coal continues to be one of the top fuels of choice for power generation.
At this pace, the world is on track for a temperature increase of between 2.5C and 3C by 2050, according to ExxonMobil Economic and Energy Director Prasanna Joshi.
The world is “nowhere close” to the 2C target laid out by the United Nation’s Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change to avoid the worst effects of climate change, he said.

ExxonMobil’s Energy Outlook typically shows strong demand for oil and natural gas for decades into the future even as the world attempts to reduce emissions. While such an approach may be self-serving, the oil explorer maintains its forecasts are grounded in scientific and economic data that take into account realistic changes in government policies and consumer behavior.

Phasing out coal, the dirtiest fossil fuel, has been a key focus of the United Nations COP conference for at least the last five years in favor of cleaner alternatives like natural gas, wind, solar and nuclear. But with rising prices for liquefied natural gas and the intermittent nature of some renewables, coal has remained a key energy source for many countries, particularly in Asia.
“We are seeing clear signs that coal is sticking longer from an energy security and other perspectives, specifically in parts of Asia-Pacific, China, and others,” Joshi said.

Coal has also received support in the US from the Trump administration, which “ended the war on beautiful clean coal,” according to US Department of Energy Undersecretary Kyle Haustveit. “It is still by far and away the largest fuel source for electricity and that’s great.”

Other changes in ExxonMobil’s outlook include fewer emission-reduction technologies. Projections for carbon capture and storage, and use of low-carbon hydrogen, dropped by about one-third from last year.
“That is essentially slowed down versus what we had in the last outlook because of affordability and the lack of willingness to pay,” Joshi said.

Electricity demand globally will rise 65% by 2050, driven mainly by economic growth in developing countries, ExxonMobil said. Data centers will double as a proportion of power usage in the US in the next five years but face major hurdles.
“We do see real constraints on chips, power infrastructure, and essentially the rate and pace of permitting of these projects,” Joshi said.

items.title: Risk of Midterm 'Blue Wave' Leaves Defense Stocks Out of Favor
body: After two years of breakneck gains, shares of military contractors have hit a wall this year. Traders are expecting the pain to deepen further as they position for protracted negotiations and funding delays should Democrats take control of one or both houses of Congress following the midterm elections.

Stocks of companies that manufacture everything from tanks, fighter jets and Navy ships to missiles, drones and other defense technologies have deeply lagged behind the broader market this year amid doubts about President Donald Trump’s ambitious budget for the Pentagon and steep valuations.

Hopes that Trump’s pledge to turbocharge the budget to $1.5 trillion would lead to a bonanza for weapons makers had sent defense stocks on a historic rally. But now polls and prediction markets are pointing toward the strong likelihood that Democrats gain control of the House of Representatives next year following the Nov. 3 vote, while the outlook for which party controls the Senate is closer to a toss-up.

“If Democrats win and split Congress, then the fight for additional defense spending will be under a much tighter microscope where justifications for each program will undergo greater scrutiny,” said Wayne Sanders, an analyst with Bloomberg Intelligence. “This means that munitions will most likely be looked at individually instead of a larger pool of money that could cover air defense platforms and other weapon systems.”

A gauge for the group of stocks — the S&P Composite 1500 Aerospace & Defense Index — is down 13% since Feb. 27, right before the Iran conflict started. The S&P 500 Index has gained nearly 10% over the same period. A fund tracking the sector — the iShares US Aerospace & Defense ETF — is on pace for two back-to-back quarters of net outflows, for the first time since 2023.

The biggest decliners in the group include space and missile systems provider Karman Holdings Inc., defense-tech company Kratos Defense & Security Solutions Inc., and drone maker AeroVironment Inc with drops of at least 38% since the end of February. Larger traditional big-ticket defense contractors such as Northrop Grumman Corp., Lockheed Martin Corp., Huntington Ingalls Industries Inc. and L3Harris Technologies Inc. have also fallen by at least 18%.

“There might be some more pressure on the group just because of its elevated price-to-earnings ratio, at least as it relates to its average over the past 30 years,” said Eric Sterner, chief investment officer at Apollon Wealth Management. “We could see some more weakness between now and election day.”

The defense stocks index is currently trading at 27 times forward earnings, according to data compiled by Bloomberg. That compares with a 30-year average of about 18, and S&P 500’s current multiple of 19.

The Trump administration has requested a budget of $1.5 trillion for national defense in fiscal 2027, including $1.15 trillion in discretionary funding and $350 billion through reconciliation — a fast-track approval process Congress can use to provide mandatory defense funding. The 2027 fiscal year starts Oct. 1. Senate Majority Leader John Thune has said he doesn’t expect Republicans to take up the budget resolution before the midterm election.

With temporary fiscal 2027 funding set to run through Dec. 11, the post-election lame-duck period could become an important test of whether investors view the sector’s recent weakness as an opportunity to buy or a reason to keep money elsewhere, analysts said.

The current pullback in the sector is “actually a healthy thing,” said Apollon’s Sterner. “Typically you see the markets trade sideways ahead of an uncertainty and then once that uncertainty is removed, we could see some of these stocks re-energized.”

And the longer term outlook for defense remains strong, analysts and investors said. While congressional uncertainty could shape appropriations, oversight and program priorities, the broader push to modernize the military remains intact, they said.
“There’s still a strategic case for modernization of the military, and it does really kind of cross across most of the political spectrum,” said Don Hagan, chief investment officer at Arax.

The ramp-up in geopolitical tensions around the globe, along with a push toward higher defense spending in Europe and around the world, bode well for military contractors, analysts and investors noted.

“We’re in a scenario where we have no choice but to continue to actively add to defense because of the changing face of what the defense industry is building and requiring,” said Philip Blancato, chief market strategist at Osaic Holdings.
Nevertheless, even bullish investors agree the next few weeks will be turbulent for the stocks.
“Investors seem to be pricing in a blue wave and seemingly assuming the worst for the sector,” said Guggenheim analyst Michael Ciarmoli.

items.title: Citigroup Raises $12 Billion in Its Biggest-Ever Bond Sale
body: Citigroup Inc. raised $12 billion in its largest-ever US dollar bond sale, seizing a chance to sell debt as credit markets rallied a day after the Federal Reserve hiked rates.
The Wall Street heavyweight drew about $40 billion of peak demand for Thursday’s deal, according to people with knowledge of the matter, or about 3.3 times the size of the offering.
Its timing coincided with a broad risk-on rally after the Fed’s first interest-rate increase since 2023, a move that helped calm investors worried about inflation.
A measure of US high-grade corporate credit risk plunged the most in more than a month on Thursday, while average spreads hit a five-week low on Wednesday at 77 basis points.
Read More: Stocks, Bonds Rise After Fed-Day Drop as Oil Falls: Markets Wrap

Pricing on the longest 11-year maturity tightened to 0.93 percentage point above the benchmark rate from early discussions of around 1.25 percentage points, a separate person said, asking not to be identified because they’re not authorized to speak publicly.

Banks are particularly savvy when it comes to timing borrowing, typically selling bonds after quarterly reports. But as credit spreads tightened and bond yields dropped, conditions were especially attractive after a volatile start to the week.
Wells Fargo & Co. also tapped the market Thursday, attracting roughly $28 billion of peak demand for its $6 billion offering, the people said. It priced notes due in four and 11 years.
There is further evidence that investors are seeking more exposure to longer-dated debt, which has become increasingly scarce in the high-grade market as borrowers shy away from more expensive rates.

Citigroup had about $18 billion of demand for its longest-tenored note, the most among the deal’s tranches, the people said. The company’s sale overall is tied for the fourth-largest dollar bond deal by a US bank, according to data compiled by Bloomberg.

Including Thursday’s deals, the six big US banks have sold a combined $177.3 billion of investment-grade bonds this year. Citigroup’s volume had far trailed its peers but is now at $18.3 billion, with Wells Fargo reaching $24 billion. Goldman Sachs Group Inc. leads the way at $44 billion, which includes January’s record $16 billion sale.
The high-grade market had six offerings on Thursday, as this week’s volume neared dealers’ forecasts.

items.title: Three New ETFs to Watch: From Tax Avoidance to AI Winners
body: Listen and subscribe to Trillions on Apple, Spotify, iHeart and the Bloomberg Terminal.What’s a new way to invest in artificial intelligence? And what’s the latest tax strategy for wealthy investors? There’s no shortage of exchange-traded funds, but some of the latest launches reveal important trends.

In this week’s New ETFs to Watch episode, Eric Balchunas and Joel Weber — joined by Bloomberg News reporter Isabelle Lee — sift through the latest launches. They highlight the Investment House ETF (TIH) and the growing use of ETFs to defer taxes, how the Yorkville America MANGOS Plus Index ETF (FRUT) is betting on the next generation of AI winners and whether investors really want a hedged version of Bitcoin (HBIT). Money goes where it’s treated best. That simple truth is a big reason why more and more money (trillions of dollars, in fact) flows into a powerful, low-cost tool that’s quietly transformed investing. Exchange-traded funds let you invest in everything from the stock market to gold like never before. This biweekly podcast will demystify them — and hopefully delight you in the process.

items.title: US Housing Starts Drop Unexpectedly on Multifamily Projects
body: New US residential construction declined unexpectedly in August to one of the weakest paces since the pandemic, reflecting a plunge in starts of multifamily projects.

Housing starts decreased 2.6% to an annualized rate of 1.28 million, according to federal government data released Thursday. The median forecast in a Bloomberg survey of economists was a 1.32 million pace.
Starts of multifamily projects decreased nearly 22%. Single-family home construction rose 7.6% to an annualized 918,000, the fastest pace since March and fueled by increases in the West and Midwest.

Despite the advance in one-family home starts last month, the residential real estate market remains challenged in an environment of rising mortgage rates and constrained affordability. Builders may also be hesitant to ramp up work on new homes considering inventories remain well above pre-pandemic levels.
Housing completions dropped nearly 12% to the slowest pace since the end of 2018. Completions of one-family houses slid to the lowest since before the pandemic.

“The big picture remains that elevated and rising borrowing costs are holding developers back, supporting our view that the downward trend in housing starts has further to run,” Bradley Saunders, North America economist at Capital Economics, said in a note.
In August, overall building permits, which point to future construction, dropped 2.7%. Permits for one-family homes decreased 1.8% to an annualized 878,000.

Home construction has subtracted from economic growth in five of the last six quarters. The Federal Reserve Bank of Atlanta’s GDPNow forecast is penciling in residential investment to subtract 0.16 percentage point from third quarter growth.

The average 30-year mortgage rate neared 7% last week, the highest level in over a year, according to the latest data from the Mortgage Bankers Association. Rising home financing costs are keeping a lid on purchase activity and undercutting builder sentiment.
Greater shares of builders are offering incentives and cutting prices in an effort to attract potential buyers, figures from the National Association of Home Builders showed Wednesday.
Read More: US Homebuilder Sentiment Drops to Match Lowest Level Since 2022

Revenue and new orders at Lennar Corp. declined in the latest quarter from a year ago, the homebuilder reported on Wednesday. Margins are under pressure from price reductions and the elevated use of incentives to shore up sales in the higher-rate environment.

Across the US, housing starts in the South, the nation’s largest homebuilding region, decreased 1.3% to a three-month low. Starts jumped in the West to a five-month high. Despite a pickup in single-family starts in the Midwest, multifamily home construction slumped.
The new residential construction data are volatile, and the government report showed 90% confidence that the monthly change ranged from a 14.6% decline to a 9.4% gain.

items.title: US Jobless Claims Fall to 196,000 During Holiday Week
body: Applications for US unemployment benefits fell to the lowest since July and recurring claims dropped to a more than two-year low, adding to signals of labor market stability.

Initial claims fell 10,000 to 196,000 in the week ended Sept. 12, one of the lowest readings since 1969, according to Labor Department data released Thursday. That period included Labor Day, and the data can fluctuate around holidays.
The four-week moving average of new applications, a metric that helps smooth out volatility, fell to 203,250 — a five-week low.

The decline in initial claims could reflect seasonal swings related to Labor Day and the start of the school year. Even so, the broader trend highlights how subdued layoffs are across the economy outside a few high-profile announcements.
Continuing claims, a proxy for the number of people receiving benefits, fell to 1.73 million in the week ended Sept. 5, the lowest since 2024.
Despite limited job cuts, Americans remain hesitant to leave their jobs amid uneven hiring, reinforcing a low-hire, low-fire labor market.
Read More: America’s White-Collar Workers Feel Stuck in Jobs They Dislike
Unadjusted for seasonal fluctuations, initial claims fell sharply. That was led by declines in California, Texas, Michigan and New York.

items.title: Ryanair Dangles $1.6 Billion Baltic Investment as Rival Stumbles
body: Ryanair Holdings Plc proposed a five-year investment plan in Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania that includes more routes and planes, as the Irish discount carrier seeks to capitalize on the woes of Air Baltic Corp AS that just sought creditor protection.
The initiative stands to add 11 million annual seats, 16 based aircraft and thousands of new jobs in what Ryanair called a $1.6 billion investment, according to a statement on Thursday.

The proposal calls on the Baltic governments to abolish aviation taxes and cut airport fees if they wish to compete for the spending plan. The move shows Ryanair’s clout as it uses its considerable leverage to push planes and business into markets — or retract them from places deemed less amenable to its demands.
The Irish carrier also faulted the Latvian government for sinking €550 million of taxpayer money into Air Baltic, which Ryanair called a shrinking “zombie” airline.
Air Baltic filed for bankruptcy protection this week, seeking restructure its hefty debt burden after buckling under the weight of high fuel prices and travel disruptions.

items.title: Czechs Keep Door Open for Rate Hike as Inflation Risks Persist
body: Czech policymakers may deliver a second interest rate increase this year to tame persistent domestic price risks should inflationary pressure grow, according to the central bank’s governor.

After the Czech National Bank board unanimously voted to hold the benchmark at 3.75%, Ales Michl said the first rate hike for four years in June had “for now” sufficiently tightened conditions. But officials will still decide between lifting borrowing costs or keeping them stable at the next meeting, he said.

“We are prepared to tighten monetary policy further if it turns out that inflation risks are really happening,” Michl told reporters in Prague on Thursday. “As we proved in June, we won’t hesitate to raise interest rates if the situation requires.”

Michl and his colleagues are weighing a policy response to a gamut of risks stemming from rising costs of services, the housing market, wage growth and prospects of bigger state spending financed by debt. That’s been compounded by a surge in oil prices that’s sent Brent above $100 and helped push up market expectations of more interest-rate hikes.
Forward rate agreements indicate market expectations of about two more quarter-point hikes this year and four such increases in total within the next 12 months.

Michl said the Czech market interest rates are currently “significantly influenced” by US monetary policy — the Federal Reserve raised rates this week — and that he didn’t want to “get into speculations about market expectations.”

Headline inflation in August remained below target, but the central bank expects price growth to accelerate early next year. Officials are also closely watching core inflation, which excludes the most volatile items like food and energy and remains at levels that central bankers call “elevated.”
“The persistence of core inflation is a risk in the coming months,” Michl said. “A more lasting reduction in core inflation can be achieved with continued tight monetary policy.”

That’s unlikely to sit well with Prime Minister Andrej Babis, as his administration seeks to ramp up spending on infrastructure, health care and defense. The billionaire premier himself this week called the central bank’s policy “incomprehensible,” saying high mortgage rates are making housing less affordable.
Michl declined to comment on the criticism, reiterating only that the board will decide on whether to raise rates again when it next debates policy in November.

The bank board’s approach of not rushing with more hikes may stem from key economic data recently developing in line with the central bank’s latest forecasts or undershooting the projections, according to ING Bank strategist Frantisek Taborsky.
“I expect the situation to change by November, leading the CNB to adopt a more hawkish stance in the interim and making the November meeting a ‘live’ one,” he said.

items.title: KKR Passes Partners Group as Europe's Top Evergreen Fund Manager
body: KKR & Co. has overtaken Partners Group AG as Europe’s largest manager of open-ended private market funds, with the US firm expanding its business as the Swiss asset manager has grappled with withdrawal requests.

“We recently became the largest manager of evergreen private markets funds in Europe. Previously the number one was a Swiss company,” KKR’s managing director and head of global wealth solutions international Markus Egloff said in an interview in Zurich, citing data compiled by industry research firm Novantigo.

The US private equity firm became the largest manager of European-domiciled evergreens by assets under management in the first quarter, with €13.6 billion ($15.6 billion) across its evergreen platforms. Partners Group’s asset under management also grew, to €13.4 billion at the end of the first quarter, up €0.4 billion from the end of 2025.
“We have been doing this business for three years, so it goes to show that at least in the private wealth space we have clearly been winning significant market shares,” Egloff added.

KKR launched its first European-domiciled evergreen fund for its wealth channel in May 2023, joining a flurry of alternative asset managers opening offices in Zurich to tap investors through partnerships with private banks.
Private equity firms have increasingly tapped wealthy retail investors to boost inflows as institutional buyers reach their limits for allocations to private markets.
Read More: KKR Starts Private Credit Fund With More Flexible Access to Cash
In some instances, the pursuit of new investor types has backfired.

Private credit funds — including some managed by KKR — have faced investor redemption requests this year amid broader worries over debt quality and the impact of AI on the software companies in PE portfolios.
The withdrawal requests put Partners Group, Europe’s second-largest listed PE firm, in the spotlight.

The firm placed a cap on redemptions for its flagship $14.5 billion evergreen fund following a surge in requests. The move underscored a broader systemic crunch for evergreen private market funds, where high-profile asset mismatches and liquidity crunches have sparked intense regulatory scrutiny and forced managers to drastically restructure how they handle retail investor exits.
Read More: Partners Group Caps Withdrawals at Top US Evergreen Fund (1)
The turbulence might now present an opportunity, according to KKR.

“There are lot of our competitors, private asset managers, and traditional asset managers also trying to get into that space. So the number of evergreen funds and access points have hugely increased,” he said.

items.title: Hedge Fund Manager Seeks Alpha in Strong El Niño Trades
body: Traders are betting on markets mispricing the consequences of a super-El Niño and they’re moving to take advantage.

Today’s newsletter brings you an exclusive interview with a London hedge fund manager that expects El Niño to produce an “unusually alpha-rich environment.” We also talked to Al Gore, and have the latest on renewable developers struggling in Germany.
Subscribe to Bloomberg.com for unlimited access to all our coverage.
By Gautam Naik
A former Balyasny Asset Management trader who now runs a boutique hedge fund in London says he expects to be able to amplify returns by anticipating how an evolving super El Niño will affect markets.

The cyclical climate phenomenon associated with warming across the equatorial Pacific Ocean is already reshaping weather patterns across the globe. Zulfiqar Ali, founder and chief investment officer of energy commodities trading hedge fund ZAMS Asset Management, says that as El Niño gets “stronger and stronger,” his fund “is positioned to take advantage of dislocations as they happen, with a quick turnaround.”

More opportunities are likely to emerge toward the end of the year, when El Niño is expected to produce an “unusually alpha-rich environment,” he said. So far, the strategy helped ZAMS deliver its clients a 5.7% return in August and 13% year-to-date.

The 34-year-old Cambridge University mathematics graduate says he and his team of half a dozen traders, quants and weather strategists have been analyzing energy futures contracts and weather models to find price anomalies. ZAMS buys climate models from specialist weather-forecasting companies like MetDesk, and then tries to improve on them using in-house expertise.

It’s an idea that’s gaining traction. Bloomberg reported in June that Moreton Capital Partners is targeting $500 million to bet on all the ways in which El Niño will upend food prices. At Man Group, the world’s largest publicly traded hedge fund firm, the assessment is that the full range of contagion risks associated with El Niño has yet to be priced in.
By Eva Brendel and Libby Cherry
Germany’s renewable-energy developers are entering a shakeout after years of rapid expansion, with worsening project economics pushing a growing number into financial distress.

Hamburg-based solar developer Enerparc AG, one of Europe’s largest solar park operators, filed for insolvency this month with around €3 billion ($3.5 billion) of debt across the group. That follows the insolvency of wind developer Sowitec Group GmbH, while others including BayWa r.e. and ABO Energy have embarked on restructuring efforts.

The difficulties mark a reversal for an industry that expanded rapidly on cheap financing and supportive subsidies as Germany accelerated its transition away from fossil fuels. Developers now face higher borrowing costs and weaker returns on new projects — pressures that are also weighing on the industry across Europe.

Germany’s rapid buildout has created problems of its own. Wind and solar capacity has expanded faster than the power grid and energy storage needed to accommodate it, making some new projects harder to connect. And when renewable generation surges, the glut of electricity can push prices below zero or force producers to curb output, undermining the economics of both new and existing projects.

Wildfire resilience is largely funded by governments and utilities, but rising losses are putting pressure on public budgets, utility balance sheets and ratepayers. California, Southern Europe and the Australian state of Victoria show that raising more capital is not the only answer. Each region has innovated to protect the ability of utilities to finance from catastrophic losses, tap public funding where benefits are widely shared and introduce incentives to further encourage resilient outcomes.

When it comes to green tech, China is a list of superlatives. It produces more solar panels, wind turbines, electric vehicles and batteries than anywhere else in the world. But is finance the real climate hero? This week on Zero, Akshat Rathi is joined by Ma Jun, chairman of the Hong Kong Green Finance Association and former chief economist of China’s central bank. They discuss how the country became a green-finance superpower and how other nations can speed up their own transitions.
Listen now, and subscribe on Apple, Spotify or YouTube to get new episodes of Zero every Thursday.

Europe is set for one of its smallest ever potato harvests after a succession of heat waves and lingering drought battered the water-hungry staple. The summer heat is likely to curb the crop in Europe and the UK by about 3.5 million tons, according to analysis from the Energy and Climate Intelligence Unit. For consumers, the squeeze could soon show up on supermarket shelves in the form of smaller baked potatoes, shorter fries and ultimately higher prices.

items.title: Radiant World Reveals Near-Empty Coffers to Jefferies Fund
body: Radiant World, the iron ore trading group that’s under fire amid allegations of fraud, has revealed to lawyers for a Jefferies Financial Group Inc. fund that it has hardly any cash left.

The Jefferies fund is seeking to continue a worldwide freezing order of $499 million, from a London court last month. In court filings ahead of a hearing in London on Thursday, lawyers for the Jefferies fund said that Radiant World had disclosed to them “enormously lower” cash and inventories than was shown in their most recent annual accounts.
Simon Salzedo, a lawyer for LAM Trade Finance Group II LLC, the fund that’s managed by Jefferies unit Point Bonita, said in court that Radiant World was part of a a “very large scale fraud.”
“They are party to a very sophisticated, large scale international conspiracy,” Salzedo said, arguing to continue the freezing order over Radiant World founder Pinkesh Nahar.
Nahar’s lawyer in court on Thursday denied the allegations made against him, including those about alleged breach of orders to disclose his assets.

Several top commodity traders stopped doing business with Radiant World amid concerns it had provided falsified documents to banks to raise financing. Radiant World denied wrongdoing and said it conducts its business to the highest commercial and legal standards.

When the Jefferies fund earlier this year began to investigate unpaid receivables it had been financing for Radiant World, it “gradually uncovered that many of the documents purportedly supporting the unpaid receivables had been falsified, including invoices, contracts, and notices of assignment,” according to the judgment imposing the freezing order, which was cited by the Jefferies fund’s lawyers.

The fund also discovered that payments that it had received had in fact not been paid as a settlement of the invoices it believed, but “in satisfaction of completely different debts,” according to the judgment.
Radiant World hasn’t produced any evidence that “casts doubt on the claim that they are in fact party to sophisticated fraud,” Salzedo said in court.

Radiant World Corporation Pte, the company’s main Singapore operating company, disclosed assets of $1.07 billion to the Jefferies lawyers, but more than $1 billion of this was made up of trade and other receivables which Jefferies argued could not be relied on. The values of inventories and cash were “enormously lower” than in the company’s most recent annual accounts for the year ended September 2025, they said.

Radiant World Holding Ltd., the company’s Hong Kong holding company, disclosed just $10,000 in cash, compared to more than $200 million in its most recent annual accounts. And Sapphire Minmetals Corporation Ltd., a legally separate but closely related company, disclosed cash of $3.8 million, compared to $66.5 million in its most recent annual accounts.

It was normal for commodities trading companies to have amounts owed to them as trade receivables, a lawyer representing Sapphire Minmetals said in court. The assets, including receivables, were enough to cover the claim.
Radiant World and related companies have been reducing their headcount and selling inventories since Bloomberg first reported in late July the concerns over falsified documents.

items.title: Torrential Rain Brings Deadly Floods Back to East Coast of Spain
body: Torrential rain lashed the east coast of Spain, flooding roads and leaving at least one person dead.
The heavy rainfall started Wednesday in Valencia and Catalonia, reviving fears of a repeat of the devastating floods that killed more than 200 people in 2024.

The latest storm is being blamed for one death in Olivella, in the region of Barcelona, after a man was found 500 meters away from a vehicle that appeared to have been swept away by floodwaters, local firefighters said in a post on X.

At the end of October 2024, an intense “dana” storm — a common phenomenon in Spain at the time of year — devastated the Valencia region. Global warming is intensifying those systems in the Iberian peninsula, as the Mediterranean warms and higher air temperatures allow storms to hold more water.

A scheduled football match on Wednesday evening between Valencia’s Levante and Athletic Bilbao was suspended because of the storm. Valencia airport was closed Wednesday night due to heavy rains, but was reopened Thursday morning.

Conditions improved on Thursday, but government forecaster AEMET warned that heavy rainfall is expected to continue further south, with up to 60 millimeters (2.4 inches) an hour falling near the port city of Cartagena.

Heavy rain, strong winds and hail are forecast to continue across the region through Friday, with similar conditions also expected along Spain’s north coast and the Balearic Islands, according to AEMET.

items.title: Pentagon, Lockheed to Accelerate Production of New Missile
body: The Pentagon and Lockheed Martin Corp. are moving to speed up the production of a new classified air-to-air missile for US Air Force and Navy jets that’s seen as vital to deterring China.

The company and the Defense Department said they have struck a broad framework agreement that will eventually result in a multi-year production contract for the Joint Advanced Tactical Missile, or JATM, which is still in development but close to entering production.

When it’s deployed, the projectile will be the most advanced air-to-air missile in the US arsenal. That role has long been held by increasingly sophisticated versions of RTX Corp.’s AIM-120 AMRAAM, for Advanced Medium-Range Air-to-Air Missile, which was introduced in 1993.
In a statement released Thursday, the Pentagon said the agreement was critical to ensuring Lockheed Martin and the munitions supply chair can make long-term workforce and capacity investments.

“We will deliver JATM at the speed our nation and allies demand while providing value for taxpayers and our shareholders,” Tim Cahill, the president of Lockheed Martin Missiles and Fire Control, said in a statement.

It’s the first framework agreement of a classified system orchestrated by Michael Duffey, the Defense Department’s top acquisition official. His office has completed numerous framework agreements for high-profile systems such as the most advanced version of the Patriot surface-to-air missile, Tomahawk cruise missile and interceptors for the Terminal High Altitude Area Defense, or THAAD, system.
“Speed, scale, and stability drive acquisition excellence, and these gears must turn in unison,” Duffey said in a statement.

The new missile program received a $2 billion boost in the Trump administration’s proposed budget for the fiscal year beginning October 1, a sign it could see accelerated production and be deployed soon. The Air Force and the Navy are seeking $2.9 billion for missile development and orders in 2027, compared to just $894 million this fiscal year.

Lockheed Martin first received the classified development contract in August 2017. The Pentagon also disclosed in March it was selling Australia 460 missiles, plus test equipment, in a $3.1 billion deal.
The new JATM, also known as the AIM-260, is designed to fit in the internal weapons bays of the F-22 and F-35 fighters, but the Air Force said it would also be integrated with F-16 and F-15 jets.

items.title: San Francisco's AI Wealth Boom Skirts Engineers as OpenAI, Anthropic IPOs Near
body: The coming IPOs of Anthropic and OpenAI are set to rain down riches in San Francisco. Just across the Golden Gate bridge, a recent gathering captured the flip side of the AI boom.

A group of more than four dozen laid-off workers gathered at 11 a.m. on a Monday to hike Mount Tamalpais, a majestic peak overlooking the San Francisco Bay. They descended the mostly deserted trail in groups of about a dozen, led by Basem Istanbouli, a former Google employee sporting a bucket hat and a pair of toe shoes.

Among them was a former Meta Platforms Inc. worker considering leaving tech altogether to pursue her passion for illustration. A software engineer, out of work for more than a year, lugged a large camera he’d bought a week before he was laid off.

Istanbouli has been organizing the weekly outings since December, when he started un(PTO), a community for people navigating unemployment. The group’s first hike included him, a friend and a “random dude off Reddit.” The online community has since grown to more than 1,700 people, and sometimes more than 80 show up to the outings.

Trillion-dollar startups, once-unthinkable compensation packages and bidding wars for workers who can build and deploy artificial intelligence have created the impression of a Bay Area labor market on fire. But even as debate swirls about AI’s potential dangers and the need for regulation, the technology has already had a profound disruption on jobs. Many of the workers who helped power San Francisco’s last boom are struggling to find their place in this one.
Read more: Are We Losing Control of AI? What’s Driving New Fears

Tech-industry employers filed layoff notices for more than 14,500 Bay Area workers in the 12 months that ended in June, almost double the count for the previous fiscal year, a Bloomberg analysis of data from California’s Employment Development Department shows. Across all industries, San Francisco and nearby San Mateo County have added more than 10,000 jobs in the last 12 months, but have lost more than 60,000 since February 2020, according to a report by Ted Egan, chief economist of the city and county of San Francisco.

Just as many once-booming software companies are trying to reinvent themselves for the age of AI, tech workers are now having to adapt. Demand for software engineers in the Bay Area has fallen 42% since 2022, according to Lightcast, a labor-market analytics firm. Jobs tied to AI-related IT and computer science, meanwhile, have jumped 37%.

Nico Crisafulli, a 55-year-old single dad who’s part of the un(PTO) group, worked as a full-time front-end web developer for an e-commerce company before being laid off in July. He was thrust into a labor market he didn’t recognize.
“Hard coding is sort of not really a thing anymore,” he said. “Getting a front-end engineer job seems a little bit of yesterday’s problem. I don’t know if that’s even possible.”

Crisafulli decided to become a software engineer at a very different moment in Silicon Valley. In 2013, he paid $15,000 for a coding boot camp and made a career out of skills like JavaScript and front-end development. Now he’s parsing job titles like “AI strategist” and “AI engineer,” trying to figure out where his experience fits in a labor market that increasingly prizes a different kind of technical worker.

While the AI boom is responsible for a lot of San Francisco’s revival, tech isn’t driving hiring in the area. In the last 12 months, the information sector, which includes most of tech, lost about 2,000 jobs. In fact, the industries driving the labor recovery are private education and health, as well as leisure and hospitality, according to Egan.

There’s a “sort of a seesaw between the labor market stimulating effects of the AI investment and then the depressive effects of the layoffs of the legacy tech companies,” said Egan. “It is clear that you’ve got a lot of people getting laid off and a smaller number of people at this point getting hired for AI-specific skills.”

Just this month, Uber Technologies Inc., one of the standout startups of San Francisco’s 2010s boom, announced it was cutting about 3,300 roles, or 10% of its staff globally, in a restructuring aimed at reducing management layers.

Istanbouli, the un(PTO) founder, started the group to help ease the isolation that comes with having a tough time finding a job. It has evolved beyond hikes to also include career-related gatherings such as interview preparation. Still, he’s concerned to see so many people joining.

“You wonder, how held back are people gonna be in their careers?” he said. “And you also wonder how much of these people are going to actually face financial instability to a point where a lot of really smart people are actually going to end up leaving San Francisco.”
Adding to the financial pressure, AI wealth is making the city more expensive: San Francisco rents are rising at the fastest pace in the country.

While one class of worker is watching the skills that once made them indispensable become easier to automate, the premium is shifting toward those who can keep pace with AI, where the skills in demand can seem to change almost by the day.

The market is particularly unforgiving for engineers at the beginning of their careers. In California, employment among workers ages 22 to 25 in the occupations most exposed to AI has fallen 16.8% since the launch of ChatGPT, compared with a 4.6% decline among other workers, according to workforce intelligence platform Revelio Labs.

Tawni Cranz, an operating partner focused on talent at venture capital firm SignalFire, said the traditional “on-ramp” for new graduates has been “completely stifled.” Larger technology companies, she said, face the challenge of figuring out how to redesign the entry-level experience while still “building a pipeline for future founders and future leaders.”

Now, one of the most popular jobs in tech may be forward deployed engineers, a once-obscure role popularized by Palantir Technologies Inc. in the early 2010s. It blends engineering with the customer-facing work of figuring out how businesses can actually put AI to use.

Postings for the position in the Bay Area are up nearly 600% since 2022 and command a median advertised salary of $202,300, according to Lightcast. OpenAI currently has almost 20 job postings for forward deployed engineers, with salary offerings running from around $145,000 to $325,000 plus equity. At Anthropic, forward deployed engineers  command a salary ranging from $280,000 to $320,000. Salesforce Inc., one of San Francisco’s largest private employers, has committed to hiring 1,000 workers for the role.

At Taktile, which sells AI software to banks and insurers, forward deployed engineers increasingly do work that previously might have required software engineering, product and business teams, said Hao Li, who leads the company’s FDE team in North America.
“You can combine these three things into one role and that becomes this unicorn called FDE,” Li said.

Crisafulli, the laid off tech worker, is eager to embrace AI in his next role. At his former job, he had used it to build a workflow that compressed roughly two days of work into about an hour. He doesn’t blame AI directly for his layoff, but believes the technology made it easier for the company to do the same work with fewer people.
Since losing his job, he’s built five applications with AI and is trying to learn as much as he can about the technology. Yet some days he feels more hopeful than others.
“Some days I wake up and I’m like, maybe I’ll just open a flower shop,” he said. “That sounds much nicer, to be honest.”

items.title: How Buffalo Scored a $2.2 Billion NFL Stadium for the 'Bills Mafia'
body: Quarterback Josh Allen, now in his ninth year with the Buffalo Bills of the National Football League, is still knocking on the door of his first Super Bowl appearance. This year, he’ll take most of his snaps inside what some fans have dubbed “The House That Josh Built.”

Allen’s rise to NFL stardom and his team’s success since 2020 has lifted the spirits of Buffalo, New York — as well as the team’s profits. The team has taken advantage of the momentum: This season, the Bills open Highmark Stadium, the first new NFL venue to break ground since the end of the Covid-19 pandemic.

Located across the street from the rubble of its previous home of 52 years, the $2.22 billion venue is filled with amenities and flourishes previously foreign to the “Bills Mafia,” as the team’s passionate fanbase is known. After decades of uncertainty over the team’s future in Buffalo, those same fans can now direct all of their fears towards Allen’s risky runs and the Bills’ narrowing Super Bowl window.

The old stadium was infamous for the beer-soaked game-day antics that unfolded in its vast parking lots. But the scrimmages and preseason games the new Highmark Stadium hosted in August had a different kind of buzz. Spectators gravitated to the illuminated bison sculptures that anchor a finely landscaped public plaza before entering a family-friendly tailgate zone. Many purchased $25 cocktails served in plastic mini bowling balls (an homage to a tailgate classic). Upon reaching their seats, they shared a laugh over how much money they had to put down for a personal seat license.

It would be easy to imagine things going differently. In the last five years, the NFL has extended its regular season schedule, expanded its international footprint and signed a new broadcasting rights deal. Franchise valuations have grown well beyond the threshold for traditional ownership models. Signaling this bonanza and the spell the league has over city leaders, even more expensive venues with significant public subsidies are under construction in Nashville, Cleveland, and Washington, DC, with future stadiums planned for Denver and Kansas. Chicago may stumble into one as well. Nine franchises have relocated since the Bills joined the NFL, three over the last decade.

The Bills are everything to Buffalo, the league’s second-smallest market, and the memorable images of a wind-whipped, snow-covered gridiron surrounded by working-class fans in various states of dress and sobriety seem to carry a branding value great enough for the NFL to write off the region’s financial limitations. With the new Highmark Stadium, Buffalonians can now feel assured that its NFL team, considered one of the league’s most iconic, will stick around for at least another generation.

Inside the new stadium’s club level, a replica of a telegram appears at the scale of a mural. It was a message sent by Bills founder Ralph Wilson Jr. to American Football League commissioner Lamar Hunt in September 1959 that simply states: “COUNT ME IN WITH BUFFALO.”

Wilson paid $25,000 for his franchise in the upstart AFL, formed by businessmen spurned by the NFL. The splinter league’s quick success led to a merger in 1966, putting Buffalo — a 19th century boomtown struggling to keep up with a modernizing global economy — in the big leagues. The Bills made Buffalonians feel like their city mattered, so much so that the rest of the country would have no choice but to be aware of its existence for at least a few Sundays every year. (The Buffalo Bills did not respond to a request for an interview.)

“At a very early age I understood Buffalo’s status in the country, the scarcity of NFL teams, and the significance of Buffalo having one,” says Bills fan Nicholas Mendola. He grew up watching the team’s historic run of four straight conference championships (and four straight Super Bowl losses) in the early 1990s and became known for his “Bills raps” through much of the team’s historic playoff drought of the 2000s and 2010s. “There is a different feeling around football and Buffalo,” he adds.

War Memorial Stadium, the WPA-funded multipurpose facility the Bills first called home, offered little beyond two goal posts and a certificate of occupancy. The 45,000-seat stadium was located in the city’s East Side on the corner of Jefferson Avenue and Best Street, a predominantly Black neighborhood in the early stages of economic collapse by the time the team played their first game in 1960. The neighborhood’s perceived lack of safety and the stadium’s small size and ramshackle condition (its nickname was “The Rockpile”) made a replacement necessary.

Early visions of a domed facility to replace War Memorial fell through, leading Erie County and the Bills to settle on a solution that would partially define Buffalo football to national television audiences: an outdoor venue on a site fully exposed to some of the worst of the region’s lake effect weather. An unremarkable county-owned stadium in Orchard Park, a suburb 10 miles south of downtown Buffalo, was built by 1973 to put a stop to Wilson’s flirtations with other markets. The venue, known as Rich Stadium for its first decades, received modest updates following each anxiety-inducing lease renewal negotiation until the team owner’s death in 2014. Terry and Kim Pegula, already owners of Buffalo’s NHL team, purchased the Bills for a then-record $1.4 billion from Wilson’s estate. The lease they inherited expired in 2023.

Rumors spread in the spring of 2021 that negotiations for a new stadium were going nowhere and the Bills were open to relocating to Austin. But after the resignation of New York State Governor Andrew Cuomo, Western New York native Kathy Hochul assumed the office and quickly moved the ball in Buffalo’s direction. In 2022, Hochul signed off on a deal for the new home of the Bills, providing the most public money ever (at the time) for a NFL stadium: New York State would own the venue and contribute $600 million while Erie County would provide $250 million. The Bills would pay for the rest of the estimated $1.6 billion project plus cost overruns, which ended up adding more than $500 million to the tab.

Populous, the architects behind the new Highmark Stadium, have promised a more comfortable experience this time around. With 60,108 seats, it’s smaller than its predecessor, too, with 11,500 fewer seats. “Highmark Stadium is bespoke to Buffalo,” says Populous managing director Jonathan Maille.

The dark brick, metal and glass facade of the new stadium form an homage to two Buffalo architectural icons: Eliel and Eero Saarinen’s Kleinhans Music Hall and Green & Wick’s Memorial Auditorium. Kleinhans is an internationally renowned venue completed in 1940, instantly recognizable for its curved roofline and vertical limestone sections that wrap around its northeast-facing exterior. The Aud, also completed in 1940 but demolished in 2009, served as the longtime home of the NHL Sabres; spectators would walk through large vertical facade cutouts on their way in and out of the otherwise modest art deco structure.

At Highmark, those two elements are brought over to the large vertical indentations on the east and west sides of the stadium’s metal screen-panel facade, wrapping around the facility and establishing the roof’s distinct curve, instantly recognizable from miles away.

Inside, the design team looked at ways to let in the snow and cold that make Buffalo a memorable football experience while still being comfortable enough to attract people to a late-season game barely safe enough to drive to. “We were designing for December,” explains Maille. “We wanted to make the building and the experience feel as intimate for the fans and as intimidating for the opposing team as possible.” the architect says.

The concourses are well worth a few excursions. Fans can easily look back out onto the field should the roar of the crowd make them regret getting in line for a beer. And when the game gets too painful to watch, a giant cut-out of the facade in the upper concourse frames a clear view of Lake Erie and the skyline of downtown Buffalo, about 10 miles away. There are also a wide variety of installations by local designers and artists that celebrate the team and the region. The sculptural replica of a smashed folding table — an international symbol of the tailgate debauchery of the Bills Mafia — is already a hit.

In 2022, during community-benefits agreement negotiations for the new Bills facility, a white man drove 200 miles to a supermarket on Buffalo’s East Side, just a few blocks away from where War Memorial Stadium once stood, killing 10 people and injuring three others in a racist mass shooting. The alleged shooter picked the site for its high concentration of Black residents, igniting conversations afterwards around how to meaningfully improve the quality of life for people living on Jefferson and beyond.

One week after the shooting, the Bills’ extremely private owner Terry Pegula paid a visit to the neighborhood, visibly shaken by what had transpired. Even though War Memorial had been demolished in 1989, current and former Bills players also appeared, handing out groceries and spending time with residents. “That reality and trauma and devastation also helped us get to a good CBA,” says then-county legislator and current state senator April Baskin.

While CBAs are not new to large developments, they are rarely implemented on projects in wealthy suburbs. The median income in Orchard Park is around $100,000 — double that of the city of Buffalo and much more than the neighborhood where the Bills got their start. Because the agreement was negotiated by Erie County, the benefits for the city of Buffalo will be more diffuse.

The CBA holds the Bills to prioritizing local and minority workers and business for construction and vendor contracts. The team also committed to giving at least $3 million each year for the duration of the lease towards community priorities such as affordable housing, food insecurity, educational access, social justice and mental health initiatives. The team gave $4.1 million in FY 2025, although $1.4 million of that total was through in-kind donations.

Accessibility in the CBA covers transportation, too. To get to the old Highmark Stadium, fans parked on front lawns and surface lots, passing a smattering of standalone restaurants; the absence of stadium amenities and isolated suburban setting is partly responsible for the Bills Mafia’s tailgating culture. That won’t go away, but now there will also be consistent public transit service on game days. A permanent, weather-protected transportation center has been constructed with 10 bus bays for the regional transit authority to run special routes from the city. Baskin hopes that the service can eventually expand to include workforce shuttles.

The Bills are now on a 30-year lease with financial punishments in place should they leave Western New York beforehand. The lease provides more than just emotional security, according to Baskin, who led the efforts to establish a community benefits agreement as part of one of the largest construction projects in the region’s history.

“The Bills were held hostage in the late ’90s and early 2000s, so as a fan, the fear of them going away never really leaves you,” says Mendola. “I have accepted as a Buffalonian and as a football fan that this is just how it works.”

To pay its share, the Bills took advantage of the NFL’s “G-5” stadium construction loan program for $250 million and raised an additional $260 million through personal seat licenses, which gives fans the exclusive right to purchase season tickets. With the team valued at $5.8 billion at the time of construction, the Pegulas sold a 20.6% stake to two separate private equity groups. The Bills are now worth $8.13 billion.

Many Bills fans will end up paying five times toward the new stadium: As a county taxpayer, a New York State taxpayer, and then — if they have the disposable income — as a personal seat license holder. That’s in a stadium where all point-of-sale transactions come with a 6% surcharge to help cover maintenance.

The NFL has so far avoided the ownership volatility and fan alienation emerging in other leagues since the arrival of private equity. Buffalo is all too familiar with what happens when outside investors run out of ways to extract profit. It is also the home of the most passionate fanbase in the league (scientifically proven). And despite the limitations of its market size, the Bills have managed to stretch their footprint out east to Rochester and northwest to southern Ontario. (Historically, as many as 15% of season ticket holders are Canadian residents.) Aside from the flashing red lights 30 years ahead, the Bills are securely in Buffalo, while generating a relatively modest chunk of annual funding for community needs through its CBA.

The new Highmark stadium represents the Bills’ ability off the field to make the most of their run as a must-watch football team with a superstar quarterback. Despite the great architectural leap forward, the crowds so far look no different than the ones that used to show up across the street.

Fandom in Buffalo now requires a more substantial investment in time and money, according to Mendola. Personal seat licenses have been sold out since December 2025, and there’s a wait list for fans who paid $150 to vie for a chance to buy season tickets. The father of three doesn’t expect to take his family to a game soon. “We’re likely priced out for a few years,” Mendola says. “The Bills are essentially the sports equivalent of ‘too big to fail.’”
