items.title: US Bonds and Tina Turner: What Is the True Price of Safety?
body: This article is adapted from      Worth the Risk: The Seven Myths That Keep Us From Taking the Chances We Need to Take       by Allison Schrager, to be published by Yale University Press. Copyright © 2026 by Allison Schrager. Excerpted by permission. All rights reserved.
What does Tina Turner have in common with a US Treasury bond? They both show that the meaning of safety is not always straightforward.

Born into poverty in rural Tennessee, Anna Mae Bullock sang in the church choir as a child and eventually made her way to the St. Louis music scene, where she became a teen mother and married a band leader who already had two children of his own. They started singing together and became rich and famous, traveling the world as the duo Ike and Tina Turner.

Before long, however, the relationship turned abusive, both emotionally and physically. Tina eventually summoned the courage to leave Ike Turner in 1976. You might think that a divorced woman, especially of that era, would need money to feel safe — and she was certainly entitled to plenty of it, having created hits like Proud Mary with him. But Tina Turner made a surprising decision during the divorce proceedings: She said she didn’t want the assets from the marriage, including royalties from the songs she made famous. She left with nothing except custody of the four children, two cars, and the right to keep using her stage name.

Tina Turner chose her name over money in the bank because she knew that doing so would make her feel safer. The assets she left behind were part of a life in which she didn’t feel safe. It wasn’t clear if her decision would work out in her favor, and those first few years were very difficult. She went on food stamps, and her career did not seem to be going anywhere as she approached middle age. But in her mid-forties, Turner released the album Private Dancer, which went multi-platinum and made her an even bigger international superstar than when she was married.

Money in the bank might seem like a universally safe concept — especially to Americans accustomed to the government insuring their deposits. But the idea that a universally safe investment or situation exists and can protect your future is a myth that prevents many people from taking risks like Turner did.

Safety isn’t a real place. It’s a feeling. It’s deeply personal, and it can change with your life circumstances. What you need to feel safe is not what someone else needs. What’s safe in one era doesn’t feel so safe in the next. But defining your personal feeling of “safety” is key to making good decisions about risk.

For Turner, her name meant her career and identity, which felt more secure than money from the past. What you see as safe defines how you perceive, value, and take risks. In financial economics, what safe means depends on your goals.

For example, we think of bonds as a safe investment. But not all bonds are a safe way to meet your goal. If you are saving for the long term, like for retirement, a long-term bond will likely protect your money from all the changes that will happen in markets over the decades, especially if it is inflation-protected. Yet a long-term bond still has risk: Because its price fluctuates more than a short-term bond’s, its market is less predictable in the near term. Only if you are investing to feel safe several decades from now, and no sooner, are you assured of long-term security.

If your personal definition of safety is long term, beware that the financial industry usually defines a safe asset as something different: one that offers a certain rate of return each year, and can be sold whenever you need it for at least what you paid for it. The industry regards a US Treasury bill (a short-term government bond) as a safe asset since it is backed by the government and its price doesn’t change. This makes sense if you are saving for an upcoming vacation or are a company with extra cash waiting a few months for the right investing project.

The distinction is important because bonds are how the financial industry values safety, and by extension how it defines risk. And yet it gets what’s safe wrong all the time by choosing the wrong bonds as safe and by assuming that bond prices don’t change as much as they do. Price changes in the bond markets tell us more about the state of risk and the economy than any other asset, because bonds represent the current price of safety. To be precise, the price of the “risk-free asset,” as US Treasury bonds are colloquially referred to, appears in almost every asset-pricing formula used in finance; it is the standard of how all risk is priced. It influences bank rates for loans to individuals, and it is used as collateral. It is the single most important asset in finance. The development of sovereign debt markets is one reason that Europe is thought to have industrialized first, and why the North prevailed during the US Civil War.

Most important, the value of US Treasury bonds has changed over time, as the way we view safety has evolved. Mirroring how we have come to value safety ever more highly, the price of a risk-free bond has been rising over time. And the more a bond costs, the lower the rate of interest paid to the bond holder.

Why did safety become so expensive (and thus yields so low)? There are many reasons, and some have been more important at different points in time. For most of history, these bonds were not really that safe, and gold was considered the ultimate risk-free investment. Now it is US Treasury bonds. Someday, though probably not anytime soon, it could be another country’s bonds or even German renewable energy stocks. No one knows. Anything can happen.

The idea that a relatively young country’s sovereign debt could be considered risk-free would have been unthinkable a century ago. For most of history, governments had problems paying debt or inflating it away. Rates of bonds trended down partly because the asset became safer and more valuable as governments got richer and more stable. Once they did, they had no need to offer high rates to entice buyers.

But events over the past several decades have proven especially telling when it comes to our mounting risk aversion. As the demand for safety increased across all parts of our lives — from the removal of seesaws on children’s playgrounds to everything else — the price of low-risk assets increased. After the 1997 Asian financial crisis, many countries wanted to reduce their risk exposure. So they bought lots of safe bonds — those issued by big rich countries like the United States and European Union members. Regulators wanted to ensure less risk in markets and demanded that financial institutions hold more low-risk assets. This created more demand for bonds, so they got a lot more expensive. It was a low-rate and low-risk time. Inflation was very low and predictable. Bonds from rich countries were the established safe asset of the world, and yields kept falling and falling.

After the 2008 financial crisis, central banks also started to buy many of their own countries’ bonds, which further increased the demand. Tremendous demand for low-risk assets that were in limited supply combined to make them even more expensive. As the price of safety grew significantly, it transformed how financial markets worked because if you wanted to invest in a low-risk asset, it would not return very much.

This sky-high demand for safety in recent years explains why investing in low-risk assets like a government bond or savings bank account earns you so little. It explains why mortgage rates fell — from 13 percent in the 1980s to 3 percent until the early 2020s. It explains why so much money went to crypto or tech startups: if you wanted your savings to grow, you had no choice but invest it in riskier assets. Gone was the time a bank would pay you 8 percent for a twelve-month certificate of deposit; now you are lucky to a get a rate that keeps up (barely) with inflation. If you are pension-fund manager who needs to make a certain return to pay benefits, you turn to risk. Safety has become very expensive.

In short, going into the early 2020s it became cheaper to be on the other side of a risk. It became better to be a borrower instead of a saver. It was cheaper to borrow for mortgages or cars. The low rates also trickled throughout the global financial system, which meant even developing countries, which normally pay a fortune, could borrow at lower rates and so help finance their development. It was also cheaper for businesses to fund an expansion or hire more people. Cheaper debt in many ways makes the world less risky, because cash is readily available from lenders when needed. Alternatively, it is easier to take on leverage, a riskier position. If anything changes suddenly and interest rates increase or the bond market freezes, we are more vulnerable.

What’s happened to the risk-free asset and its impact on financial markets offers a useful metaphor for the rest of the economy and our approach to risk in other areas of our lives. As the world became hungrier for safety, the entire financial system changed. In some ways, the world became safer as we valued safety more — most of the time, anyway.

But in other ways, this shift made us more vulnerable. For example, recessions became more difficult for central banks to counter, because interest rates were so low there was less room to cut rates further to spur new growth. Rates got so low that many investors needed to take on more risk to reach their goals: they became open to assets that seemed safe and offered some extra return. But Greek bonds or mortgage-backed securities turned out to not be as safe as they once appeared.

After decades of falling rates, especially after 2010, bond rates have started to rebound, with rates in the 2020s increasing and current rates seeming to stay higher. This turnaround has surprised many people — even economists. People in the financial industry and government had started to believe that interest rates would either keep falling or at least stand still. We all should have known better. Research on rates over many decades shows that rates still do go up and down, even if they have slowly trended down over the centuries. And it suggests that much of what happened since 2010 was a blip, not a permanent fall.
The price of safety is not stable. It never has and never will be, because how we value it changes over time.

items.title: Shareholders Revolt After Crypto Hoarders' $50 Billion Crash
body: Investors are ramping up scrutiny of how much crypto hoarders pay their employees, as shareholders nurse losses totaling about $50 billion.
Retail and institutional investors alike have been burned by what was a red-hot trade in crypto markets last year. Both groups are now turning to activism to try to limit the damage.

Last week, SkyAI Inc., a syringe-maker-turned-Solana-buyer, was pressed over a proposed equity incentive plan for staff worth millions of dollars, as well as related-party transactions, while Tokyo-based Bitcoin accumulator Metaplanet Inc. on Friday sought to quell a social-media storm by scrapping some $220 million in warrants.

The pressure comes with shares in digital-asset treasury companies, or DATs, languishing well below the value of their crypto holdings. The fully diluted market value of listed treasury companies that invest in Bitcoin and Ether currently stands at about $90 billion, some 40% beneath its peak, according to analytics firm Artemis.

“Executives whose strategy is to invest in risky cryptoassets with no real utility should not be rewarded when that strategy inevitably fails,” said Ben Schiffrin, director of securities policy at Better Markets, an advocacy group.

The decline in crypto treasury stocks broadly tracks a wider selloff. Bitcoin, the largest cryptocurrency, is trading about 40% below its record price of over $126,000, which it reached on Oct. 6. The market sold off sharply days later and has failed to recover.

SkyAI, formerly Sharps Technology, last year raised over $400 million from major crypto funds to transform itself into a treasury vehicle for Solana, the seventh-largest cryptocurrency. Since the deal closed in August 2025, SkyAI’s shares have nosedived nearly 90%.

Rival Solana accumulator Forward Industries had offered to buy the company at a 20% premium to its share price in June, but the bid didn’t succeed. In a statement last week, Forward upped the ante, urging SkyAI shareholders to vote against a proposed equity incentive plan at an upcoming annual meeting. If approved, that plan would set aside 7.2% of SkyAI shares — worth about $4 million at current prices — for its 30 employees, subject to shareholder approval.
A SkyAI spokesperson said the proposal is below the median equity incentive plan offered by comparable DATs, and that only a portion of the awards would go to executives.

Forward also drew attention to consultancy payments worth millions made to Sol Edge Ltd., in addition to warrants issued to Sol Markets valued at $101 million as of Dec. 31, according to a SkyAI filing. Both companies are owned by James Zhang, brother of SkyAI Chief Investment Officer Yuwen Zhang.

“It’s extremely abnormal,” Ryan Navi, Forward’s chief investment officer, said in an interview, pointing out that the warrants are worth roughly twice SkyAI’s market capitalization. “I don’t even know how that makes sense.”
SkyAI’s spokesperson said the arrangements were reviewed by its board, publicly disclosed and entered into before the fundraise closed.

Tian Zeng, chief executive officer of crypto hedge fund Third Eye, participated in the round and contends that the disclosures were inadequate. Had investors been told more explicitly about the warrants, “no one would have invested,” he said in an interview.
For Metaplanet, whose shares are down 84% from a June 2025 high, the criticism came not from would-be acquirers but from an army of individual investors online.
The drama centered on an arcane incentive structure which social-media users said had enriched executives while diluting ordinary shareholders.
On Friday, Metaplanet Chief Executive Officer Simon Gerovich relented.

“One thing is increasingly clear: we are no longer the company we were when the incentive structure at the center of this dialogue was created,” he said in a post on X. The company made adjustments to the pay program, including canceling some warrants that were planned for an employee incentive pool.

“We are engaging independent external experts to help create a new compensation program to ensure it appropriately aligns management incentives with long-term shareholder value creation,” Gerovich said.
Gerovich directed Bloomberg News to his post on X when asked for comment.
This isn’t the first time crypto treasury companies have drawn attention for how they spend the hundreds of billions of dollars they’ve collectively gathered from investors.

Shares in David Bailey’s Bitcoin buyer Nakamoto Inc. are down 99% from last year’s peak. In February, Nakamoto used stock to acquire two other companies led by Bailey, who is widely credited with converting Donald Trump into a Bitcoin believer. Bailey has said the purchases are part of a broad plan to diversify Nakamoto’s earnings.
However, some observers characterized it as a clear conflict of interest. Short-seller Jim Chanos put it this way in an X post: “Theater of the Absurd.”
A Nakamoto spokesperson declined to comment.

Executives and boards of directors should prepare for more shareholder activism as long as values remain depressed and investors question the underlying business model of DATs, according to a memo written by three Goodwin Procter attorneys and published by Harvard Law School this week.
“Those pressures create a landscape that shareholder activists may find increasingly attractive,” they wrote.

items.title: Australia Mulls Ban on Smart Glasses in Federal Office Buildings
body: Australia’s government is considering a ban on smart glasses in federal buildings, citing privacy and security concerns over using the devices to record people without their knowledge.

“Smart glasses can raise legitimate privacy and security concerns, particularly because of their ability to record and capture information, and we need clear and consistent guidance for public servants,” Minister for the Public Service Katy Gallagher said in a statement Thursday.

The Australian Public Service is one of the nation’s largest employers, with almost 200,000 people as of last year, and a ban in federal workplaces could set a precedent for other local and state jurisdictions, as well as companies. The government said it sees the move as a step toward “a potential world leading ban.”

The Brisbane city council last month banned the non-consensual use of smart glasses, phones and other wearable technology to film at public pools. Those rules allow lifeguards to eject people who film anyone without permission, and a number of other councils in Australia are following suit.

items.title: AI Fuels 440% Surge in Hackers Using Blockchains in Attacks
body: Open-source artificial intelligence is making it easier for hackers to hide malicious code on blockchains, opening a new front in a crypto industry already grappling with rising cybercrime.

Instances of malware instructions written into on-chain transactions and smart contracts are up 440% in less than a year, averaging 11 cases per day, blockchain analytics firm Chainalysis said in a report published on Thursday. Such cases averaged two per day prior to the release in the middle of last year of powerful Chinese open-source AI models with no restrictions on generating malicious code, according to the report.

A malware attack uses malicious software planted on a computer or network to steal information, passwords or funds. In the attacks documented by the report, hackers use a blockchain to leave instructions for that software, telling it where to send information, a technique known as “blockchain dead drop”. This can make an attack harder to stop because information recorded on a blockchain cannot be easily removed.
State-backed groups — including those linked to North Korea and Iran — now account for the majority of this activity, the report said.

The findings add to evidence of generative AI contributing to a boom in cyber threats, by spotting more software vulnerabilities and allowing cybercriminals to carry out more attacks. In crypto, the number of hacks rose roughly 150% to 207 in the first half of the year, according to blockchain intelligence firm TRM Labs.
Read More: Hackers Armed With AI Stoke Fears for $130 Billion Crypto Sector

Blockchains are typically not involved in the initial infection of a machine, which often happens through conventional means such as supply-chain attacks or malicious downloads, Eric Jardine, head of research at Chainalysis, said in response to questions over email. The firm has not tracked how many attacks were successful, or how much money was lost.

Hiding malware on a blockchain is not new, Chainalysis said, but powerful new open-source AI models are allowing hackers to carry out attacks on a larger scale, while growing involvement by state actors is making them more sophisticated.
Read More: A $320 Million Hack Exposes the Cracks in Crypto’s Plumbing (1)
Worsening the threat, open-source AI models can be run independently, allowing hackers to modify them or remove safeguards against cybercrime.
“This gives malicious developers greater control over the model and more privacy,” said Vitaly Kamluk, founder of cybersecurity consultancy TitanHex.
By contrast, companies such as OpenAI and Alphabet Inc.’s Google can block access to their AI services when they detect abuse.

The transparency of blockchains cuts both ways, though. Every update attackers post is permanently recorded, letting investigators map their infrastructure and connect campaigns that would otherwise look unrelated, according to Chainalysis.

items.title: Sweden Center Left Seals Election Win to Keep Far Right Out
body: Sweden’s center-left opposition bloc won Sunday’s tight general election by a narrow margin, prompting Prime Minister Ulf Kristersson to resign and closing off the prospect of the far right entering government for now.

A final tally of late votes and overseas ballots was completed Thursday, giving the Social Democrat-led bloc 176 seats against 173 for the current premier and his allies. Just over 50,000 votes separated the sides.

After the result became clear, Kristersson submitted a letter to the parliament speaker, seeking to be relieved of his duties as prime minister effective immediately, to open the way for negotiations on a new government.
Social Democrat leader Magdalena Andersson is now expected to begin what could be tricky talks with allies who disagree with each other over key areas from tax policy to the future of nuclear power.

“The Swedish people have voted for a new direction for our country, voted for unity and against division,” Andersson said in a speech posted on social media. “The Swedish people have voted to move Sweden forward. And I want to realize the new direction that you have voted for.”

The count was paused for two days after Sunday failed to produce a result, as election officials awaited the arrival of some advance votes, as well as the remaining ballots from Swedes residing abroad. Turnout rose to almost 85%, matching the previous election.
Read More: Swedish Voters in Limbo in Election Race Too Close to Call
Markets have taken the uncertainty in their stride, with the OMX Stockholm Index up 0.6% from Friday. The krona is trading little changed versus the pre-election level of 11.2531 per euro.

Eking out a narrow majority shows how the Social Democrats are suffering from the fragmentation of the political landscape. Their 28% backing is the worst in more than a century and far from their mid-20th century heyday when the party regularly pulled in nearly half of the vote.

Still, the outcome supports a flickering revival of the center left across parts of Europe. UK Labour Prime Minister Andy Burnham is seeking to build on a recent bounce in opinion polls and Social Democrats already govern Denmark, Norway and Iceland. Center-left candidates will be tested again in Spain, France, Poland and in Sweden’s neighbor Finland over the coming year.

The result deals a blow to Kristersson’s bid for reelection after his gamble backfired. He had promised to bring his Sweden Democrat allies under leader Jimmie Åkesson into government for the first time.

“It will now require constructive openness from the parties in parliament for a prime minister to be tolerated — and for a new government to be able to secure support for its budget,” Kristersson wrote in a resignation letter. The outgoing premier’s bloc which relied on backing from the anti-immigrant Sweden Democrats had governed with a similarly narrow majority.

By readily adopting a stronger position on crime, Andersson was able to outflank the right on its own turf. She also succeeded in drawing on her party’s history of strengthening public welfare to reassure Swedes feeling the pinch of weak growth and an uncertain job market.
In absolute numbers, the Sweden Democrats lost the most seats, totaling 11, while Andersson’s Social Democrats didn’t fare much better, giving up eight.

Andersson is likely to try and form a government made up of or supported by the Green Party, the Center Party and the Left Party in what appears a daunting challenge. The two latter parties have outlined mutually exclusive red lines, but Andersson insists it will be possible to persuade them to compromise.

A key sticking point will be economic policy with the Left Party favoring higher taxes on income and business earnings to boost pensions and other welfare investments, positions which the Center Party firmly rejects.
Before the final results were clear, Center leader Elisabeth Thand Ringqvist, who has emerged as a kingmaker in the election, said her party will be “constructive” in the talks.
Read More: Sweden’s Small Pro-Business Party Emerges as Election Kingmaker
If Andersson fails to stitch together the support to be appointed prime minister, Kristersson will be next in line to try.

Under the Swedish system, a prime minister doesn’t need backing from a majority of lawmakers, but needs to ensure most members of parliament don’t actively oppose them. There can be four parliamentary votes on a new prime minister before a new election must be called.

items.title: Schlumberger Heirs to Auction Never-Exhibited Monet at Sotheby's
body: Schlumberger heirs are set to auction a rare Claude Monet masterpiece at Sotheby’s in Paris next month, a sale that could fetch a record price for a painting sold in France.

Monet’s Iris is considered a masterpiece from the artist’s final years, painted between 1924 and 1925 at his house in Giverny near Paris where he famously produced his water lilies series, Sotheby’s said Thursday. The painting is coming under the hammer on Oct. 22.

The auction house estimates the piece could fetch between €22 million ($25 million) and €30 million. The Monet belongs to heirs of Jeanne Schlumberger, the wife of Marcel Schlumberger, one of the two brothers who founded the eponymous firm. The company, which became an oil-services giant that was renamed SLB four years ago, now has a market value of about $78 billion.

Jeanne, a famous art collector, became the owner of exceptional pieces including Paul Cezanne’s La Ferme and Gustave Moreau’s Reve d’Orient thanks to her friendship with the gallery owner Katia Granoff. Those pieces are also set to come under the hammer next month.

Thomas Bompard, Sotheby’s France co-head of modern and contemporary art who will oversee the auction next month, told reporters that the sale of the never-exhibited Iris comes as the art world this year commemorates the 100th anniversary of Monet’s death, with special exhibitions notably at the Musee de l’Orangerie in Paris that displays his famous water lilies.

The Schlumberger heirs considered “the time had come and the market is strong enough to organize the big revelation and the big presentation of the collection of their ancestor,” Bompard said Thursday.

Bompard said Jeanne had always refused to lend the Iris for exhibitions and held it at her private residence located on Paris’ left bank, where she lived — a decision that has helped preserve it in a “miraculous” state, Bompard said. The work has been left untouched, unvarnished, unlined, a rare condition for a painting of this caliber, he added.

Monet’s “paintings from this period are among the most sought-after,” Bompard said, adding that Jeanne was drawn to them by their contemporary and abstract elements rather the impressionist touches for which Monet is known.

The highest price for a Monet Iris painting was reached at a 2015 auction in London by Christie’s, where it was sold for £10.8 million, or $17 million at the time. The record price commanded by a Monet is $110.7 million, when Meules, was auctioned by Sotheby’s in New York in 2019.

items.title: Mexico's Superpeso Requires Careful Handling
body: A Big Mac in Mexico already costs almost $6.50. So does a gallon of premium gasoline. The shiny new iPhone 18 Pro? That will set you back 29,999 pesos, or about $1,765 at 17 to the dollar, nearly 50% more than the US pre-tax list price. And I won’t get into what private-school tuition costs in Mexico City even before converting it into dollars.
The steady appreciation of the peso is making Mexico an expensive country.

In recent weeks, the currency strengthened past the 17 peso-per-dollar threshold, touching on Sept. 4 its strongest nominal level against the greenback in more than two years before losing some ground. In real terms, the run of the superpeso is even more striking: Mexico’s inflation-adjusted real exchange rate, weighted across 49 trading partners, is hovering near its highest level in almost 24 years, according to data compiled by Banxico, the central bank.

The consequences are already emerging: In the key tourism sector, international air travelers dropped 5.7% in July from a year earlier, while their spending fell 3.3%, reflecting weaker demand for Mexico’s beach destinations. Mexican tourists, by contrast, are taking full advantage of their powerful peso to see the world: Outbound flying tourists grew 4.9% in the same month, and their spending jumped more than 21%.

Remittances have lost 25% of their real peso value since their July 2022 peak, largely because of FX gains, eroding the purchasing power of millions who depend on money sent by relatives in the US. Consumption of domestic goods seems to be losing ground to imports. And although exports continue to set records, manufacturing employment and production volumes declined year over year in June.

That’s growing evidence the superpeso is doing more harm than good to the Mexican economy. It’s time to stop pretending that a stronger FX is always good news, as Mexico’s leftist government has oddly done since the days of President Andrés Manuel López Obrador, who turned the macho peso into a leitmotif of economic soundness.

The harder question is what to do about it. In an era of growing bouts of currency warfare, from Japan to Colombia, Mexico should instead tread lightly and resist the temptation to intervene in the foreign-exchange market in ways that could easily backfire. There are macroeconomic, geopolitical and strategic reasons why a rushed intervention could do more damage than the superpeso itself.

That doesn’t mean Mexico should sit back and watch its currency become an even bigger drag on competitiveness. Having authorities acknowledge the superpeso’s downsides, instead of cheering it, is a sensible first step. But policymakers should weigh the risks carefully and deploy any creative solutions at a gradual pace that doesn’t threaten the country’s hard-won financial reputation.

The easiest way to weaken the currency — short of a catastrophic devaluation that nobody is advocating — would be for Banxico to resume its cycle of interest-rate cuts, making the peso less attractive to carry-trade hunters. That would also be the preferred option for Mexican businesses, which would love to see the key policy rate fall to 5% or less from 6.5% now, with the exchange rate ideally moving closer to 18 or 19 per dollar.

The problem is that this could dent Banxico’s inflation-fighting credentials. The central bank, whose recent forecasts have been erratic at best, only expects to reach its 3% inflation target by the final quarter of 2027. Perhaps the inflation outlook improves significantly in the coming months and a new window to cut borrowing costs opens up again. But easing monetary policy now could be interpreted by investors as a deliberate attempt to weaken the peso, undermining the central bank’s credibility and making its inflation-targeting mandate harder to achieve.

A higher-impact option would be for the Foreign Exchange Commission — made up of officials from the Finance Ministry and Banxico — to announce dollar purchases to expand international reserves. An explicit goal of, say, $10 billion or $20 billion would reinforce the country’s foreign-exchange buffers, much as Colombia is doing with a similar program that it announced in late July.

Yet while such policy would give Banxico greater firepower if external flows suddenly reverse, it’s unlikely to meaningfully correct the peso’s appreciation. Worse, it could confuse the market about the central bank’s priorities. Mexico’s international reserves are already adequate, at about 12% of GDP; investors would surely read the strategy as a foreign exchange intervention instead.

Even riskier, announcing such a program while Mexican negotiators are trying to convince US President Donald Trump to renew their trade pact would amount to declaring war on Washington. Any major move that even implicitly seeks to weaken the peso, at a time when Mexico runs large trade surpluses with the US, could trigger unwanted political conflict with the country’s top trading partner. That’s a nonstarter.

As things stand, the best strategy for Mexico may be to achieve a narrower interest-rate differential with the US, currently standing at between 250 and 275 basis points after the Federal Reserve’s announcement on Wednesday. By breaking the historic pattern of following the Fed, Banxico can make the carry trade — already offering the smallest gap since Mexico implemented the overnight policy rate in 2008 — even less attractive. As an initial taste of that, the Mexican currency has lost about 1.3% against the dollar during this Fed week.

“Mexico’s only feasible option is to show a bit of independence from the Fed,” Pablo Garcia Silva, a former vice president of Chile’s central bank, told me. “Attempting to intervene in the currency market today will be very complex, very risky.”

Some may find all this underwhelming. Trust me, as someone whose salary is being smashed by the peso’s strength, I wish for more powerful options. But regaining currency competitiveness through national policy in a country that ships almost 85% of its products to the US is tough because direct market interventions can do little to tame structural cycles, especially at times of high uncertainty.

Mexico is also the victim of a happy problem: Part of the peso’s allure comes from its growing importance in international markets. Already the world’s third-most-traded emerging-market currency, it’s liquid, convertible and functioning around the clock. Global investors love it. That institutional framework, together with the flexible exchange-rate regime adopted after the 1994 Tequila crisis, have served Mexico remarkably well and should be preserved. It’s not here where the problems of the Mexican economy start.

Only gradual options that don’t jeopardize the country’s credibility and stability should be considered, including authorities jawboning the peso. In a convoluted world where the US economy is facing serious challenges, suggesting more volatility ahead, Mexico’s smartest response to the superpeso may for now be prudence and patience.

items.title: CoreWeave Seeks to Raise $3 Billion in Convertible Bonds
body: CoreWeave Inc., a provider of computing that powers artificial intelligence systems, kicked off a fresh round of fundraising that includes a $3 billion convertible bond issue and a vehicle for potential share sales.

The artificial intelligence cloud firm agreed a so called at-the-market offering program that allows it to sell as many as 35 million shares from time to time, according to a statement Thursday. The program will provide financing flexibility and help CoreWeave migrate its credit profile toward investment grade, the statement showed.

CoreWeave’s senior convertible bonds will be due in 2033 and the proceeds will be used for general corporate purposes, with a portion set aside for a series of derivative agreements related to the offering, according to a separate statement on Thursday. There is an option to increase the size of the offering by $500 million, the statement shows.
The company’s shares fell 1.7% to $81.97 each in pre-market trading on Thursday in New York.

The relentless drive to fund AI infrastructure has prompted companies involved in the rapid buildout to tap a wide range of potential sources of cash. Investors have begun to show signs of fatigue after companies borrowed about $419 billion in global debt markets this year alone, according to Bloomberg-compiled data, driving funding costs higher for some as demand dipped.
In July, CoreWeave had to sweeten the pricing on a $2.6 billion leveraged loan deal to help get it over the line.
Read More: CoreWeave’s Wild Stock Ride Takes Toll on Its Cost to Finance AI

The ramping up of AI fundraising has propelled US convertible bond sales to their highest annual total on record, according to data compiled by Bloomberg. Companies with US listings have raised $137.3 billion from the sales of securities that potentially convert into stock under certain conditions, the data show.

CoreWeave is offering a coupon on the convertible bonds of 2.375% to 2.875%, according to people familiar with the matter. The offering is expected to price later Thursday, the people said, asking not to be identified as the information isn’t public.

Morgan Stanley, Goldman Sachs Group Inc., JPMorgan Chase & Co. and Wells Fargo & Co. are working on the convertible bond offering, the people said. A spokesperson for CoreWeave declined to comment. Representatives for the banks didn’t immediately respond to requests for comment.

items.title: Kamala Harris Ramps Up Travel as Pressure to Decide on 2028 Mounts
body: I’m Jonathan Tamari, senior Washington reporter for Bloomberg Government, and each weekday I’ll be coming to you with inside-the-room reporting and insights that reveal what’s really happening in Washington—and how it impacts you. Email me with feedback and comments here. If this newsletter was forwarded to you sign up here.
Today: Will Kamala Harris get another shot?, Trump’s Fed response, and crypto learns a lesson in lobbying.
Would Democrats take another chance on Kamala Harris?

It’s a question moving closer to the forefront as the party takes early stock of its options for 2028, with some high-profile Democrats this week suggesting she might not take the plunge or would have a difficult run.

Harris consistently leads polls of the possible 2028 field and will ramp up her public presence next week when she heads to Michigan to campaign with Abdul El-Sayed in a crucial Senate race, hoping to help unify Democrats.
She’s also slated to campaign in key contests in Georgia and Nevada next month.
The events will give us an early chance to assess another key question Democratic strategists are asking about Harris’s chances: Can she evolve?
The 2028 race is almost certain to center on change and disruption after more than a decade of presidents born in the 1940s.

Harris, however, is tied to an old administration and old president. She’s already had two swings, with her 2020 and 2024 campaigns marked by caution, convention, and a struggle to convey authenticity. Both ended badly.
But, he told me, Harris has to “be honest” about her mistakes.
She’ll also have to show she can offer a break from status quo politics, despite being a former VP, said Ashley Etienne, a Democratic strategist who has previously worked for Harris and Nancy Pelosi.
Harris being out of public office for the first time in more than 20 years may help her gain a new perspective and speak more freely, Etienne argued.
(Etienne, who said she’s not working with Harris or any potential 2028 contender, spoke with me at the request of the ex-VP’s office. Harris’s spokesperson declined to comment for this piece.)
Some Democrats look ready to move on.

Battleground candidates in Alaska and Iowa have waved away Harris from their races, and LinkedIn cofounder and Democratic mega-donor Reid Hoffman told Politico on Wednesday that 2028 “would be a very challenging path” for her.

Pressure for Harris to more clearly signal her intentions grew this week after Gavin Newsom told CNN “I don’t know if she runs” but that he’ll stand down if she does. (There’s no sign yet he’s pumping the brakes on his own bid, while other hopefuls are drawing early attention.)
Democrats’ most successful recent presidents have been fresh, forward-looking figures such as Bill Clinton and Barack Obama.
Even if Harris can show a new side, it could create problems after facing accusations of being too malleable in the past.
But Harris would also begin any campaign with major assets, including being the most well-known Democrat in the mix, with the biggest national network of supporters.
Democrats moving their first nominating contest to South Carolina, where Black voters play a central role, could also help.

The former VP says said she’s focused on the midterms (she’s been fundraising and urging people to vote), but hinted at getting back in the arena more directly on a recent podcast with former soccer star Megan Rapinoe.
Sounds like Democratic voters may have to soon start weighing if they’ll put their hopes in her again.
Trump floated new tariffs on the EU or cutting off some trade if he decides that its invite to Canada to become an “associate member” is “a hostile act.”
Mark Carney, meanwhile, today called for a closer alliance between Canada and the EU to ward off threats from powers like the US and China.
Trump blamed a “very hostile board” for the Fed’s first rate hike in three years but stopped short of criticizing Kevin Warsh — a marked difference from his repeated attacks on Jerome Powell.
Crypto just learned an age-old lobbying lesson: it’s a lot easier to block a bill than to pass one. Here’s what the industry is doing as it looks to Plan B.
Sonia Sotomayor renewed her sharp criticism of fellow justices, saying that while many citizens don’t understand the US system of government “some of my colleagues don’t either.”
Apple’s Tim Cook and OpenAI’s Sam Altman will attend the state dinner with Trump and China’s Xi Jinping next week.
King Charles III is urging leading AI execs to keep their products under control as he hosts officials from Nvidia, OpenAI, Google DeepMind, and Anthropic today.
OpenAI reported several undisclosed incidents of its models misbehaving and unveiled a new framework for tracking and disclosing such events.

“Obviously, we don’t want anybody to cheat in the election,” Representative Mike Lawler told Bloomberg Government. Other vulnerable Republicans brushed off Trump’s call to “cheat like hell” in the midterms.
Trump has appointed a smaller percentage of Asian Americans to the bench this term. He’s nominated fewer judges overall due to fewer vacancies.
A bill giving Trump new powers to impose tariffs on countries buying Russian oil passed the House and is headed to his desk, a victory for Ukraine and its supporters.

A House panel advanced a bill aimed at giving the US an edge over China in the use of open-source AI models. Democrats knocked the GOP for sending lawmakers home before the election without passing AI safety legislation.
People using GLP-1 pills for weight loss curbed their snacking less than those using shots, according to new research from Bloomberg Intelligence.
Russia’s attacks on Europe are getting more brazen and dangerous as they reach deeper into the continent.
Snap is detailing more on its forthcoming $2,195 smart glasses, hoping to make consumers comfortable wearing a computer on their faces.
Hundreds of billions of market cap in the pharma sector remain without a White House deal for lower prices on consumer drugs, BGOV’s Andrew Ramonas writes.

More than two dozen drugmakers have agreed to discounts on some of their most popular drugs, covering about 90% of the US market. Eli Lilly & Co., Johnson & Johnson, and AbbVie Inc. were among drugmakers to sign onto pacts with the Trump administration.
The “most favored nation” deals came with calls by the companies for the US government to hold off on mandatory pricing requirements.
Trump signs executive orders, participates in a tele-rally in the evening, and attends a Rose Garden dinner.
Pennsylvania Governor Josh Shapiro speaks at the AI Horizons Conference.
The Senate Banking Committee holds a markup at 10 a.m. and considers multiple nominations.
The Senate takes its next procedural vote on college sports legislation.

items.title: Trump Turns His Canada Ire Toward the EU
body: Good morning. Donald Trump redirects his ire toward Canada at the European Union. King Charles III holds court with AI’s elite. And Snap’s heavy Specs come with a hefty price tag. Listen to the day’s top stories.
— Angela Cullen and Harry Black

Donald Trump threatened to “put very serious tariffs or stop trading with Europe on many things” if he deems a push by Brussels to make Canada an associate of the European Union to be “a hostile act.” Prime Minister Mark Carney welcomed the EU’s outreach, calling for a closer alliance between Canada and the EU in a speech to European lawmakers in Strasbourg, France, on Thursday. “We do not seek power to dominate others,” Carney said. In a separate escalation of his trade spat with Ottawa, Trump directed agencies to remove Canadian goods from US government contracts.

The president returned to the campaign trail, traveling to North Carolina, where Republican Senate hopeful Michael Whatley trails Democrat Roy Cooper in opinion polls. The trip kicks off what Trump has billed as a nationwide sprint to Election Day with a number of hotly-contested Congressional races. North Carolina could be critical to determining which party controls the Senate, and Trump’s rally at an airfield outside Charlotte offered a sign of the deep concern within GOP ranks over their prospects of holding onto the chamber.

Congress gave final approval to a bill that would give Trump new powers to impose tariffs on countries that buy Russian petroleum products. It’s a setback for a coalition of business lobbyists concerned the legislation creates a legal underpinning for a broad new tariff regime against US trading partners. India, for one, isn’t happy. Meanwhile, Russia’s attacks on Europe are getting more brazen, and more dangerous.

Not again? OpenAI reported several undisclosed incidents of its AI models misbehaving, and unveiled a new framework for tracking and disclosing such happenings. The company’s finance chief, Sarah Friar, is set to join Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang and Google DeepMind co-founder Demis Hassabis at a meeting with King Charles III in Scotland today. Britain’s monarch wants assurances they’ll protect mankind in AI’s march into the future. Away from the AI world, a Venice exhibition is celebrating handmade crafts, featuring more than 700 objects that showcase traditional techniques now at risk of disappearing.

With weeks to go before Brazil’s presidential election, President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva and right-wing challenger Flávio Bolsonaro are locked in a dead heat. A new poll by AtlasIntel suggests fallout from a major bank scandal is hitting both campaigns. Next door in Peru, one central banker has weathered  political turbulence as a pillar of economic stability. Ten presidents have come and gone since Julio Velarde took charge of monetary policy in 2006. The 74-year-old draws standing ovations the world over for his longevity.
Across America, college teams are betting big on swanky arenas and higher salaries for players and coaches, a financial model that’s starting to resemble the pros, on and off the field.

Kevin Warsh, who a year ago criticized the Fed for keeping borrowing costs too high and predicted a tech-driven, non-inflationary boom, has been forced to hike interest rates just four months into his tenure as Fed chair — defying President Trump — as war, tariffs, and AI upend his outlook.
Big Take Podcast
Markets are pricing a series of Fed rate hikes, Jonathan Levin writes. But a look back at the Alan Greenspan Fed shows Kevin Warsh has ample room to prove the consensus wrong.
More Opinions
Our daily word puzzle with a plot twist.
Today’s clue is: Mob rule
Play now!

Snap’s augmented reality glasses are set to launch with a hefty price tag: $2,195. They’re more technically advanced than Meta’s highest-end $799 spectacles but fall short of the visual clarity and immersion of Apple’s $3,699 Vision Pro, Chris Welch and Mark Gurman write. And they’re heavy.

items.title: UK Bonds Flip to Gains as BOE Scraps Long-Dated QT Sales
body: UK government bonds gained after the Bank of England left interest rates unchanged and scrapped plans to sell long-dated gilts as part of its quantitative tightening program.

The yield on 30-year gilts reversed an earlier rise to fall 12 basis points, the most since May, to 5.74%, while two-year rates dropped six basis points to 4.70%. Traders trimmed bets on further BOE tightening, with about an 85% chance of a hike priced in for the November meeting. Less than four hikes are now priced in by this time next year.

The BOE announced a major overhaul of its quantitative tightening program that will see the £488 billion ($652 billion) portfolio unwound by September 2034. It also hit pause on planned QT auctions until April and will seek to sell shorter-maturity gilts to the Debt Management Office instead of actively to the market.

Markets were on a knife edge over the QT decision, and slashing long dated sales provided some relief for the battered bonds. The 30-year yield had climbed to its highest since 1998 in recent days, with the move exacerbated by a broader global bond selloff.
Read more: BOE Scraps Long-End Gilt Sales, Helping Ease Pressure on Yields
“It is a positive for gilts particularly at the long end as it would improve the supply demand picture for gilts,” said Mohit Kumar, chief European strategist at Jefferies.

Persistent inflation remains a key concern among Monetary Policy Committee members, with the conflict in the Middle East keeping energy prices elevated. Six rate-setters chose to leave rates unchanged, including Governor Andrew Bailey.

In the statement of the decision, Bailey said the global energy shock has so far had a limited effect on prices and wages in the UK. “But the longer this volatility persists, the bigger the impact it will have on inflation, and the more likely it is we will need to raise Bank rate,” he said.

items.title: Canada's Oil Sands Get a Boost From Mark Carney
body: Welcome to our guide to the commodities driving the global economy. Today, commodities editor and Calgary bureau chief Iain Boekhoff looks at the growing alignment between Ottawa and Canada’s oil industry.
Canada’s oil industry this week found itself in the rare position of giving the federal government a rave review.
The reason: a change to the tax regime for a broad range of industries, including oil production and pipelines, that will now be able to immediately expense some investments.
A federal government official told a conference in Edmonton on Tuesday that the marginal effective tax rate of 6.4% for new investments would be the lowest of advanced global economies.

That’s good news for an industry set to spend north of C$100 billion ($71.8 billion) in the next decade to simultaneously expand production, build a new million-barrel-a-day pipeline to Canada’s west coast and construct a major carbon capture and storage project in the oil sands.
“They really delivered ahead of schedule,” said Kendall Dilling, head of the Oil Sands Alliance, a group representing the five largest producers in the region.

The alignment of interests between Ottawa and Alberta, the center of the country’s oil sector, is a relatively new phenomenon. In recent years, pressure from the federal government on the oil sands to reduce emissions generated resentment in Alberta and fueled the province’s separatist movement.
But Prime Minister Mark Carney’s government has been supportive of oil and gas as a way to cut Canadian reliance on the US as the relationship between the two neighbors has deteriorated.

That said, energy exports from Canada to the US are exempt from the tariffs imposed by President Donald Trump — both countries’ energy sectors are simply too entwined (and fuel prices already too elevated) for Washington to risk dragging oil into the trade war.
But around 90% of Canadian oil currently goes to the US. Boosting output and ensuring more is shipped to Asia are key planks of Carney’s strategy.
The industry is still looking for more concessions. Alberta Premier Danielle Smith has indicated she’s considering changes to the royalty scheme the province charges companies on their production.
And then there’s the Pathways carbon removal project, billed as the world’s largest, which would curb some of the emissions associated with Alberta’s oil industry.

The Canadian and Alberta governments and the oil sands majors are now negotiating to meet a Nov. 15 deadline to move ahead with the plan. The Pathways project is costly, ambitious and controversial, and its future is by no means assured.
But if it advances, that would be another vote of confidence for the sector.
—Iain Boekhoff, Bloomberg News

Thailand is using the oil shock caused by the Iran war to accelerate a shift toward electrification and domestically-sourced energy, trying to turn a supply crisis into a push for greater security. The government is seeking to reduce dependence on imported crude that accounts for about 90% of Thailand’s oil supplies by promoting greater adoption of battery-powered vehicles and increasing electricity use.
Oil extended a decline on signs that supply disruptions in the Middle East are set to ease, with a key pipeline in Saudi Arabia being restored.

India warned that a US bill allowing Trump to impose tariffs of as much as 100% on top buyers of Russian oil could hurt bilateral ties. Meanwhile, Indian state-owned refiners are facing the most significant supply uncertainty in months.

Ukraine damaged a major Russian oil refinery less than 200 miles northeast of Moscow while Russian forces attacked Ukrainian infrastructure overnight, a fresh indication the sides haven’t agreed to an energy truce despite Trump’s claims.
Holtec Nuclear Corp., a supplier of specialty services to the nuclear power industry, postponed a planned US initial public offering which was expected to price Thursday.
Germany’s renewable-energy developers are entering a shakeout after years of rapid expansion, with worsening project economics pushing a growing number into financial distress.

Bloomberg Green returns to New York on Sept. 23 during Climate Week, convening industry leaders, policymakers and climate innovators to explore what’s next in the transition to a more resilient and future-ready world.

items.title: Almonty to Supply Tungsten to Sandvik From Spain Mine Tailings
body: Almonty Industries Inc. has signed a deal to supply tungsten, one of the most sought-after critical minerals, to Swedish mining equipment maker Sandvik AB.

The supply will come from recycling leftover mining waste, or tailings, from a long-shuttered Spanish mine called Los Santos, Almonty said in a statement Thursday. The tungsten will be supplied to Sandvik’s Wolfram Bergbau und Hütten AG unit as part of a long-term deal.

“The agreement is intended to create an expedited tungsten supply solution with the ability to deliver concentrate in notably less time than the development of a traditional mine,” Almonty said. The deal is “structured on a take-or-pay basis.”

Europe and the US are increasingly looking for new supplies of the strategic mineral to cut reliance on China, which accounts for about 80% of global production, especially after the Asian nation set tighter export curbs in 2025. Spain is home to Western Europe’s largest reserves of tungsten, an extremely hard, heat-resistant metal used in everything from weapons and semiconductors, but projects to bring new production online have been marred in red tape.

Almonty’s main mine is in South Korea, and it also produces in Portugal. In Spain, the company has also held the license to a mining project called Valtreixal since 2013, but is still waiting for the requisite permits to start operations. In July, a regional government issued a non-binding negative environmental assessment against it.

The European Union in 2024 passed the Critical Materials Act to try to foster more production in the bloc, and in April the Commission included tungsten in its joint-purchasing plans for critical minerals — alongside rare earths, gallium, magnesium, germanium, and graphite.
At Los Santos, Almonty’s plan consists of employing specially developed technology to process tailings, rather than mining. Tailings offer far lower-grade tungsten than newly mined ore.

The plan is fully driven by the price of tungsten, which has surged since China placed its controls on exports, and by the need of European users such as Sandvik to find new suppliers, said Almonty Chairman and Chief Executive Officer Lewis Black in an interview.

Los Santos “could be a success or a total failure,” he said. If it succeeds, the company aims to replicate the model at “multiple similar sites across Iberia,” he said, adding that there could be as many as 100 in the peninsula.

items.title: UK Seeks to Slap Fees on Battery Projects Clogging Up Grid Queue
body: The UK’s energy watchdog proposed new measures to reduce a ballooning queue of battery-storage projects for power-grid connections, seeking to squeeze out those that are unlikely to come to fruition.

Ofgem wants to introduce a fee for battery projects to wait in line, starting at £3,000 ($4,019) per megawatt and potentially rising to £25,000 per megawatt if the queue remains significantly oversubscribed, it said Thursday in a statement. The fee is refunded if projects get connected.

Britain is rapidly transforming its energy system, adding more renewables as it moves away from a power mix dominated by gas. Batteries are crucial to balancing swings in wind and solar output, but an increasingly congested grid and an overcrowded queue have stymied efforts to get viable projects online.

“Britain needs the major deployment of large-scale battery storage to meet future electricity demand,” said Eleanor Warburton, Ofgem’s director for energy system design and development. But it has “three times more battery capacity in the connections queue than the system is expected to need by 2035.”

The bottleneck has become a constraint on the energy transition and more broadly on economic growth. Ofgem’s plan to ease the logjam follows a similar measure put forward earlier this year targeting data centers in the queue.

That proposal suggested a fee of £237,500 to £712,500 a megawatt, equivalent to about 2.5% to 7.5% of a project’s estimated capital expenditure. For batteries, Ofgem estimates the maximum commitment at about a quarter of capex for short-duration batteries and 7% for medium-duration projects.
Read More: UK Plans Fees to Weed Out Speculative Data Center Projects
Ofgem’s latest proposals are now out for consultation.

items.title: Peso fuerte de Milei golpea economía de Argentina
body: Read story in EnglishLos esfuerzos del presidente Javier Milei por controlar la inflación mediante una moneda fuerte están teniendo un impacto cada vez mayor en la economía argentina.

El peso se ha debilitado apenas un 3,7% frente al dólar, mientras que los precios al consumidor acumulan un aumento del 21,3% entre enero y agosto. Esa apreciación real se ha sostenido cada vez más en las últimas semanas mediante intervenciones oficiales en los mercados de bonos y futuros, mientras siguen vigentes los controles cambiarios para las empresas.
Suscríbase       aquí     al boletín Morning Briefing Español y conozca nuestro canal de       WhatsApp

El Instituto Nacional de Estadística y Censos (Indec) publicará este jueves por la tarde las cifras del producto interno bruto del segundo trimestre, y los analistas prevén una contracción del 0,9% respecto del período de tres meses anterior. Para muchos, la fortaleza de la moneda bajo Milei es uno de los principales factores que frenan el crecimiento de Argentina.

“A estas alturas, está más que claro que la actividad económica no primaria de Argentina muestra un desempeño débil, lo que plantea riesgos para la continuidad de la política económica”, señaló Iván Stambulsky, analista de Barclays, en un informe a inversores la semana pasada. “En nuestra opinión, la principal explicación es simplemente que el tipo de cambio real efectivo es demasiado fuerte para la actual combinación de políticas”.

El líder libertario ha moderado los aumentos de precios durante gran parte de su presidencia, en parte manteniendo un férreo control sobre el peso, lo que ha provocado una apreciación de la moneda en términos reales.

Durante el primer semestre del año, ingresaron dólares procedentes de la cosecha de soja, en medio de una fuerte emisión de deuda en el exterior por parte de empresas argentinas, lo que proporcionó abundantes divisas y ayudó al banco central a recomponer reservas sin ejercer demasiada presión sobre el peso.

Ese contexto comenzó a cambiar en el segundo semestre. Los ingresos de dólares provenientes de las exportaciones agrícolas se desaceleraron tras el pico de la cosecha, mientras también disminuyeron los fondos obtenidos mediante el endeudamiento corporativo. A medida que escaseaban los dólares, el banco central recurrió cada vez más a la venta de títulos vinculados al tipo de cambio y contratos de futuros para satisfacer la demanda de cobertura y aliviar la presión sobre el peso, al tiempo que seguía intentando acumular reservas.

Como resultado, el volumen de coberturas vinculadas al tipo de cambio aumentó más del doble en apenas cinco meses, según estimaciones de la corredora local Facimex. En total, las tenencias del sector privado de contratos de futuros, bonos duales e instrumentos dólar linked aumentaron a alrededor de US$12.000 millones a fines de agosto, desde US$5.200 millones a fines de marzo.

“Hay un fuerte grado de intervención del BCRA”, señaló Stambulsky. Cuando el mercado comenzó a desarmar operaciones de carry trade tras el pico de la cosecha, la autoridad monetaria “intensificó la intervención mediante la venta de coberturas, redujo el ritmo de compras en el mercado spot y permitió que subieran las tasas”.

Agosto, septiembre y octubre suelen ser meses en los que el banco central vende dólares directamente en el mercado spot. Pero este año el gobierno cambió de estrategia y optó por vender instrumentos vinculados al dólar fuera de ese mercado.

La estrategia ha ayudado a mantener el tipo de cambio cerca de 1.500 pesos por dólar, mucho más fuerte de lo que habían previsto los economistas. Hace un año, los analistas encuestados por el banco central esperaban que el peso se debilitara hasta 1.811 por dólar para diciembre de 2026. Para el mes pasado, habían revisado esa previsión a 1.629.

En una economía que ya soporta una elevada carga tributaria y altos costos, un peso fuerte reduce la competitividad de los productores nacionales y abarata las importaciones, perjudicando a la industria local.
Esa dinámica está pesando sobre una economía que ya pierde impulso. Los economistas han recortado su previsión de crecimiento para todo 2026 al 2,1%, desde el 3,5% hace varios meses.

Las políticas de Milei han reducido drásticamente la inflación mensual, que pasó del 25,5% en que se encontraba en su primer mes en el cargo hasta el 1,7% en agosto. Sin embargo, los avances se han vuelto más difíciles desde que estalló la guerra con Irán. La inflación, que Milei esperaba que ya hubiera caído por debajo del 1%, se ha mantenido obstinadamente más cerca del 2%.

“Lo que el gobierno quiere, y rápido, es que la inflación baje”, señaló Osvaldo Giordano, presidente del centro de estudios económicos Ieral de la Fundación Mediterránea. La fortaleza del peso refleja tanto la determinación del gobierno de alcanzar ese objetivo como la expectativa del mercado de que cuenta con las herramientas para seguir haciéndolo, señaló.

Las mismas políticas que sostienen la moneda están generando presión en otros frentes. Las tasas de interés más altas están afectando al crédito, que se había convertido en un importante motor de la recuperación después de que años de elevada inflación dejaran en gran medida a hogares y empresas sin acceso al financiamiento. Sin embargo, desde las elecciones legislativas de octubre pasado, la morosidad de los hogares ha batido récords mes tras mes.

La presión es particularmente evidente en la industria manufacturera, el comercio minorista y la construcción, sectores intensivos en mano de obra que emplean a un gran número de argentinos y que han quedado rezagados frente a la expansión de áreas como energía, minería y agricultura. La construcción se contrajo un 4,5% interanual en agosto, mientras que la industria manufacturera cayó un 4,9%.
Eso plantea un creciente dilema político para Milei mientras se prepara para buscar la reelección el próximo año.

Según Giordano, tal vez “sería menos arriesgado decir que no es tan importante con qué velocidad termino de bajar la inflación y trato de generar un alivio, sobre todo en estos sectores urbanos, como industria, comercio, construcción, que son de los que vive la mayoría de los argentinos y que son los que muestran las estadísticas que fueron donde más actividad económica y empleos se destruyeron”.

items.title: Warsh Suggests Fed Rate Hike Is Good-News Story, Touting Growth
body: I’m Chris Anstey, a senior economics editor in Boston. Today we’re looking at Kevin Warsh’s hawkish Fed message. Send us feedback and tips to ecodaily@bloomberg.net. And if you aren’t yet signed up to receive this newsletter, you can do so here.

For the first time in three years, the Federal Reserve is hiking again. While the dominant narrative in the 2022-23 cycle was a desperate move to contain the biggest inflation surge in decades, this time around the US central bank head has thrown in a feel-good message.

Asked in his press conference why the Fed pulled the trigger on a quarter-point rate increase on Wednesday when it stood pat in July, Chairman Kevin Warsh cited three things. Number one, he said, “the economy has strengthened.” He went on to say it “appears to be strengthening,” which added some forward momentum to his initial observation.

“New hiring, private sector earnings, business capital investment — each of these markers has improved in recent months and is pointing in a good direction,” Warsh said. “Credit flows have been robust, particularly for businesses.”
Stephen Stanley at Santander US Capital Markets, said “perhaps the most striking development from Chairman Warsh’s press conference was the degree of optimism regarding the economy.”

How far tying a rate hike to economic strength may go in mollifying Donald Trump — who has long demanded the Fed slash rates — remains to be seen. The president’s initial response was a generic call for rates to go to 1%. (The Fed’s new target range is 3.75% to 4%.) In comments after the decision, Trump blamed the hike on a “hostile” board and said he’s “relying on Kevin.”

Warsh cited two other dynamics for the rate rise. One was that “too many categories” in US inflation reports continue to post annualized increases above 3% on a six-month and 12-month basis. This metric will now clearly be a big focus for investors and economists.

Finally, he effectively pointed to the Iran war pushing up costs, without using the word “Iran” — potentially another move to lessen the risk of direct conflict with the president. Warsh instead referred to “geopolitics” and “hotspots around the world.”

Having voted with all his colleagues to pull the trigger, Warsh secured his credibility, many Fed watchers said — an opinion arguably supported by the bond market. And while he again forswore offering “forward guidance,” some viewed him as hinting he’s ready to do more.
“Today’s action starts to show we’re serious about this,” he said. “We removed a dose of accommodation.” Note the words “starts” and “dose.” Both could convey there’s more to come.

“This is certainly not ‘a one and done,’” rate hike, said Stephanie Roth, chief economist at Wolfe Research, on Bloomberg TV. She said Warsh’s hawkish signals suggest “considerable more accommodation to be removed.”

On this week’s episode of Trumponomics, host Stephanie Flanders speaks with Bloomberg Opinion columnist John Authers and Jamie Rush of Bloomberg Economics to discuss how demographics, rising government debt and the artificial intelligence investment boom are reshaping the price of money. Listen on Apple, Spotify or wherever you get your podcasts.
Global gender parity remains more than a lifetime away for women — even though the gap with men is now smaller than ever, according to the World Economic Forum.

As we explain here, the organization’s annual report on the matter found current progress means it will still take 120 years to reach full equality. That’s a marked improvement, and up from 170 years measured a decade ago, but still means that no-one alive today is likely to experience it.

The WEF’s report combines indexes of political empowerment, economic participation and opportunity, health and survival and educational attainment to assess gender disparity across the world. The overall gap across 145 economies has narrowed to 69.4%, the best result recorded in two decades of such reports.

items.title: EU's Slow Regulation Is Finding Fans in AI Age
body: Welcome to Tech In Depth, our daily newsletter about the business of tech from Bloomberg’s journalists around the world. Today, Tanya Falenczyk looks at Silicon Valley’s search for some humorless technocrats who can oversee the development of AI.

SK Hynix’s next move: The South Korean memory chipmaker said it’s exploring options to boost global competitiveness after a report it may team up with Intel to make semiconductors in the US. SK Hynix indicated it hasn’t decided on an Intel deal specifically.
ByteDance billionaire: TikTok founder Zhang Yiming has become Asia’s richest person. He was already the wealthiest individual in China.
Salesforce’s outlook: The software company projected $63 billion in sales for fiscal year 2030. Investors have been worried about the future.

Headspace, a popular meditation and mental health support app, is being acquired by Sword Health, an AI startup focused on healthcare. The all-cash deal is valued near $300 million. Once the transaction closes, Sword plans to add more personalization features to the Headspace app.
EU regulation has long been the setup to a punchline. Like, how many faceless bureaucrats does it take to calculate the optimal curve for a banana?

Germany, where I’m from, is often regarded as a byword for bureaucracy. Regulations carry the stigma of stifling innovation and making it difficult for startups to take off — one of the European Union’s perennial problems, especially compared with the US.

Tech chief executive officers like SpaceX’s Elon Musk have underlined that narrative. “In the EU, for example, we find that the regulation level is extraordinarily high, and things are generally default illegal, and this inhibits progress with new technologies,” he said at the G20 Innovation Summit in early September.

When I arrived in San Francisco this summer, I expected this idea to be amplified. In the city where self-driving taxis roam the streets and you’d have a hard time meeting someone not working at an AI startup, surely innovation without constraints would be the prevailing ideal.

Instead, the talk now is all about regulation — at least a version of it that fits in with Silicon Valley’s foundational ideas. Even Musk backed Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei’s call to “slow the pace” of artificial intelligence development. With the biggest AI companies in recent days making louder calls for stricter laws, Europe could lead the way, or at least offer a starting point.

Silicon Valley’s long-standing philosophy has been to ask forgiveness, not permission. But recently, that has led to a wide array of problems, some very expensive for the companies, like Meta’s legal settlement running in the billions of dollars for the effects of social media on younger users. And the high-profile AI security breaches, which some have said are harbingers of intelligence that could potentially threaten humanity, also have AI employees and CEOs disturbed.

Politico EU described the current mood in Brussels as a “splash of Schadenfreude,” a German term for taking pleasure in someone’s misfortune. After a former Anthropic employee’s warning that AI models could kill us all by the end of the decade, European policymakers were quick to point out that the bloc already has legislation in place to prevent that: the EU AI Act.
Under the law that took effect in August, companies like OpenAI and Anthropic must take into account and counter what are called systemic risks. These include the risk of losing control of a model.

“If it gets bad or worse, we can definitely evaluate models. We can require risk mitigation measures, and in extreme cases and where necessary, we can also restrict, withdraw, or even recall AI models,” EU spokesman Thomas Regnier told AFP last week.
Now, US companies seem to be warming to the idea that a more cautious, regulated approach could lead to more predictable outcomes.
Joanna Bryson, professor of ethics and technology at Berlin’s Hertie School, advised the EU on its AI Act. She pushes back on the idea that regulation harms companies.

“The control problem becomes simpler when you externalize parts,” Bryson told me. “Of course, there can be bad external control, but it is much easier to keep safety processes intact when you don’t have to defend them internally.”

While advising a big tech company, Bryson was told how much time they spent monitoring other players in the sector, making sure they don’t misbehave. “I said: ‘This is what the government is for.’ Mature sectors have figured out how to have oversight done outside, because it is an insane amount of effort,” Bryson said. “It is a chance to throw the hard questions over the wall and let the government figure it out.”
About the US companies calling for regulations, Bryson tells Bloomberg: “There’s no reason for them to write something that’s very different from what the AI Act is.”

There’s another part of the EU legislation that seems to have left its mark on American AI companies. In his essay published last Saturday, Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei stated that the company committed to embed external evaluators such as METR – a nonprofit research organization based in California and the same organization aiding the EU in its oversight. Amodei calls on the government to require other frontier companies to do the same.
With its invisible watermark on all of Claude’s text and file output, Anthropic had already decided to comply with the EU AI Act’s transparency rules. The watermark was applied globally.
It’s too early to tell if the current mood of prioritizing safety and risk mitigation will last, but the EU’s standards could have even more ripple effects in the months ahead.

This week I attended the Dreamforce conference in San Francisco, where, in his opening keynote, Salesforce CEO Marc Benioff talked about spending the past two months in Europe. “I didn’t see a single autonomous vehicle. That was kind of a metaphor for me. I didn’t see the same kind of transformation.”

Later, he was joined onstage by OpenAI CEO Sam Altman. “When you look back at what’s happened with social media, what lessons should we take about this idea that companies should be held responsible for their actions?” Benioff asked.
Maybe he should have taken a closer look at Europe.
The day’s most read story in tech and entertainment:

After nine months as president, vice chairman and co-leader of Meta Compute, Dina Powell McCormick’s responsibilities extend far beyond helping to hash out AI infrastructure deals. Interviews with more than a dozen company insiders, outside executives and government officials and Powell McCormick herself show she’s an executive trusted by CEO Mark Zuckerberg and his top deputies to tackle the company’s thorniest problems.
