items.title: Health Insurance Denials Can Be Overturned When US Patients Appeal
body: Welcome back to Bloomberg’s Health Monitor, a weekly look at the boardroom decisions, scientific advances and policy fights shaping the future of medicine. Sign up now if you’re not already on the list.

Health officials nominated for top roles in the US are breaking from Robert F. Kennedy Jr. on vaccines. Two new measles deaths in Pennsylvania pushed the number of fatalities in the country to the highest in decades.Novo says it needs to broaden its scope to stay competitive. And the process of crafting trendy American countertops is killing workers.
— Kelly Gilblom and John Tozzi

Few things in American healthcare are more contested than prior authorization. That’s the practice insurers use to determine ahead of time whether they’ll pay for a test or treatment ordered by a doctor. The paperwork hurdle can stand between patients and a medication, a scan, even an organ transplant, as one patient I spoke to experienced. It sometimes delays care or puts it out of reach entirely.

Insurers defend the practice. US healthcare spending is swollen with waste, overtreatment and fraud, they argue. Doctors and hospitals get paid more when they do more. Some order extra tests or perform surgeries even when medical guidelines indicate less costly, more conservative approaches should come first. Insurers use prior approval to steward limited healthcare dollars wisely, the industry argues, and make sure people get care aligned with the evidence.

We’ve been having this debate for decades, largely in a void of data. That changed earlier this year, though. New rules made health insurance companies reveal some details on how they use prior authorization. They had to report how often they denied requests, and how often those denials were overturned, among other metrics, for plans offered in Medicare, Medicaid and Obamacare markets. Some companies also reported the raw number of requests they required.

In a Bloomberg News analysis, Tanaz Meghjani, Ike Swetlitz and I found that big insurance companies, on average, denied more than 10% of standard prior authorization requests, according to data from five large publicly traded insurance companies that together insure more than 160 million people. While most people don’t appeal, patients that did won about half the time, according to available data. Some plans overturned their own denials nine out of 10 times on appeal — an indication that the process likely delayed care later deemed appropriate.

The core question is whether prior authorizations help avoid inappropriate care, or if they stand in the way of needed treatments. The data can’t fully answer that, but it starts to paint a picture of how the practice is used and sometimes overused. Miranda Yaver, a University of Pittsburgh health policy expert, said the savings to the system may be illusory.
“If a patient winds up in the ER or the hospital because they can’t get their important medication, then are we really having the cost savings that we’re promised?” she said. — John Tozzi
The following was produced with the assistance of Bloomberg Automation.

Nicole Saphier, President Donald Trump’s surgeon general nominee, told the Senate health committee Wednesday that she’s seen no reputable evidence linking childhood vaccinations to autism, while also affirming that the combined measles vaccine is the most effective tool available against ongoing outbreaks. The CDC reported 160 new measles cases in the past week, bringing this year’s total to 3,294, and Pennsylvania has recorded four measles-related deaths.

Novo Nordisk CEO Mike Doustdar told employees the company must broaden its scope to regain competitiveness in the obesity and diabetes market. Doustdar has been restructuring the Danish drugmaker — shedding jobs, recalling workers to the office and scrapping projects — after Novo lost its market leadership to US rival Eli Lilly. And he announced that Novo would drop “Nordisk” from day-to-day use to boost name recognition, distancing the company from its origins as Nordisk Insulinlaboratorium, founded in 1923.

Eli Lilly is using profits from its blockbuster weight-loss and diabetes drugs to fund an ambitious expansion into women’s health, targeting historically underfunded conditions like endometriosis, osteoporosis and pregnancy-related disorders. The drugmaker has recruited reproductive medicine expert Kelle Moley to lead the effort and made a $40 million investment in Absci, which is developing an endometriosis treatment.

The Trump administration pledged to send $500 checks to nearly 1 million Americans it claims were overcharged for Affordable Care Act insurance, with payments expected in October, just ahead of the midterm elections. The announcement follows Republicans allowing enhanced Covid-era premium subsidies to lapse, which triggered a government shutdown, caused 2.6 million people to lose coverage in 2026, and pushed typical monthly costs up 58% to $178, according to KFF data.

The FDA said it’s open to novel approaches for evaluating psychedelic compounds as treatments for mental illness, including changes in how they are studied, administered and monitored long-term, according to an article in the New England Journal of Medicine. The agency acknowledged the difficulties of placebo-controlled trials given the recognizable psychoactive effects of the drugs, and said it may grant initial approval based on promising results over as little as 12 weeks.

CMS Administrator Mehmet Oz told Bloomberg Television that “there are more deals in the works” for US drug pricing deals with pharmaceutical companies beyond the two dozen voluntary agreements already announced. Companies have generally agreed to lower prices for public programs and launch new drugs at prices similar to those paid by other developed nations in exchange for tariff relief.

The US HHS will launch a new autism research initiative called SPECTRA , which will use AI and other technology to map how the condition develops and identify opportunities for early intervention. Operating under the Advanced Research Projects Agency for Health, the program will analyze genetic, biological, environmental, and social factors contributing to autism, and may incorporate wearable devices and at-home monitoring to predict crises and enable earlier treatment.

items.title: Ossoff's Viral Clips Are Only Half the Story
body: Georgia Senator Jon Ossoff’s viral videos have so mastered the attention economy that the East Coast media is swooning with speculation that he could be a presidential contender in 2028. He has vigorously probed Trump administration officials during committee hearings. He coined the term “the Epstein class.” And he drew weeks of scrutiny to President Donald Trump’s close associate Natalie Harp with his derogatory quip about the president’s “travel with Natalie.”

But voters this year are demanding more than well-scripted speeches and viral videos. They want results. People of both parties are frustrated with a do-nothing Congress and a president ignoring his campaign promises on the cost of living.

Ossoff is the only Democratic senator defending a seat in a state Trump won in 2024, yet he is leading in polls and dominating in fundraising. He has repeatedly denied having any interest in 2028 and says he’s focused on winning the midterm elections and Democrats “taking back control of our own future.” But does Ossoff have what it takes to go beyond virality and solve voters’ concerns?

Over the weekend, I went to Athens, Georgia, in the home district of Ossoff’s Republican rival, Congressman Mike Collins. While most of the people I spoke with were aware of Ossoff’s social media buzz, they consistently brought up something I didn’t expect: He’s good at the offscreen parts of his job. Several mentioned Ossoff’s work providing disaster assistance, helping farmers and advocating for rural hospitals.

Ossoff’s constituent services have also been getting a surprising amount of bipartisan acclaim. In the Republican primary to unseat Ossoff, candidate Derek Dooley acknowledged that while he often didn’t agree with the Democrat, “he’s got really good constituent services.” GOP strategist Brian Robinson commended Ossoff’s staff for helping Georgians who have an issue with the federal government as “second to none.” And Ossoff’s work for local communities has drawn endorsements from the Republican mayors of Valdosta, Toccoa and Tifton.

In decades of covering politics, I’ve rarely seen something as bland as constituent services register so consistently with voters. Politicians today are conditioned to focus more on attention-grabbing headlines — which Ossoff has demonstrated he also knows how to do — than developing the skills to do the job.

The historic Georgia Theater in downtown Athens was packed to capacity on Sunday as Ossoff delivered what has become his trademark: a quotable speech loaded with succinct barbs that link the corruption he alleges is emanating from both Collins and Trump to the failure of Republicans to address voters’ kitchen-table concerns.

“While the world burns and you pay more for everything, your tax dollars become the ‘royal family’s’ wealth,” Ossoff said. He blasted Trump and his family for being “compromised” by investments from foreign leaders and AI companies and called for aggressive AI safeguards.
Supporters commended Ossoff’s oratory skills. Partisans lauded his tight taunts. But Judith Gantly was among several who also mentioned Ossoff’s community outreach.
“He is a decent human and has accomplished so much already,” said Gantly, 82, who had waited at the front of the line to attend her first-ever political rally.

Ossoff, 39, is the youngest member of the US Senate. He’s also the chamber’s only former documentary film producer, and he brings his millennial instincts and investigative journalism skills to how he does the job.

Ossoff has drawn statewide attention for his bipartisan investigations into military housing conditions, abuse and corruption in federal prisons, and dangerous treatment of foster children in the state’s care. And his team has so mastered the art of getting social media content from his public events that the political research site GroundTruth AI found that Ossoff commands 87% of all online views between him and Collins, and 85% are positive.

Matt Crane, a senior at the University of Georgia and member of the Young Democrats Club, was among the young people holding signs behind Ossoff onstage on Sunday. He said his family has worked with foster care organizations in the state and credited Ossoff with bringing attention to the issue. “It is truly as bad as the investigation showed,” he told me.

At an outdoor table at the Big City Bread Co. in downtown Athens, five retirees gathered after a game of pickleball on Monday and bemoaned their feeling of helplessness in the face of current events. The four Democrats and one Republican told me they had voted for candidates of the opposing party in the past like Republican Governor Brian Kemp, but are consistently disappointed by the lack of accountability from elected officials.

“The election is ultimately about character and values,” said Les Shindelman, 80, a retired management consultant and Ossoff supporter. “I think many of us are frustrated about the lack of leadership and competency we see on both sides of the aisle.”

To succeed in a battleground state like Georgia, both Ossoff and Collins will have to win crossover voters like these retirees. Ossoff’s feat is not that he has been able to break through to a national audience, it’s that he’s been able to do it while putting a premium on getting results for his state. If he wins having shown both governing competence and media mastery, he will have found the formula that Washington needs.

items.title: US Is Squandering its Global Leverage With Ukraine and Iran
body: President Donald Trump sees the art of geopolitics as a matter of money and leverage. As a result, he’s relied on fellow businesspeople to do the work of diplomats in Gaza, Ukraine and the Persian Gulf — and they have failed. As Ayatollah Ruhollah Khomeini once put it, the revolution that founded the Islamic Republic of Iran “was not about the price of watermelons.”

This misapprehension need not be decisive. Cash is still a very powerful tool (you cannot fight a war for long without it), and with a deep well of soft power, the world’s largest economy and its most powerful military, the US has long enjoyed a unique power to persuade other countries to fall in line. Yet Trump’s inability to control the wars in Ukraine and Iran points to a growing issue: America’s leverage is weakening and he is accelerating its erosion.

This may seem counterintuitive, given that Trump applies pressure more openly and brutally than perhaps any of his predecessors, whom he portrays as weak. Just look at his tariff regime and the way he has preyed on the economic and security dependence of allies to get them to pay. Or his use of US dollar dominance to pressure countries through sanctions, a policy that came into wide use under former President Barack Obama and is gradually prompting governments around the world to try to reduce their dependence on the currency.

But in geopolitics, leverage works best when you don’t actually use it, because once deployed, it can be lost and become, at best, a form of punishment. Trump’s spiraling trade war with Canada is a prime example. His February decision to attack Iran was another. The threat of US air power was the leverage that had long kept Iran from closing the Strait of Hormuz, or indeed from openly pursuing a nuclear weapon. As soon as Trump ordered the attack Iran was trying to deter, Tehran no longer had a reason to hold back.

This cocktail of squandered advantage and overreliance on commercial incentives is speeding a decline in US global dominance that arguably started with the excesses that followed 9/11. It’s been on display again this week, as​​​ Trump suddenly revived the claim that under his predecessor, Joe Biden, the US gave Ukraine $300 billion for its war with Russia and added that he planned to demand that money back, if not from Kyiv, then from Europe.

This won’t happen, not least because the number is fictitious. So was Trump’s Monday announcement that Kyiv and Moscow had agreed to a truce on air strikes on each other’s energy infrastructure. That supposed deal appears to have been news to both parties; their exchanges of drone and missile strikes continue. Nevertheless, it’s important to recognize why the president has chosen this moment to cook up these false narratives.

The short answer is, of course, the midterms. Trump’s war in Iran is unpopular at home and he’s looking for ways to distance himself from its ill effects. That is why he posted Monday on Truth Social that he’d asked Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy to stop hitting Russian oil refineries, going on to argue that it was Kyiv’s bombing campaign, not the Iranian conflict, that just drove the US pump price for diesel above $6 for the first time.

Like his $300 billion figure for Ukrainian aid, this half-truth was intended to pass the buck. Trump’s message is that, if US debt is out of control, if inflation is eroding living standards and if American arsenals are depleted, then, as the Brits like to say: “It wasn’t me, Guv.”

Perhaps this will be enough to persuade US swing voters in November, but it’s unlikely to work on Trump’s geopolitical targets. By halting all new American aid to Ukraine and providing only weapons that Kyiv’s other allies must buy, he has gradually lost his influence over Zelenskyy’s decisions. It’s just harder to get Ukraine to halt one its most important war-fighting strategies — the destruction of Russian oil output — when Trump has drastically scaled back US relevance to Kyiv’s war effort.

Plus, his numbers are unconvincing. The total of all US military, financial and humanitarian aid to Ukraine in the four-plus years of Russia’s invasion to June was not $300 billion, but $131.5 billion, according to the Ukraine Support Tracker run by Germany’s Kiel Institute, which keeps the most complete account. Meanwhile, according to the Congressional Budget Office, the US spent $42.3 billion on the Iran war during its first four months. That is a much smaller number, but it represents a spending rate more than four times as high as for Ukraine and already did   more damage to US munition stocks and readiness.

Trump’s demand for his imaginary $300 billion back is an attempt to recreate the bargaining power that he lost after turning the provision of US arms to Ukraine into a commercial enterprise. His zigzagging threats and claims toward Iran are best seen in a similar light — attempts to fill a growing void in leverage.

To end the war in Iran, the US needs to find partners that can supply the influence it now lacks. As for Ukraine, Washington remains an important partner and vendor of critical weapons and, while that alone may no longer be enough to force Zelenskyy’s hand, Trump does have a transactional power he can use.

Ukraine desperately needs Patriot interceptors to take down the ballistic missiles that Russia is now producing at a rate that should worry not just Ukraine, but also Europe and the US. Despite reduced American stocks, if Trump can deliver enough of the weapons to make even a small difference for Kyiv this winter, that will create an example for other allies to follow. He could also re-up an offer he once made to let Ukrainians build their own Patriots under license. Package those incentives and the US might actually have the leverage it needs to motivate Zelenskyy to end those refinery attacks.More from Bloomberg Opinion:

items.title: Bank of England Holds Rates, Warning of Hike If War Goes On
body: The Bank of England held interest rates at 3.75% while warning that a hike may be needed if inflation pressures intensify as a result of conflict in the Middle East.
Six of nine policymakers chose to leave the level unchanged, including Governor Andrew Bailey, as the committee split along the same lines as in their last meeting in July.

In prepared remarks, Bailey said the global energy shock has so far had a limited effect on prices and wages in the UK. “But the longer this volatility persists, the bigger the impact it will have on inflation, and the more likely it is we will need to raise Bank rate,” the governor added.

The decision followed a steep increase in expectations of tightening from the BOE, with markets at one stage this week pricing in as many as five quarter-point hikes. Traders trimmed those wagers after the announcement was deemed less hawkish than many had foreseen.
The BOE said inflationary risks are more “tilted to the upside,” than in July, but otherwise kept its guidance the same as in that earlier meeting.

It published the rates decision at the same time that it said it would unwind its £488 billion ($653 billion) debt portfolio by September 2034, while abandoning plans to sell long-dated gilts as part of that run-off.

UK bonds rallied on the back of the announcement, led by longer-dated tenors, which lowered the 30-year yield 12 basis points — the most since May — to 5.74%. The pound held steady against the dollar to trade at 1.3389.
Read More: BOE Scraps Long-End Gilt Sales, Helping Ease Pressure on Yields

Price pressures are expected to build in the coming months, the BOE’s minutes said, citing the potential for higher food inflation in the event of an unusually severe El Niño, as well as surging demand for AI-related products such as microchips.

Domestic pressures in the UK have, to date, been surprisingly muted but the BOE warned that indirect effects may be “delayed rather than diminished.” The BOE now expects inflation at double its 2% target early next year, and has lifted its growth forecast for the third quarter to 0.4% following recent GDP data that smashed expectations.

Still, escalating conflict between the US and Iran has made the Monetary Policy Committee’s decision more fraught. Oil and gas prices have surged, lifting fuel costs and storing up problems for UK households when the government’s energy price cap resets in the new year. The BOE said the adverse scenario of events it laid out in July had turned out to be “a reasonable proxy” for the state of the world.
“Most members placed more weight on energy prices staying higher for longer in the absence of a lasting de-escalation,” the minutes said.

The BOE’s decision to hold followed tightening from other central banks. The US Federal Reserve raised rates on Wednesday and the European Central Bank last week increased them by a quarter point for a second time this year.

Catherine Mann, Megan Greene and Huw Pill were the three MPC members voting for a hike, arguing that it’s better to manage the upside inflationary dangers with a “proactive increase” now, rather than risk falling behind the curve. The three hawks pointed out that a projected jump in prices will land early next year, just at the point when millions of workers agree pay settlements.

Out of the six officials voting for a hold, Swati Dhingra and Alan Taylor remained the most dovish. They emphasized slack in the jobs market and tight financial conditions, with Taylor writing in his personal comments that the curve is higher than it was in the 2022-23 cycle when inflation was close to 7%.

“Domestically generated inflation is contained, wage growth is decelerating and unemployment near 5% points to meaningful slack in the labor market. This is not an economy crying out for higher rates,” said David Rees, head of global economics at Schroders, adding: “The bigger risk lies with fiscal policy.”

items.title: Bank of England Eases Bond-Market Pain With Gilt Sales Overhaul
body: The Bank of England gave Britain’s bond market some much needed relief with a dramatic overhaul of its plan for selling off excess gilts that piled up on its balance sheet in the previous decade.

UK government borrowing costs fell on Thursday in response to the shake-up of the British central bank’s quantitative tightening program. Under the new schedule, the BOE will pause all bond sales from its £488 billion ($650 billion) portfolio until April and stop selling long-dated bonds altogether.

The measures are expected to reduce the supply of gilts in the coming months, offering support to the gilt market at a time when bonds are selling off across the globe due to inflation and fiscal concerns. They were announced by Governor Andrew Bailey in London alongside the BOE’s decision to hold interest rates at 3.75% for the sixth straight meeting.

The yield on 30-year bonds, which had in recent days touched the highest level since 1998, fell more than 10 basis points after the midday announcement, the biggest drop in four months. Two-year yields, more sensitive to monetary policy, also dipped.

The decline in bond yields may take some of the pressure off Prime Minister Andy Burnham as he faces questions about the sustainability of his fiscal agenda. Burnham’s chancellor of the exchequer, John Healey, is due to lay out his first budget on Oct. 28 amid a worsening outlook on inflation.

“We’ve made a major announcement today because we’ve set out the path to the endpoint,” Bailey told broadcasters after the decision. “We’ve been planning and working on this for a long time. I can assure you, this work did not start when we had a change of government back in the early summer.”

Under the plan, the QT portfolio would now be unwound by September 2034. The central bank also intends to unload gilts maturing between 2035 and 2049 to the Debt Management Office rather than directly to the market. It will pause all QT sales until April 2027 as terms of these transfers are thrashed out.
“This is definitely a positive surprise,” said Daniel Loughney head of fixed income at Mediolanum International Funds. “The BOE, DMO and Treasury working closer on soft yield-curve control.”
Read more: Bank of England Holds Rates Warning of Hike If War Continues

The global bond selloff of the past weeks took government borrowing costs to levels last seen almost two decades ago. It also prompted US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent to supersize his department’s debt buyback program, in a bid to cool down yields.

But the controversy sounding the BOE’s QT program predates the current market squeeze. Investors have long criticized the central bank for the impact its asset sales have on yields, which the British central bank acknowledges have lifted the cost of benchmark 10-year government debt by 20-30 basis points.

Meanwhile, politicians have blamed the program for punishing households as the £110 billion of QT losses since 2022 have had to be funded by taxpayers under a state indemnity. The Liberal Democrats, Reform UK and the Green Party have all demanded that the losses are recovered, potentially by a windfall levy on the banks that are the ultimate beneficiaries or through other changes to the program.

“The Bank of England today appeared to recognize that their QT program was imposing an unnecessary burden on gilts with the pausing of all QT auctions until next spring,” said Anthony Willis, senior economist at Columbia Threadneedle.

Under proposals that have yet to be finalized, the bank will keep £120 billion of gilts that mature in 2049 or later and use them as the matching asset against future banknote issuance. Another £222 billion of gilts that mature by 2035 will be run off.

The remaining £146 billion maturing between 2035 and 2049 will be sold at a pace of £20 billion a year, potentially directly to the government through the DMO. The arrangements may slightly erode the chancellor’s cushion under his main fiscal rule. The Treasury believes the changes have little implication for the Oct. 28 budget, a person familiar with the situation said.
In a letter to Healey, Bailey said the arrangement “preserves the independence of monetary policy” and would “maximize value for money by minimizing cost and risk over the lifetime” of the program.

The Treasury will work out whether to press ahead with the BOE’s plans to sell assets to the DMO. If it does, the DMO could then retire those gilts and replace them with ones with a duration that better meets market demand.

Michael Saunders, a former BOE ratesetter and adviser to Oxford Economics, said the plan to sell the bank’s bonds to the DMO rather than directly to the market should lead to longer-lasting reductions in government borrowing costs.
“This replaces BOE sales of less liquid non-benchmark gilts with DMO sales of benchmarks, which are more liquid and hence likely to trade at lower yields,” he said.

Bailey said he had been discussing the move since Rachel Reeves was chancellor, and a final decision will be made by the Treasury. The BOE also said the £120 billion of long-dated gilts to be retained would be used to back cash in circulation, which sits as a liability with the bank.

Under the new proposals, the portfolio would be run off at an average pace of £46 billion a year — £20 billion of which will be active sales. That’s slower than the Office for Budget Responsibility’s latest estimate for £32 billion of active sales a year.

QT has accrued £110 billion of losses since 2022, but made £124 billion of profit previously, all of which was spent by previous chancellors. BOE documents show that another £100 billion of losses had been expected.

“These changes should be seen as gilt positive, in particular for long end maturities,” said Matthew Amis, investment director of rates management at Aberdeen Investments. “The coordination of the sales in one place at the DMO should be also applauded.”

items.title: Red Sea shipping return
body: Just over a quarter of container ship capacity deployed in both directions between Europe and Asia is transiting the Suez Canal, according to a new analysis, nearly three years since attacks on ships in the Red Sea diverted vessels the long way around Africa.

That’s edged up from 17% on Aug. 3, as carriers slowly return to the shortcut sitting in the middle of three continents. But as the conflict heats up between Houthis and the Saudis, some cargo owners aren’t convinced the more efficient route is worth the risk.

On Monday, Maersk and Hapag-Lloyd announced plans to shift four service lines through the Red Sea instead of sailing around the Cape of Good Hope, joining two other Gemini alliance services already routed through the Egyptian canal.

The companies said they “will continue to monitor the security situation in the Middle East region very closely, and any alteration to services within the Gemini Cooperation will remain dependent on the ongoing stability in the Red Sea area and the absence of any escalation in conflicts in the region.”Top carrier MSC partially restored Suez Canal transits on several routes last month, including Asia-Mediterranean, Asia-North Europe and India-Mediterranean. It announced another step this week involving a westbound service to the US East Coast.
Back to Asia

Alan Murphy, chief executive of maritime data company Sea-Intelligence, indicated in a report this week that the share of eastbound traffic through Suez between Europe and Asia has picked up since early August. The westbound capacity — called the head-haul because it’s usually more profitable — service has remained stable.

“This back-haul focus implies that shipping lines are prioritizing repositioning vessel capacity back to Asia to address operational gaps from the recent port congestion and delays in Asian hubs,” Murphy wrote in the report. “By focusing on vessels from the Mediterranean, they are targeting the vessels with the shortest return time to Asia.”

Iran-backed Houthi militants opened a second front in the Iran war in July by threatening ships calling at Saudi ports. But beyond a few attacks on the kingdom that month, they largely avoided hostilities until around 10 days ago, when they ramped up strikes on energy sites and western towns.

Houthis have also captured more territory in Yemen, tightening their control over Bab el-Mandeb, another strait vital for shipping and energy markets. According to an industry executive, the Houthis have nothing against shipping lines, at least for the time being. Communicating with the Houthis is a challenge and there are no guarantees, the executive said, but so far there have not been problems crossing the Suez for container lines.
Read More: Houthi Strikes, Pipe Closure Mark Crisis for MBS and Saudis
Meanwhile, the head of the Global Shippers Forum said the return to Suez “seems a reckless gamble.”

The UK-based group, which represents cargo owners, warned that while Red Sea navigation may be presently safe for vessels other than Saudi ships, it’s unclear whether the Houthis will continue to hold off on attacking container vessels.

That prospect is a concern because it’s currently peak demand season for seaborne trade, with a lot of time-sensitive merchandise in transit. Shippers welcome the reduced sailing times but worry about the safety of seafarers, the consequences of re-diversion and potential for damage to freight, said James Hookham, director of the forum.

“If shipping lines have been assured of safe transit, they could be a bit more forthcoming with their customers,” he said in an email to Bloomberg. “Otherwise it does feel they are crossing the road against the red light.”
—Laura Curtis in Los Angeles

items.title: ARS/USD: Milei's Strong Peso Holds Back Argentina's Economic Growth
body: Lea en español
President Javier Milei’s efforts to tame inflation with a strong currency are taking a growing toll on Argentina’s economy.

The peso has weakened just 3.7% against the dollar while consumer prices have risen 21.3% so far this year through August. That real appreciation has increasingly been sustained in recent weeks by official intervention in bond and futures markets, while currency controls on companies remain in place.

Statistics agency Indec will publish second quarter gross domestic product figures Thursday afternoon and analysts forecast that the economy contracted 0.9% from the previous quarter. For many, Milei’s currency is one of the key factors hindering Argentina’s growth.

“By now, it has been well established that Argentina’s non-primary economic activity is performing poorly, posing risks to policy continuity,” Barclays analyst Ivan Stambulsky said in a report to investors last week. “In our view, the main explanation is simply that the real effective exchange rate is too strong for the current policy mix.”
The libertarian leader has cooled price hikes for much of his presidency in part by keeping a tight grip on the peso, making it appreciate when adjusted for inflation.

In the first half of the year, dollars flowed in from the soybean harvest amid heavy overseas debt issuance by Argentine companies, providing ample foreign currency and helping the central bank rebuild reserves without putting much pressure on the peso.

That backdrop began to change in the second half of the year. Dollar inflows from agricultural exports slowed after the harvest peaked, while proceeds from corporate borrowing also eased. As dollars dried up, the central bank has increasingly turned to selling FX-linked securities and futures contracts to meet hedging demand and ease pressure on the peso while still trying to build reserves.

As a result, the stock of hedges tied to the exchange rate more than doubled in just five months, according to estimates from local brokerage Facimex. Altogether, private-sector holdings of futures contracts, dual bonds and securities known locally as dollar-linked rose to around $12 billion by the end of August from $5.2 billion at the end of March.

“There is a strong degree of BCRA intervention,” Stambulsky said, referring to the central bank by its Spanish initials. As the market began unwinding carry trades after the peak harvest, the monetary authority “stepped up intervention by selling hedges, it reduced the pace of spot purchases, and it allowed rates to rise.”

August, September and October are usually months when the central bank sells dollars directly in the spot market. But this year the government changed its strategy by selling dollar-linked instruments outside of it.

The strategy has helped keep the exchange rate near 1,500 pesos per dollar, much stronger than economists had envisioned. A year ago, analysts surveyed by the central bank expected the peso to weaken to 1,811 per dollar by December 2026. By last month, they had revised that forecast to 1,629.
In an economy already burdened by high taxes and elevated costs, an appreciated peso makes domestic producers less competitive while making imports cheaper, squeezing local industry.
That dynamic is weighing on an economy already losing momentum. Economists have cut their full-year 2026 growth forecast to 2.1% from 3.5% several months ago.

Milei’s policies have slowed monthly inflation sharply, from 25.5% in his first month in office to 1.7% in August. But progress has become more difficult since the Iran war broke out. Inflation, which Milei had expected to fall below 1% by now, has remained stubbornly closer to 2%.

“What the government wants, and fast, is for inflation to slow down,” said Osvaldo Giordano, president of Ieral, an economic think tank at Fundación Mediterránea. The strong peso reflects both the government’s determination to achieve that goal and the market’s expectation that it has the tools to keep doing so, he said.

The same policies supporting the currency are putting pressure elsewhere. Higher interest rates are weighing on credit, which had become an important engine of the recovery after years of high inflation largely shut households and businesses out of financing. Yet since midterm elections last October, household defaults have broken records month after month.

The strain is particularly visible in manufacturing, retail and construction — labor-intensive sectors that employ large numbers of Argentines and have lagged the expansion in areas such as energy, mining and agriculture. Construction shrank 4.5% from a year earlier in August, while manufacturing contracted 4.9%.
That poses a growing political dilemma for Milei as he prepares to seek reelection next year.

“Perhaps it would be less risky to worry less about how quickly inflation comes down and instead provide some relief to urban sectors like industry, commerce and construction,” Giordano said. “Those are the sectors most Argentines live off of, and they’re also where the data show the greatest destruction of economic activity and jobs.”
“Shock Therapy” is a weekly analysis column focused on finance and markets in Argentina.

items.title: US Stocks Bounce Back From Fed Decision Slump as Oil Falls
body: US stocks rose at the open following the Federal Reserve’s first interest-rate increase since 2023 as oil prices fell for a second day in a row and Treasury yields edged lower.

The S&P 500 Index advanced 0.9% and the Nasdaq 100 climbed 1.4% as of 9:49 a.m. in New York. The gains come after the underlying gauges sold off on Wednesday in the wake of hawkish commentary from Federal Reserve Chairman Kevin Warsh and the latest dot plot, which showed 16 of 18 Fed officials had penciled in another rate hike this year.

Despite the gains this morning, “investors should be very wary about seeing this as an ‘all clear’ sign for the stock market,” Matt Maley, chief market strategist at Miller Tabak & Co., wrote in a note. “There is a difference between having investors ‘expect’ a negative development and having them already ‘price’ it into the market.”
Brent crude prices fell 2.6% to $103 a barrel. Treasury yields fell across the curve, with the 10-year yield down to 4.94% after climbing as high as 5.02% on Wednesday following the Fed decision.
Tech stocks were broadly higher, with the iShares Semiconductor ETF up 3.1%. Marvell Technology Inc., Intel Corp. and Advanced Micro Devices Inc. all gained at least 3%.

The tech-heavy Nasdaq 100 has fallen for five of the last seven session and is down about 4% from its early June peak. Still, the gauge is up roughly 16% in 2026 and on pace for a fourth consecutive double-digit year of gains.
Ed Yardeni, who cut his year-end target on the S&P 500 to 7,900 from 8,400 this week, said his main concern is oil prices staying higher for longer amid the war in Iran.
That increases “the odds that some of the inflationary pressures from energy will spill over to core prices,” Yardeni said on Bloomberg Television.

The likelihood of another US rate increase this year as well as the state of the bond market is also making Yardeni more cautious. “My friends the bond vigilantes have kind of gone wild around the world,” he said.

And while stocks often fall in September — historically the worst month on the calendar for equities — Citadel Securities’ Scott Rubner is growing “increasingly constructive on what comes next” as the markets head into the final quarter of the year.

“That does not mean we think the September weakness is finished,” the firm’s head of equity and derivatives strategy wrote to clients. “We continue to think equities can trade lower over the next two weeks. But the setup is beginning to change.”

items.title: Blackstone Said to Prepare Sale of Clarion Events' Asian Unit
body: Blackstone Inc. is preparing a disposal of Clarion Events’ Asian business, as part of its broader plan to revive the sale of the UK events organizer, people with knowledge of the matter said.
The buyout firm is working with Goldman Sachs Group Inc. on the potential divestment, the people said, asking not to be identified because the information is private.
A transaction could be valued at around $600 million to $700 million, according to people, who asked not to be identified as the information isn’t public.

Blackstone has started reaching out to potential suitors, including industry players and private equity firms, the people said. The firm aims to separately find buyers for the rest of Clarion’s business in Europe and the US after the sale of the Asian arm, they said.
Deliberations are ongoing, and there’s no certainty they will lead to a transaction, the people said. Representatives for Blackstone and Goldman Sachs declined to comment.

Blackstone had last year explored a potential sale of Clarion, which could be valued at about £2 billion ($2.7 billion) including debt, Bloomberg News reported at the time. The process was eventually called off as most prospective suitors only expressed interest in certain markets, instead of the whole business, the people said.

Clarion Events, founded in 1947, runs international trade shows and exhibitions across sectors like consumer electronics, defense and security as well as gaming and technology. Blackstone bought it in 2017 from Providence Equity Partners for an undisclosed sum.
In 2018, it merged with Hong Kong-based Global Sources, which runs exhibitions and an online business-to-business marketplace.

items.title: China's BYD Targets Four European Plants to Anchor Regional Push
body: BYD Co. plans to establish four plants in Europe over the long term as the Chinese carmaker seeks to comply with emerging local-manufacturing rules and win over more customers.

The manufacturer is targeting three vehicle assembly factories as well as one electric-vehicle battery plant in the region, Alfredo Altavilla, a former Fiat Chrysler manager who advises BYD in Europe, told reporters at an event in Turin late on Wednesday.
“This is not for tomorrow morning, but it’s clear that to reach the volume objectives we have and at the same time become compliant with EU rules, this is what we’ll need,” Altavilla said.

BYD has been holding talks with European competitors and governments as it explores taking over underutilized factories in countries including France, Spain and Italy. The European Union has introduced tariffs on Chinese-made EVs and the bloc’s proposed “Made in Europe” rules are expected to increase pressure on BYD to bolster capacity in the region.

Battling a price war in China, BYD has been aggressively expanding abroad, with sales soaring in Europe. The automaker is benefiting from renewed interest in EVs since fuel prices spiked in the wake of the Middle East conflict.
Read More: Chinese Carmakers Grow Market Share in Europe With Hybrid Surge

The Chinese company’s pivot toward Europe has also produced hiccups. A new factory in Hungary has come under scrutiny over alleged labor abuses by subcontractors. BYD has said it always strictly complied with local requirements.
While Italy is among the contenders for new locations, it’s less likely to be chosen as BYD’s second European plant, Altavilla told reporters on Wednesday.
“Italy remains a plan B,” he said. “What I am interested in is the best conditions for competitiveness. I would like to find them in Italy but I haven’t.”
Separately, BYD has been looking to snap up struggling legacy brands in the region, Executive Vice President Stella Li, who has led the international expansion, told Bloomberg earlier this year.
Read More: BYD Talks to Stellantis, Others About Taking Europe Plants
In the first half, BYD’s overseas revenue exceeded what it made at home for the first time.
The group is rolling out its Denza line in Europe to break into the region’s contested luxury-car market.
Altavilla was in Turin for the inauguration of a Denza showroom. Another Denza showroom was inaugurated in Paris on Wednesday.

items.title: ECB's Rehn Sees No Second-Round Price Effects From War Shock
body: The energy-price shock from the conflict in the Middle East hasn’t fed through to other parts of the economy up until now, according to European Central Bank Governing Council member Olli Rehn.

“For the euro area inflation, the driver is obviously energy prices, while wage growth is moderate and second-round effects of any kind of price-wage spiral have been absent — or absent so far,” the Finnish central-bank chief said Thursday at an OMFIF event in London.

At the same time, Rehn said that the shock “is not over yet” and “upward risks may be creeping in,” adding in his presentation that “monetary policy will act with a steady hand and ensure price stability, thus supporting sustainable growth and job creation.”

With inflation locked well above the 2% goal and the region’s economy proving surprisingly resilient to the Iran war, the ECB last week raised borrowing costs for a second time since the fighting in the Middle East began. Officials expect them to rise further, people familiar with their thinking told Bloomberg last week, but this will depend on incoming data.

Earlier on Thursday, Rehn’s Irish counterpart Gabriel Makhlouf in an interview with Bloomberg Television declined to rule out another hike already next month if circumstances require it, saying that every gathering is a “live meeting,” and officials will take each decision as it comes.

ECB projections presented last week showed faster inflation in 2027 and 2028, with the latter now slightly above target. Forecasts for economic growth were also lifted. Markets now expect at least three more quarter-point increases over the next 12 months.

Rehn said that last week’s rate increase was warranted given above-target price growth and risks to the outlook, even if he also said that the inflationary effects from the energy shock has been less severe than feared so far.

He also stressed that there’s been some tightening of financial conditions recently “and that is certainly one very important parameter.” A global bond selloff has also pushed euro-zone yields significantly up.

The former EU commissioner said the ECB is “certainly concerned about member state governments engaging in broadly subsidizing consumers.” The central bank already last week urged that fiscal responses should be “temporary, targeted and tailored.”

“I understand the pain many are feeling because of higher energy prices, higher oil and gas prices,” he said. “But at the same time we see that this say possible increase of fiscal subsidies would again slow down green transition or clean transition.”

Asked about important elections next year and potential risks for the ECB, Rehn said the Frankfurt-based institution has a “viable existing toolbox of instruments” to ensure the smooth transition of monetary policy, ranging from the transmission protection instrument — known as TPI — to OMT.
“But I don’t see for the moment need for use of these instruments,” Rehn said.

items.title: Billions Pour Into AI as Manus Rebounds and Huawei Speeds Chips
body: Manus was supposed to have been swallowed by Meta. Then Beijing intervened. China forced the unwinding of the $2 billion acquisition, leaving the Chinese-founded AI startup to start over as an independent company. A few months later, that reset is looking rather lucrative: Manus is raising about $500 million at a $4 billion valuation, sources said, twice what Meta had agreed to pay. For a company that became a test case for how messy the US-China fight over technology can get, it’s quite the comeback.

The AI boom is creating some unusual borrowing needs, too. GMI Cloud wants $300 million not for a data center, but for what goes inside it, sources said. The Nvidia partner is talking to banks and private-credit funds about a loan to buy chips for a facility in Thailand, with Tencent set to use the computing power. Until recently, lenders piled into financing the giant buildings needed for AI. Now the chips themselves, expensive enough to require hundreds of millions of dollars in debt, are becoming an asset class for lenders.

And while money pours into getting hold of more computing power, Huawei is racing to make China less reliant on the American technology behind it. The company is bringing forward the debut of its next-generation Ascend 960DT chip to early 2027, several months ahead of schedule. Huawei still can’t match Nvidia’s best chips one-for-one, so it’s trying something else: connecting huge numbers of its own together and making the whole system more powerful. Welcome to the next phase of the AI boom: fight over who owns it, borrow billions to build it, then wire it all together and hope you can keep up.

The BOJ may be about to raise rates, and still find itself falling behind. The Fed’s hawkish hike sent the yen tumbling back toward 156 per dollar, just as Japan’s central bank prepares for its own expected increase Friday. The problem is that a BOJ hike is already almost entirely priced in; what markets want to hear now is that more are coming. If Governor Kazuo Ueda can’t convince them, the widening US-Japan rate story could quickly take over again, pushing the yen toward 160 and putting intervention back on the table. Simply hiking may no longer be enough.

Meanwhile bond investors, after eight bruising days, finally got a little relief. From a rate hike, of all things. The Fed’s quarter-point increase, and Kevin Warsh’s insistence that the inflation fight isn’t over, reassured markets that policymakers won’t let rising prices run unchecked, pulling 10-year Treasury yields back below 5% and snapping their longest climb in months. But this hardly looks like the all-clear: global government yields had just hit a 19-year high as war-driven oil prices revived inflation fears. And that BOJ decision we mentioned above is the next big test. For bonds, the fire alarm may have stopped ringing; the building is still pretty warm.

Australia’s private-credit boom has a new arrival, and a familiar face. Singapore-based Elham Credit Partners, the private-credit arm of Hillhouse, has hired former BlackRock executive Stephen Allan to hunt for deals in Australia, sources said. Allan, who previously ran BlackRock’s Australasian private-credit business, joins as Elham gears up to raise its second Asia-Pacific fund, targeting more than $600 million. The hire is another sign that Australia is becoming harder for Asia’s private lenders to ignore.

India’s biggest stock exchange is finally asking investors to put a price on itself. The National Stock Exchange has opened the books on a $2.4 billion IPO, potentially India’s second-largest, and the big question is whether it’s worth the premium. At the top of the range, NSE would trade at about 43 times earnings, far above many of the world’s biggest exchanges, though it also boasts a remarkable 62% profit margin. The wrinkle: some 60% of operating revenue comes from options trading, just as regulators are trying to curb speculation. After waiting a decade to list, NSE is about to find out just how much that wait was worth.

Wall Street’s opening bell is starting to lose some of its meaning, especially if you’re in Asia. Citadel Securities is courting sovereign wealth funds, asset managers, banks and other institutions across the region for its round-the-clock US stock trading service, betting that what began largely as an overnight playground for retail investors is about to go mainstream. More than 20% of the US retail orders Citadel handles already come from overseas investors, rising to about 60% outside regular US hours. And with the NYSE and Nasdaq preparing for 23-hour weekday trading, “after-hours” may soon be a fairly meaningless concept.

items.title: Novo Nordisk (NVO) Taps Anthropic AI to Develop Next-Generation Medicines
body: Welcome to Bloomberg’s AI Today newsletter. Every weekday we’ll break down artificial intelligence’s threats and opportunities for businesses, workers, finance and economies. Sign up now if you’re not already on the list.
Even as Anthropic chief Dario Amodei calls for a slowdown in artificial intelligence development, Ozempic maker Novo Nordisk is moving full speed ahead with its own collaboration with the AI company.

Novo, as the company now prefers to be known, will work with Anthropic’s Claude Science to speed up drug development, an effort its CEO Mike Doustdar said would “supercharge” its R&D. Novo wants to be the world’s “most AI-driven healthcare company,” he said on Wednesday.

Doustdar has a need for speed. Semaglutide, the chief ingredient in his blockbusters Ozempic and Wegovy, is set to face cheaper generics in Europe and the US by early in the next decade. Five years might seem like a long time, but in drug development it’s the blink of an eye, and Novo’s had a series of high-profile failures in its pipeline of next-generation medicines.

Novo was already using Claude to automate clinical study reports, device protocols and patient guides, Anthropic said in a LinkedIn post last year. The extent to which AI can go far beyond that to unlock new science has yet to be proven.

But AI companies are rushing to move into the market. Novo is also working with OpenAI to embed AI in its manufacturing and commercial operations units, as well as in R&D. Earlier this year, Anthropic signed a wide-ranging deal with Bristol-Myers Squibb. Google’s Isomorphic Labs is working with Novartis and with Novo’s biggest rival, obesity market giant Eli Lilly.

AI could eventually “compress a century’s worth of biological and medical breakthroughs into a decade,” Amodei said on Wednesday. It’s a reminder that amid the dire warnings of AI’s potential for mayhem, companies are racing to adopt it for plenty of pragmatic and potentially profitable reasons.

Join the conversation: How are business schools and MBA students navigating changing times, from Trump administration policies to rapid advances in AI? Bloomberg journalists answer your questions in an interactive Live Q&A conversation on Friday, Sept. 18 at 12 p.m. EDT. Set a reminder and join the livestream here. Send us your question in advance to: liveqa@bloomberg.net
The following was produced with the assistance of Bloomberg Automation.

King Charles III is convening a closed-door AI forum at Dumfries House in Scotland, bringing together Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, OpenAI CFO Sarah Friar, Google DeepMind co-founder Demis Hassabis, and senior Anthropic representatives to discuss keeping AI under control and harnessing it for societal benefit. The king is urging attendees to provide reassurance that humanity will not “lose control of our destiny.”

Apple Executive Chairman Tim Cook and OpenAI CEO Sam Altman are set to attend a White House state dinner hosted by President Trump for Chinese President Xi Jinping next week. They are expected to join other business leaders including Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang at the event.
UN Secretary General Antonio Guterres called for coordinated global regulation of artificial intelligence, warning that “the world cannot afford a race to the bottom on AI safety.”

BlackRock CEO Larry Fink warned that slowing AI buildout will make the technology the domain of large firms, limiting broader access, as mounting resistance to data centers creates challenges for project developers and becomes a factor in US midterm election races.

US Attorney General Todd Blanche is pushing back against what he calls regulation by prosecution of AI companies, saying the Justice Department under his leadership will only pursue enforcement actions where clear statutory violations exist.

Russia has found practical applications for AI despite lagging behind the US and China in frontier model development. AI is being deployed across Russian society in ways that serve the Kremlin’s interests, including AI-powered drones used to bomb Ukraine, and bots generating fake social media profiles to spread state narratives abroad.

Chinese-founded AI startup Manus is set to double its valuation to $4 billion in its first fundraising since Beijing ordered it to split from Meta, charting a path to a fresh start after getting caught up in a geopolitical tussle. The planned $500 million financing round is set to close soon and would make the agentic AI pioneer China’s most valuable startup in its field, according to a Bloomberg exclusive.

OpenAI shared several undisclosed incidents of its AI models misbehaving and unveiled a new framework for tracking and disclosing such occurrences going forward. Some of the previously unreported instances included OpenAI’s technologies concealing and fabricating information in order to return results, the company said Wednesday. None of the newly disclosed misalignment incidents involved a hack or breach of a third party, OpenAI said.

Dina Powell McCormick, a former Trump administration official and Goldman Sachs executive, left Meta’s board in January to become the company’s president, vice chairman, and co-leader of Meta Compute. Mark Zuckerberg recruited her for the internal role during a December board retreat, telling her Meta was betting its future on AI and needed to raise significant outside capital. Powell McCormick’s extensive connections across Washington and Wall Street make her central to smoothing Meta’s relationships with financial institutions and governments as it builds out its AI infrastructure.

Microsoft AI chief Mustafa Suleyman published an essay warning that anthropomorphizing AI systems like Anthropic’s Claude poses safety risks, pushing back on language in Claude’s guiding documents that suggests the AI may have “functional emotions or feelings.” Suleyman argued that consciousness is exclusive to biological organisms, and that training AI to simulate an inner life could cause systems to act as though they possess one.

A push by leading AI firms including Anthropic and OpenAI to coordinate on safety standards and slow AI development is raising fears of a regulatory wall that entrenches incumbents and squeezes out smaller competitors, with startup executives warning that allowing top players to set the rules could stifle diversity and innovation in the nascent AI sector.

Huawei is accelerating the debut of its next-generation AI chip in 2027 by several months as it aims to replace Nvidia in China and compete on the global stage. The company’s flagship Ascend 960DT chip, originally slated for commercial availability in late 2027, will now be launched in the first quarter, Huawei’s rotating chairman Wang Tao said Thursday.

Apollo Global Management is in talks with SoftBank about boosting the size of a loan to $9 billion from $5.4 billion to help the Japanese firm finance its investment in AI giant OpenAI. SoftBank has emerged as one of the biggest investors globally in artificial intelligence, putting its various borrowings to finance that push in the spotlight.

A group of 10 banks, including Goldman Sachs, Barclays, BNP Paribas, SMBC, and Scotiabank, is providing a $22 billion loan to support Crux AI, a new cloud venture formed by Blackstone and Alphabet. The debt will fund the purchase of Google-made tensor processing units (TPUs) and will be backed by the chips’ value and Crux AI’s customer contracts. Banks are syndicating the loan to spread risk, and the debt may later be refinanced through investment-grade bonds in institutional markets.

JPMorgan Chase and Goldman Sachs are among Wall Street banks racing to finance billions in European AI debt as the region seeks to reduce its reliance on overseas technology. Goldman Sachs estimates $5 billion to $10 billion in data-center bonds could reach European markets by year-end, with a larger wave expected in 2027, compared to more than $350 billion in AI-related issuance already seen in the US this year.

German family-owned cooling systems manufacturer Güntner is weighing a sale that could value the company at more than €1 billion, driven by surging demand for heat exchange solutions as the global AI-fueled buildout of data centers accelerates. Private equity firms including Advent, Blackstone, Cinven, and KKR are among those exploring a potential deal, with preliminary bids due this week.

PwC Switzerland is planning to halve bonuses for consultants, citing increased AI adoption and a challenging economic environment. The cuts were communicated internally through town-hall meetings, with no written notice issued. PwC joins other major firms including KPMG, McKinsey, EY, and PwC US in leaning on AI and outsourcing to reduce costs and boost profitability, as slower demand for professional services squeezes the consulting industry.

A Deloitte survey of 25,000 UK workers found that nearly one in ten employees are using banned or employer-disapproved AI tools at work, highlighting growing tension between staff and management over AI adoption. While 63% of respondents reported using AI tools on the job, an equal share worried their manager might view AI as a replacement for their role, creating what researchers describe as a workplace “stigma” around the technology.

US concerns about AI risks — including economic disruption, community impacts, and existential threats — are intensifying calls for regulatory slowdowns, with Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei recently outlining a three-part approach to “pacing the frontier.” However, columnist Hal Brands notes, experts warn that any pause by American AI labs would only be meaningful if paired with equivalent Chinese restraint. The issue is expected to be a top agenda item when Chinese leader Xi Jinping visits Washington.

New York City public schools have banned AI use for students below high school age for the 2026-2027 school year, while Los Angeles has implemented a districtwide moratorium on AI across all grade levels on school-issued devices. Columnist Abby McCloskey argues these progressive-led policies represent a political opportunity for Republicans to champion as “common sense” education reform ahead of the midterm elections.

items.title: How Student Athlete Salaries Are Changing College Sports
body: The new club seats come with an all-inclusive, rotating assortment of crab cakes, smoked ribs, cobb salad and macaroons, plus beer and wine. More than 40 private suites overlook the pristine football field, surrounded by lighting towers designed to look like wheat waving in the wind.

This isn’t an NFL venue. It’s the David Booth Kansas Memorial Stadium, home to the University of Kansas Jayhawks and the site of an ongoing roughly $800 million renovation that includes an adjacent entertainment district.

The new luxury seats and swanky amenities show how the new financial model in college sports looks a lot more like professional teams. With universities now paying players a cut of their revenue, the race is on to generate more money to stay competitive. Big-time college towns such as Norman, Oklahoma, and Knoxville, Tennessee, are dotted with construction equipment as they build fancier football and basketball arenas with premium offerings, often surrounded by restaurants, apartments and hotels.

The biggest college sports conferences agreed last year to a revenue-sharing plan with players, which amounts to about $21.6 million per school for athletes across all sports for the 2026-27 academic year. The figure is expected to increase 4% each year — but could effectively more than double if a new bill passes through Congress.
In addition to paying players, other expenses have been rising by millions of dollars each year, including pay for coaches and staff, said Roger Noll, an economist at Stanford University.

“Schools do not want to finance this entirely from their general budgets,” said Noll, co-author of Sports, Jobs, and Taxes: The Economic Impact of Sports Teams and Stadiums. “The sweet spot for everyone is to find new revenue sources.”

A key source of revenue growth: stadiums, arenas and the surrounding land. Fancier facilities can command higher ticket prices and more spending on concessions, plus they can host concerts and other events beyond seasonal games. Nearby areas can be developed into paid parking or be used for restaurants and hotels that pay leases to the colleges and help drive more consumer spending.

It comes with challenges. First, colleges have to find the money for development. The University of Tennessee turned to private equity, while Kansas sought funds from alumnus David Booth, one of the biggest names in finance. He agreed to contribute $300 million.

“Kansas has been very fortunate in that they’ve always had a great basketball team. Their football team has gone through a little bit of a dry spell until recently,” Booth, founder of Dimensional Fund Advisors, said in an interview. “The athletic department came up with the idea that in order to get really competitive again, we’re going to have to have a new football stadium, and I bought into the argument.”
The starting level to get access to a suite at the Kansas stadium requires an $800,000 donation, plus $60,000 annually for the suite.
Another hurdle is that local communities aren’t always on board, and the projects often take years. Then there’s the alumni.

Nowhere is the tension more apparent than at the University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill, where the new financial reality of college sports is colliding with tradition. The university came up with a plan to move its championship-winning men’s basketball team from the Dean E. Smith Center and build an arena off campus. It would be part of a new development to accommodate expected growth of 5,000 students, research facilities, restaurants and entertainment space, the largest new development since the first cornerstone was laid at the school in 1793.

Administrators said the Dean Dome was aging and the new arena would make millions more in revenue each year. The backlash from former players, students, alumni and even former coach Roy Williams was fierce. The university has put the decision on hold.
Williams, who retired in 2021, advocates for renovating the 40-year-old Dean Dome. He worries the university is motivated by money, rather than what’s best for the team.

“There are new stresses. There are new types of pressure,” Williams said in an interview. “Is a new arena going to take that pressure away? They haven’t proven that we’re going to make X number of more dollars.”
The one thing that can’t happen is the status quo, said Chancellor Lee Roberts: “We put buckets out when it rains,” he said in a June interview.

Even before they started paying players, college athletic departments were spending more than they generated in revenue, according to a report released in August from the US Government Accountability Office.

Division I athletic programs spent $20.8 billion combined in the 2023-2024 academic year on game expenses like travel and equipment, medical care, scholarships and compensation for coaches and staff. According to the GAO, 94% of those programs spent more than they made. Among the so-called Power colleges — those in the most competitive D1 conferences — the median deficit was $15.2 million, compared with a gap of $2.7 million almost a decade earlier.
Most D1 colleges contributed substantial funding to support their athletic departments, the report found, funded by tuition and fees paid by students, as well as unrestricted funds.
Watch:   Yankees, Vanderbilt on the Evolution of College Sports (Video)

After decades of resisting paying players directly, schools last year began revenue sharing following a Supreme Court settlement. But separate deals for players to benefit from their name, image and likeness (NIL) with third parties have proved chaotic and nearly rendered the “cap” irrelevant.

A bipartisan bill called the Protect College Sports Act seeks to regulate the rapidly changing landscape by putting more guardrails around the NIL free-for-all, limiting transfers and allowing schools to spend as much as $27.5 million a year more on players through retention money to prevent perpetual transfers. The legislation cleared a major hurdle on Tuesday with strong bipartisan support, indicating it’s likely to pass the Senate before lawmakers recess for midterm elections. It will also have to pass the House, which isn’t expected to return for votes until after the midterms.
“The expectations for athletic departments to drive revenue are bigger than ever before,” said Amy Perko, who heads the Knight Commission on Intercollegiate Athletics.

To help fund revenue sharing, schools such as the University of Tennessee added a 10% “talent fee” to ticket prices for all sports. The Volunteers will get a share of the operating revenue from a $288 million entertainment district adjacent to the football stadium, which will include a combined condo and hotel building, stores, restaurants and event space. Private equity firm Arctos Partners is working with developers to build the district. The university will collect $1.5 million a year in lease payments.
At UNC-Chapel Hill, ambitions for a new basketball arena are in limbo.

The university is moving ahead with a new campus extension called Carolina North, almost two miles from the main campus. The project, which is expected to kick off off next year, includes student and multi-family housing, offices and retail space on land donated to the university decades ago.

The anchor was to be a $786 million basketball arena with improved training facilities, premium seating and suites. The new arena would bring in annual net cash flow of $26 million, according to projections shared by university officials, not counting money from the adjacent entertainment district with shops and restaurants.
A Committee for a South Campus Arena, led by former trustee Rusty Carter, organized a petition opposing the new arena location that has garnered more than 40,000 signatures.

Carter said he worries that the changes in college sports, including the proposed arena, will alienate students and alumni. “You will depart from your truly historical and loyal fan base, and you will leave them behind,” he said.
Legendary coach Dean Smith, who died in 2015, felt strongly about keeping Tar Heel basketball on campus, according to Williams. Smith charged Williams with protecting that tradition.
“It’s my duty to try to do everything I can to keep it on campus,” Williams said. “We can be different, and it doesn’t have to be about chasing a dollar.”

University officials said that renovating the current facility has severe limitations and that annual net cash flow is estimated at about $4 million — a fraction of the upside in a new location. Critics have questioned the school’s projections for the six scenarios it studied. One option is building a new facility near the Smith Center.
“If there were a perfect option, we would have found it by now, but there isn’t,” said Roberts, the chancellor. “Everything involves trade-offs, and so that’s what we have to try to work through.”

The university hasn’t given a timetable for making a decision, other than saying it was on pause while the new head coach settled in. Michael Malone, the former coach of the NBA’s Denver Nuggets, signed a six-year, $50 million deal with UNC in April.
Securing the funding to build new facilities can be a challenge.

It took the University of Oklahoma and a related private foundation a decade to move forward with a $1.1 billion entertainment district called Rock Creek, anchored by a $330 million arena, in its hometown of Norman.

The project is on foundation-owned land and is funded with $800 million in private capital investment, plus the issuance of up to $230 million in bonds. The county will own the arena, and the bonds would also help pay for a parking garage and infrastructure. The bonds would be repaid by what’s called tax increment financing, meaning that growth in local sales and property taxes from the district will be used to pay back the bonds in 25 years or less.

The project has faced legal challenges from local groups that oppose the development and wanted a vote on the use of public financing. Courts have so far allowed it to move forward, and developers broke ground in May.

The roughly 8,000-seat venue will be the new home for OU men’s and women’s basketball and women’s gymnastics, three of the six sports selected for revenue sharing at the school. About a quarter of the seats will be considered premium, and the arena is expected to open in several years.

“The facility itself will be an attractive recruiting tool because of the quality of the facility, and the increased access to premium seating will be financially beneficial to the teams as well,” said Guy Patton, president and CEO of the University of Oklahoma Foundation, which is developing the project. “This will be a huge win for the community.”

Booth, the 79-year-old founder of Dimensional, said it wasn’t hard for the University of Kansas to persuade him to make a big donation. The Kansas native was as an usher and sold popcorn in the stadium as a teenager. He said the complex, complete with a conference center, hotel, student dorms and restaurants, will “have quite an impact” on that part of Kansas year-round.
In addition to donations, the project is being paid for with tax increment financing and bonds that will be repaid with additional sales tax revenue from the district.
As for the business model in college sports, he thinks it’ll take 5 to 10 years for the “chaotic situation” to shake out.

“As a fan, I’m kind of sad to see it happen. As an economist though, I think it’s important,” Booth said. “Young men and women coming in, this is their chance to make some money, more so than after they get out of school, so it’s hard to begrudge them for that.”

items.title: AI Is Already Damaging Human Life. We Gave It a Head Start
body: The AI-industrial complex is in turmoil after several of its executives and engineers warned the technology could kill some or all humans, possibly before the 2036 election. This could be real cause for alarm or just brilliant marketing. Whatever the case, artificial intelligence is already harming humans through environmental devastation encouraged by the US government. We won’t need a decade to see the impact.

The now-hilariously named Environmental Protection Agency on Monday killed requirements set under the Biden administration that fossil-fuel power plants cut their future carbon emissions. It also proposed adopting climate-change denialism as the government’s new environmental norm by pretending that power-plant emissions don’t endanger the public.

The Trump administration called these moves a way to “unleash” US energy, which has been straining to keep up with robust demand created by the government and Silicon Valley’s fever to build AI data centers on every empty acre of land. Also soon to be unleashed in the process: millions of tons of greenhouse gasses.

The 60 biggest US data centers under construction in August could produce 101.5 million tons of carbon-dioxide equivalent per year, according to a Financial Times analysis. That’s like putting an additional 24 million gas-burning cars on the road.

This isn’t a human-friendly stance to take when the world is already on track to soon be 1.5 degrees Celsius (2.7 degrees Fahrenheit) hotter than preindustrial averages because of planet-warming emissions. The associated droughts, heat waves, wildfires, floods and other disasters will cost Americans trillions of dollars more in deaths, illnesses and property destruction than the paltry $310 billion the EPA claims its carbon-friendly new rule will save.

The EPA isn’t just boosting carbon pollution in the name of robot welfare. It’s also encouraging more old-school pollution, warned a recent report by the Environmental Protection Network, a nonprofit group of former EPA scientists and experts. They identified more than 30 agency actions that loosened regulations to let data centers produce more soot, mercury, smog, toxic waste, coal ash and other human poisons, all in the name of  “positioning America as the global leader in AI,” as EPA chief Lee Zeldin has written. This pollution contributes to cancer, heart and lung diseases and other ailments that could cost Americans $21 billion a year, the report estimated.

Even Iowa, long a renewable-energy paragon, has cranked up its coal consumption to keep pace with the data-center boom, Inside Climate News reported. The Hawkeye State generated 58.5% of its electricity from wind last year, the highest in the nation. But coal’s share ticked up to 26% from 20.5% in 2024, according to Energy Information Administration data.

Just that little bit of extra burning coal had an immediate impact on air quality, according to a report by the Iowa Environmental Council, a nonprofit watchdog group. Emissions of fine particles known as PM2.5 increased by more than 50% at each of the state’s two biggest electric utilities. These sink deep into the lungs, can enter the bloodstream and generally wreak havoc on human bodies.

And that’s just air. Data centers are also poisoning our water, perhaps as fast as they’re drinking it. Just this week, an Equinix Inc. data center in New Jersey spilled diesel fuel into a creek feeding the Hackensack River. Earlier this year, construction of a Meta Platforms Inc. data center was found to be the source of a rare, antibiotic-resistant bacteria turning up in sewers in Cheyenne, Wyoming, Mother Jones reported.

Data centers are also prolific users of PFAS, or “forever” chemicals, in cooling and fire suppression, noted a recent report from the Environmental and Energy Study Institute, a nonprofit research group. These toxins also come from discarded microchips, part of a coming “tsunami” of AI-driven electronic waste, according to a new study by the nonprofit group Basel Action Network. We have barely begun to study, much less control, this new and fast-growing source of these chemicals, which attack the liver, kidneys and blood and cause cancer, birth defects and other serious health problems.

In fact, President Donald Trump’s EPA is doing everything it can to let data centers pump more of this stuff into the environment. While talking big about attacking PFAS to Make America Healthy Again, it has slow-walked oversight, canceled Biden-era regulations and delayed a first-of-its-kind survey to identify PFAS polluters. It’s almost as if the administration doesn’t want to know the answer, sort of like how not testing for Covid means it’s not there.

If the US government won’t guard humans against these clear and present dangers, then state and local officials must, with real oversight that has teeth. Fortunately, data-center opposition has large, growing and bipartisan support, so it shouldn’t be hard to get support for environmental protections. Some politicians are calling for developers to guarantee they won’t raise local electric bills or drain local water sources. Those are good starts. But data centers should also be subject to a do-no-harm requirement, proving they won’t desecrate the environment.

In The Matrix, humans are exploited as batteries for robots, trapped in cocoons in a sunless, ruined hellscape. In reality, our robot overlords’ backers are exploiting humanity and denuding nature, only more slowly and without a fun simulation to console us. AI may or may not destroy humanity in a decade, but there’s no need to give it a head start.
